News.title: Oscar winner Michael Douglas declares his love for Wales, Butlin's, seaweed and lava bread
News.content:
Oscar winning actor Michael Douglas astonished fans at an event in Swansea this week when he confessed to “loving Butlins.” Worth an estimated £300 million, professing his love of all things Welsh, Michael, 82, says: "Most of you know, I have been married to Catherine [Zeta Jones] for 26 years. Let’s just say, I have been to Swansea and the Mumbles area a few times. It has always been wonderful.”

Michael owns five luxury properties in the US, Canada and Mallorca and he and Catherine had a £1 million four-bedroom house built in Mumbles, Swansea - where she comes from - mainly for her parents Dai and Pat, in 2004. "I have so many memories over the years. My kids Dylan and Carys have spent several holidays with their grandparents, David [Dai] and Pat Jones,” says Michael. "We used to love to go somewhere - this place they call Butlin's - and I did not realise it was a whole family affair when you go there. They had a wonderful time when they were there.”

The star didn’t specify which Butlin’s they visited. But the closest Butlin’s on Barry Island, South Wales, closed in1996, while Butlin’s Pwllheli was rebranded in 1987 and is now run by Haven Holidays as Hafan y Môr. They may have gone to Butlin’s Minehead Resort, a three hour drive from Swansea. Michael continues: "Also, when I first came here [Swansea] I ate seaweed. I could not believe it and I tried lava bread. Fish and chips you can’t beat over here and I love all the golf courses."

To see more of the stories you love from The Mirror and to find them easily in Google then make us your preferred source. Free and easy-to-do, just click on the link here to find more from The Mirror at the top of your feed.

‌



View 5 Images Michael Douglas, Catherine Zeta Jones and their children at the Gower Heritage Centre near their Mumbles home in 2011 (Image: Shutterstock)

Catherine's parents were in the audience for Michael’s talk at the 3,500 capacity Swansea Building Society Arena. But his wife sent her apologies, as she was filming for a new movie, psychological thriller Cupid, in Mississippi - having just finished playing Morticia in the Netflix show Wednesday.

Enjoying rousing cheers from his audience, when he shouted "Go Swans" - the rallying cry for Swansea University Women's Rugby Football Club - Michael reassured fans that Catherine would not be betraying her South Wales roots by appearing in Ryan Reynolds' Netflix series, Welcome to Wrexham. The show documents the fortunes of the North Wales football team Wrexham F.C which Ryan co-owns with American actor and comic Rob McElhenney. Michael says: "Catherine wants you all to know no matter how many times they ask her, she is not going to be on the Wrexham series. That is out of the question."

The star, who won a best actor Oscar for his portrayal of Gordon Gekko in Wall Street (1987) found little to wax lyrical about when he turned his focus to his native America. In a blistering attack on US President Donald Trump, the star pf 1995 movie The American President, who also played America's founding father, Benjamin Franklin, in the 2024 Apple TV+ series Franklin, says his research on the constitution for these roles means the present incumbent’s behaviour has enraged him. He says of Trump's actions: "It's just so king of embarrassing the way he has [behaved] our President. " And of the upcoming midterms in the US, he says: "It will be a massacre."

‌



View 5 Images Michael Douglas promotes his book in Swansea (Image: Supplied)

Currently conducting a global tour, promoting his memoir One Helluva Ride, Michael - who famously wooed Catherine when they first met at the Deauville American Film Festival in France in 1998, telling her on their first date, "I am going to be the father of your children" - also name checked some famous pals.

Speaking of his “wonderful friendship” with Jack Nicholson, 89, star of 1976 film One Flew Over the Cuckoo’s Nest, which Michael produced and which won a best picture Oscar, he says: “He’s not working anymore. He’s well. He has disappeared. I know that. I still see him but he is fine. He is up there by his house and walking around in his slippers. It happens. He deserves it. I understand. He is a few years older than me, but I understand.”

He also compliments his great friend Glenn Close - his co-star in the 1987 film Fatal Attraction - who he is appearing with on Friday’s The Graham Norton Show at 10.40pm on BBC1. Despite the thriller spending eight consecutive weeks at number one at the box office in the US and 10 weeks at number one in the UK and being nominated for six Oscars in 1988, Glenn lost out on Best Actress to Cher, for her movie Moonstruck. But she will be awarded an honorary Oscar for her prolific 52-year acting career next year.

‌



View 5 Images Michael Douglas and Glenn Close in Fatal Attraction (Image: Corbis via Getty Images)

Michael says of Cher’s win: "I have nothing against Cher, but it was a shocking situation. Glenn is to get an honorary Oscar, as she has been nominated eight times. It was amazing to work with her on Fatal Attraction. That was some movie and Glenn even kept the knife from the movie and hung it up in her kitchen."

Meanwhile, Michael - who was diagnosed with throat cancer in 2010, but was declared cancer free the following year - says his experience has made family more important than ever. He says of his cancer: “It made me a better actor and better human being. My career was no longer the most important thing in my life. My family was and that has lasted since the cancer, 16 years ago.”

But Michael is still planning future projects. Next, he will be playing former US President Ronald Reagan in the upcoming TV mini series Reagan & Gorbachev - a dramatic account of the 1986 Iceland summit, which proved a turning point in the Cold War. And he is close to finishing the new Oliver Stone movie, White Lies, with co-stars Josh Hartnett and Willem Dafoe.

‌



View 5 Images Michael Douglas and Catherine Zeta Jones on the 10th Anniversary of the Noahs Ark Appeal at the Children's Hospital for Wales (Image: Phil Rees/Shutterstock)

Family, however, remains his primary concern. Waxing lyrical about Catherine, he recalls them bonding over a shared love of golf when they first met, saying: “The first thing we found out was we have the same birthday, 25 year age difference and I asked her if she liked golf. She said ‘I love golf.’ And that did it.”

But, despite their shared love for their children, for Wales, golf and acting, Michael says there is one major thing over which they will always disagree … Marmite. He says: “I don’t understand why people eat Marmite. My wife,I Iook at her [eating it] and I don’t know what we have in common. Oh my gosh, I am like, ‘how can you eat that?’

‌



*Michael Douglas's memoir One Helluva Ride is out now, price £25.

News.title: 'Working families deserve a fairer deal — and Labour's Budget makes a start'
News.content:
'Working families deserve a fairer deal — and Labour's Budget makes a start'

Millions of people will get £100 towards their energy bills funded by a tax on bumper bank profits in a Budget to provide "breathing space" for households, it's emerged

View Image Voice of the Mirror has its say...

For millions of families struggling to make ends meet, the real test of any Budget is simple. Will there be enough money left at the end of the month to put food on the table, heat the home and give the children a decent life?

‌



‌



John Healey’s first Budget offers welcome reassurance at a time when Donald Trump’s reckless war in Iran threatens to send household bills soaring.

‌



The £100 winter fuel payments to 20 million households will provide much-needed relief, while cuts to gas standing charges will help ease the pressure of rising energy costs.

‌



A higher minimum wage for 2.3 million workers means more money in the pockets of those who need it most. And support for shops, restaurants and other high street businesses will protect jobs and communities.

These are practical, worthwhile measures from a Labour government determined to stand up for working families.

There is also reason to welcome the Chancellor’s commitment to investing in British businesses, creating jobs and laying the foundations for future prosperity.

‌



After years of Conservative economic mismanagement, Britain desperately needs that stability.

Of course, there is room for greater ambition. Britain’s biggest banks are enjoying enormous profits, while oil and gas giants stand to benefit from global turmoil. They can afford to contribute more.

‌



And the case for asking the super-rich to shoulder a fairer share of the burden remains compelling.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has promised an economy that rewards hard work and gives ordinary families a fair chance. This Budget represents another step towards delivering that change.

Article continues below

There are difficult decisions ahead, and families will rightly expect further action to ease the cost of living.

But Labour deserves credit for putting money back into people’s pockets while investing in Britain’s future. For households worried about the next bill, that support matters. And after years of hardship, there is finally reason to hope that better days lie ahead.

News.title: John Healey unveils energy bills help for millions in Budget to weather 'economic storms'
News.content:
John Healey unveils energy bills help for millions in Budget to weather 'economic storms'

Chancellor John Healey unveiled a £2.6billion support package for 20 million households in council tax bands A-D in England, who will get £100, paid directly into their bank accounts

View 3 Images Chancellor John Healey unveiled a Budget focused on giving 'breathing space' to hard-pressed households (Image: Jordan Pettitt/PA)

Millions of people will get £100 towards their energy bills funded by a tax on banks bumper profits in a Budget to provide "breathing space" for households.

‌



‌



Chancellor John Healey set out measures to shield families and businesses from “global economic storms" as he heaped blame on Donald Trump’s disastrous Iran war for the grim state of the public finances, as well as higher prices at the pump, higher energy bills and higher mortgages.

‌



With energy bills predicted to surge to an average £2,200 a year in January, Mr Healey unveiled a £2.6billion support package for 20 million households in council tax bands A-D in England, who will get £100, paid directly into their bank accounts.

‌



A temporary scrapping of VAT on electricity bills was extended from next March to July, saving the average customer around £50 a year, and a green levy has been stripped from bills. Mr Healey also confirmed he would axe standing charges on gas - a flat fee paid regardless of energy use - with plans to do the same for electricity bills.

View 3 Images Andy Burnham and Chancellor John Healey meet with local residents in the cafe of the Abbey community centre in Westminster (Image: Getty Images)

“We didn’t want this war,” the Chancellor told MPs. But he added: “Those are the storms we face. We can’t wish them away. We must choose the course we steer through them.”

‌



He promised “to steer us through the global economic storms today, to chart a new course for Britain in the years ahead, to give people fresh hope for Britain’s future”.

Mr Healey chose to slash his headroom - a cushion against future turmoil - to £15billion to avoid putting up taxes. Instead, he went after the banks with a smaller-than-expected hike to a levy on profits, which will rise from 3 per cent to 6 per cent for 15 months from January.

‌



An ally of the Chancellor said: “Just as the public supported banks during the financial crisis, banks are now being asked to contribute towards giving families breathing space.”

He also announced an increase in gambling taxes to pay for business rates relief for high street firms. Some 70,000 shops, restaurants and gyms will be taken out of paying rates altogether.

‌



The Budget was a low-key affair compared to Rachel Reeves's tax-hiking statements as she sought to repair damage done by years of Tory rule. But while the help was broadly welcomed, the Chancellor was accused by some critics of failing to do enough to mitigate the grim pressures on living standards.

Households will barely be better off in 2029 than they were before the pandemic, as energy shocks from wars in Ukraine and Iran and Covid contributed to a dismal period for living standards, according to the OBR.

‌



Real household disposable income - a measure of how much spare disposable income people have got - has shown "virtually no growth" since the Covid crisis in 2009. The OBR predicted that by 2029, a whole decade on, it might have grown by a pitiful 1%.

View 3 Images John Healey's maiden Budget was a more low-key affair than in previous years (Image: PRU/AFP via Getty Images)

‌



"That is practically unheard of in the history of the UK,", said the OBR's Professor David Miles. "It has been a dismal period in British economic history".

Analysis by the Joseph Rowntree Foundation (JRF) found average annual household disposable incomes are projected to fall by £450 over the course of the current parliament after adjusting for inflation.

‌



Andy Burnham said the Budget contained “significant measures” to help Brits with the cost-of-living squeeze. The Prime Minister told reporters: “Well, we aren’t immune, obviously, to the pressures on finances coming from the situation in the Middle East and the impact that that’s having on the cost of fuel, on the cost of energy.

“We can’t insulate people completely from all of those pressures, but within that, we are doing meaningful things to give people that breathing space.”

‌



JRF Group chief executive Julian Hartley said: “People need to feel that paying the rent, heating their home and putting food on the table is becoming easier. Today’s Budget recognises that pressure but falls short of what’s needed. We live in an uncertain world and need long-term policies that build resilience for those who need it most.”

The Resolution Foundation thinktank warned that using the council tax system to deliver energy bill support means around one in eight poorer households who live in higher band properties would miss out.

‌



Chief Executive Ruth Curtice said: “Conflict in the Middle East and global economic turmoil have brought higher inflation and borrowing costs to Britain, challenging the Chancellor to deliver a delicate balancing act of providing cost of living support while keeping borrowing down.

"The Chancellor has missed the mark with badly targeted support that has left families facing a tough winter as energy bills rise."

‌



Some charities raised alarm at the failure to unfreeze housing benefit which they claim has failed to keep up with the cost of soaring rents. Foodbank organisation Trussell's Helen Barnard said support for energy bills "will make a real difference as the colder months draw in".

But she added: "The decision to keep housing support for private renters on low incomes frozen is a misstep that will continue to drive people towards homelessness and to the doors of food banks".

Article continues below

Big decisions on defence spending and welfare reform have been deferred to next year. The Chancellor said details of how the UK will hit its target of spending 3% of GDP on defence by 2030 would come at the spending review.

News.title: EasyJet flight to Glasgow 'reports mass vomiting' with medics rushing to runway
News.content:
EasyJet flight to Glasgow 'reports mass vomiting' with medics rushing to runway

Flight crew aboard an easyJet flight bound for Scotland were reportedly forced to alert operational command and prepare ground support after a suspected stomach virus broke

View 2 Images An EasyJet flight to Glasgow was reportedly hit by a suspected norovirus outbreak (Image: Zoe Head-Thomas/Press Association)

At least eight passengers onboard an easyJet flight to Scotland were reportedly left vomiting after a suspected sudden sickness bug outbreak.

‌



‌



Flight crew on board the jet had to "notify operational command and arrange ground support" after the outbreak erupted mid-flight, AirLive reports.

‌



Flight U23116 took off from Sharm el-Sheikh late on Wednesday evening for an overnight journey across Europe to Glasgow.

‌



The trip descended into chaos during the early hours of Thursday, October 22, while the aircraft was travelling through Dutch airspace. According to reports from the cockpit, the pilots made contact with the easyJet Flight Operations Centre to flag up a rapidly developing medical emergency.

View 2 Images The plane landed safely at Glasgow Airport (Image: Ross Turpie/Daily Record)

‌



British teacher fights for life in Dubai after her 'precious' baby boy dies at 30 weeks READ MORE :

Plane crashes at UK airfield as 999 crews swarm and casualties rushed to hospital READ MORE :

The crew reported a suspected norovirus outbreak on board, reportedly saying that at least eight passengers were simultaneously suffering severe nausea and vomiting.

Norovirus, an extremely infectious bug which causes acute gastroenteritis, can transmit swiftly in confined environments such as commercial aircraft cabins, frequently triggering sudden onset symptoms including vomiting and watery diarrhoea.

‌



Despite the difficult conditions, the crew maintained control of the aircraft and continued on the planned flight path toward the UK.

The plane landed safely on Runway 23 at Glasgow Airport at around 2:45am BST. Medical personnel and airport operations were briefed ahead of the landing to assist the affected holidaymakers upon arrival.

Article continues below

The Mirror has contacted easyJet for comment.

News.title: 10 nasty Budget surprises in small detail - from price of pint to household income
News.content:
10 nasty Budget surprises in small detail - from price of pint to household income

John Healey admitted Britain cannot wish away the tough 'global economic storms' - the Mirror looks at some of the nasty details included in the Budget, the forecasts and the reactions

View 5 Images John Healey has promised British families he will 'to steer us through the global economic storms' (Image: Wiktor Szymanowicz/Shutterstock)

John Healey has promised British families he will “to steer us through the global economic storms".

‌



‌



The Chancellor admitted the country cannot wish away the tough times it faces amid the financial impact of the wars in Ukraine and Iran. He sought to provide “breathing space” he promised for households and high street businesses.

‌



Among help for struggling Brits, he announced £100 payments for millions of Brits to help with energy bills, the abolition of standing charges on gas bills, and higher taxes on banks to help tackle the cost-of-living crisis.

‌



But many experts and campaigners have been left underwhelmed by the lack of brave or transformational policies, with some criticising the Budget as a "hodgepodge" of small changes.

The Mirror looks at some of the nasty details included in the Budget, the forecasts and the reactions.

Stay up to date with everything announced in our Budget 2026 live coverage.

‌



View 5 Images The Chancellor admitted the country cannot wish away the tough times it faces amid the financial impact of the wars in Ukraine and Iran (Image: PRU/AFP via Getty Images)

‌



Budget 2026 - What John Healey is most likely to announce and how it affects you READ MORE :

1. Households to be £450 worse off

Average annual household disposable incomes are projected to fall by £450 by 2029 after taking inflation forecasts into account, analysis shows.

The Joseph Rowntree Foundation warned that cost of living help - including energy support - in the Budget does not do enough to "address the hit to incomes from rising energy prices".

‌



The charity says that, if incomes were to grow in line with the average for the period from 1961 to the pandemic, households would have been on course to be around £5,000 better off in 2029 than they were in 2024. Chris Belfield, senior economist at JRF, said: " To unlock economic growth we need to see bolder interventions that give families and our economy the firm foundation of better living standards."

2. Grim growth figures

The Budget watchdog's 200-page document does not make for happy reading, describing the UK’s economic position as remaining "challenging".

‌



The OBR makes clear that the economic picture has got worse since its last projections in March, which were finalised before the start of the Iran war. It downgrades next year's GDP growth figures from the spring forecast dramatically - from 1.6% to 1%.

Helen Miller, director of the respected think tank IFS, admitted Mr Healey's statement is unlikely to improve figures. He added: "This Budget has a raft of fiddly measures but very little that will move the dial on growth."

‌



View 5 Images Average annual household disposable incomes are projected to fall by £450 over the course of the current parliament (Image: Getty Images/iStockphoto)

3. Inflation could go either way

The volatile world means the outlook for inflation is "highly uncertain", with the OBR remarking how "energy prices have increased sharply since our last forecast".

‌



The watchdog admits inflation could go either way, with a one-in-five chance that CPI inflation next year will be above 4.5% and a similar probability that it will be below 2.5%.

It predicts inflation to return to the Bank of England's 2% target by 2028 "assuming energy prices subsequently decline in line with market pricing".

‌



4. 'No growth' to earnings or income

In depressing reading, the OBR's figures on earnings growth and disposable income show why households are still feeling worse off.

The watchdog says real household disposable income (RHDI) - a measure of how much spare disposable income people have got - has shown "virtually no growth" since the Covid crisis in 2009. And it predicted that by 2029, a whole decade on, it might have grown by a pitiful 1%.

‌



"That is practically unheard of in the history of the UK," said the OBR's Professor David Miles. "It has been a dismal period in British economic history." The reasons include a series of energy shocks that have hit households and businesses hard, along with the impact of frozen income tax thresholds.

On top of this, the OBR admits that inflation on wages and a loose labour market "means we expect no real earnings growth in 2027". The watchdog says real wage growth then recovers to around 0.5% a year by 2030, if energy prices drop.

‌



View 5 Images The Iran war has impacted the UK's economic picture (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

5. Higher borrowing

Government borrowing - which has to happen when more money is spent than is brought in by taxes - is set to go up by billions of pounds.

‌



While Mr Healey told MPs borrowing as a share of GDP will fall over the next five years, the figure has increased by £11billion per year since the the OBR's last forecast because of interest rates and rising inflation.

And it could get worse, the watchdog warns: "If energy prices reach a higher and more sustained peak, borrowing could be £17billion above the central forecast in 2027-28, while a lower energy price path could reduce borrowing by £12billion."

‌



All that borrowing leads to more government debt. And in more bad news, the OBR predicts some £14billion more will be paid on debt interest this year.

6. Housing benefit remains frozen

One issue notably missing from the Chancellor's Budget statement was the housing benefit freeze.

‌



More than a dozen charities called on him to end the freeze at the weekend - and just last year Andy Burnham said restoring Local Housing Allowance (LHA) would make a real difference in preventing homelessness.

Foodbank Trussell's Helen Barnard describes it as a "misstep" not to act on this issue. Crisis's Matt Downie praised the extra cash to eradicate rough sleeping and investment in social housing, but added: "The missing piece of the puzzle is taking action to prevent people being forced into homelessness in the first place."

‌



7. Booze prices to go up

Drinkers will nurse another price rise hangover when booze duty goes up again next February. The Budget didn’t include another new rise in the tax but Treasury documents show previously planned increases are set to go ahead.

Alcohol duty will increase in line with the retail price measure of inflation, which is higher than the more widely used consumer price index.

‌



We don’t know for sure what month’s data for RPI will be used, but September’s figure was 3.9%. That would mean another 2p to the price of a pub pint, 13p to a bottle of red wine, gin by 42p and whisky by 37p

Miles Beale, chief executive of the Wine and Spirit Trade Association, said: “No-one will be toasting yet another RPI increase on top of rising inflation." The Treasury expects to collect £13billion from alcohol duty this year, driven by increases to the rate offsetting an assumed average 1% decline in alcohol consumption in each year.

‌



View 5 Images Drinkers will nurse another price rise hangover when booze duty goes up again next February (Image: Getty Images)

8. Wage hike slows for younger workers

John Healey confirmed a wage increase for younger workers is to slow down - after the Chancellor announced a 3.9% minimum wage increase for all age groups.

‌



Labour's manifesto committed to scrapping "discriminatory" age bands, by increasing wages for 18 to 20-year-olds so young workers are paid the same as those over 21. To balance this, the national minimum wage for those aged 18 to 20 has been hiked by more than the rate for older workers. For instance, the minimum wage for younger workers rose by 8.5% this year, reducing the difference to £1.86 an hour. But this has now slowed.

Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds earlier this week said: "The manifesto pledge on equalisation still applies but we were always clear it could happen over time."

‌



9. Energy department cuts

The Department for Energy Security and Net Zero has suffered cuts to its budget to help fund the defence investment plan.

This includes cutting the flagship Warm Homes Plan by £1billion. Launched under Keir Starmer, the plan seeks to invest in home upgrades to help cut bills and lift people out of fuel poverty. Its offers include grants and loans to make it easier for households to install heat pumps, solar panels and batteries, as well as direct support for home upgrades for those on low incomes and in fuel poverty.

‌



The government says the "majority" of funding for low-income households and social housing is protected - but not all. It adds that it is committed to the rollout of heat pumps and will maintain the Boiler Upgrade Scheme at current funding levels of £400million in 2027‑28. It will rise "broadly" in line with inflation after that.

10. Many to miss out on energy support

One in eight households of the poorest half of earners in the country are expected to miss out on a £100 energy discount announced in the Budget, grim analysis shows.

Article continues below

Respected think tanks the Resolution Foundation and the IFS both questioned the energy support policy - which gives a £100 payment to households living in council tax bands A to D - was being linked to the outdated council tax system, which is based on the value of properties in 1991.

The Resolution Foundation's research showed around one in eight households in the bottom half of the income distribution live in higher band properties and are expected to miss out And the IFS questioned "relying on the outdated council tax system to provide one-off payment of £100 to around 80% of households in England, rather than just those on low incomes".

News.title: 'We’re cutting back on everything - the Budget does nothing to stop the squeeze on families’
News.content:
'We’re cutting back on everything - the Budget does nothing to stop the squeeze on families’

As the Chancellor unveils a £100 energy handout and freezes fuel duty, families across the UK tell the Mirror why the measures will barely touch the reality of soaring food and heating bills this winter

Millions to get £100 off energy bills

As the Chancellor delivered the Autumn Budget today, headline measures including a £100 energy payment for council tax bands A to D, a rise in the minimum wage, and a freeze on fuel duty were pitched as relief for struggling households.

‌



‌



But across the UK, working families say the measures barely scratch the surface as prices rise.

‌



Iram Malik, 44, an NHS frontline health advisor and mother of three children, aged 12, 10, and four, in Hounslow, relies on strict budgeting and working opposite shifts with her husband to keep their household afloat without paying any childcare fees. For her, rising energy and food bills remain the primary pressure point.

‌



Stay up to date with everything announced in our Budget 2026 live coverage.

To see more of the stories you love from The Mirror and to find them easily in Google then make us your preferred source. Free and easy-to-do, just click on the link here to find more from The Mirror at the top of your feed.

View 6 Images NHS health advisor and mum-of-three Iram, 44, from Hounslow, west London, says soaring food bills remain her family's biggest financial pressure

‌



Budget 2026 winners and losers revealed from energy bill payers to state pensioners READ MORE :

"Food is the most expensive thing, out of anything basically, hands down," she told the Mirror. She keeps costs manageable by turning bargain-hunting into an activity for her children, or avoiding eating out. She added: "I'm not going to lie, sometimes I do try and say to them, 'Let's just eat snacks [when we’re out] so we can have a main meal at home’. And I think that's not so bad, because when we did it, we turned out okay.”

The mum channels her spare time into volunteering with grassroots community project C-Change West London, which she credits with offering invaluable local support - and says more people could benefit from.

‌



Pragmatic about the future, she is already encouraging her 12-year-old son towards vocational training: "I want him to do an apprenticeship. I don't want him to get into debt - I want him to turn what he enjoys into a solid career.”

At Hounslow Charity Foodbox, a local foodbank, senior operations manager Alexander Robertson said demand was increasing rapidly.

‌



In the last quarter, they supported over 2,100 individuals - a new high.

Surrounded by shelves half-empty after a busy half-term, he told the Mirror: "Historically, we have supported many people experiencing ongoing difficulties associated with their mental and, or physical health.

‌



"But we are increasingly seeing people accessing a food bank for the first time because of a sudden change in circumstances.

"Some of the people we support have said that they prioritise others over themselves, particularly their children or their pets. Quite often, we'll hear people say, "I need food for my children, I need food for my pet,” reflecting the priority they place on the wellbeing of their family and pets, even when they are experiencing financial hardship themselves."

‌



Earlier this week, the Government announced it would be removing tariffs from 100 food items, which could save households up to £21 per year - or 40p a week.

"A lot of people may welcome the prospect of making a saving over the course of a year, but if you're living from one day to the next, that annual saving doesn't quite correlate with the immediate pressures they face," Alexander said.

‌



View 6 Images Alex spoke to the Mirror at the food bank (Image: Ian Vogler / Daily Mirror)

"A saving of £40 or £45 over a year does not necessarily translate into a meaningful improvement in someone's day-to-day circumstances. When money is already stretched, relatively small savings may not provide sufficient immediate relief to cover essential expenses."

‌



He added: "When people are having to manage from one meal to the next, talking about an annual saving can feel quite remote from the immediate financial pressures they are experiencing."

In Merthyr Tydfil, interpretation and translation assistant Gareth Clement, 37, lives with his wife and three children on a combined income under £55,000 in a rented house. He is acutely aware of the rising cost of utilities as winter sets in.

‌



View 6 Images Dad-of-three Gareth Clement, 37, from Merthyr Tydfil, fears rising energy bills are forcing low-income families to choose between heating their homes and putting another jumper on

"The energy bill is probably the biggest one because it's a non-negotiable with gas and electric." Gareth told the Mirror. "It's getting colder, we're using more gas and I'm always conscious in the back of my mind how long the heating is on for, and how much the bill is increasing."

‌



He feels that they’ll see little benefit from tariff cuts at the checkout, despite cutting back on vaping and swapping to supermarket brands.

He said: "We get our food shop delivered weekly - it's anywhere between £70 and £80 per week but we've noticed the number of products we're getting for that amount of money is getting less and less but the prices are increasing, it just doesn't look like value for money."

‌



The dad-of-three added: "I think more help with fuel bills would help.

"I think there should be a social tariff that gives you unlimited usage if you're on benefits - I think that needs to be looked at because the increasing energy charges are pushing lower off families into a corner where they're choosing whether to heat their homes or put another jumper on.

‌



"We're living in the UK and it shouldn't be happening."

6 View 6 Images Widowed mother-of-two Philippa Smith, 42, from Berwick-upon-Tweed, says the £100 winter energy payment offers zero relief (Image: Kennedy News/Philippa Smith) 6 View 6 Images Philippa, who is currently undergoing breast cancer treatment following the death of her Royal Navy husband Richard in 2023, is urging the government to extend bereavement support payments for children (Image: Kennedy News/Philippa Smith)

‌



For Philippa Smith, 42, an academic and widowed mother of two in Berwick-upon-Tweed, who is currently on sick leave after being diagnosed with breast cancer, the £100 energy rebate offers no respite.

Her annual income is £60,000, with sick pay and a widow’s pension after her Royal Navy officer husband Lieutenant Commander Richard Smith died in 2023, aged 38.

‌



"It doesn't help me because my council tax is E or F. I think the whole council tax system needs reforming," she said. “I think they need to do a lot more. Getting rid of standing charges on gas or freezing fuel duty isn't a huge amount.”

View 6 Images Chancellor John Healey outside 11 Downing Street (Image: Jordan Pettitt/PA)

‌



Facing three-hour round trips for medical appointments alongside £300 monthly energy bills, she adds: "My earning potential has drastically dropped since my husband died because I'm limited with being able to do work outside school time.

"With my cancer diagnosis I have all my medical appointments too. Once my kids are a bit older and I have kicked cancer, I'll be able to earn again."

‌



Philippa had hoped to see more action taken to improve the lives of bereaved parents.

Bereavement support payments can be claimed by a spouse or partner following the death of a loved one and people can receive an initial payment of £3,500, followed by 18 monthly payments of £350, before they end.

‌



Philippa said: "It hasn't been updated in a really long time. Widows and widowers would receive ongoing payments until their children were 18 from their partners' contributions to national insurance. Now it disappears after 18 months.

"I know a lot of people who spend a large sum of the money on funeral costs.

‌



"I would ask the chancellor to uprate bereavement support payment in line with inflation like the other benefits and extend it until children turn 18."

Jodie Reid, co-CEO of family charity Home-Start UK, said today's Budget will make a difference to many families.

‌



Home-Start, which has supported families across the country for over 50 years and helped nearly 60,000 households last year, works on the front line with parents navigating the cost of living crisis, postnatal mental health, and cuts to local services.

Last week Children’s Commissioner for England, Dame Rachel de Souza, called for a national Children’s Emergency Fund to address inequalities in children’s services, after a new report showed the stark differences in support available to children across the country.

‌



In response, Reid warned that early intervention is now facing a "postcode lottery", with rising living costs leaving 1 in 5 parents of under-fives feeling cut off from meaningful adult contact outside the home.

The charity boss had hoped to see more details released on a possible Children’s Emergency Fund, alongside improving family's finances, but warned more steps are needed.

Article continues below

"Many parents Home-Start works with struggle to get the basics on the table, bringing stress and a sense of isolation which makes it incredibly hard do their best for their children. The Chancellor’s announcements today will make a difference to many families, but to give every child a fair chance of success as they grow, far bigger steps are needed.

"We want to see more action to tackle hardship in the first year of a baby’s life, where costs are high and parental pay is poor and more to strengthen services such as ours, which provide trusted early support for families at their most vulnerable moments.”

News.title: UK Budget 2026 Live: Millions to get £100 off energy bills as bank tax rises and Martin Lewis 'delighted' over ISA
News.content:
Chancellor John Healey has delivered his first Budget of Prime Minister Andy Burnham's government - millions are set to be given help towards energy bills, while banks will pay an extra 3% on profits

UK Budget 2026 Live: Millions to get £100 off energy bills as bank tax rises and Martin Lewis 'delighted' over ISA

Chancellor John Healey has unveiled a "budget for the working people of Britain" as he announced energy bills discounts, help for state pensioners on low incomes, bank tax hikes and fuel duty freezes.

He said it is a budget "for British businesses, big and small", built on "fiscal discipline". He warned of "global economic storms" with trade tensions and Putin's illegal invasion of Ukraine as he opened his Budget statement in the House of Commons.

Directly blaming rising energy costs on Donald Trump's war with Iran, the Chancellor says he's taking immediate action and extending the VAT cut on electricity bills until the summer next year. Also 20 million households in council bands A-D will get a £100 energy bills discount - a £2.6billion scheme to take pressure off as winter bites. An announcement that crashed the government's council band checker website.

The Chancellor also announced the fuel duty freeze will be extended until July and the national minimum wage and national living wage will increase by 3.9% for 2.3 million workers. Mr Healey said he was "looking to our banks to help fund breathing space for British families", and hiked taxes on banks by an extra 3% for 15 months from January.

Mr Healey said Britain will commit £10 billion of additional economic and military support to Ukraine, and half a billion in urgent military funding this winter and said he is “getting work under way” to reach spending of 3% of GDP on defence by 2030.

This evening, Prime Minister Andy Burnham backed his Chancellor's first budget - telling reporters he was taking "bold" action on the cost of living.

"It’s pretty bold to help 20 million households with energy costs through the council tax cut this winter", he said.

"It’s bold to lift 70,000 businesses out of business rates altogether, and that will give a real lift to high streets up and down the country."

Money Saving Expert founder Martin Lewis meanwhile said he was "delighted" at changes announced to to the Lifetime ISA, which will axe the withdrawal penalty first-time buyers are charged when purchasing homes above £450,000.

Follow our live blog for the latest updates.

News.title: Nigel Farage claims he skipped Budget to avoid 'physical altercation' with MP
News.content:
Nigel Farage claims he skipped Budget to avoid 'physical altercation' with MP

The Reform UK leader claimed he’d previously had an issue with an unnamed MP at the state opening of parliament, and wanted to dodge a 'potential conflict' so skipped the Budget

View 2 Images Nigel Farage claimed he skipped the Budget to avoid an altercation (Image: Getty Images)

Nigel Farage has claimed he skipped the Budget because he wanted to avoid a “physical altercation”.

‌



‌



The Reform UK leader claimed he’d previously had an issue with an unnamed MP at the state opening of parliament, and wanted to dodge a “potential conflict”.

‌



Mr Farage, who declined to name the MP, also suggested his seat reservation had been moved, a claimed branded “total bull” by a senior Tory.

‌



Speaking at a press conference, he said: “At the State Opening of Parliament, I didn't want to, but I got involved in a physical altercation with an MP in the chamber.

View 2 Images The Reform UK leader wanted to avoid a fight (Image: Stefan Rousseau/Press Association)

“I didn't make a fuss about it, I didn't complain, but I could see, given that my prayer card had been removed, I was heading towards another physical altercation, and just sometimes it's better to avoid conflict, that's one reason.

‌



“Second reason is actually, I sat going through the budget with our senior economists in the office, so I actually had the time to go through it line by line, knowing I had to come and face all of you at three, and I don't spend my whole life studying this in a way that Jenrick does”.

He added: “So it was actually more useful for me to sit in the office with a team of economists around me. But I was going to go to PMQs, but I could see potential conflict, and being a very quiet, shy, modest kind of person, I decided to give it a wide berth”.

‌



Earlier MPs had dismissed his claims his reservations had moved, claiming it never happened.

Writing on X, Tory MP Alicia Kearns said: “This is total bull. Any of the Reform MPs could have given their seat up for him.

‌



“There were lots of seats without reservation, when exactly did Farage come into the chamber looking for a seat?”

Lib Dem MP Tim Gordon said: "The idea that Farage couldn't attend the Budget because his prayer card was moved is the latest eye-rollingly predictable attempt at grievance politics. I didn't put a prayer card in. I turned up just before prayers and there were loads of spaces. Farage, as far as I could tell, didn't turn up to prayers to guarantee a seat. A pretty poor and easy-to-disprove excuse for not turning up to actually do his job".

Article continues below

Responding, a House of Commons Spokesperson said: “There are clear and long-established arrangements for Members to reserve their own seats in the Chamber using Prayer Cards displaying a valid date stamp. 'Today, a Prayer Card placed on a seat did not display a valid date stamp and was removed in line with the usual Chamber protocol.”

News.title: Healey unveils £100 for energy bills and bank tax in first Budget
News.content:
Millions of households will get Â£100 to help with soaring energy bills to be paid for by a tax on bank profits, John Healey has announced in his first Budget.

The chancellor said he wanted to give hard-pressed families "breathing space now" and "hope for the future" as the UK economy is battered by "global economic storms".

He also unveiled tax breaks to boost high street businesses - but confirmed that many big decisions, including on defence spending and welfare, will not be made until next year.

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said Healey's plans were "not bold enough" and the government was "overspent, overborrowed, overtaxed and drowning in an out-of-control welfare system".

In an hour-long speech to a packed House of Commons, with Prime Minister Andy Burnham and other frontbench colleagues cheering him on, the chancellor unveiled a string of measures aimed at cutting the cost of living.

These include:

One-off Â£100 energy payment for people living in council tax bands A to D in England, with Wales saying it will match the payment and the Scottish government planning to "replicate" it

Gas standing charges in England, Scotland and Wales, to be scrapped during 2027 "or as soon as possible after". These fixed daily fees will be shifted onto the price of each unit of energy, meaning heavy gas users will face higher bills

Extending the 5p "temporary" cut in fuel duty on petrol and diesel to July

Increasing minimum wage rates by 3.9% in April, although there will be no progress on narrowing the gap between rates for older and younger workers

Healey increased the tax on the profits of big banks from 3% to 6%, which will last from January next year to April 2028, and increased taxes on high-stakes gambling machines.

News.title: Key points at a glance
News.content:
Chancellor John Healey has set out the government's tax and spending plans in his Budget â the first since Andy Burnham became prime minister.

Here is a summary of the main points.

LIVE: Follow all the Budget coverage

News.title: Chris Mason: Budget felt cautious despite its range of small measures
News.content:
This was a Budget I would describe as a flotilla of small measures.

Westminster is poring over the 150 page Red Book, external in which the Budget is printed and also what is formally called the Economic and Fiscal Outlook published, external by the watchdog and forecaster the Office for Budget Responsibility, the OBR.

The Red Book sets out the measures the chancellor will implement and how much they will cost. There are 98 of them, considerably more than normal and more than in either of Rachel Reeves' budgets.

But nearly all of them are pretty small in terms of their impact on the Treasury's spreadsheets.

This gets to the heart of why those involved in compiling this Budget have been irritated by commentary in the build up to it suggesting there would be nothing to see in John Healey's address â but also why those suggesting that were arguably onto something as well.

Firstly, as expected, it was a much smaller Budget in overall tax and spending terms than plenty of recent ones have been. But there were plenty of measures here and there which the chancellor will hope enough people notice and value â and others that some will likely curse.

There are more taxes for savers and landlords, for instance, and too for banks.

When a government has promised, as Labour have, to not put up income tax, national insurance or VAT â the big revenue generators â they end up looking elsewhere if they conclude putting up tax is necessary.

That runs the political risk of choosing particular sectors who might respond rather noisily. Think of the plenty of farmers who were incensed by the changes to inheritance tax Rachel Reeves was keen on.

News.title: The main announcements from the Budget - and how they will be funded
News.content:
Chancellor John Healey has set out the government's tax and spending plans in his Budget â the first since Andy Burnham became prime minister.

The BBC's Joe Pike outlines what the key points are and how they will be funded.

More on this story here.

News.title: How the Budget affects you
News.content:
Families facing cost-of-living pressures are being offered some help, or "breathing space" as Chancellor John Healey is calling it.

The help comes as prices are rising faster than expected with annual energy bills in particular likely to increase by hundreds of pounds in January.

Here's how the key announcements in the Budget affect you and your money.

News.title: What the Budget offers for under 25s - and what it leaves out
News.content:
The Budget contained plans to help people get onto the housing ladder, including the introduction of a "First Time Buyer Isa". This is an account in which savers can build up a deposit, with the government topping up contributions of up to Â£4,000 each year with a 25% bonus.

The new savings account will be introduced in 2029, replacing the existing Lifetime Isa, which has been criticised by some for imposing harsh penalties on those buying homes for more than the Â£450,000 cap.

The cap will remain, but the new "First Time Buyer Isa" will ensure savers are not penalised by losing their own money when making withdrawals. Savers will only lose contributions made by the government when making withdrawals which are not eligible for the account.

The penalty for withdrawals from existing Lifetime Isas will be lowered, too, to address concerns about savers being punished.

The government had already revealed a Â£4.7bn scheme for first-time buyers in England dubbed Your First Home. It is aiming to help 70,000 individuals and couples get on the housing ladder

The scheme will allow people to buy a new-build home with a deposit of 2.5%. It will provide them with a loan worth 20% of their property's value to help pay for the purchase.

Capped at Â£110,000 outside London and Â£140,000 in the capital, it is aimed at those hoping to get on the housing ladder without help from "the bank of mum and dad".

News.title: Watch: At the scene of Spain's deadly train crash
News.content:
Dozens of people have died and others have been injured after two high-speed trains collided south of the Spanish capital Madrid.

Prime Minister Pedro SÃ¡nchez said it was "unacceptable" that Spain had suffered its second fatal rail crash in a year.

The BBC's Guy Hedgecoe reports from the scene of the crash.

Follow our live coverage here.

News.title: What we know about the crash so far
News.content:
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro SÃ¡nchez has said "the whole of Spain is grieving" and that "lives have been shattered, families have been torn apart".

"The pain is immense," he said on a visit to the crash site.

The government was "trying to determine what was the origin of this tragedy, of this terrible accident," he added.

"We will get to the bottom of this, and if there has been any negligence, it will come to light.

"If there have been failures in the security system, they will be addressed with the utmost firmness."

SÃ¡nchez and other Spanish politicians have cancelled all public engagements on Wednesday, including campaigning for next month's parliamentary elections.

Spain's royal family posted on X that it was "shocked and concerned" and expressed condolences for the relatives of the deceased and those affected by the crash.

A spokesperson for the EU said the bloc was ready to help Spain if needed.

A huge emergency response is under way with fire crews and helicopters at the scene.

Hospitals in the area have suspended planned surgeries as they deal with an influx of patients from the crash, Spanish media have reported.

A blood transfusion centre in Madrid has also appealed for "urgent" donations. In a post on X, Centro de TransfusiÃ³n said it made the request "in the face of a possible sudden increase in care needs".

It reported that facilities in Toledo, Ciudad Real and AlcÃ¡zar de San Juan have cancelled procedures as casualties from the crash begin to arrive.

This is the second high-speed rail tragedy in Spain this year.

In January a high-speed train derailed in southern Spain, its rear carriages going into the path of a state-run Renfe train, claiming the lives of 46 people.

News.title: Russell Brand tells trial sexual consent is 'fundamental'
News.content:
Warning - this report contains graphic content

Russell Brand has told the jury at his trial he believes sexual consent is "fundamental" and "more important than sex itself".

Brand, 51, is accused of three counts of rape, three counts of sexual assault, and one charge of attempted indecent assault.

The allegations, made by six female complainants, span a 10-year period between 1999 and 2009. He denies all the charges.

Giving evidence on Wednesday, Brand said the allegations had been "deeply traumatic" and had a "devastating" impact on him.

The media personality gave evidence as his defence case began at his trial at Southwark Crown Court in London.

Asked whether consent was important to him, he told the court: "Consent is fundamental, essential, necessary and indeed in many ways more important than sex itself."

Brand told the court he had previously been "comfortable" allowing his fame to "facilitate sexual access, which I agree with you was wrong".

But asked by the prosecution whether he "needed and was prepared to go to any lengths", Brand replied: "Absolutely no."

Prosecutor Riel Karmy-Jones KC suggested to Brand there were inconsistencies between his previous prepared police statement and what he told the jury.

"Ms Karmy-Jones, I completely agree," he replied. "Since these events occurred there's been escalating recollection.

"It's been a deeply traumatic episode of my life. I've focused on it at the expense of my marriage, my children and health.

"I recognise that this recollection includes small details that are inconsistent and I acknowledge that."

He said: "I do recognise I have been a very determined and focused man.

"With women, of course, which is the subject of my trial, I've been persuasive, seductive, begging and flirting, and dedicated a lot of my life to what seems now beyond reckless philandering, and idiocy."

He told the jury: "Regrettably I've had a lot of consensual sex, which I see has caused harm."

News.title: Tommy Robinson guilty of harassing two Daily Mail journalists
News.content:
Political activist Tommy Robinson has been convicted of harassing two Daily Mail journalists.

A jury at Southwark Crown Court found the 43-year-old, real name Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, guilty of two counts of harassment causing fear of violence.

The case concerned Robinson's response to Daily Mail and Mail Online articles from August 2024, showing him on holiday in Cyprus while riots took place in England following the Southport murders.

The court had heard how Robinson, from Bedfordshire, used "bully-boy, intimidatory tactics" to frighten reporters Andrew Young and Jacob Dirnhuber, forcing them to employ security or leave home.

Robinson had denied the charges, saying he had "panicked" and had been "scared" when the Daily Mail published a story accusing him of "stoking race riots from his sunbed".

He told the jury he felt the article had "endangered" his family by revealing they were staying in a hotel near Ayia Napa in Cyprus.

After the guilty verdicts, Frank Ferguson, the head of the Crown Prosecution Service's Special Crime and Counter Terrorism Division, said Robinson had "weaponised social media and subjected two journalists to a campaign of harassment which caused them serious fear of violence".â

Robinson was granted bail ahead of his sentencing, scheduled for 16 Decemberâ.

Harassment causing fear of violence can carry a maximum sentence of 10 years in prison, or up to 14 years if the offence is racially or religiously aggravated.

News.title: Terminally ill mum who can't talk, walk or dress herself refused Pip payment
News.content:
A terminally ill mum who has been given three years to live has been denied disability benefit despite being unable to eat, talk, dress or use the toilet independently.

Rachael Field, 56, from Rhondda Cynon Taf, who has tongue cancer, was first diagnosed six years ago.

She uses a feeding tube, has had her tongue and voice box removed, and had her windpipe reconstructed using chest tissue. Field also has mobility issues.

Earlier this year, she was denied Personal Independence Payment (Pip), to support people with disability-related extra costs.

The Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) said it needed further evidence to complete the claim and was sorry for "any distress" to the family.

Field said she has had cancer four times in six years, and now cannot do anything for herself.

"I need help to wash, dress and use the bathroom. I can only walk a few steps with help. I cannot eat or drink, everything has to go through my feeding tube," she added.

News.title: Huntingdon train attacker asked man 'do you want to die?', trial hears
News.content:
Train passengers fled "in sheer terror" from a knife attacker who asked one victim "do you want to die?", a trial has heard.

Anthony Williams, 33, is accused of attempting to murder 10 passengers and staff on a train that had to make an emergency stop in Huntingdon, Cambridgeshire, on 1 November 2025. He is also accused of trying to kill three people in Peterborough the day before and then a boy at a London railway station.

Opening the prosecution case at Cambridge Crown Court, Christopher Paxton KC said that of those on the train "some stood tall, to protect others trying to de-escalate his rampage".

Williams, of Langford Road in Peterborough, denies 14 counts of attempted murder.

Williams is accused of attempting to murder Jonathan Gjoshe, Sachin Balakrishnan, David Presland, Scott Bletcher, Scott Green, Kevin Deely, Stephen Crean, Raza Aslam, Michael Paffett and Samir Zitouni on the train between Peterborough and Huntingdon on that Saturday evening.

He is also accused of attempting to murder a 14-year-old boy and Dawid Taborski on a footbridge near Henry Penn Walk in Peterborough on 31 October, and William Ogelby at Railworld car park in the city shortly afterwards.

Williams was then seen swigging from a bottle of alcohol outside Ritzy Barber Shop in Fletton in Peterborough, before going into the shop brandishing a knife.

The jury heard he then travelled to east London, where he stabbed a 17-year-old on a Docklands Light Railway train at Pontoon Dock in Silvertown in the early hours of 1 November.

During that attack, jurors were told a witness said she heard the defendant repeatedly say: "Are you trying to beef with the devil?"

News.title: Bonfire Night policing in Scotland will be 'largest operation since Trump visit'
News.content:
Scotland's biggest police operation since the visit of President Donald Trump last year is to take place on Bonfire Night, in the face of a "unique" combination of safety concerns.

As many as 1,700 officers could be deployed on and around 5 November to deal with fireworks-related disorder, a European football match involving Celtic and potential protests in Glasgow.

Additional public order vehicles and drivers are being brought in from 18 English and Welsh police forces under mutual aid arrangements.

Police Scotland says the plan, titled Operation Amberlight, is intended to ensure the safety of the public and emergency services.

The force has already vowed that anyone caught up in disorder around Halloween and Bonfire Night will face "very real consequences".

This will be enforced through Fireworks Control Zones (FCZs), which ban the use of pyrotechnics in certain areas of Edinburgh and Glasgow from 30 October.

In recent years, emergency crews have been pelted with petrol bombs and missiles - though police said there were fewer instances of this last year.

News.title: Legal bid to overturn Drumcree march ban fails
News.content:
An attempt to overturn the Northern Ireland secretary's decision to ban the Drumcree parade has failed.

The High Court in Belfast has ruled that Sir Chris Bryant's decision made on 9 October was lawful.

The judicial review was brought by a Portadown Orangeman against Sir Chris and the Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) Chief Constable Jon Boutcher.

The secretary of state's intervention to stop the parade came after he received security advice from Boutcher.

A lawyer for the Orangeman told the court that an appeal of the judgment is "likely".

The Drumcree dispute led to a stand-off between Orangemen and nationalist residents of the Garvaghy Road in Portadown lasting almost two weeks.

Mr Justice Scoffield said: "The secretary of state's decision was lawful and within the margin of discretion properly afforded him, although it is highly regrettable that it was required in the circumstances which arose."

He said those who opposed the march should "take no particular joy in the outcome of this case".

The judge added that "the position which has now been reached has been brought about at very significant cost to the people of Northern Ireland - financially, through the diversion of police resources, and in terms of community relations".

"Depressingly, the threat of serious and widespread disorder has loomed large," he said.

He went on: "Significant concerns have now been expressed about respect for the rule of law in this jurisdiction.

"That includes among some elected representatives, by reason of their participation in the unnotified protest."

Speaking afterwards, Sir Chris said that he was "grateful that he (the judge) has said that not only did I act lawfully but this was the right decision".

He said it was "not a cause for celebration," and said prohibiting the parade was a "last resort".

He said: "I also wholeheartedly agree with the judge that the rule of law must be upheld. Everyone and especially elected officials must uphold the law at all times and not just when they agree with it."

News.title: Burnham rules out early general election in next 12 months
News.content:
Andy Burnham has ruled out an early general election in the next 12 months, after opposition parties suggested one would be called.

The next UK general election must be held by August 2029, and there has been speculation that the prime minister is preparing for an earlier poll.

Asked directly if he would call a snap election within the next year, the prime minister told broadcasters: "I don't know how many times I've done this now but yes, I can rule out calling a general election in the next 12 months."

He said he was focusing on people over the Labour Party, adding: "I'm not thinking about myself. I'm not thinking about my own party and its prospects."

Earlier this month, Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch suggested Burnham may go to the country early.

She said the Conservative Party was "coming back" after it slumped in popularity at the end of 14 years in government, telling BBC South East: "This is an era of political volatility and multi-party politics."

She added: "I do think Andy Burnham is going to call an election sooner than he is saying... all the policies he announced are for after an election."

Reform UK leader Nigel Farage said in September he believed there would be an election "next spring".

"I believe there must be a general election because Andy Burnham has no mandate - the messiah without a mandate, we deserve a general election on who continues to govern this country."

Burnham was elected MP in June after the Makerfield by-election, before securing the Labour Party leadership and becoming prime minister after Sir Keir Starmer lost the support of Labour MPs and quit Downing Street.

He has since outlined a number of ambitions, which has led some to question whether he will try to secure a fresh mandate before 2029.

One of these issues is Brexit, where Burnham has said he wants an "honest conversation" about the UK's future relationship with the EU.

On Wednesday, he promised to stick to the red lines in his party's 2024 manifesto on EU freedom of movement, the single market and customs union "for the whole of this Parliament".

The current Parliamentary term runs until the next general election.

Burnham has repeatedly denied he is seeking a snap poll. He told broadcasters on Wednesday: "We've got a 10-year plan to come, and that will inform the spending review next year. These are my priorities, not looking at our own internal party political advantage."

News.title: King acknowledges 'suffering of the past' as Caribbean tour begins
News.content:
King Charles III has begun his tour of the Caribbean by acknowledging the "great suffering of the past" as he faced calls for slavery reparations.

Speaking an event in the Bahamas celebrating local youth, the King said the country's culture was "born out of darkness", and it was "only right" to acknowledge historic injustices.

His nine-day tour will culminate in the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM), where the King has confirmed leaders will discuss the region's legacy of slavery.

The visit, his first as monarch, comes in the wake of renewed calls from Caribbean nations for Britain to apologise for its role in selling enslaved people for profit.

Prior to the trip, Buckingham Palace said the King would not shy away from "colonial legacy" and the impact of the slave trade during his visit but, in line with the UK government position, he will not apologise for Britain's role in the slave trade or offer reparations.

Upon his arrival on Tuesday, the King met Governor General Dame Cynthia A. Pratt and its Prime Minister Philip Edward Davis, before speaking with members of the Royal Bahamas Defence Force as he inspected a guard of honour.

King Charles, wearing sunglasses and a grey suit, was then met with cheers as he arrived for his first engagement at a youth rally at Clifford Park - where he attended independence celebrations for the Bahamas as Prince of Wales in 1973.

The young people in the crowd had been given time off school for the event. "It's my first time seeing him in person out of TikTok so he's out there, it's cool," one student told the BBC.

A small group of protesters gathered close to the rally shouting "pay us what you owe us" and "return artefacts you've stolen."

The group of around a dozen protesters was kept outside the main venue as they called on the King to help change the UK government's position on apologising and offering reparations.

"He's a man of influence. The Crown still has influence. And if they do not do it then we will become a republic and we will turn our backs on England if you do not show respect to the former colonies," said one protester, Sharon Purcer-Cooper.

News.title: What Brian Jones wrote to Charlie Watts before he joined the Rolling Stones, revealed for the first time
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

“Dear Charlie, if you consider this letter impertinent, please excuse me…”

This was the opening line in Brian Jones’s bid to poach drummer Charlie Watts for the Rolling Stones, delivered to “Mr C Watts” at his childhood home in Wembley.

The historic handwritten letter, postmarked 3 June 1962, is being auctioned by Watts's sister after remaining in the family for six decades, with its contents revealed to the public for the very first time.

Band co-founder Jones made a strong case for Watts to quit Alexis Korner’s Blues Incorporated and join the ambitious new group he’d formed with Keith Richards and Mick Jagger.

“I don’t know at the moment what your relationship with Korner’s band is,” he wrote. “I noticed Nick Nicholls was drumming last night at Ealing. If you are not going to work with Alex in the future, and still want to play R&B, we are looking for a good drummer.”

Jones continued: “Already we consider our band far better than Alex’s – we are getting a very tightly-knit sound.”

He told Watts that the band were rehearsing three times a week, on Mondays, Wednesdays and Fridays: “Anyway, if you have time, let me know what’s happening.”

open image in gallery Brian Jones urged Charlie Watts to ditch his current band and join the group who would go on to become the Rolling Stones ( Sotheby's New York )

In a “PS”, he added a rundown of the current set-up for the band (”two guitars, harp, piano and drums. We are going to use a bass guitar eventually”).

open image in gallery The letter from a young Brian Jones as he attempted to recruit Charlie Watts to the Rolling Stones ( Sotheby's New York )

He also delivered a rather scornful assessment of their drummer at the time, whom he branded “atrocious!”.

It is unclear who he was referring to: it could have been the Stones’ first drummer, Tony Chapman, who played with them at their live debut at the Marquee Club on 12 July 1962, then left in January when Watts joined. Carlo Little also had brief stints with the Stones in 1962, again before Watts joined.

At the time Jones made his pitch, Watts – who went on to be regarded as one of the greatest drummers of his generation – was still working a day job in advertising while playing with Korner’s band, and resisted the Stones’ early attempts to recruit him.

open image in gallery The letter along with the envelope it was mailed in, addressed to "Mr C Watts" at his childhood home in Wembley ( Sotheby's New York )

Despite Jones’s plea, it was another seven months before Watts agreed to officially join the Stones in January 1963. He remained with the band for almost six decades until his death in 2021.

Indeed, the band had been so determined to get him on board that they were prepared to sacrifice luxuries like food to be able to afford him: “We starved ourselves to pay for him!” Keith Richards later recalled in his autobiography, Life.

Watts, for his part, joked in a 1986 interview that he “worked five years” then spent “20 years hanging around”. He died aged 80 in August 2021.

“What’s so fascinating about this letter is that it shows just how highly regarded Charlie Watts already was at this incredibly early stage,” Craig Inciardi, Sotheby’s music and pop culture specialist, told The Independent.

“The Rolling Stones band name didn’t yet exist, but Brian Jones clearly understood how important the right drummer would be to the sound they were trying to create.”

open image in gallery L-R: Mick Jagger, Keith Richards, Brian Jones, Bill Wyman and Charlie Watts ( Getty )

He added: “There’s something wonderful about seeing that history unfold in real time, especially knowing that Charlie’s distinctive drumming style would go on to define the band’s sound.”

The letter, which is estimated to fetch between $70,000 to $80,000, will be on public view along with its original envelope at Sotheby’s New York between 2 - 8 December, with online bidding open from 2 - 15 December ahead of its sale on 15 December.

The Stones released their latest album, Foreign Tongues, to critical praise in July this year, with The Independent praising the band for “melding pop polish with good old-fashioned rock’n’roll grit” in its four-star review.
