News.title: Trump demands Alaska ballot change after report on Dems recruiting Dan Sullivan to campaign
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

President Donald Trump has demanded that Alaska change its ballot after The New York Times reported that Democrats spent months trying to recruit a man named Dan Sullivan to run against Dan S. Sullivan, the state’s Republican senator.

“It has just been determined that the Democrats in Alaska illegally searched for, and recruited, a man named Dan Sullivan to run against our distinguished Republican Senator, Dan Sullivan, in order to defraud, confuse, and obfuscate the Election, thereby taking votes away from the REAL Senator, Dan Sullivan,” Trump wrote on Truth Social Wednesday.

He added that Democratic candidate Mary Peltola “should suffer the Legal and Political consequences for what she has done, A FRAUD ON THE AMERICAN PUBLIC, and Dan Sullivan should be allowed to run without either Mary Peltola or FAKE Dan Sullivan on the Ballot.”

The previously undisclosed effort to enlist a same-name challenger involved staff members at the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee and on Peltola’s campaign, The New York Times reported Wednesday, citing documents and sources familiar with the matter.

The effort paid off: Dan J. Sullivan, a retired teacher from Petersburg, is now on the ballot as unaffiliated alongside the incumbent senator, Peltola and Republican challenger Gerald Heikes.

open image in gallery Democrats spent months trying to recruit a man named Dan Sullivan to run against Alaska’s Republican senator, according to a new report. Pictured: Dan J. Sullivan (left) and Republican Dan S. Sullivan (right) ( Sullivan for Senate/Getty )

Peltola’s campaign and the DSCC have denied involvement with Dan J. Sullivan’s team, and Sullivan has said the decision to run was his alone.

The contest has become one of the nation’s most closely watched Senate races in the 2026 midterm cycle. Democrats hope a victory could help them regain control of the upper chamber, while many Republicans contend that Dan J. Sullivan is a plant intended to undermine the incumbent’s reelection bid.

Last week, the Justice Department filed a federal lawsuit seeking to bar Alaska officials from certifying a Peltola victory if Dan J. Sullivan remains on the ballot. The Alaska Supreme Court had previously rejected Republican efforts to remove him.

The Independent has reached out to Peltola’s campaign for comment.

The Alaska effort, dubbed the “ballot composition project,” was a sweeping, coordinated operation that included secret trips to remote parts of the state to find potential candidates, The Times reported.

“Alaskan voters need to know,” Elisa Rios, Peltola’s former campaign manager, told the outlet. “There was a lot of speculation, and voters should get the full picture when making their decisions.” She added that the Democratic candidate was not personally involved in the recruitment effort, but that she was “definitely aware.”

The project got underway last summer, Rios said. In one meeting, DSCC staffers introduced her to Jerid Kurtz, a longtime Democratic operative. Kurtz later took part in a video call, where he said he had successfully contacted a man named Dan Sullivan in the small fishing community of Petersburg.

open image in gallery Democratic challenger Mary Peltola’s campaign has denied involvement with Dan J. Sullivan’s Senate bid ( Reuters )

Kurz “said he hated Trump, and if it was going to help Mary, he liked Mary. He didn’t have any interest in being a politician, but if this could help,” Rios said.

A pro-Peltola super PAC 49th State reportedly paid Kurtz’s firm roughly $87,000 this year. When reached by the Times, a spokesperson for the PAC said it had “never hired or paid Jerid Kurtz.” Kurtz didn’t respond to the outlet’s request for comment.

According to the Times, Peltola’s team also attempted to recruit other potential spoilers into the race.

So-called “ballot-stacking” tactics are thought to be legal and have been used before. Two years ago, when Peltola sought re-election to the House, state Republicans pushed to keep an incarcerated Democrat on the ballot.

Namesakes have also shared a ballot. In 2004, Rep. José E. Serrano, a New York Democrat, faced a challenge from Jose Serrano, a retired loading dock worker who withdrew after reporters began asking questions. Decades earlier, John F. Kennedy’s opponent in his first congressional race faced a similar namesake challenge.

President Donald Trump, who pushed the DOJ to file its lawsuit, has also publicly weighed in on the Alaska Senate race.

​“I am very concerned about the Dan S. Sullivan Race for the U.S. Senate in Alaska in that it is totally confusing, with the Dumocrats putting up another man, totally unrelated to Politics, named Daniel J. Sullivan, Jr,” Trump wrote on Truth Social earlier this month. “It’s ridiculous that the Court didn’t stop this SCAM.”

Peltolta has called the lawsuit an example of “flagrant corruption.” Senator Sullivan, she said in an October 23 Facebook post, is “using his DC allies to try to keep himself in power and put his own interests ahead of Alaskans.”

The federal lawsuit remains pending, with Election Day less than one week away.

News.title: High speed train crash leaves at least 68 dead and 77 injured in one of Spain’s worst rail disasters
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

At least 68 people have been killed and 77 injured after two high-speed trains collided in Spain, the country’s second major rail crash this year.

There were 544 people on board the two services between Madrid and Seville when they crashed at around 9am Wednesday morning. The incident is one of Spain’s deadliest rail disasters, and the worst since 78 people were killed when a high-speed train derailed near Santiago de Compostela in 2013.

Passengers were travelling between Madrid and the southern Andalusia region when an express train operated by Iryo was struck by a train operated by Renfe in Toledo. The Iryo train had been stationary due to a signal fault, a person briefed on the disaster said.

Footage showed a derailed train with several carriages remaining on an elevated section of track while twisted metal, broken panels and wreckage could ⁠be seen strewn across an embankment beneath the line.

open image in gallery The two high-speed trains were travelling between Madrid and Seville when the crash occurred ( AP )

open image in gallery Multiple carriages derailed during the deadly collision, with 544 people on board the two services ( AFP/Getty )

Survivor Jesús Jerónimo, 54, told El Pais that people were thrown from the train by the “brutal” impact of the collision. He had been travelling in carriage two of the high-speed train en route to Seville, where he often goes for work meetings as a medical consultant.

“I was working on my laptop when I felt a very strong acceleration and I crashed into the seat in front of me,” he said.

“People were thrown from the train. We thought we had derailed. Then, little by little, we got out and saw that our train was tilted. There were many injured people and a lot of people shaken up. I saw papers on the floor and a child who was fine.

“Right now, we were helping the emergency services, holding IV bags with our hands… The firefighters, however, are working on the most damaged section of the train.”

open image in gallery Rescue personnel work at the site of the collision of two high-speed trains between the towns of Mora and Orgaz, near Toledo ( Reuters )

open image in gallery At least 68 people have died after the train collision with 77 more injured ( AP )

Eduarda, a passenger on the Iryo train, told Cadena SER radio she had initially thought it was making an emergency stop as she was thrown forward by the strong impact. She only realised the seriousness of the accident after seeing injured people and being told to evacuate.

After climbing down an embankment to safety, she saw what she described as a catastrophic scene, with part of the train hanging down the slope and a fire in one carriage.

Emergency responders, including a helicopter, police and ambulances, arrived within about 20 minutes. “I saw dead people,” she said.

Miguel, a passenger travelling with ​several ⁠colleagues in the rear car of one of the trains, said he heard a “massive roar” from the impact.

“We heard a massive roar, a truly enormous thud that went on for ⁠10 seconds, as if the train were about to derail. Through the right-hand window, we could ​see a ⁠wrecked train – I imagine it must have ‌been the other one,” he told Reuters.

Andalusian politician Juanma Moreno declared three days of official mourning in Andalusia, from 2pm on Wednesday until 2pm on Saturday.

“We are devastated,” he said. “All of Andalusia stands with the victims of this new railway accident.”

Jesús Pérez Martín, mayor of the nearby town of Los Yébenes, told RTVE he’d heard reports of “mutilations and very serious injuries”. Meanwhile, health minister Mónica García amplified calls from Madrid authorities urging people to donate blood amid the tragedy.

Renfe said it had activated a special line for families of victims and expressed its condolences, while Iryo activated emergency protocols.

Transport minister Oscar Puente said the fatal train crash occurred after a Renfe high-speed ⁠train ​was ⁠authorised to continue its ⁠journey despite an active ​red ⁠signal because ‌of a stationary train on the ‌tracks ahead, breaking protocol.

Politicians cleared their agenda for the day following the serious crash, with prime minister Pedro Sanchez offering support to all the victims and their families.

open image in gallery The crash has renewed criticism of transport minister Óscar Puente ( AFP/Getty )

open image in gallery A video provided by Guardia Civil shows an aerial view of carriages and first responders on the site ( Guardia Civil )

“Shocked by the serious train accident in Toledo,” he wrote on X. “I remain in constant contact with the Minister of Transport, and with the president of Castilla-La Mancha.

“Emergency services are working on the ground to assist those affected and ensure their safety, in coordination with all the involved administrations. My affection, solidarity, and support to all the victims and their families.”

It’s the second major train collision this year on Spanish railway lines, after 46 people were killed and more than 120 injured after a high-speed train derailed and collided with an oncoming one on 18 January near Adamuz, in the province of Cordoba.

The accident is still under investigation, but a preliminary report by Spain's Civil Guard in February pointed to defects in the track, rail, or weld between two ⁠sections of track as the main hypothesis for the accident. That crash triggered a debate about the level of investment in railway maintenance in recent years.

Following the latest crash, Jose Trigueros, president of the Association of Roads and Civil Engineers in Spain, renewed these criticisms of Mr Puente.

“It’s unacceptable that our infrastructure is being managed by incompetent people who should be focusing on their Ministry instead of tweeting. The state of our infrastructure is a disgrace. I hold the Minister responsible,” he told Europa Press.

Mr Puente has refused to say whether he’ll resign after a second fatal train collision this year. He said that the railway system is “reliable and safe” but had “some limits”, like every system of transport.

News.title: Broadcasting legend Ernie Johnson announces 'Inside the NBA' exit
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Ernie Johnson will step down as host of "Inside the NBA" once the 2026-27 season is over.

"It's just time," Johnson, 70, said Wednesday in a video posted to social media.

The announcement makes clear the decision is his alone. Johnson said in his message that he was neither pushed out of the role nor retiring, but simply "just cutting back".

He also said he intends to keep working, with CBS and Turner Sports' coverage of the NCAA men's basketball tournament the most notable part of his schedule.

A Sports Broadcasting Hall of Fame inductee, Johnson cited heart issues in recent years as one factor behind the move.

"This is by no means the end. It's just a turning of the page. And I'll forever cherish every chapter we have written with 'Inside the NBA,'" Johnson said.

open image in gallery Ernie Johnso said: 'It's just time' ( Getty )

The 2026-27 season is Johnson's 37th as host of "Inside the NBA”, the popular pre- and post-game show that also features retired NBA players Shaquille O'Neal, Charles Barkley and Kenny Smith.

O'Neal joined the programme in 2011, Barkley in 2000 and Smith in 1998. The show moved from TNT to ESPN and ABC last season and has won 21 Sports Emmy Awards.

Barkley said in September that he expects the 2026-27 NBA season to be his last on the show.

"Ernie Johnson is one of sports media's most respected and beloved figures," ESPN chairman Jimmy Pitaro said in a statement. "For more than three decades, he has been the heart of ‘Inside the NBA,' helping create one of the most iconic and entertaining studio shows in sports. We are grateful for Ernie's extraordinary contributions and look forward to celebrating him throughout the season."

The 2026-27 season began last week, with LeBron James leading his new side the Philadelphia 76ers to a win over defending champions the New York Knicks at Madison Square Garden.

News.title: King tides inundate streets and flood homes and businesses along both US coasts
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

King tides have inundated parts of both U.S. coasts, flooding streets and sending seawater into homes and businesses in beach communities in California, Florida and the Carolinas.

The tides began with the full moon earlier this week and could cause flooding in some areas into the weekend, forecasters said. King tides are caused by the gravitational pull and alignments of the Earth, moon, and sun. They can occur several times a year and last several days.

This week's king tides have been exacerbated by additional factors, forecasters said Wednesday.

In Florida, strong high pressure to the north and low pressure over the Caribbean were causing increased swells, Chris Fisher, a National Weather Service meteorologist in Miami, said.

Along the California coast, the ongoing super El Niño has warmed the ocean, leading to an increased volume of seawater. Another factor was the occurrence of Kelvin waves, a series of pulses of warm water that lift the sea level, said Roger Gass, a meteorologist with the weather service's Bay Area forecast office in Monterey.

King tides, like their name, are definitely noticeable. Residents don't need a beach to see the ocean. The ocean came to them.

In Southern California, Huntington Beach residents placed sandbags outside of homes Wednesday to try to keep floodwaters out. Some people used paddleboards and surfboards to move about the streets. Stretches of the Pacific coast Highway were closed, and tides were expected to approach record levels in Orange and San Diego counties.

In the northern part of the state, minor flooding was expected through Saturday in low-lying areas along shorelines and tidal waterways during peak high tides, the weather service said.

Gass said the coastal flooding generally occurred within 1 1/2 hours before and after high tides, which are peaking 1.9 feet (about a half-meter) above normal in Northern California.

Most of Florida’s Atlantic coast was under flood warnings through early Friday. Street flooding also was reported in South Carolina coastal cities, including Charleston and Myrtle Beach, and rip currents were possible as far north as North Carolina's Outer Banks.

“It’s been a rough beach week,” Fisher said. “We’ve had a high risk of rip currents and some high surf out there. The beach conditions are going to continue to be rough through the weekend. It’s been a good week to stay out of the water and stay away from the beaches.”

In Fort Lauderdale, Florida, getting to the multiple waterfront venues at what’s billed as the world’s largest-in-water boat show was tricky, requiring driving through flooded streets next to marinas, hotels and convention centers.

Virginia Key, a barrier island in Miami, saw its highest king tide and the third-highest water level since records were first kept going back three decades, Fisher said.

“The only times we've seen higher was during hurricanes,” Fisher said. “It's historical from a king tide perspective.”

News.title: Putin hails Elon Musk as ‘genius’ weeks after Starlink access slowed down for Ukraine
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Vladimir Putin hailed Elon Musk as a “genius” and said he was in contact with the tech billionaire as Russia develops its answer to his ⁠Starlink satellite internet system.

It comes just weeks after Ukraine, which uses a version of Starlink as a key component of drone operations and battlefield communications, complained of speed restrictions that hampered its ability to intercept Russian attack drones and forced the cancellation of some operations.

The Russian president made the remark about Mr Musk on Wednesday as he listened to a presentation by digital development minister Maksut Shadayev, ⁠who said Russia had launched more than 30 satellites ​as ⁠it builds its own Starlink equivalent.

"Just a second, I want to point out this is just our first step. Elon Musk is a genius, he's just a real genius," said Mr Putin.

open image in gallery ( Reuters )

Mr Shadayev ‌said in reply to a question from Mr Putin that Mr Musk had more than 5,000 low-orbit satellites up and running — although the actual number is close to 10,000, according to independent tracking site ‌Orbital Radar.

"Over 5,000 while we are only taking our first steps. But we are proud that we have begun to do this, and started to do it independently," Mr Putin said, adding that the task now was "to move from quality to quantity".

"We are in close contact with our American partners — including ⁠Mr Musk — because it is very important, in orbit, not to get in each other's way and to maintain a certain level of discipline and order," he said.

Starlink, which does not work in Russia, uses a constellation of satellites that orbit far lower than traditional geostationary communications satellites, reducing signal travel time.

Ukrainian leader Volodymyr Zelensky earlier this month accused the United States of withdrawing vital intelligence and weakening the Starlink service at a crucial time in the Russian invasion.

Starshield - the military version of Starlink - has provided a lifeline to Ukraine in helping to defend against incoming attacks, as well as striking Russian targets.

open image in gallery ( AFP/Getty )

However, on October 14, Ukrainian officials began reporting trouble with terminals moving at speed.

The problems with Starlink in Ukraine added to tensions between Kyiv and the US after Donald Trump announced a deal to buy Russian diesel.

He also pressed the country to stop striking Russian oil refineries and saying it was time for Ukrainians to replace their president.

At the weekend, Ukraine said Starlink and Starshield were again ⁠fully functional, but Musk accused the Ukrainian military of violating SpaceX's terms.

Neither Mr Musk nor the US government, which operates Starshield ‌using Starlink technology, have ​taken responsibility for imposing the speed curbs.

Russian officials have spoken highly of Mr Musk before. In 2025, Putin's investment envoy Kirill Dmitriev said Russia would like to work with him on a mission to Mars.

News.title: Burnham rules out calling early election
News.content:
Thanks for joining me. John Healey has promised to offer households “breathing space” in his maiden Budget today.

The Chancellor insisted the economy has shown “resilience” in the face of the energy shock from the Iran war.

However, he admitted the conflict has pushed up the cost of living, “piling pressure on the families, on businesses, and on our public finances”.

Among the measures the Chancellor is expected to announce are plans to scrap standing charges on household gas bills – saving families up to £50 a year.

Mr Healey said: “We can’t stop these shocks that hit Britain, but we can make Britain more resilient when they do.

“So, this Budget is designed to give households breathing space from some of the everyday costs, provide targeted support for businesses and self-employed people, and to start the long-term action needed to get energy costs down for good.” Here is what you need to know.

5 things to start your day

1) Healey prepares to slash household gas bills by £50 | Chancellor to scrap standing charges on gas bills and curb Energy Secretary’s power

2) Minimum wage rise will drive up food prices, Healey warned | Manufacturers say they are already struggling to cover soaring production costs

3) Poundland directors quit in stand-off over administration | Board members fear owner wants to steer retailer into insolvency

4) Google attacks UK over ‘unlawful’ AI plans | Search giant fights plans by competition regulator to force it to promote rivals

5) Netherlands to cut 25,000 civil service jobs in AI push | Police and defence will be exempt from plans to trim 15pc of government workforce in next decade

What happened overnight

Ahead of the Budget, oil prices rose after an attack on a refinery in Saudi Arabia, the world’s biggest crude exporter, which has renewed concerns around the risks to supply in the Middle East.

Brent crude was up 1.7pc to nearly $116 a barrel, maintaining inflationary pressure on the global economy. It traded around $70 before the start of the Iran war.

Meanwhile, Asia stocks rallied amid fresh enthusiasm about AI.

South Korea’s Kospi surged more than 6pc and was on track for its largest one-day gain since July, after chipmaker SK Hynix reported a more than seven-fold jump in quarterly profit and said it would return about $75 billion to shareholders this year.

The AI rally faces its next test when technology giants Alphabet and Microsoft report earnings after market close later today, with investors looking for evidence of returns that would justify the hefty cost of the AI build-out.

In Asia, MSCI’s broadest index of Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan was up 1.7pc, with Japan’s Nikkei adding 1.1pc and ⁠China’s CSI300 blue-chip index climbing 0.7pc.

News.title: Government remains tight-lipped on aid spending in Autumn budget
News.content:
The government made no mention of plans to restore aid spending in the Autumn budget and is on track to miss its current aid commitment.

It had been rumoured that a Burnham government planned to reverse the overseas aid cuts made by Sir Keir Starmer, who reduced an already shrunken aid budget from 0.5 to 0.3 per cent of gross national income (GNI) in February 2025.

The current 0.3 per cent allocation is the lowest proportion of national income spent on aid since 1999.

It was expected the reversal would be drawn up as part of a wider shake-up of the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO) under Ed Miliband as foreign secretary, The Telegraph reported in September.

But there was no mention of any timeline for restoring Britain’s overseas development assistance to the legally enshrined 0.7 per cent of gross national income GNI target on Wednesday.

The UK is now also on track to miss its 0.3 per cent aid spending commitment, equivalent to £9.2 billion per year, following a failure to confirm any upwards adjustment to the UK aid budget to account for inflation.

The shortfall is estimated to fall at £410 million this year, an analysis from the Centre for Global Development (CGD) found.

Britain’s aid money is spent across the world in sectors like health, education, disaster relief, and helping to promote democracy.

News.title: Fleetwood knock out Arsenal in one of the biggest shocks in League Cup history
News.content:
An unfamiliar opponent at a very familiar sounding venue, Arsenal play Fleetwood Town for the first time this evening at the Lancashire club’s Highbury Stadium.

Fleetwood, 18th in League Two, are the lowest-ranked team remaining in this season’s League Cup, having booked their place in the fourth round thanks to a victory at Sheffield United.

They were playing in English football’s sixth tier in 2009, and so while their stadium may share its name with Arsenal’s former home, the two clubs are worlds apart.

The League Cup is fourth of four competitions on Arsenal’s list of priorities, but Mikel Arteta should be able to rotate extensively while progressing to the quarter-finals. With a trip to Anfield on Sunday, that is a welcome luxury.

Kepa Arrizabalaga, Piero Hincapie, Cristhian Mosquera, Martin Zubimendi, Mikel Merino and Viktor Gyokeres are seasoned internationals in need of minutes and in line to start.

Max Dowman lit up Arsenal’s third-round victory at Ipswich Town, and 17-year-old centre-back Marli Salmon was not far behind him. Young striker and Northern Ireland international Ceadach O’Neill is also expected to be involved, and he may be joined by other academy players.

While attention is fixed on Premier League and Champions League success, Arsenal’s stinging defeat by Manchester City in last season’s final of this competition will not have been forgotten by Arteta or his players.

Matt Lawlor, Fleetwood’s manager, was full of praise for Arsenal in his pre-match press conference: “The champions are coming to town and they’re coming to our patch. The players need to be excited by it, not overawed by it. The respect is through the roof, but the fear can’t be through the roof.

“We’ve earned a game like this. We’ve had to go through round upon round of tough games, and none of them were easy. To get to where we are, we deserve that.”

Arteta has told his players that they must keep their standards high, with a lack of concentration or professionalism potentially their worst enemy against fourth-tier opposition.

Arteta said: “Our reputation, our pride, everything is in play. So every time you play a football match, and especially against a team in a different division, respect the game, respect every opponent because they deserve that, and then try to win and try to play a bit better than them.



“We know the risk, and in football, things can get very equal the moment you are able to match certain things, and that’s why our basics and habits have to be through the roof to be able to win the game.”



Full team news on the way shortly.

News.title: High temperatures linked to more than 700,000 deaths in 2023, study estimates
News.content:
Record-breaking temperatures killed an estimated 710,00 people globally in 2023, an increase of more than 36 per cent since 2015, according to new research.

A report on climate change and health by the Lancet medical journal shows that since the Paris climate agreement was introduced in 2016 the number of deaths linked to heat has rocketed.

Between 2006 and 2015 the average annual number of deaths attributed to heat stood at around 398,400 but between 2016 and 2023 the number increased to an annual average of 540,800, hitting a high of 710,000 in 2023.

The authors of the Lancet study say that extreme heat, which is linked to cardiovascular problems and is particularly dangerous for older people, pregnant women and those with other health conditions, must be considered a global health emergency. And they warn that the risks from high temperatures have accelerated in recent years.

News.title: Nigeria’s women and girls impacted the most by British and US funding cuts, committee is told
News.content:
UK and US aid funding cuts in Nigeria have impacted the country’s women and girls more than other groups, MPs were told on Tuesday.

Nigeria has been among the hardest-hit countries as many Western governments have slashed overseas development budgets to increase defence spending.

At the International Development Committee’s first hearing on the impact of aid cuts on global health in Africa, MPs were told that UK government cuts had impacted water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) programmes in Nigeria significantly, putting women and girls at risk.

“WASH is one of the lowest-funded areas in UK government support to Nigeria. WASH enables girls to stay in school, enables them to manage their menstruation effectively, enables women to give birth safely, and protects the lives of children under 5,” Evelyn Mere country director of Water Aid Nigeria said.

“The UK government says one of its priorities is that it will educate girls, empower women and make sure their voices are heard. It means that the UK says one thing, but with the aid cuts does another,” she added.

The British Foreign, Commonwealth, and Development Office (FCDO) announced earlier this year it would reduce its aid spending in Nigeria by 50.2 per cent over the next three years, from £136 million in 2025 to £68 million by 2029.

Nigeria has also faced substantial funding reductions from the US after the Trump administration shuttered USAID, the government’s foreign assistance arm. This included more than $600 million (£450 million) in health funding.

An FCDO internal impact assessment, published in July 2025, acknowledged that the biggest casualties of African funding cuts would be frontline WASH and women’s health programmes.

“Overall, any reductions to health spending risk an increase in disease burden and ultimately in deaths, impacting in particular those living in poverty, women, children and people with disabilities,” the assessment concluded.

News.title: Taliban forbids ‘un-Islamic’ sight-saving operations
News.content:
Hundreds of people each year will be denied sight-saving operations in Afghanistan after the Taliban forbade corneal transplants, doctors have told the Telegraph.

Officials have ruled that the transplant procedure is not permitted under Islamic teachings and have ordered surgeons to halt operations.

It is the latest in a stream of edicts limiting access to health care issued by the regime since it swept to power in 2021.

The edict came just months after a medical charity had helped train up local doctors to conduct operations in the Afghan capital, Kabul, and the eastern city of Jalalabad.

Doctors say there is a severe need for corneal transplants in Afghanistan to restore sight in patients injured in explosions and accidents.

Dr Noor Zaman Hashim of Noor Eye Hospital in Kabul said his staff had conducted 90 transplants in recent months, before the programme had been halted by the Taliban order.

He said the hospital had a growing waiting list, comprising mostly young people who had lost their eyesight because of trauma, injuries, explosions and welding-related accidents.

“Decades of violence have devastated Afghanistan’s healthcare infrastructure. We neither have sufficient ophthalmologists nor locally available corneas to meet the demand for transplants,” he said.

“The Taliban have verbally instructed us to stop the transplants. Nobody has the courage to defy their orders because of the risk of severe punishment,” he said.

Sports.title: Norris, Verstappen among 10 F1 drivers to miss Mexico first practice
Sports.content:
Lando Norris and Max Verstappen are among 10 Formula 1 drivers who will miss first practice for the Mexico City Grand Prix this Friday.

During the season, each Formula 1 team must run a rookie in at least two practice sessions for both of their cars and the relative simplicity of the Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez - which is not a street circuit, nor is the race a Sprint event - means most teams are taking the opportunity to fulfil the requirements.

Only Ferrari will run both full-time drivers for the opening session of the weekend, live on Sky Sports F1 at 6.30pm on Friday.

Which rookies will be running in Mexico City GP first practice? Mercedes - Frederik Vesti (George Russell)

Red Bull - Ayumu Iwasa (Max Verstappen)

McLaren - Leonardo Fornaroli (Lando Norris)

Racing Bulls - Nikola Tsolov (Liam Lawson)

Alpine - Gabriele Mini (Franco Colapinto)

Haas - Ryo Hirakawa (Esteban Ocon)

Audi - Freddie Slater (Gabriel Bortoleto)

Williams - Luke Browning (Alex Albon)

Aston Martin - Jak Crawford (Lance Stroll)

Cadillac - Colton Herta (Valtteri Bottas)

Verstappen will be replaced by Ayumu Iwasa, who drove for Red Bull in first practice in Barcelona and Monza earlier this year.

Reigning F1 world champion Lando Norris will hand his McLaren to Formula 2 champion Leonardo Fornaroli and George Russell will be on the sidelines for Mercedes reserve driver Frederik Vesti.

Formula 2 title contender Nikola Tsolov will make his F1 practice debut in place of Liam Lawson at Racing Bulls, who are the only team to not announce any of their 2027 drivers.

Lawson's impressive season and Arvid Lindblad's solid rookie campaign means many people are expecting Racing Bulls to retain the same line-up, but that would leave up and coming star Tsolov without a seat.

Formula 1 2026 remaining races Mexico This weekend Qatar November 27-29 Brazil November 6-8 Abu Dhabi December 4-6 Las Vegas November 20-22

Former IndyCar star Colton Herta wlll have a fifth practice outing of the season at Cadillac, Jak Crawford will complete his fourth Aston Martin appearance of 2026 and Britain's Luke Browning will be in Alex Albon's Williams.

Formula 2 driver Gabriele Mini will make his F1 practice debut and Haas' Ryo Hirakawa returns in place of Esteban Ocon.

British teenager Slater to make F1 practice debut in Mexico

British teenager Freddie Slater will make his Formula 1 practice debut for Audi in Mexico on Friday in Gabriel Bortoleto's car.

Slater, who became the first signee to the Audi Driver Development Programme, will also feature in practice at the Sao Paolo Grand Prix next week.

The 18-year-old finished as runner-up in the 2026 Formula 3 championship, with his strong campaign featuring a streak of eight podiums in eight weekends.

"We have seen Freddie making great progress throughout recent years, both on and off the track; it is the right time for Freddie to step up," said Audi racing director Allan McNish.

"These appearances in Mexico and Brazil will give him valuable experience of a Formula 1 race weekend, and another chance to continue his development before he steps up to Formula 2 next season. We are looking forward to seeing him in the R26 and supporting him through these two important FP1 sessions."

Image: Audi junior Freddie Slater will make his first F1 practice outing in Mexico (Credit: Audi Revolut F1 Team)

Slater added: "Getting behind the wheel of a Formula 1 car at a Grand Prix weekend is a big moment for me and something I've been dreaming of since I was a kid.

"I've learned a lot this year, and these Free Practice outings with Audi Revolut F1 Team will be another opportunity to keep gaining on-track experience.

"I'm really looking forward to getting out on track: my focus will be on doing the best job I can, helping the team with its programme and taking as many learnings as possible from both sessions."

Sports.title: Liverpool v Chelsea: Carabao Cup fourth round – live
Sports.content:
42s ago 15.51 EDT Xabi Alonso – a European champion with Liverpool but having suffered two defeats out of two as a visiting manager with Bayer Leverkusen and Real Madrid – speaks to Sky Sports. “The cups are important for us this year … we have a good challenge here coming to Anfield … it’s make or break … we want to make it happen today … we know we need a great performance … we have taken [this competition] from the beginning seriously … our players have played a few times already here … hopefully they will show it today.” Share

5m ago 15.46 EDT Pre-match postbag. “I’m loving the balance of experience and youth in the Liverpool starting XI. Jürgen had Klopp’s kids. Arne could have rolled out Slot’s Snappers more often. Today we’ve got Iraola’s Imps!” – Peter Oh “Looking at the Liverpool line-up, I can only think that Iraola has decided not to risk the prospect of drawing the mighty Fleetwood Town in the next round” – Vanessa Edwards “For the sake of the integrity of the Carabao Cup I think we are all Brighton fans tonight. If City stay in the competition and then lose their appeal (almost inevitable) then how on earth does that get resolved?” – Rick Harris “Anfield is nine miles from where I currently slouch and I can feel the anticipation from here. Something might just be afoot. Hope? Hendo also returns. But am glad he has scored his one cracker for the season already” – Ian Copestake (and readers who enjoy making speculative investments may be interested to note that, now Ian’s said that, you can get 28s on Henderson scoring the first goal tonight) Share

37m ago 15.14 EDT Andoni Iraola speaks to Sky Sports. “We need fresh legs … a lot of players are waiting for this competition to have their starts, their minutes … they are pushing hard … so I have trust that they can perform well … the bench is always important … we have good options … according to how the game goes, we will decide one way or another … we need to keep winning games … we need to keep going … it does not stop … the level of our opposition is very high … everyone has to play their part … I hope today they do … Chelsea have a very strong starting XI … we have to respect them … we have to be at our very best if we want to beat them … we always practice [penalties] … I don’t know if it is better or worse, I think Fleetwood didn’t practice and they were incredible! … but we always do it!” Share

Sports.title: Arsenal v Benfica: Women’s Champions League – live
Sports.content:
“I was stunned when I read that Renée Slegers was under pressure,” writes Kári Tulinius . “ It’s only just over a year since the greatest triumph in the club’s history, not only winning the Champions League, but beating that Barcelona side. Yes, Arsenal have started horribly, but I think Slegers has shown she’s a great coach.”

“Don’t forget Servette!” writes Jez Smith. “We are at Servette, where we saw our team put in a commanding performance to beat Leuven 5-1. We are, at least briefly, be above the likes of Manchester City. Which feels incredible after our first two defeats in the campaign.”

Ellie Carpenter has put Chelsea 1-0 up at home to Roma , and Momoko Tanikawa has scored Bayern Munich’s second equaliser at home to Real Madrid. Yep.

Renee Slegers makes three changes from the win at Spurs. Elisa De Almeida , Ona Batlle and Geraldine Reuteler come in for Leah Williamson, Emily Fox and Lisa Baum

Hello, hello and welcome to live coverage of Arsenal v Benfica in the Women’s Champions League. Arsenal will hope their 2-1 win at Tottenham kickstarts a hitherto disappointing season. They’re sixth in the WSL, with two wins from seven, and have four points out of six in the Champions League. It should really be six from six – they led 2-0 away to Paris FC last month before being pegged back.

This is what the head coach Renee Slegers had to say in her programme notes for tonight’s game.

double quotation mark Let’s make Saturday’s success against Tottenham Hotspur the beginning of something. We have been on such a frustrating run of games and to be able to break that cycle on Saturday, at the north London derby no less, meant so much to all of us. You all deserved that win. Your dedication to this team throughout a difficult start to the season has been nothing short of incredible and we are all so grateful for your support. We wanted to make sure you knew that. The supporters were on our minds all week in the lead-up to the match. We’d spoken within the group about how everyone wanted to play for something bigger than themselves, and there’s no greater symbol for that than a sold-out away end of nearly 4,000 people. So we said: let’s do this for you. In times like these, actions speak louder than words. You could see that when Leah sprinted to you the moment the final whistle blew, with Isabella Damm and Amy Liddiard right there in the crowd alongside you. Saturday was an outpouring of relief, but it was also more than that. It was a sign of the connection we share. You are all a part of this team.

Kick off 8pm.

Sports.title: Burnley turn to former CSKA Moscow manager Fabio Celestini as new head coach
Sports.content:
Burnley have announced former Switzerland midfielder Fabio Celestini as their new head coach four days after sacking Nicky Hayen.

Burnley, who have won only one of their 12 league games this season following relegation from the Premier League, have not disclosed the length of Celestini’s contract. They heralded his appointment by saying in a statement that the 50-year-old “arrives with a proven capacity to win and to adapt to different football environments”.

The club’s chief football officer, Diego López, himself a new name at the club this week, said: “Fabio brings the passion, experience and knowledge we were looking for. He showed extraordinary determination and conviction to come to Burnley. We want people who truly want to be here and help this club grow. Fabio is a clear example of that.”

Celestini’s last managerial role was at CSKA Moscow, who he left in May this year, and he has also had spells at Swiss clubs Lugano, Luzern, Sion and Basel. He led the latter from bottom of the table to a league and cup double in the space of 18 months.

The new head coach told Burnley’s website: “I look at Burnley and I see a club with big potential and players with real quality, who can help us achieve our supporters’ ambitions. I know the situation we are in, and I have lived it before. Our supporters deserve to see a team playing with belief from the first whistle.”

The former midfielder, who spent 10 years as a player in France and Spain and won 35 caps for Switzerland, will take charge of his first match in Saturday’s home league game against Portsmouth.

Sports.title: Lise Klaveness: ‘Certainly there are people that can challenge Infantino’
Sports.content:
As the rain whips around Oslo’s government quarter, Lise Klaveness is shielding herself from the wind, trying to work out tactics. “Of course we cannot probably do everything alone, but we have a voice, we have the right to speak, we have the right to suggest, so let’s see,” she says. “We will at least try to be a spearhead.”

The president of the Norwegian Football Federation wants to re-engage Fifa, and other governing bodies, on the topic of remedy. A slightly arcane aspect of human rights policy in normal times, the importance of remedy became very clear in the aftermath of the World Cup in Qatar, when the families of those injured or killed in the work that led up to the tournament were left without financial compensation after Fifa chose to direct a legacy fund elsewhere.

At Klaveness’s prompting, Fifa conducted a review into the process. The report ultimately found the organisation did have a responsibility to provide remedy, but Fifa chose not to redirect the money. Klaveness wants to focus minds on the topic once again and make sure new practices are in place for Euro 2028, co-hosted by England, Scotland, Wales and the Republic of Ireland, as well as the 2034 World Cup in Saudi Arabia, where labour movement sources suggest there is little to no external scrutiny on worker’s conditions.

She is doing so at a delicate juncture. While Gianni Infantino has assured those listening that the “vast, vast majority” of Fifa’s electorate will back his re-election as president next year, many within the game regard this as an opportunity for change. Klaveness is one of them, having been a thorn in Infantino’s side since she first raised the topic of remedy on the floor of the Fifa congress in 2022 and having called for him to resign this summer after the scandals of the Balogun red card and the Fifa Forward Enterprise fiasco.

The 45-year-old Klaveness has been touted as a possible candidate in the Fifa presidential election, earning a perhaps less than desirable endorsement from Sepp Blatter. The disgraced former president said Klaveness “deserved the utmost respect” and that “the time has come for a woman to take over the leadership”. Klaveness responded by recalling that Blatter “wanted us to play with shorter shorts”. Her position on a run for president today is to almost, if not entirely, rule it out.

View image in fullscreen Lise Klaveness prefers a collaborative approach to achieving solutions, rather than deals struck behind closed doors. Photograph: Stian Lysberg Solum/NTB/Alamy

“My name has come up a few times and I take it as a sign that [people are concerned] about governance because we have been very outspoken about governance,” she says. “We’ve had a role internationally that is not the most efficient way to get votes. I think we’ve been very outspoken so this time around I don’t think that would be a possibility for me and it’s not been a real subject for me either.”

Not quite a no, then, but whether she runs or not Klaveness is a consistent champion for reform. She believes there are other candidates out there who could challenge Infantino and deliver change. She says it is crucial that any such individual is persuaded to stand before the deadline for nominations on 18 November. “It’s really important to have a candidate and one who can win,” she says. “We will welcome any candidate, but just putting up somebody who will lose is …” She shrugs. “I think it’s important to now discuss who can have a platform to win.

View image in fullscreen Lise Klaveness has been a thorn in Gianni Infantino’s side since she first raised the topic of remedy on the floor of the Fifa congress in 2022. Photograph: MB Media/Getty Images

“There has been distrust, and not just in Europe, many other places than Europe,” she says of the challenge to Infantino. “Of course, it’s become very political, that’s why I refer to it as the Game of Thrones. Candidates need to have a base in different confederations. We don’t know how challenged Infantino can be until there’s a counter-candidate like that. But certainly there are people that can challenge him.”

On this day at least Klaveness is reluctant to make too many pugnacious remarks about Infantino or Fifa. “People ask me all the time about Infantino, but it’s not about him,” she says. “For me it’s about the governance going forward. He was elected on a platform of reform, which we really believed in, but it was not really implemented and that disappointed us.”

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Klaveness says she wants any reforms around remedy to apply to all organisers and competitions. She talks about building alliances to back proposals that would ensure funds are set aside for remedy before a tournament takes place and that mechanisms are established for how any money should be distributed. She wants to submit such proposals at the next Fifa congress. “It should also be in Uefa and other places, but let’s start with Fifa, let’s start at the top, and now that governance is on everybody’s lips let’s make this part of the suggestions we will make to the congress, together or alone.”

View image in fullscreen Klaveness (fourth row, second left) joined Norway men’s football team in a viking row on their homecoming in Oslo after their successful 2026 World Cup. Photograph: Trond R Teigen/EPA

A collaborative approach to achieving solutions, rather than deals struck behind closed doors, is Klaveness’s preferred way and on Tuesday the former midfielder, with 73 Norway caps, made her case on remedy to a gathering of politicians commemorating the 50th anniversary of the OECD’s guidelines for “responsible business conduct”. No longer the lone voice speaking out on the conference floor, Klaveness has allies and a growing number of people who – at least in private – would claim to share her values. That she also presides over two successful national sides doesn’t hurt.

Norway’s women’ face a playoff against Wales to qualify for next year’s World Cup. The men, meanwhile, won hearts and matches in the US this year. Klaveness recalls with some bemusement the World Cup experience. “I was on the road for seven weeks with 65 men,” she says. “I also saw Erling Haaland with a dead raccoon. Football is a lot of things, a sport, a competition, a cultural phenomenon. It’s also a social tool, but if we want the game to be for everyone there is going to be conflict.” It won’t be too long before that conflict resumes.

Sports.title: Howe, Nagelsmann, Pochettino: can anyone end Manchester United’s doom loop?
Sports.content:
In January 2014 the 13th series of Celebrity Big Brother aired in the UK, the show so popular that its run time was extended by five days before a public vote anointed Jim Davidson the winner. Then, two years later when Brexit happened, people wondered where their tolerant country had gone, lamenting the ephemeral spirit of London 2012 as though the 2011 riots were some kind of fever dream, not a desperate response to decades of structural and institutional racism exacerbated by the cruelty of unnecessary austerity.

The truth is that if security is quickly upended, it was built on quicksand to begin with. Which brings us to Manchester United, easing effortlessly from an uplifting third-place finish to some of the worst football in their history.

It is entirely possible that Alex Ferguson made a deal with the devil to the effect that United would be great until he retired and hilariously dreadful thereafter. But assuming not, his l’état, c’est moi mentality was busy setting up the post-him fall even at the height of the success – itself a consequence of what had gone before.

A day after the Munich air disaster, Louis Edwards – later a seller of condemned meat to schools – joined the board, eventually assuming control thanks to a dodgy rights issue. He bequeathed the club to Martin – his substellar son – who floated it for personal gain, turning an institution that sought to win, entertain and unify into a business legally compelled to return value to shareholders.

This left United vulnerable to acquisition by anyone and, when Ferguson fell out with two directors – a horse, a horse, his kingdom for a horse’s ejaculate – they sold to the Glazers, who loaded the purchase price and accordant interest obligation on to the club, with government and football authorities waving through a move since outlawed. Ferguson, meanwhile, must have feared exactly what the takeover would entail and known that without his support the banks might not have lent the money, while the chief executive David Gill admitted opposition to it but stayed in his role anyway, and so the pillaging began.

View image in fullscreen Manchester United fans let their feelings know about Malcolm Glazer’s proposed takeover of the club in May 2005. Photograph: John Peters/Manchester United/Getty Images

The English game then exploded, with investment in United left available only to those of wealth so extreme it necessarily casts aspersions over their character – such as arch polluter and anti‑immigration zealot, Jim Ratcliffe. Proclaiming inaccurate and divisive rhetoric contrary to the inclusive, cosmopolitan spirit of Manchester and United, jobs were culled and fights picked with fans, Old Trafford’s most desirable seats socially cleansed so the club could sell them to day-trippers for astronomical prices, with longstanding supporters banned after trumped-up charges of touting – a deeply principled stance the club fails to apply to itself.

Not untypically for a billionaire, Ratcliffe seemingly believes that correct opinions reflect exchequer not expertise, giving himself final say on footballing decisions. And rather than the “best in class” executives he promised, his United operate according to what political analysts call the “Boris principle”, no‑marks in thrall to their own self‑image given jobs for which they lack the ability and character, the consequent chaos being effective sabotage.

So the patterns continue: Champions League qualification is missed, insufficient funds are released; a new unsuitable manager spends heavily on players below requisite standard; Champions League qualification is achieved via unsustainably reactive style; the manager is denied necessary funds amounting to less than the bounty of Champions League qualification; the manager imposes a proactive style without the necessary materials; the manager is belatedly fired for a fee far exceeding that saved by cutting jobs; a new unsuitable manager, with entirely different requirements to his predecessor, is appointed; executive accountability is absent.

View image in fullscreen Eddie Howe is the preferred choice of director of football Jason Wilcox if there is a change of manager at Old Trafford. Photograph: Lee Smith/Action Images/Reuters

It is thus no surprise that Michael Carrick remains unfired, despite exuding the vibe of a man who’s mentally fired himself. Perhaps it’s a stay of execution, but more likely there’s bizarre hope of a turnaround, partly to save paying him off, partly because the relevant executives can’t achieve consensus on a replacement, and partly because surely even Omar Berrada and Jason Wilcox accept that, following another catastrophe, after dismissing Carrick they are honour-bound to dismiss themselves.

Except they and United don’t work like that.

So, just as they failed Carrick by not recruiting properly; failing to add experience to his coaching team; failing to replace outgoing fitness and set-piece coaches and failing to interrogate details of his new game-model, they are now failing him by having him continue in a job that is too much for him, destroying a season that remains salvageable. Meantime, the Glazers’ dividends continue unabated.

As such, the question isn’t so much who should be United’s next manager as can anyone manage United? Increasingly, it looks like the answer is – to quote Don Logan in Sexy Beast – “No”.

There are immediate on‑pitch issues: the team are unfit and their collective mentality weak; after years being lied to, the captain has finally broken; and the players hate the suits, the package toxic. Those are the minor problems.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Roughly, football management comprises five aspects: coaching, tactics, talent ID, pastoral care and presence. And, though no manager excels in every department, at this version of United surely they must. Moreover, given this is no job for a novice, track record is also important – and it might be here that Unai Emery’s candidature falls down, his brilliance in transforming mid‑ranking clubs undermined by failures at two high-profile basket cases.

View image in fullscreen Mauricio Pochettino has recently signed a contract extension which puts him in charge of the USA men’s team until 2030. Photograph: Kirby Lee/Imagn Images/Reuters

Which brings us to pastoral care and presence. In the postwar era, only Erik ten Hag has won a trophy at United without tangible charisma, the size of the club now demanding it more than ever. This is not a quality associated with Eddie Howe, while Antonio Conte does not scream pastoral care and, brilliant though his career has been, he failed miserably at Spurs, the only environment he has inhabited that is remotely similar to United.

Should United miss Champions League qualification, financial strictures will make an elite coach and tactician essential. But in any event, football has changed such that the alchemic art of combining players and personalities no longer guarantees success.

Which leaves us with talent ID, player quality and intelligence being the best coaching and tactics there are. Of the 78 players purchased post-Ferguson, only Bruno Fernandes and perhaps Zlatan Ibrahimovic could be classed as cast-iron successes, so the next man – assuming United don’t target Emma Hayes, who embodies more of the right stuff than almost anyone else – must have a keen nose. Even Jürgen Klopp, the other manager who fulfils these criteria – and of all the damage Ed Woodward wreaked on United, turning him off was most costly – benefited from a department which delivered the greatest run of transfers ever.

View image in fullscreen Germany’s coach at the 2026 World Cup, Julian Nagelsmann, speaks to his squad. He is believed to be admired by Manchester United’s executives. Photograph: Pilar Olivares/Reuters

Which leaves Mauricio Pochettino, who built something at Tottenham despite the environment, and Julian Nagelsmann. But had Pochettino not signed a new contract with the USA men’s team, the sense is that, as when Mourinho arrived at Old Trafford after years of speculation, he’s past his magical best, while Nagelsmann may be the free-thinking genius of his own imagination, just as he may be an emperor’s new clothes bluffer.

All of which is to say that failure has many fathers and, once ingrained, is not easily eradicated. Yet just as society has too much going for it to ever move quite beyond the pale, so too does Manchester United. Even the longest journey starts with one step; but does anyone have the nous to ensure it’s taken in the correct direction?

Sports.title: Football Daily | Fleetwood go their own way to down Arsenal and live Carabao Cup dream
Sports.content:
CODSWALLOPPED

Having made a passing reference to Mick Fleetwood in Tuesday’s thrilling edition of your favourite email, Football Daily genuinely wasn’t expecting to be repeatedly typing that particular F-word in our lead story in today’s edition. While we were aware Arsenal were in the coastal town of Fleetwood for a Fizzy Cup tie that could scarcely have been less glamorous than the previous evening’s Ballon d’Or ceremony at the Palladium, the needle on our patented Potential Shock-o-Meter had barely moved before a match pitting the Premier League champions against a side struggling in League Two. Even with the residual winds from Storm Boelo still buffeting the ground, we presumed Arsenal’s second string would have enough about them to record a comfortable win at Highbury, over 20 years after they left a London stadium of the same name to begin their residency at the Emirates. It was not to be and almost five months to the day since exiting a cup competition on penalties following a curiously flat and uninspired display, Mikel Arteta’s side exited a cup competition on penalties following etc, and so on.

Considering their team came into this game on the back of consecutive defeats by Cheltenham and Exeter, Fleetwood’s Cod Army would almost certainly have settled for seeing their players avoid embarrassment but after watching them go ahead against a team of Fancy Dans who were visibly labouring in the miserable conditions expectations were duly raised. Arsenal equalised courtesy of a scrambled Viktor Gyökeres effort that is unlikely to trouble the Puskas Award jury, before all hell broke loose when young Max Dowman was sent off for retaliation following a Harrison Neal challenge that – depending entirely on what team you support – was a potential career-ender or wasn’t even a foul. While he is not yet old enough to drive, get a tattoo or vote, Dowman has apparently been around long enough to earn himself a stinging rebuke from his manager, who conveyed the impression the 16-year-old could look forward to being sent to bed without any supper and having his screen-time vastly reduced.

A penalty shootout in which yet another Brazilian missed a crucial spot-kick for the Gunners ended in victory for Fleetwood, when Conor Haughey fired past Illan Meslier to make it five successful kicks out of five for the hosts. The second teenager to disgrace himself on the night, the young man from Norn Iron proceeded to drop a different kind of F-bomb in a post-match interview with Sky Sports. Asked what had been going through his mind before he took his penalty, Haughey replied: “Hit the top corner and run like f**k.”

Despite the post-watershed lateness of the hour, Sky’s pitchside reporter felt compelled to apologise to viewers for the youngster’s forthright response. While Arteta is left to focus on making sure his players get their act together ahead of Sunday’s trip to Liverpool, Fleetwood head coach, Matt Lawlor, can look forward to tonight’s quarter-final draw. “I’ve got no preference whatsoever,” he said. “We’ve got a big game at home [against Bristol Rovers] on Saturday and I want to win it. I would absolutely love to make an amazing night into an amazing week.” For Arsenal, on a night when heroes were hard to find, the dream of a domestic treble went its own way.

LIVE ON BIG WEBSITE

The MBM OGs are in tandem tonight for steaming hot live action. Join Scott Murray from 8pm GMT for Carling Cup fourth-round updates from Liverpool 3-2 Chelsea while Rob Smyth will be on deck at the same time to talk us through Arsenal 1-1 Benfica in the Women’s Champions League.

QUOTE OF THE DAY

“Our club holds deep respect for China, its history, its culture, and its citizens, as well as for the millions of Chinese fans who feel affection and admiration for Real Madrid. The club joins the public apology expressed by Kylian Mbappé, in which the player himself has conveyed his regret for his words and reiterated his respect for the Chinese people” – Real Madrid are in crisis PR mode as Mbappé’s Chairman Mao comments reach the second day of saying sorry.

View image in fullscreen Fallen idol. Photograph: Wu Hao/EPA

double quotation mark Your headline Mbappé’s China Crisis leads me to point out he was born in Paris and is not one half of a synth pop duo from Kirkby, Merseyside – Kev The Poet, Tiverton (born in Kirkby).

double quotation mark So pathetic Arsenal get knocked out of the Carabao Cup by plucky Fleetwood Town. I think that Michael Carrick should be sacked immediately! – Nigel Sanders.

double quotation mark The Nevada in Florida story reminded me of my coaching time with under-11s in Maryland in the 90s. The rule from the league was clear, if you’re leading by six goals at half-time, take off the star(s) for the second half. Football was designed to develop as well as to win. As for parents, I had them stand in an area I designated where during game-time they could encourage their scions but not encroach. This was unusual but they understood this strange Brit in a faraway land and it worked well for everyone. Happy times and no police needed, except welcomed as parents! – Jeremy Foxon.

double quotation mark Regarding the quote of the day from Wayne Rooney in yesterday’s Football Daily, he seems to be inferring that players from Brentford and Wolves are not good enough for Manchester United. This is from a man who signed for said United in the summer of 2004 from Everton, who (checks online encyclopaedia) finished 17th in the Premier League a couple of months earlier. Pot/kettle? – Tracey in Leicester.

If you have any, please send letters to the.boss@theguardian.com. Today’s prizeless letter o’ the day goes to … Kev The Poet. Terms and conditions for our competitions, when we run them, are here.

Sports.title: Max Dowman’s Fleetwood fracas leaves him, Arsenal and Arteta red-faced
Sports.content:
Mikel Arteta’s reaction said it all. As Max Dowman trudged towards the touchline after becoming the youngest player sent off in a League Cup match at 16 years and 300 days, the Arsenal manager could not help himself.

Arms folded across his chest like an angry father who has caught his teenage son sneaking in after midnight, Arteta leaned over and aimed a few choice words in Dowman’s direction before the forward headed sheepishly down the tunnel. What he said remains unknown, although that hasn’t stopped the amateur lip-readers speculating on social media. “Get in the changing room. Now,” appears the most likely guess.

There is no doubt Arteta had made up his mind about the incident that ended with Dowman seeing red for reacting to an overaggressive sliding tackle from Fleetwood’s Harrison Neal. Although Arsenal intend to appeal and Arteta told Sky after the shock penalty shootout defeat by the League Two side 84 places below them in the pyramid that he wanted to watch it again before “assessing the situation”, the Spaniard made no excuses for Dowman in his post-match press conference.

“It was something that we discussed before the game,” he said when asked about their touchline exchange. “We knew when we prepared the context of the match, we were very clear on the things to expect, the things that emotionally we have to dominate.”

Whether Dowman’s reaction warranted a straight red card remains open to debate given there was minimal force when he lifted his right knee towards Neal. The referee, Michael Salisbury, could easily have decided to give both players a yellow and defused the situation, especially given Cole Palmer was booked for barging into Tottenham’s Matheus Fernandes off the ball on Saturday in what seemed a far more aggressive act. But, as Wayne Rooney and David Beckham infamously found to their cost while playing for England at the World Cup, acts of petulance are not usually tolerated by officials. Dowman was deemed to have overstepped the line.

It is a pressure Arteta has warned the record-breaking teenager would have to deal with as Dowman’s reputation has grown. Only last month Dowman was sent off playing for England Under-19s against the USA after a poorly timed tackle that most present at the behind-closed-doors match deemed a harsh decision. He was said to have been on the receiving end of a host of strong challenges in that match. Last year, Arteta urged Dowman to follow the example of Bukayo Saka after revealing Dowman was fouled nine times in a the first half of an England Under‑19s game against Spain.

View image in fullscreen Max Dowman is the centre of attention for Fleetwood’s players after the teenager’s reaction to a tackle from Harrison Neal. Photograph: Ryan Browne/Shutterstock

“It’s going to happen, he’s going to have to learn when to release the ball and when to attract his starting position,” Arteta said. “Very similar to Bukayo in the beginning as well. Those players are going to attract players, contact, attention and they have to be very smart about when you want that contact and when you don’t want it, and what you have to do to avoid it.”

Asked how Dowman tends to react, he said: “He just gets up … very rare! Sometimes I get surprised emotionally how cool he can be. I think it’s about repetition. He’s so used to it that now he knows to let the referee deal with it and my teammates probably to defend me, and I will carry on playing.”

When the dust settles after a seismic defeat that ranks alongside Arsenal’s League Cup upsets against Swindon, Birmingham and Bradford, Arteta may come to regret such a public admonishment of a 16-year-old. His actions were criticised by Paul Merson, who questioned whether Areta would “do it differently” given another chance. But part of Arteta’s frustration will be that Dowman took the bait. He also knows opponents will now target Dowman even more to see whether they can provoke a reaction.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

If Arsenal’s appeal fails, Dowman’s immediate punishment will be a three-match domestic suspension, causing him to miss Sunday’s trip to Liverpool and games against Hull and Newcastle. The timing is far from helpful: Saka’s thigh injury, expected to keep him out for several weeks, had opened up the possibility of more game time in the Premier League and Noni Madueke did not travel to Fleetwood owing to an ankle issue.

Dowman burst on to the scene last year by becoming the first 15-year-old to play in the Champions League, then broke the Premier League’s youngest goalscorer record against Everton in March, and this is the first major setback in his fledgling career.

He has been training with the first team since he was 14 and Arsenal have been extremely careful not to overexpose one of the most talked about players to emerge from their Hale End academy. Arteta resisted the temptation to give him many more minutes in the Premier League after Dowman scored twice against Ipswich in the previous round of the Carabao Cup last month. The challenge will be how Dowman responds to the extra scrutiny – on and off the pitch – that is bound to come his way.

Sports.title: Kylian Mbappé’s China crisis shows how sensitive Mao’s legacy remains | Rebecca Bailey
Sports.content:
It’s been a bad start to the week for the Kylian Mbappé. The France forward missed out on joining the elite roster of Ballon d’Or winners and instead became the latest high-profile addition to a far less illustrious list – that of foreign brands and individuals charged with “hurting the feelings of the Chinese people”.

The saga began when a video of the Real Madrid player making light of a meme involving him and China’s former leader Mao Zedong began spreading.

Within hours Mbappé found himself condemned online, before being unceremoniously dropped by brands, then held responsible for state television suspending the entire top Spanish league from its schedule. On Tuesday Mbappé apologised – “My comment was ill-judged, and I now understand that it hurt many people in China” – as did La Liga, which released a statement saying it “deeply regrets the offence that Kylian Mbappé’s recent comments have caused among Chinese fans”.

Foreign brands from Mercedes to Versace and celebrities from John Cena to Katy Perry have previously been sent to the sin bin for crossing China’s political lines on Tibet, Hong Kong and Taiwan.

Mbappé’s case shows how sensitive Mao’s legacy remains in China 50 years after his death – to the extent that most Chinese coverage of the affair does not even mention what the footballer said.

In the video, Mbappé references a meme of himself and “a guy … I think he was a Chinese dictator”, before a composite image of Mbappé’s face on Mao’s body pops up. (Mbappé has been nicknamed “the dictator” since his time at Paris Saint-Germain, a joke referring to his perceived influence at the club.)

The football app Dongqiudi was among the first to release a statement condemning the “inappropriate remarks”, but said: “Because his comments were offensive to China and the Chinese people, we cannot translate them.” Chinese media have reported on reactions such as the brand desertions, and the China Football Association’s lodging of a “stern protest” with Real Madrid – who apologised on Wednesday “to the Chinese people for any offence caused” – but have generally steered clear of outlining Mbappé’s precise offence.

The topic was still trending on Chinese social media on Wednesday morning, with one hashtag relating to the superstar’s apology boasting more than 600m views. Some posts asked variations on a simple question: “What did he actually say?”

Manya Koetse, editor of the Eye on Digital China newsletter, said in a post on X: “Many netizens without a VPN are still left in the dark about why all the talk about boycotting Mbappé is actually happening.”

Still, many expressed anger at what was characterised as disrespect for, as well as a misunderstanding of, China’s history. “For the majority of the [Chinese] people, Mao was and is still not seen as negatively as it is believed in the west,” said Mobo Gao, professor of Chinese studies at Adelaide University.

Mao was the founding leader of modern China, but his legacy includes radical policies such as the Great Leap Forward, an industrialisation policy blamed for a famine that killed as many as 30 million people by some estimates.

View image in fullscreen An  for a drink brand, featuring Kylian Mbappé, in Shanghai. Photograph: Ying Tang/NurPhoto/Shutterstock

The ruling Communist party (CCP) maintains Mao was a revolutionary hero, though after his death it acknowledged another extreme policy, the violent Cultural Revolution, was a “grave mistake”.

Gao said: “There has been intense tension between Mao hatred and Mao support among the Chinese themselves. This tension is even more keenly felt since the economy has slowed.”

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Some scholars have pointed to a resurgence of interest in Mao among younger Chinese, with a yearning for a time they regard as more idealistic and egalitarian – something the CCP is keen to keep in check.

Jennifer Pan, professor of communication at Stanford University, said the difficulty of doing independent social science surveys in the past decade meant “our understanding of what Chinese people actually think is weak”. Pan said: “Social media doesn’t fill that gap. It’s noisy, unrepresentative, and censored … What we see is that companies, platforms, broadcasters and the foreign ministry moved together quickly. Did this follow public anger, or did this produce public anger? Either is possible, and we can’t tell which came first.”

Whichever way round, the financial cost for Mbappé is the same. His face is a common sight on Chinese buses, in subways and in online ads, and his commercial deals could be worth “as much as $30m (£22.6m) per year”, said Mark Dreyer, author of Sporting Superpower, a book about China’s ambitions in the sector.

However, “as soon as someone else has decided you’ve crossed the line, it’s a race to who can cut ties quickest, who can be the most patriotic”, he said. “Then you have to kiss the ring – there really is no other way if you want to stay in the market.”

Mbappé’s and La Liga’s swift apologies suggest they are trying to avoid a fate like the NBA, whose lucrative pre-season matches were shut out of China for six years after the Houston Rockets’ then general manager Daryl Morey voiced support for Hong Kong pro-democracy protests in 2019.

La Liga may have better luck, with the state broadcaster CCTV saying it would listen to what Mbappé had to say, and “more importantly” watch what he does.

On Wednesday a foreign ministry spokesperson, Guo Jiakun, said: “We take seriously the apology the individual concerned has made.”

Dreyer said: “It doesn’t sound like it’s an instant ‘all is forgiven’. But it sounds like they’re going to be a little bit more, for want of a better word, reasonable.”

Sports.title: Liverpool vs Chelsea - Carabao Cup: Xabi Alonso returns to Anfield for a place in the quarter-finals up with grabs plus updates from Manchester City vs Brighton
Sports.content: Michael Carrick CAN still save his job at Man United - these are the three things he must do in last roll of the dice at Chelsea, writes NATHAN SALT

Sports.title: Michael Carrick holds Carrington summit with Bruno Fernandes amid tension between Man United boss and captain after Bournemouth snub and 'loyalty' dig
Sports.content:
Michael Carrick has held clear-the-air talks with Bruno Fernandes after dropping the Manchester United captain to the bench for Sunday’s defeat to Bournemouth at Old Trafford.

Carrick confirmed that Fernandes was fit and available for the game in a clear indication that the Portugal star was being punished for criticising United’s tactics in the Champions League defeat in Como last week.

The two men had a meeting at Carrington on Wednesday to iron out their problems after United confirmed that Carrick will stay in charge for now despite a run of eight games without a win. With Carrick's future still uncertain, though, it made sense to get his captain and best player back onside.

Sources say that Fernandes is more settled after a difficult week in which he appeared to pin the blame for United's embarrassing 4-1 loss to Como on Carrick, and then discovered that his home in Cheshire had been raided by a gang on the night of the match. Fernandes' family were not home at the time, and the burglars made off with jewellery and other expensive items.

Speaking after he was substituted shortly after the hour mark in Italy, Fernandes discussed United's tactics by saying: 'It's a decision from the staff to not press man to man and sometimes leave space behind and try to get the ball, wait for them.

Michael Carrick has held clear-the-air talks with Man United captain Bruno Fernandes

Fernandes was seen in training on Wednesday as Man United prepare for a crunch clash against Chelsea

The captain then liked an Instagram post which read: 'Never push a loyal person to the point where they no longer care'

'It's not the first time. We started on the wrong foot and they scored very early. Not much pressure on the ball, not many good movements with the ball, not many things going our way.

‘Conceding early makes us go into game with a mood of defeat, it's difficult to get out of that, trying to be brave, to have the ball and make something happen. If we are not able to do that, it is going to be very difficult to get out of this situation.’

Asked if he meant that Carrick got his tactics wrong, Fernandes added: ‘That's on the manager and staff to say, not me. Sometimes you have to be more brave under pressure, take the risk of pressing high and making them uncomfortable.

‘As you saw with Como, the centre-back was coming to mark me in my own half. We need to do that as a team but we were unable to.'

When Carrick was told about Fernandes’ comments, the United boss gave a pointed response by suggesting that his players weren’t willing to run enough.

Fernandes was dropped for the Bournemouth defeat after questioning the team's tactics

‘We actually were half-pressed man-to-man in the second half and then conceded a goal from that,’ he said. ‘There's a little bit on whatever system you play, whatever tactics you play, but if you don't run – you don't run forward and you don't run back – you aren’t going to win.’

Carrick dropped Fernandes to the bench against Bournemouth and then left him stewing there while he brought on four other substitute including teenager Shea Lacey.

Afterwards, Fernandes was among the United players targeted for abuse by fans as they made a public show of support for Carrick and then turned on the team.

He seemed to respond with a veiled dig at Carrick on Sunday night when he liked a cryptic Instagram post that read: ‘Never push a loyal person to the point where they no longer care.’
