World.title: Fed leaves interest rates unchanged despite inflation in the US
World.content:
Rates will remain 3.75-4 percent even as inflation continues to rise.

Share Fed leaves interest rates unchanged despite inflation in the US on social media

The United States Federal Reserve is set to hold interest rates steady in its final monetary policy decision before the US midterm elections.

The central bank will maintain rates at 3.75-4 percent, following a 10-2 vote, in line with expectations.

CME FedWatch, which tracks the likelihood of monetary policy decisions, indicated that there was more than a 90 percent chance rates would remain unchanged.

“Economic activity is expanding at a strong pace,” the Fed said in its press release announcing the decision on Wednesday. “While uncertainty remains elevated owing, in part, to geopolitical developments, domestic spending has been resilient. Productivity growth is strong, and capital investment is robust. Job gains have kept pace with the workforce, and the unemployment rate has changed little.”

The Fed noted how inflation continues to rise.

It also added, “The accumulation of more information will help the Committee determine the policy stance appropriate to ensure a timely return of inflation to the Committee’s 2 percent goal.”

The most recent Consumer Price Index (CPI) report showed the annual inflation rate increasing to 3.7 percent in September, up from 3.4 percent in August, with energy prices largely accounting for the monthly surge.

There were signs earlier this month that the central bank would maintain benchmark interest rates, with the Fed’s chair for supervision, Michelle Bowman, advocating a “wait and see” approach.

“I don’t feel any urgency for taking further action at this point,” she said at this month’s International Monetary Fund-World Bank meetings in Bangkok, Thailand. “We really need to take some time and understand how things will evolve.”



The decision comes before Thursday’s release of the Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) Price Index report, which is used by the central bank to assess inflation and inform its decisions.

Today’s Fed announcement follows an interest-rate hike rise last month, amid surging inflation – the first increase by the central bank since July 2023. The move drew criticism from US President Donald Trump, who has repeatedly pressed the Fed to cut rates since taking office. At the time, he wrote on Truth Social that “interest rates in the United States should be 1% or less.”

The Fed’s next monetary policy meeting is scheduled for December 8-9, when it will give its final rate decision of the year.

Current forecasts point to a quarter-point interest rate increase.

World.title: What are the implications of Israel’s elections?
World.content:
No clear winner in Israel’s first election since the October 7 attacks and genocidal war in Gaza.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s alliance, made up of right and far-right parties, is short of a majority after the most consequential elections in decades.

Tuesday’s poll saw a record turnout. And the main opposition bloc, led by former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, also does not have the numbers to form a government on its own.

Meanwhile, parties representing the Palestinian citizens of Israel have made unprecedented electoral gains.

While Netanyahu has refused to work with Arab-led lists, could the opposition alliance reach a deal with them?

Or is cooperation a bridge too far while the Israeli military’s assaults on Gaza and the occupied West Bank continue?

Presenter: Sami Zeidan

Guests:

Mairav Zonszein – senior Israel analyst, International Crisis Group

Mustafa Barghouti – secretary-general, Palestinian National Initiative

Phyllis Bennis – fellow, Institute for Policy Studies, and author of Understanding Palestine and Israel

World.title: US jury convicts Rwandan American of lying about role in genocide
World.content:
Jurors heard competing witness testimony on where Eric Nshimiye was and what he was doing in April 1994.

A federal jury in Boston, Massachusetts, has convicted a Rwandan American man of perjury and obstruction of justice for lying about his role in the 1994 Rwandan genocide.

Eric Nshimiye, a 55-year-old father of four and a United States citizen, was accused of lying in his testimony in a 2019 trial, also in Boston, for Jean Leonard Teganya, a former medical school roommate who was later convicted of helping to perpetrate the genocide. At the time, Nshimiye told the court neither he nor his friend had taken part in the killing and rape of Tutsis in Butare, where the pair were studying at a medical university.

Investigators from the US Department of Homeland Security arrested Nshimiye at his home in Ohio in 2024, alleging he had lied to them in an interview about his time in Rwanda during the genocide.

Nshimiye was originally charged with multiple counts of perjury, obstruction of justice and committing fraud on his immigration paperwork because prosecutors said he had told immigration officials he did not take part in the genocide when he moved to the US several years after the violence. He became a US citizen in 2009.

The immigration charge was dropped by prosecutors before the trial began. On Tuesday, the jury convicted Nshimiye on four counts of perjury and one count of obstruction of justice.

“For nearly three decades, this defendant concealed his involvement in the 1994 Rwandan genocide and the heinous acts of violence he committed, including clubbing people to death,” Assistant Attorney General A Tysen Duva in the Department of Justice’s Criminal Division said in a statement on Wednesday. “Then, he lied to immigration officials in order to become a US citizen, and he lied to a federal jury to protect himself and a fellow perpetrator of the Rwandan genocide.”



After the verdict, Nshimiye’s attorneys filed a request with the court to count the time he had already spent in prison before the trial towards any sentence. In a court filing, the attorneys argued Nshimiye should be set free because the two and a half years he had already spent in custody were longer than the usual sentence for the charges he was convicted of.

Nshimiye’s family, including his US-born children, were in attendance when the verdict was announced in court.

“It was quite shocking, difficult to process at first because we were expecting a different outcome. We were expecting to bring him home,” his son Tresor Nshimiye, told Al Jazeera.

Prosecutors brought a series of experts to help the jury understand the scope of the crimes in Rwanda, starting with academics who pointed out where the country was on a map of Africa.

Witnesses from Rwanda told jurors they recalled Nshimiye taking part in killings and other violence in Butare directed at minority Tutsis in 1994. They were part of a nationwide outbreak of genocidal violence by hardline majority Hutus that killed more than 800,000 people over about 100 days. Others said Nshimiye was part of the pro-Hutu National Revolutionary Movement for Development and the Interahamwe, the paramilitary group blamed for most of the killings during the genocide.

The defence argued Nshimiye had never been implicated in domestic and international tribunals after the genocide, including the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda as well as an informal transitional justice system inside Rwanda, called gacaca, which tried more than a million people for their roles in the atrocities.

Defence lawyers pointed out apparent inconsistencies in government witnesses’ testimonies and brought other witnesses who said Nshimiye was with them in the capital, Kigali, and other parts of the country during the genocide.

Nshimiye’s attorneys also argued in court that Rwandan authorities had interfered with the investigation because they had met with some witnesses before they testified in Boston.

“At the end of the day, it was just two competing stories, and so much is lost with this all happening 30 years or so ago. … I guess the jury was more convinced of the prosecutor’s witnesses because they victimised themselves in their stories,” Tresor Nshimiye said.

Nshimiye’s case is one of several currently under way in the US related to the Rwandan genocide.

In April 2025, prosecutors charged Faustin Nsabumukunzi, a 65-year-old beekeeper in Long Island, New York, who had applied for US citizenship, with similarly concealing his role in the violence. And in June 2025, authorities charged 65-year-old Vincent Nzigiyimfura of Dayton, Ohio, who had also applied for US citizenship, with concealing his role in the genocide.



Both men were previously listed publicly as fugitives by Rwandan authorities.

World.title: Putin tells African leaders Moscow will not pursue ‘neo-colonialism’
World.content:
Speaking at the third Russia-Africa Summit, Putin frames Russia as an alternative partner to former colonial powers.

President Vladimir Putin has told African leaders visiting Moscow that Russia does not engage in “neo-colonial exploitation” of the continent, unlike former colonial powers.

Speaking at the third Russia-Africa Summit in Moscow on Wednesday, Putin said the West is still trying ‌to exploit the continent’s resources and uses debt to hold back development.

“Africa is increasingly asserting itself as one of the key players in the global economy and politics. However, the emergence of a multipolar world is, of course, no easy task; it faces resistance from countries that are not prepared to accept this reality,” Putin told the summit.

Russian-backed government forces in a broad swath of North Africa are fighting armed rebellions as many countries in the region emerge from military coups that have shaken regional security.

Putin criticised “active attempts by Western countries” to drive Africans back into debt and to force them to accept much-needed financial resources on predatory terms, which he said slowed their long-term development.

“Our business does not engage in the predatory, neo-colonial exploitation of natural and human resources, but rather expands the processing of raw materials locally, thereby creating new jobs and generating tax revenue,” said Putin.

Disruptions to agriculture

Putin told delegations from 48 African countries, including 22 represented by their heads of state, that Russia was prepared to expand the geographical reach of agricultural product shipments.

Russia had supplied 13 million metric tonnes of agricultural products to Africa in the first nine months of this year alone, he added.



The remarks come as attacks in the Black Sea continue to disrupt exports of grain from both Russia and Ukraine, while the United States-Israel war on Iran has interrupted global fertiliser supplies.

Putin is due to hold one-on-one talks with individual African leaders who are attending on topics ranging from trade to security, grain supplies and arms deals.

The summit is expected to end with a final declaration on deepening cooperation between Russia and African nations.

World.title: Five key takeaways from the UK Autumn Budget
World.content:
The government says its policies are for the ‘working people of Britain’.

The United Kingdom’s government has announced its first budget since Andy Burnham became prime minister and leader of the Labour Party three months ago.

Chancellor of the Exchequer John Healey unveiled his Autumn Budget on Wednesday, announcing a series of policies that he said were for the “working people of Britain”, who have experienced a dramatic decline in living standards in recent years. Healey said the budget would give the country “breathing space” after years of economic stagnation fuelled by austerity, Brexit, the coronavirus pandemic, privatisation and rising energy prices.

So, what did Healey announce, and what will it mean for the average Brit?

Energy costs

Global fuel prices have soared in recent months because of the US-Israel war on Iran, which has prompted Tehran to close the Strait of Hormuz, a crucial waterway through which about 20 percent of the world’s oil and liquefied natural gas (LNG) would normally transit.

In response, Healey said on Wednesday that 20 million households will receive a one-off payment of 100 British pounds ($133) towards their energy bills. People living in homes valued at 88,000 British pounds ($117,000) or less will receive the payment. The valuations are based on prices in April 1991, not current house prices.

Healey also said a temporary cut to VAT – a sales tax – will be extended until 1 July. The measure will reduce the annual price cap by 50 British pounds ($66.50).

However, James Meadway, an economist and co-director of the left-wing think tank Verdant, told Al Jazeera that these measures will not tackle the cost-of-living crisis in “any serious way”.



“There’s quite a lot of small things. These are not nothing. They’re just not approaching the scale of the problem that people are already facing and [which] is expected, according to the government’s own figures, to get worse over the next year,” Meadway said.

Earlier on Wednesday, the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR), an independent public body that analyses the country’s finances, said it expected no growth in real earnings next year. The body also sharply downgraded its growth forecast for 2027 to 1 percent, from 1.5 percent.

“There are forecasts out there saying that by the end of Parliament, it will be the worst Parliament for living standards in modern history. Put in those terms, what you got in this budget was nothing like enough,” Meadway added.

Defence spending

Healey said he would fund the government’s additional Defence Investment Plan, worth 15 billion British pounds ($20bn), and pledged to plug a gap of 4.7 billion British pounds ($6.2bn) by “reprioritising” budgets across other departments.

However, he did not detail how the government would meet its NATO commitment to spend 3.5 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) on defence by 2035, with an interim target of three percent in 2030. Instead, Healey said he would set out how these targets would be met during a spending review next year.

In response, NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte welcomed the British government’s budget plan, saying it showed a “strong commitment” ⁠to defence.

“Good news on the new budget from MP John Healey with ‌a strong commitment on defence,” wrote Rutte on X.

“The UK role in Transatlantic security is vital, and I welcome ⁠this move to ⁠put Britain on a credible path towards meeting the commitment ⁠made by all NATO Allies ⁠in The Hague – ⁠to ensure we’re all investing what’s needed to remain ready ‌and able to deter aggression and defend our freedom ‌and ‌security,” Rutte added.

Ukraine was also on the agenda during Healey’s budget statement, with the chancellor pledging an additional 10 billion British pounds ($13.2bn) in economic and military aid for Kyiv in its war with Russia.

Salaries

The National Minimum Wage and National Living Wage will both increase by 3.9 percent in April, at the start of the new tax year. The former currently sets a minimum hourly rate of 10.85 British pounds ($14.44) for workers aged 18 to 20, while the latter sets the rate at 12.71 British pounds ($16.91) for workers aged 21 and over.



Taxes on banks’ profits

To raise funds for additional support for households and businesses, the government will temporarily increase the Bank Corporation Tax Surcharge from three percent to six percent. The increase will last for 15 months, ending on March 31, 2028. The surcharge is levied on top of standard corporation tax and is expected to raise 1.5 billion British pounds ($2bn).

Housing crisis

Affordable housing is a significant problem in the UK. The latest data from the Office for National Statistics (ONS) shows that 35 percent of men aged 20 to 35 were living at home with their parents last year, compared with 22 percent of women in the same age range.

To tackle this, Healey announced a new First Time Buyer savings account. Interest earned in such accounts, commonly referred to as Individual Savings Accounts (ISAs), is tax-free.

The First Time Buyer account will launch in 2029, replacing the current Lifetime ISA. The exact details of the new account are not yet clear. However, like the Lifetime ISA, it will pay savers a bonus of 25 percent on deposits of up to 4,000 British pounds ($5,320). That means savers can benefit from an annual government bonus of up to 1,000 British pounds ($1,330).

Healey also announced that the penalty for first-time buyers using funds from a Lifetime ISA to purchase a house worth more than 450,000 British pounds ($598,853) will immediately be reduced to 20 percent. That means savers will get back at least what they put in. The penalty was previously 25 percent.

A further 432 million British pounds ($574.9m) will also be spent over the next two years to reduce the number of people sleeping on the streets, a problem that Burnham has pledged to end.

World.title: At Least 68 Killed in Train Crash in Spain, Officials Say
World.content:
Pinned

A high-speed passenger train rear-ended another in Spain on Wednesday morning near the central city of Toledo, killing at least 68 people and injuring dozens more, officials said, in one of the deadliest train crashes in Spanish history.

The accident happened after traffic control operators told a high-speed train to continue its journey when another train was stopped farther along the tracks, Spain’s transportation minister, Óscar Puente, said. He called the operators’ instruction “inexplicable.”

The deadly crash was the second this year involving the same two rail operators; the first, in January, killed 46 people. The latest accident, and its timing months after the previous crash, was likely to deepen doubts about the security of Spain’s once-vaunted rail system.

In Spanish news reports, passengers described an awful impact that tossed people from a dining car, broke limbs and piled passengers atop one another. People crawled out of windows and others were carried by fellow passengers into a nearby field on makeshift stretchers. Local workers, who had heard the crash, rushed to help and guide survivors to safety.

The crash came about a month ahead of national election in Spain, and it had the potential to become an issue in an already bitter campaign about the competence of the left-wing government of Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez.

Spain’s rail authority, the Adif, said the trains involved were a “Renfe train and another from the Iryo company,” both covering the route between Madrid, the capital, and the southern city of Seville. Renfe is the national rail provider.

Mr. Sánchez visited the scene of the crash, saying that Spanish rail’s security systems clearly needed to be reinforced. “If there has been negligence, it will come to light,” he said. “If there have been failures in the safety system, we will respond with the utmost firmness.” He declared three days of official mourning.

The conservative opposition leader, Alberto Núñez Feijóo, voiced his own concern.

“I am very concerned about the information we are receiving regarding another train accident,” he wrote on social media soon after the crash. “The priority now is to assist the victims and support their families. My full support goes to the emergency teams working on the ground.” His Popular Party canceled all its campaign events around the country.

Here’s what else to know:

Survivor speaks: A passenger on one of the trains described a routine trip, a sudden jolt and an effort to tend to the dead and injured. Read more ›

An earlier deadly crash: In January, a northbound Iryo train derailed, two of its cars falling onto the opposite track, and a southbound Renfe train slammed into the carriages seconds later. An official report on what caused that lethal accident has not been released, but preliminary investigations pointed to a broken rail as the likely cause.

A detailed account: In a news conference, Spain’s transportation minister described the events that he said preceded Wednesday’s crash. Read more ›

José Bautista contributed reporting from the scene of the crash.

World.title: Rivals in Israel Election Strike Tone of Triumph, but Outcome Is Far From Clear
World.content:
Shira Shapiro, right, a candidate for the Yashar party, meeting with Gadi Eisenkot at a roadside bomb shelter where her son died during the Oct. 7 2023, attack, near Reim, Israel, earlier this month.

Several people whose relatives were killed or taken hostage in the Hamas-led attack on Israel on Oct. 7, 2023, are running for office in Tuesday’s election, the first national vote since the assault, which shook the country’s foundations and ignited its longest war.

The October 2023 assault looms large over this week’s vote. There are sharp divisions over who was to blame for failing to prevent the worst military, intelligence and policy disaster in Israel’s history.

About 1,200 civilians and soldiers were killed that day, according to the Israeli authorities, and roughly 250 were taken hostage to Gaza. Many of the family members of hostages held by Hamas rose to prominence as they campaigned for their loved ones in television interviews and at nationwide protests.

Most of them called for Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to take responsibility for the government’s failures of Oct. 7 and to prioritize negotiating the release of the hostages over continued fighting. Others supported Mr. Netanyahu’s right-wing government and urged it to keep up the military pressure on Hamas and Israel’s other enemies.

Parties from across Israel’s political spectrum have recruited candidates from what have become known as the Oct. 7 families. Here are some of the candidates with a chance to win a seat in Parliament:

Shira Shapiro is running with Yashar, the centrist party led by Mr. Netanyahu’s main political rival, Gadi Eisenkot. Ms. Shapiro’s son, Staff Sgt. Aner Shapiro, was on leave from the army on Oct. 7 when he attended the Nova music festival, one of the bloodiest targets of the Hamas-led attack. He took shelter in a crowded roadside bomb shelter and stationed himself by the entrance when gunmen attacked it. As the militants hurled grenades inside, Sergeant Shapiro repeatedly caught the grenades and threw them back out, until he was killed, according to surviving witnesses.

Zvi Mor, the father of a released hostage, Eitan Mor, is running as a candidate for the far-right party Religious Zionism, headed by Bezalel Smotrich. World.title: Israel’s opposition may not be able to form a government, but it still could control Parliament.
World.content:
news analysis

The results of Israel’s pivotal parliamentary election will not be finalized at least until Thursday and it could be weeks until it is clear what kind of government will be formed and who will lead it. But some conclusions are already inescapable.

Arab citizens of Israel turned out to vote in record numbers. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud party gobbled up many votes that his right-wing and Orthodox Jewish coalition partners had expected would be theirs. And the pre-election polls failed to anticipate both phenomena.

Much could still change. But with most of the votes counted by Wednesday afternoon, here are some initial takeaways.

Netanyahu didn’t win, but Eisenkot lost.

Mr. Netanyahu’s coalition appears to have shrunk considerably from the 64 parliamentary seats that it won in 2022: The latest results show it with around 54, well short of a majority in the 120-member Knesset, or Parliament. But he could wind up in better position to form a government than his chief rival, Gadi Eisenkot.

Mr. Eisenkot, a former Israeli military chief of staff, had two goals in the election: to lead the Jewish opposition parties to an outright majority or at least get very close to one, and to make sure his own party, Yashar, got more votes than any other. He failed on both counts, the initial results indicate.

Reuven Hazan, a political science professor at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem, said that it had been hard to imagine better conditions for Mr. Eisenkot’s alliance ahead of the election. Mr. Netanyahu and his coalition were weighed down by anger over the Hamas-led Oct. 7, 2023 attacks and their failure to do more to free Israeli hostages; by anger over ultra-Orthodox Jewish draft-dodging in wartime; and by outrage over the government’s efforts to neuter the judiciary and allow growing settler violence against Palestinians in the Israeli-occupied West Bank, he said.

“The anti-Netanyahu camp had an election handed to them on a silver platter, and they still lost,” Mr. Hazan said. “Israelis have sent an ambiguous message: ‘We don’t really like the current government, but we don’t see a viable alternative.’”

Netanyahu’s coalition shrank, but he has options.

As votes were being counted on Wednesday afternoon, Likud was poised to be the largest party in the larger of the two blocs of Jewish-led parties, meaning Mr. Netanyahu could well be given the chance to form a government, Mr. Hazan said.

The long-serving Israeli premier may try to peel away some of Mr. Eisenkot’s putative partners in order to achieve a majority of 61 seats in Parliament. A number of them are as right-wing as he is, though all have more or less ruled out entering a Netanyahu-led government.

He could also try to form a national unity government with Mr. Eisenkot — perhaps with the assistance of President Trump, who has praised Mr. Netanyahu as a “warrior prime minister” and has made clear he wants Israel to join the United States in another round of war against Iran.

Perhaps the most mind-bending option available to Mr. Netanyahu, given that he ran a scaremongering campaign that demonized Arab lawmakers and stoked fears of Arab voter turnout, would be to recruit an Arab party to join him in a government. He nearly did so once before, in 2022.

“It could very well be that they become indispensable,” said Dahlia Scheindlin, a pollster and political analyst, said of Arab lawmakers. “And Netanyahu has certainly demonstrated his willingness to do anything to stay in power.”

The liberal camp still has a shot.

Speaking of Jewish opposition parties in isolation ignores the fact that, when Arab parties are included, Mr. Netanyahu’s rivals appeared headed toward a significant majority in Parliament, with about 66 seats to roughly 54 for the prime minister’s bloc.

“There is no need to go with the racist assumption that you need not count the Arabs,” said Gayil Talshir, a political scientist at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem who is advising the opposition.

That means the Knesset in effect will be controlled by the anti-Netanyahu opposition, regardless of who ends up being prime minister. If the vote breakdown roughly holds, Ms. Talshir said she expected Mr. Eisenkot and his Jewish and Arab allies to elect a new parliamentary speaker, begin repealing unpopular laws and at least try to form a government — perhaps including some combination of Arab and ultra-Orthodox lawmakers.

“I’m not saying it’s a good scenario to take the Knesset and not be able to form the government,” Ms. Talshir said. “It’s a disaster. But this is the hand they’re dealt, and they have to play it.”

Arab voters broke records but could face rejection.

Tuesday’s election appears to have had many losers. Mr. Netanyahu’s support shrank and Mr. Eisenkot came up short of his goal. The ultra-Orthodox parties were projected to lose seats, according to the latest returns, and two right-wing nationalist parties failed to make gains, despite four years in which they drove the Netanyahu government’s extreme policies in the West Bank.

The biggest ostensible winners were the Arab voters who voted in record numbers. But they could well wind up the most disappointed citizens of all, if the Jewish opposition leaders prove unwilling or unable to form a majority in an alliance with the Arab parties.

“They’re saying, ‘We believe in Israeli democracy, we believe in the system, we want to be part of the system, and we want to be treated better,’” Mr. Hazan said. “And if Netanyahu forms a government, they’ll get none of that.”

World.title: The crash comes months after a fatal accident involving the same train operators.
World.content:
Pinned

A high-speed passenger train rear-ended another in Spain on Wednesday morning near the central city of Toledo, killing at least 68 people and injuring dozens more, officials said, in one of the deadliest train crashes in Spanish history.

The accident happened after traffic control operators told a high-speed train to continue its journey when another train was stopped farther along the tracks, Spain’s transportation minister, Óscar Puente, said. He called the operators’ instruction “inexplicable.”

The deadly crash was the second this year involving the same two rail operators; the first, in January, killed 46 people. The latest accident, and its timing months after the previous crash, was likely to deepen doubts about the security of Spain’s once-vaunted rail system.

In Spanish news reports, passengers described an awful impact that tossed people from a dining car, broke limbs and piled passengers atop one another. People crawled out of windows and others were carried by fellow passengers into a nearby field on makeshift stretchers. Local workers, who had heard the crash, rushed to help and guide survivors to safety.

The crash came about a month ahead of national election in Spain, and it had the potential to become an issue in an already bitter campaign about the competence of the left-wing government of Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez.

Spain’s rail authority, the Adif, said the trains involved were a “Renfe train and another from the Iryo company,” both covering the route between Madrid, the capital, and the southern city of Seville. Renfe is the national rail provider.

Mr. Sánchez visited the scene of the crash, saying that Spanish rail’s security systems clearly needed to be reinforced. “If there has been negligence, it will come to light,” he said. “If there have been failures in the safety system, we will respond with the utmost firmness.” He declared three days of official mourning.

The conservative opposition leader, Alberto Núñez Feijóo, voiced his own concern.

“I am very concerned about the information we are receiving regarding another train accident,” he wrote on social media soon after the crash. “The priority now is to assist the victims and support their families. My full support goes to the emergency teams working on the ground.” His Popular Party canceled all its campaign events around the country.

Here’s what else to know:

Survivor speaks: A passenger on one of the trains described a routine trip, a sudden jolt and an effort to tend to the dead and injured. Read more ›

An earlier deadly crash: In January, a northbound Iryo train derailed, two of its cars falling onto the opposite track, and a southbound Renfe train slammed into the carriages seconds later. An official report on what caused that lethal accident has not been released, but preliminary investigations pointed to a broken rail as the likely cause.

A detailed account: In a news conference, Spain’s transportation minister described the events that he said preceded Wednesday’s crash. Read more ›

José Bautista contributed reporting from the scene of the crash.

World.title: Twice before, Netanyahu was ousted then returned to power.
World.content:
Shira Shapiro, right, a candidate for the Yashar party, meeting with Gadi Eisenkot at a roadside bomb shelter where her son died during the Oct. 7 2023, attack, near Reim, Israel, earlier this month.

Several people whose relatives were killed or taken hostage in the Hamas-led attack on Israel on Oct. 7, 2023, are running for office in Tuesday’s election, the first national vote since the assault, which shook the country’s foundations and ignited its longest war.

The October 2023 assault looms large over this week’s vote. There are sharp divisions over who was to blame for failing to prevent the worst military, intelligence and policy disaster in Israel’s history.

About 1,200 civilians and soldiers were killed that day, according to the Israeli authorities, and roughly 250 were taken hostage to Gaza. Many of the family members of hostages held by Hamas rose to prominence as they campaigned for their loved ones in television interviews and at nationwide protests.

Most of them called for Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to take responsibility for the government’s failures of Oct. 7 and to prioritize negotiating the release of the hostages over continued fighting. Others supported Mr. Netanyahu’s right-wing government and urged it to keep up the military pressure on Hamas and Israel’s other enemies.

Parties from across Israel’s political spectrum have recruited candidates from what have become known as the Oct. 7 families. Here are some of the candidates with a chance to win a seat in Parliament:

Shira Shapiro is running with Yashar, the centrist party led by Mr. Netanyahu’s main political rival, Gadi Eisenkot. Ms. Shapiro’s son, Staff Sgt. Aner Shapiro, was on leave from the army on Oct. 7 when he attended the Nova music festival, one of the bloodiest targets of the Hamas-led attack. He took shelter in a crowded roadside bomb shelter and stationed himself by the entrance when gunmen attacked it. As the militants hurled grenades inside, Sergeant Shapiro repeatedly caught the grenades and threw them back out, until he was killed, according to surviving witnesses.

Zvi Mor, the father of a released hostage, Eitan Mor, is running as a candidate for the far-right party Religious Zionism, headed by Bezalel Smotrich. While Eitan was in captivity, Mr. Mor, an educator, founded a forum of right-wing parents of hostages and soldiers who opposed making deals with Hamas and pushed for Israel to defeat the group militarily.

Omri Ronen, a reserve soldier, is running with the left-wing Democrats, led by Yair Golan. His grandmother, Nira Ronen, was killed in her home in Kfar Aza, one of the border communities worst hit in the October 2023 attack, along with her Filipina caregiver, Angelyn Aguirre. Before Oct. 7, Mr. Ronen had been one of the leaders of a grass-roots group of reservists protesting the government’s plan to overhaul the judiciary. He said in a recent television interview that Mr. Netanyahu, whom he called “Mr. Oct. 7,” must go. “The word responsibility has meaning,” he said.

Rafael Ben Shitrit, a former mayor of Beit Shean in northern Israel, is in Yisrael Beitenu, a right-wing opposition party led by Avigdor Liberman. Mr. Ben Shitrit used to belong to Mr. Netanyahu’s conservative Likud party, but abandoned it after his son, Staff Sgt. Elroy Ben Shitrit, was killed in battle on Oct. 7 near the Gaza border. He has been an advocate for an independent state inquiry into what went wrong that day. Mr. Netanyahu has refused such an inquiry, and the opposition parties have pledged to establish one if they are elected.

Sharon Sharabi, also on Yisrael Beitenu’s list of candidates, is the brother of Eli Sharabi, a former hostage who was released from Gaza only to learn that his wife and two teenage daughters had been killed during the Oct. 7 attack. Another brother, Yossi Sharabi, was also taken hostage and killed after 100 days in captivity. Sharon Sharabi campaigned tirelessly for his brothers’ return. When Eli Sharabi was finally released, many Israelis were outraged over how emaciated he looked. “I was shocked,” Sharon said at the time. “I’d been told he would be thin, but I didn’t imagine how thin. It was extreme.”

Tali Gvili, running with Mr. Netanyahu’s Likud party, is the mother of Master Sgt. Ran Gvili, a member of a police counterterrorism unit who was shot and severely wounded in combat on Oct. 7 and then dragged into Gaza. His remains were recovered and returned to Israel in January 2026. The Gvili and Netanyahu families have become close, and the prime minister attended Sergeant Gvili’s state funeral, saying, “Our souls are bound with yours.”

World.title: Flávio Bolsonaro lands in Miami after defeat in Brazil's presidential election
World.content:
Brazilian Senator FlÃ¡vio Bolsonaro has flown to Miami after losing the country's presidential election on Sunday.

His arrival in Florida ends days of confusion over his whereabouts, after he was reported to have travelled to Argentina, and then prematurely reported to have already entered the US on Tuesday.

The US has said it would grant visas to Bolsonaro and his family, who travelled with him. Brazil cancelled his passport, after he failed to surrender it to authorities, due to an ongoing criminal investigation. He has denied any wrongdoing.

Newly reelected President Luiz InÃ¡cio Lula da Silva has criticised the departure, saying "those who have nothing to hide have nothing to fear".

Speculation about Bolsonaro's whereabouts was first triggered by a report on an Argentine news site, which claimed that he had crossed the land border between Brazil and Argentina and then boarded a private plane en route to the US.

Brazilian police took the rumours seriously. Early on Tuesday, they checked border crossings but found no evidence that Bolsonaro had left the country, and Argentine officials said they had no reports of him crossing.

For a little while, it seemed like Bolsonaro may just be keeping an uncharacteristically low profile after being unexpectedly beaten by his left-wing rival in the presidential run-off vote on Sunday.

When he failed to surrender his passports in time to meet a 24-hour deadline, Brazilian authorities cancelled the documents and ordered police to make checks at border posts.

With Bolsonaro's lawyers saying they did not know where he was, speculation quickly grew again that he might have left the country.

World.title: Netanyahu's bloc leading Israel election but short of majority, partial results show
World.content:
Partial results from Israel's general election show veteran Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is leading his rival, former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, but is still short of a majority in parliament.

With 85% of ballots counted, Netanyahu's Likud party and its far-right and ultra-Orthodox Jewish allies were on track to win 53 seats in the 120-seat Knesset. Eisenkot's Yashar party and three other Jewish opposition parties in his bloc were set for 48.

Both leaders have said they will try to form a governing coalition.

Arab-led parties, who are on course to win an unprecedented 19 seats, could emerge as kingmakers, but all but one of the Jewish parties have pledged not to work with them.

With between 430,000 and 480,000 absentee ballots from soldiers and diplomats yet to be counted, it could still take a day or two for the final election results to emerge.

Once they are confirmed, President Isaac Herzog will hold consultations with all the political factions and invite the leader whom he believes has the best chance of success to form a government - a process that could take weeks.

If they fail, then ultimately there would have to be another election.

World.title: How could Israel break election deadlock? Here are four scenarios
World.content:
Could Netanyahu persuade Eisenkot to join him in a national unity government?

Eisenkot would have to abandon his key platform to do so. He's framed himself as the only alternative to Netanyahu, and built his campaign on ousting him from power.

Just last night, he took to the stage at his campaign HQ and called on Netanyahu to "announce his retirement from political life today," telling the crowd that Israelis are fed up with Netanyahu's "culture of lies", "division and incitement".

But that was before one of the main exit polls - which had initially projected a lead for Eisenkot's bloc - was revised, and he was overtaken by Netanyahu.

Netanyahu could try to persuade Eisenkot's Yashar Party to join his Likud Party in a unity government by ditching the far-right and ultra-Orthodox parties he is currently in coalition with. But last night at Likud HQ he thanked his "loyal partners" and called for a "strong right-wing government" - remarks some have interpreted as meaning he intends to preserve his alliance with them.

One thing that could make a unity government more likely is a renewed conflict with Iran, which could place serious pressure on party leaders to put aside their political differences and work together. In the days prior to the election, Israeli and US media reported that Netanyahu was pushing for fresh strikes on the country, and had pressed Donald Trump to approve US involvement.

This would no-doubt be framed by Netanyahu's critics as an attempt to save his own political skin by entering another regional conflict.

World.title: Luxury cruise passengers stranded in Cambodia due to soaring fuel costs
World.content:
A luxury cruise ship on a years-long voyage around the world said it suspended operations due to extraordinarily high fuel costs, leaving passengers stranded in Cambodia.

The US-based operator of the Villa Vie Odyssey said it was working with passengers on disembarkation plans and "temporary living arrangements".

It is unclear how many were on board but the nearly 200m (656ft) vessel can carry up to 650 passengers. It departed Belfast in October 2024 for a "continuous voyage around the world".

Global fuel prices have soared since the Iran war started earlier this year. The ship's operator said the monthly fuel cost per cabin in parts of Asia has risen to as much as $8,000 (Â£6,000) from $1,800.

Villa Vie Residences said it had taken "significant steps to reduce fuel consumption, including slowing the itinerary and spending more time in port". But those measures turned out to be insufficient to "offset the extraordinary increase in fuel costs".

"Passing the full increase on to residents is not a realistic solution," it said.

The company would spend the next 60 days on "restructuring and recapitalisation", though "no outcome is assured", it said.

There were reportedly around 200 passengers on board when they were ordered to disembark in the Cambodian port city of Sihanoukville, a once sleepy beach town that has gained global notoriety in recent years as a hub for Chinese casinos and scam centres.

The Villa Vie Odyssey's voyage was expected to span 3.5 years and cover nearly 150 countries, according to its website.

Its departure had faced delays as the ship underwent repairs, leaving passengers stranded in Belfast for months and costing the company millions of pounds.

The ship was more than 750 days into its circumnavigation before announcing its suspension of its journey on Tuesday - which means its passengers would now be stranded in Cambodia.

Passengers Lanette Canen and Johan Bodin told the BBC they were informed by Villa Vie Residences' chief executive at 6am on Tuesday that they had to leave by 2pm on the same day.

The couple said passengers had known for some time about the company's financial difficulties. A potential investor had previously come onboard the ship to do due dilligence, but in the end it did not work out.

"Even then, we were still hoping a miracle investor would come through," they said. "Although there were signs that this would happen, we still felt disbelief when it became real. We were heartbroken. It felt like our dream had been crushed."

"There have been a lot of hugs and tears as residents support one another and process what has happened."

Another passenger Holly Hennessey said that the ship's passengers had earlier been asked to consider paying a fuel surcharge as global prices soared, and that their itinerary had been "severely curtailed".

Some people decided to disembark and travel on land, she said.

"It was not on my bingo card of places where I'd be spending a lot of time," Hennessey told the BBC from Cambodia.

"We're all in different hotels; there are a number of shipmates in the hotel that I'm in. We're just waiting."

Canen and Bodin said the location in Cambodia was "a difficult place to disembark" because of the distance to a major international airport.

World.title: Serbian shot dead after attacking officer outside Israeli embassy, minister says
World.content:
Serbian police shot dead a young man outside the Israeli embassy in Belgrade in the early hours of Wednesday after what authorities called a "terrorist attack".

The country's interior minister, Ivica Dacic, said the attacker had rushed at a police officer with two knives while shouting the phrase "Allahu Akbar". The officer sustained a minor knife wound to the face and shot the attacker.

Dacic said the suspect has not been identified, but he was a minor and Serbian citizen who was being monitored by security services as he was "known to be a supporter of the Islamic State".

Speaking to reporters outside the embassy, Dacic said an investigation is ongoing, but security services said the suspect had posted a picture of the Islamic State flag on his Instagram.

Dacic raised the country's terrorism threat level to "red alert" - the highest threat level â meaning stricter security checks and increased police presence at places like infrastructure facilities and areas where large crowds gather.

The interior minister said he had visited the injured police officer, who was reportedly doing well and did not need hospital care for his wounds.

Armed security personnel were seen standing guard outside the Israeli embassy on Wednesday morning.

Israel's foreign ministry confirmed in a social media post that no embassy personnel were injured and the mission was closed at the time of the incident.

This is the second such attack on Belgrade's Israeli embassy in less than three years; in June 2024, a man shot a police officer in the neck with a crossbow.

The officer who was shot survived the attack and shot dead the assailant, identified as a Serbian man who had converted to Islam.

Wednesday's attack comes just one day after elections in Israel.

World.title: Tanzania celebrates first natural gas discovery in more than 10 years
World.content:
Tanzania has announced a significant discovery of natural gas in the Mnazi Bay area in the south of the country - the first such find in a decade.

Energy Minister Juma Homera attended a ceremony at the Kasa-1X ST2 well, which is jointly owned by state-owned Tanzania Petroleum Development Corporation (TPDC) and French oil firm Maurel & Prom, to mark the occasion.

He said the estimated 223 billion cubic feet (6.3 billion cubic metres) discovery was a "major milestone" in the development of the small oil and gas sector in the East African nation.

The new well is expected to start production early next month and is intended to boost domestic supplies.

Tanzania has existing natural gas reserves of 57.54 trillion cubic feet.

World.title: Anger in Kenya over extradition hearing delay for ex-British soldier accused of murdering woman
World.content:
Wanjiru's niece, Esther Njoki, told the BBC that the family had learnt of the postponement through the UK embassy and had received no official explanation.

"We have exercised patience and endured uncertainty for years, but our patience is now being taken advantage of," she said in a statement.

"Agnes deserves justice. Her daughter Stacy deserves answers about what happened. And as a family, we deserve to be treated with dignity and kept informed about proceedings that profoundly affect our lives."

The family said it had already raised money and made arrangements to travel to the UK for the hearing, which was due to take place in three weeks.

It is now calling on the authorities to expedite the proceedings, warning that the latest postponement means the case will enter its 15th year without a trial.

The family said a UK court was expected next week to give the reasons for the hearing delay.

Wanjiru disappeared in March 2012 after spending an evening at a hotel in Nanyuki, about 200km (124 miles) north of the capital, Nairobi, where British soldiers were stationed for training.

Her body was found nearly three months later in a septic tank at the hotel. She had suffered stab wounds to her chest and abdomen and left behind a five-month-old daughter.

A Kenyan inquest concluded in 2019 that she had been unlawfully killed by one or two British soldiers.

In September 2025, a Kenyan High Court issued an arrest warrant for a British national after prosecutors presented evidence they said justified bringing murder charges.

Purkiss' lawyers said he intended to contest his extradition to Kenya.

He appeared at Westminster Magistrates' Court in February via video link, where he was further remanded in custody.

Last year, the then British Defence Secretary John Healey met Wanjiru's family during a visit to Kenya and pledged his government's support for efforts to secure justice.

The UK government has previously said it remains committed to helping the family, but would not comment on ongoing legal proceedings.

World.title: Ceasefire extended across Ukraine's Kherson region, officials say
World.content:
A ceasefire that began with the aim of getting food and medicine to the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky has been extended across the wider southern region of Kherson, according to sources.

Several thousand residents are trapped in the city with no access to food, water and electricity. On one side is the Dnipro river, while Russian forces are on the other and all the roads out are too dangerous.

However, no breaches of the truce that began early on Tuesday have so far been reported.

US First Lady Melania Trump, who helped broker the ceasefire along with Pope Leo XIV, said on Tuesday that the area involved had been expanded to provide "safe passage" for humanitarian convoys.

World.title: Tinubu set to depart for Makkah
World.content:
President Bola Tinubu will depart Abuja on Thursday for Makkah, Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, to perform Umrah, an Islamic spiritual exercise involving a pilgrimage to the Holy City.

The visit gives the president an opportunity for spiritual reflection, devotion, and prayers for Nigeria’s peace, unity, stability, and continued progress.

While in Makkah, President Tinubu will perform the religious rites associated with Umrah, seeking Allah’s guidance and blessings for Nigeria and its people.

Before leaving Abuja, President Tinubu will commission at the Presidential Wing of the Nnamdi Azikiwe Airport some equipment acquired by the Nigerian Air Force for its operations.

The president is expected back in the country next week, after completing the spiritual exercise.

Bayo Onanuga

Special Adviser to the President
