World.title: No deal to split Osun legislative seats with APC – Adeleke
World.content:
Osun State Governor Ademola Adeleke

By Shina Abubakar

Osun State Governor Ademola Adeleke has disclosed that he has no agreement to split legislative seats with the APC, insisting that his agreement with the party is to deliver President Bola Tinubu victory in next year’s presidential election.

The governor, in a statement by his spokesperson Olawale Rasheed on Wednesday, said the insinuation that he has an agreement with the APC to share local government and legislative seats is not correct.

The governor, who reaffirmed his commitment to the re-election of President Tinubu, said the negotiation for the resolution of the local government crisis targets protection of the interests of both the APC chairpersons and those of the elected PDP chairmen and councillors, adding that reports of office sharing are “mere fabrication”.

“As the governor of all Osun indigenes and residents, we are working to resolve the local government matter by ensuring that all interests are protected and cared for. As at now, all stakeholders agreed that restoring grassroots governance is a condition for our successful campaign ahead of the 2027 elections,” the statement added.

While assuring that the local government crisis will be resolved before the end of the year, the governor submitted that he did not enter into any agreement to share legislative seats with Osun APC.

“As I said while inaugurating the Presidential Campaign Council, the coalition is targeted at the presidential election. Partners agreed to join hands to ensure our dear president is re-elected. All other legislative positions are open for competition. I will work and campaign for Accord candidates for Senate, House of Representatives and the State House of Assembly,” the statement added.

World.title: Moonshot 2026: Day 1 highlights as tech leaders, founders gather in Lagos [Photos]
World.content:
Moonshot 2026: Courage & Conviction kicked off in Lagos on Wednesday, bringing together technology leaders, startup founders, investors, policymakers and innovators to discuss the future of Africa’s digital economy.

The first day featured discussions on startup growth, fintech and banking, financial discipline, digital safety, privacy and the rights of technology users among others.

Speakers at the Startup Stage explored the challenges of building sustainable businesses, emphasising the importance of sound financial management, effective systems and the right teams.

The conversations also highlighted the need for technology companies to prioritise user protection alongside innovation, with TechHerNG Executive Director Chioma Agwuegbo warning against digital platforms that overlook the safety and rights of women, children and other vulnerable users.

Beyond the panel sessions, the event provided opportunities for networking, knowledge-sharing and connections among entrepreneurs, investors and other stakeholders shaping Africa’s technology ecosystem.

World.title: $21.7bn external borrowing plan is investment, not debt – Oyedele
World.content:
Taiwo Oyedele

By Johnbosco Agbakwuru

The Federal Government has put a strong defence to its proposed $21.7 billion external borrowing plan, describing it as a long-term investment in infrastructure, human capital and economic growth rather than an additional debt burden.

The Minister of Finance and Coordinating Minister of the Economy, Taiwo Oyedele, made the clarification while briefing State House correspondents at the end of the Federal Executive Council, FEC meeting, presided over by President Bola Tinubu at the Council Chamber, presidential villa, Abuja.

He said the five-year project financing plan was designed to create productive assets whose long-term economic value would outweigh the cost of borrowing.

Presenting the highlights of the Federal Executive Council (FEC) meeting, Oyedele said the plan covered critical investments in transportation, defence and security, health, agriculture, energy, digital infrastructure, small businesses, social protection, environmental protection and education.

He disclosed that about $10.6 billion had been earmarked for transportation infrastructure, including major highway projects such as the Sokoto-Badagry and Lagos-Calabar coastal highways, as well as the Kano-Kaduna Metro Rail project.

The minister, however, clarified that the proposal was a financing plan submitted to the National Assembly and did not mean the entire amount had already been borrowed or would necessarily be drawn down in full.

According to him, the Federal Government was acting as the coordinating authority for external financing covering federal, state and other public-sector projects.

He said approximately $4.8 billion of the proposed financing was allocated to projects involving state governments, the Federal Capital Territory and other subnational entities, agencies and development finance institutions.

Oyedele said about $7.9 billion would come from multilateral and bilateral development partners, including $5 billion from the World Bank at concessional rates averaging 2.1 per cent.

He added that the indicative average interest rate on the commercial component was 7.8 per cent, which he said was below the rate on Nigeria’s November 2025 Eurobond.

The minister argued that borrowing could strengthen the country’s balance sheet if the resulting investments generated assets and economic benefits exceeding their financing costs.

Using the Dangote Refinery as an illustration, he said large-scale projects often required external financing to be completed within a reasonable period, adding that Nigeria needed to adopt a similar approach to transformative infrastructure.

On the state of the economy, Oyedele said Nigeria’s economic indicators had improved since President Bola Tinubu introduced major reforms in May 2023, although he acknowledged that significant challenges remained.

He recalled that inflation stood at 22.41 per cent when the reforms began, while the country’s net foreign reserves were estimated at $859 million, insufficient to cover a month of imports.

He also cited multiple foreign exchange rates, a premium of more than 60 per cent between official and parallel-market rates, and debt-service costs consuming about 97 per cent of government revenue as evidence of the pressures facing the economy.

According to him, the government had been forced to address structural weaknesses that threatened economic stability, arguing that failure to implement the reforms could have resulted in runaway inflation and a further collapse of the naira.

Oyedele said economic growth had risen from 2.74 per cent in 2023 to 4.43 per cent in the second quarter of 2026, while inflation declined to 14.63 per cent in September from 20.98 per cent a year earlier.

He also reported that foreign reserves had risen to more than $55 billion, with net reserves exceeding $45 billion, compared with less than $1 billion three years earlier.

The minister said the naira had stabilised within the range of N1,330 to N1,350 to the dollar, adding that the International Monetary Fund had estimated that the currency was undervalued by about 25 per cent.

He further stated that the tax-to-GDP ratio had risen from approximately seven per cent in 2023 to 12.5 per cent by the end of 2025, while the debt-service-to-revenue ratio had fallen from about 97 per cent to below 60 per cent.

Federation Account revenue, he added, increased by 44 per cent between 2024 and 2025, with the government projecting growth of at least 50 per cent in 2026.

Oyedele said international confidence had also improved, citing credit-rating upgrades and positive outlooks from rating agencies, as well as Nigeria’s exit from the Financial Action Task Force’s grey list and the European Union’s list of high-risk jurisdictions.

The minister said the government’s economic programme had also provided direct support to households, students and businesses.

He disclosed that more than N372.6 billion had been disbursed through the Nigerian Education Loan Fund (NELFUND) to over 1.5 million students, while more than 10 million households had received cash transfers worth over N600 billion.

The government, he said, was targeting at least 15 million beneficiary households under the cash-transfer programme.

Oyedele added that more than 800,000 micro, small and medium-sized enterprises had accessed subsidised single-digit-interest loans, largely through the Bank of Industry.

Under the tax reforms, he said, low-income earners making up to N100,000 monthly had been exempted from personal income tax, while small businesses with annual turnover of not more than N100 million had been exempted from corporate income tax, value-added tax collection and withholding-tax obligations, subject to the applicable provisions of the law.

He also cited the expansion of the Nigerian capital market, whose value he said had risen from about N30 trillion to more than N160 trillion in three years, as evidence of growing investment activity and wealth creation.

Despite the improvements, Oyedele said FEC recognised the need to address the high cost of living, particularly food prices, and agreed to intensify efforts to improve living standards.

He said the council adopted a target of reducing inflation to single digits by the end of 2027 or earlier, while prioritising food-price stability, critical infrastructure, human-capital development and job creation.

The council also endorsed the National Economic Council’s 90-day action plan aimed at easing the cost of living through coordinated action by federal, state and local governments.

On other FEC decisions, Oyedele disclosed that the council considered 10 memoranda presented by his ministry, including financing arrangements for electricity transmission, railway infrastructure, road development and customs modernisation.

He said a €155.9 million credit facility arranged through Deutsche Bank and other lenders would support five substations and associated transmission infrastructure under Phase One of the Presidential Power Initiative.

The intervention, he said, was intended to improve electricity reliability for households and businesses while helping to reduce energy costs.

The council also considered a $970 million syndicated term loan arranged by Standard Chartered and the Africa Finance Corporation for rolling stock on the Kano-Maradi railway line.

According to the minister, the railway investment was expected to reduce freight costs, facilitate regional trade and improve logistics along the northern economic corridor.

Another €76.8 million facility from the ECOWAS Bank for Investment and Development was approved for Bauchi State’s transport infrastructure development programme, including rural and urban roads and routes linking farms to markets.

Oyedele said FEC also approved investment in non-intrusive inspection scanners, alongside technical support, repairs and maintenance for the Nigeria Customs Service, to accelerate cargo clearance, combat smuggling and improve the detection of prohibited goods and dangerous weapons.

He said the government remained committed to fiscal discipline and investment in infrastructure and social development, arguing that the success of the borrowing programme would ultimately depend on the value delivered by the projects and their benefits to Nigerians.

World.title: FG approves East, West super grids to raise transmission capacity to 19,000MW
World.content:
Tegbe

‎

‎By Johnbosco Agbakwuru

‎

‎The Federal Government on Wednesday said it has approved the commencement of procurement for the proposed East and West Super Grids as part of efforts to strengthen the national electricity network and raise transmission capacity from about 5,000 megawatts to 19,000MW within two years.

‎

‎The Minister of Power, Joseph Tegbe, disclosed this while briefing State House correspondents at the end of the Federal Executive Council, FEC, meeting presided over by President Bola Tinubu, at the Council Chamber, Presidential Villa, Abuja.

‎

‎The Minister explained that the projects would improve grid resilience and enable the country to evacuate more electricity to consumers.

“The East and West Super Grids are not projects for one part of the country,” Tegbe said. “They cut across the north and south of Nigeria, strengthening the backbone that must carry power from where it is generated to where it is needed.”

The initiative is designed to address one of the sector’s central contradictions: Nigeria has more than 13,000MW of available generation capacity, but its transmission network can reliably wheel only about 5,000MW.

Tegbe said the super grids would improve resilience, reduce grid instability and allow more electricity to reach homes, businesses and industries.

“The target is simple,” he said. “We want a grid that can evacuate the power we already have, not one that leaves generation stranded while consumers remain in darkness.”

The Minister explained that the corridors would strengthen transmission links from Sokoto through Abuja and other locations into parts of southern Nigeria.

Beyond the super grids, the council approved three immediate interventions for Abuja and the Lagos axis, two of the country’s most important electricity demand centres.

The first is a 33kV double-circuit underground and overhead line connected to the Katampe Transmission Substation, a major hub serving the North-Central region.

The second covers the design, manufacture and supply of three 300MVA, 330/132/33kV transformers for the Ikeja West Transmission Substation, a critical node supplying Lagos.

The third will reconstruct and upgrade the 35.6-kilometre Itumola–Mapasin–Shagamu 132kV single-circuit line into a double-circuit line to serve rising demand along the Lagos–Shagamu corridor.

“These are not glamorous projects, but they are the projects that determine whether power actually gets to the consumer,” Tegbe said.

He added that the high-capacity transformers would have to be manufactured abroad because Nigeria does not yet have the domestic capacity to produce equipment of that specification.

“Some companies have started assembling transformers locally, but these large units require specialised manufacturing,” he said. “They can take between three and six months to produce, and global demand is rising because of artificial intelligence and data centres.”

The ministry has also begun a nationwide technical audit of electricity infrastructure, dividing the country into three major energy zones: Lagos and its industrial corridor, Abuja–Kaduna–Kano, and Enugu–Onitsha–Benin.

Tegbe said the audit, ongoing for four weeks, would identify ageing and weak assets that require replacement or rehabilitation.

“We will no longer spend money on the wrong projects,” he said. “The audit will show us exactly where the system is failing and where investment will deliver measurable impact.”

The government is prioritising the Lagos–Ogun, Benin–Edo–Port Harcourt and Abuja–Kaduna–Kano corridors, with the Lagos–Ogun corridor alone accounting for about half of national energy demand.

On sector liquidity, Tegbe disclosed that the Federal Government had paid N1.23 trillion of the N3.3 trillion owed to gas suppliers and other power-sector stakeholders.

He said the outstanding liabilities had constrained gas supply to generation companies and weakened confidence across the electricity value chain.

“We have paid N1.23 trillion, and we intend to finish the job,” Tegbe said. “But we must also stop new debts from accumulating.”

The payment was made through bonds under the Presidential Power Sector Debt Reduction Programme, which is intended to improve liquidity for generation companies, support gas supply and restore investor confidence.

Tegbe said the government was also reviewing the electricity market structure to strengthen payment discipline and reduce the risk of fresh arrears.

Stranded equipment ordered cleared

The President has also directed the Ministry of Power, Nigerian Ports Authority and Nigeria Customs Service to clear more than 300 containers of stranded electricity equipment at the nation’s ports.

Tegbe described the backlog as unacceptable, noting that some containers had reportedly remained uncleared for between 14 and 20 years.

“It is unacceptable that equipment meant to strengthen the grid has been sitting at the ports for years,” he said. “The President has directed that this must be resolved.”

He attributed the delays to previous administrations’ failure to settle outstanding charges and complete clearance processes.

After clearance, technical experts will inspect the equipment to determine what remains serviceable and can be deployed, while obsolete materials will be appropriately disposed of.

Modern control centre, solar expansion

The government has also commenced construction of a new National Control Centre in Osogbo to replace the existing facility, which Tegbe said was built 64 years ago.

“The new control centre will give us modern tools to monitor and manage the national grid,” he said.

The ministry is also energising completed transmission substations in Kano, Katsina, Bauchi and Gombe, among other locations, to bring idle infrastructure into service.

In parallel, the government is expanding solar mini-grids for institutions facing transmission constraints. Fourteen federal universities have received installed and energised mini-grids of between 1MW and 5MW, while 11 more are being supported through TETFund.

Five teaching hospitals are also benefiting from solar installations being implemented with the Federal Ministry of Health.

Tegbe said the administration would continue to prioritise grid stability, infrastructure rehabilitation, improved liquidity and renewable energy investment.

“Our goal is not just to announce projects,” he said. “It is to build a power system that Nigerians can depend on.”

World.title: MDPCO warns against fresh $20.5bn foreign loan
World.content:
The Makinde-Daura Presidential Campaign Organisation (MDPCO) has criticised President Bola Tinubu’s plan to secure fresh foreign loans totalling about $20.5 billion and €1.04 billion, warning that continued borrowing could increase Nigeria’s debt burden and constrain future generations.

In a press statement dated October 28, 2026, signed by Richard Nnanna Ihediwa, Director of Strategic Communications MDPCO, the organisation said it opposed the proposed loans, which it put at ₦27.52 trillion and ₦1.558 trillion, respectively.

The statement, signed by its Director of Strategic Communications, Richard Nnanna Ihediwa, questioned the timing of the borrowing request ahead of the 2027 general election and demanded that the President withdraw it.

The organisation also urged the National Assembly to reject the request, arguing that the government had yet to demonstrate how previous loans had translated into commensurate development or present a credible plan for repaying the country’s accumulated debt.

The MDPCO cited a public debt figure of ₦166.7 trillion, claiming that further borrowing would place additional pressure on Nigerians, particularly younger generations.

It also questioned the government’s explanations that successive loans were needed to finance infrastructure, critical projects and budget deficits, asking for greater transparency over the utilisation of borrowed funds.

To support its position, the organisation listed several loans secured or approved during the Tinubu administration.

It cited a $750 million World Bank loan obtained in June 2023 under the Power Sector Recovery Performance programme, intended to improve electricity supply, and a separate $500 million loan for institutional strengthening and women’s empowerment.

The group also referred to an $800 million loan secured in July 2023 for conditional cash transfers, followed by another $700 million in September of that year.

It further cited a $2.25 billion loan obtained in June 2024 for economic stabilisation and transformation, as well as a $1.57 billion borrowing plan in 2025 for healthcare, education and human-capital development. The organisation also mentioned a separate $500 million loan from the African Development Bank in 2025.

The MDPCO questioned the impact of the loans, particularly on electricity supply, economic stability and household welfare, arguing that Nigerians had yet to see results commensurate with the scale of borrowing.

It also referenced a borrowing plan approved by the Senate in 2025 involving $21.19 billion, €4 billion and ¥15 billion. According to the organisation, the plan included $3 billion for the Eastern Railway Corridor linking Port Harcourt to Maiduguri, which it claimed had yet to record tangible progress.

The group also cited Senate approvals in April 2026 for $6 billion to modernise the country’s ports and another $1.5 billion for early-childhood development and household prosperity.

The organisation compared Nigeria’s borrowing trajectory with Egypt under Khedive Isma’il, who ruled from 1863 to 1879. It argued that Egypt’s dependence on foreign loans and extravagant spending contributed to a debt crisis that undermined the country’s financial independence.

The MDPCO called on Tinubu to withdraw the latest borrowing request and urged the National Assembly to act in what it described as the national interest.

“Nigeria is nobody’s personal fiefdom!” the organisation declared.

It also called on Nigerians to support the Allied People’s Movement (APM) presidential candidate, Engr. Seyi Makinde, whose RESET NIGERIA Agenda it said offered an alternative approach to economic management, national self-sufficiency and sustainable development.

The organisation said its proposed administration would focus on restructuring, economic opportunities and prosperity, contrasting its stated objectives with what it described as the Tinubu administration’s debt-dependent economic policies.

The claims and criticisms contained in the statement represent the position of the MDPCO.

World.title: Edo Reps Candidate, Paddy Iyamu, Pledges Legislative Protection for Vulnerable People
World.content:
Felix Omoh-Asun in Benin City

The All Progressives Congress (APC) candidate for Oredo Federal Constituency in the 2027 general election, Dr. Paddy Iyamu, has pledged to sponsor legislation to protect vulnerable people and promote good governance if elected into the House of Representatives.

Iyamu made the pledge when the Oredo APC chairman, Osamudiamen Osarenkhoe, led party leaders and candidates to the Edo State Council of the Nigeria Union of Journalists (NUJ) in Benin City to formally introduce the party’s standard-bearers to journalists.

The former Edo State Commissioner for Education said his legislative priorities would include education, healthcare, women’s empowerment and youth development.

He said his experience in public service had equipped him with the knowledge and contacts needed to attract development projects and deliver results for the people of Oredo Federal Constituency.

Citing his achievements as education commissioner, Iyamu said he facilitated the construction and inauguration of about 6.2 kilometres of internal roads at a state-owned polytechnic through engagements with relevant authorities in Abuja.

He said the experience had strengthened his resolve to use the platform of the National Assembly to attract federal projects and advance the interests of his constituents.

On education, the APC candidate described it as a critical tool for breaking the cycle of poverty, tackling insecurity and expanding opportunities for young people.

He said his administration as commissioner witnessed the reconstruction and remodelling of nearly 100 schools within one year, alongside improvements in classroom facilities and the provision of furniture for pupils.

Iyamu also said his administration began implementing aspects of the Safe School Initiative before the Federal Government’s intervention, adding that he would prioritise legislation and policies to make schools safer and more conducive to learning if elected.

According to him, quality education would equip children with the knowledge and skills to succeed regardless of their backgrounds.

On healthcare, the candidate promised to promote initiatives that would improve access to health services and support programmes aimed at improving the well-being of residents.

He also emphasised the need to empower women, saying that supporting women economically would have positive effects on families and communities.

Iyamu said his foundation had supported women through various initiatives, adding that he intended to expand such interventions if given the mandate.

On youth development, he said young people remained critical to societal progress and deserved opportunities to acquire relevant skills and build sustainable livelihoods.

He cited partnerships facilitated during his tenure as commissioner, including an agreement with Chinese counterparts that enabled some young people from Edo State to travel to China.

The APC candidate pledged to build on such initiatives by creating more opportunities for young people to develop their skills and become economically independent.

He said his ambition to represent Oredo Federal Constituency was driven by a desire to use his experience to improve the lives of his constituents.

Iyamu urged voters to support his candidacy, assuring them that he would work to advance their interests and promote development through effective representation.

World.title: Barau Counters Osinbajo, Defends Tinubu’s Economic Reforms
World.content:
…Blames poor communication for public discontent, cites NELFUND, highway projects

Sunday Aborisade in Abuja

The Deputy President of the Senate, Senator Jibrin Barau, has challenged former Vice-President Yemi Osinbajo’s gloomy assessment of Nigeria’s economy and democratic governance, insisting that President Bola Tinubu’s administration is addressing longstanding structural challenges but needs to communicate its policies and achievements more effectively to Nigerians.

Barau acknowledged the validity of concerns raised by Osinbajo, particularly those relating to economic hardship, declining public confidence in democratic institutions and inadequate youth participation in electoral politics.

He, however, argued that the perception of poor government performance was partly attributable to the failure of political leaders to adequately explain their policies, interventions and ongoing development projects.

The Deputy Senate President spoke on Tuesday in Yola, Adamawa State, during a public lecture titled, ‘Democracy and Development: Rethinking the Leadership Question,’ organised to mark the 59th birthday of Governor Ahmadu Umaru Fintiri.

Osinbajo, who served as vice-president between 2015 and 2023, had expressed concern about the growing dissatisfaction with democratic governance across Africa, despite nearly three decades of uninterrupted democratic rule in several countries.

Drawing on findings from Afrobarometer surveys, the former vice-president highlighted widespread economic anxiety, declining public confidence in government, rising living costs, unemployment, inadequate healthcare and diminishing youth participation in electoral processes.

He noted that although 64 per cent of Africans preferred democracy to other forms of government, only 38 per cent were satisfied with how democracy was functioning in their respective countries.

Osinbajo also cited survey findings indicating that 59 per cent of Africans considered their national economies to be in bad shape, while 51 per cent believed their economies had deteriorated.

He warned that persistent economic hardship and the failure of democratic institutions to meet citizens’ expectations could undermine public confidence in democracy, particularly among young people.

Responding to the presentation, Barau praised Osinbajo’s intellectual depth but questioned whether the gloomy picture reflected the full extent of government interventions and ongoing efforts to address the country’s challenges.

“I know he is a very good orator, a good public speaker and an intellectual to the core,” Barau said.

Explaining why he had decided to respond despite initially intending to avoid making a speech at the birthday celebration, the senator described Osinbajo’s presentation as thought-provoking.

“Having said that, I am compelled to make some comments on the paper. It is a very beautiful and thought-provoking paper,” he said.

Barau identified inadequate communication between political leaders and citizens as a major factor contributing to public dissatisfaction, arguing that governments needed to do more to explain the policies and programmes designed to improve living conditions.

He said: “What I want to say is this: one important reason for the gloomy picture portrayed by the surveys, particularly those conducted by Afrobarometer, is what the professor talked about and specifically observed: the issue of communication between the leaders and the led.

“There is no proper communication,” he said.

The senator maintained that although Nigerians were entitled to demand better living conditions and hold public officials accountable, citizens also needed adequate information about the challenges confronting the country and the measures being taken to address them.

He cited interventions in education and infrastructure as examples of the Federal Government’s efforts to tackle structural deficiencies that have constrained economic growth and limited opportunities for millions of Nigerians.

On education, Barau highlighted the Nigerian Education Loan Fund (NELFUND), introduced under Tinubu’s administration, describing it as an intervention designed to expand access to tertiary education, particularly for students from financially disadvantaged backgrounds.

He argued that access to education remained critical to addressing the long-term consequences of poverty, unemployment and social exclusion, especially in a country with a large and growing youth population.

“Before now, it was very difficult for a child who did not have the means to go to school. Now, everyone, except a child who does not want to go to school, can go to school in Nigeria with the NELFUND introduced by this administration,” he said.

The Deputy Senate President also underscored the importance of infrastructure development in stimulating economic activity, attracting investment and improving the standard of living.

He cited the Lagos-Calabar Coastal Highway, the Badagry-Sokoto Highway and road projects across the North-east and North-west as evidence of ongoing efforts to address the country’s infrastructure deficit.

According to him, investments in roads, water supply and other essential infrastructure are necessary to connect communities, facilitate trade, reduce transportation bottlenecks and create conditions for sustainable economic prosperity.

He said: “When we talk about economic prosperity, you cannot achieve it without a certain level of infrastructure, including road networks, water supply and other essential infrastructure.

“This is what is happening currently in this country under President Bola Ahmed Tinubu’s administration. Roads are being constructed everywhere to propel the process of bringing economic prosperity. That is being done.

“It is a long journey, but it is being done. Yet, there is no proper communication.”

He urged political leaders and public officials at the federal and state levels to prioritise sustained public engagement, insisting that government policies could not achieve their intended impact if citizens remained inadequately informed about their objectives and implementation.

The senator also attributed part of the pressure on household incomes and the rising cost of goods and services to international economic developments, arguing that Nigeria’s current difficulties could not be considered in isolation from global events.

He pointed to the Russia-Ukraine war and conflicts in the Middle East as factors that had disrupted international supply chains, increased energy costs and raised production expenses across several economies.

Barau also cited tensions around the Strait of Hormuz, a strategic international oil transit route, as one of the factors contributing to volatility in global energy markets.

According to him, “The fact is that these challenges are not peculiar to Nigeria; they have an international dimension. The rising cost of living is partly attributable to conflicts in different parts of the world, including the Middle East, as well as the ongoing war between Russia and Ukraine.

“These conflicts have disrupted global supply chains, driven up energy prices and increased the cost of goods and services worldwide.”

The senator, who is also the First Deputy Speaker of the ECOWAS Parliament, argued that developments in international energy and commodity markets could have significant implications for Nigeria, given the country’s exposure to global trade and the cost of imported goods and production inputs.

“Nigeria is not an island,” he said.

Barau’s intervention came against the backdrop of continuing public debate over the effects of Tinubu’s economic reforms, particularly the pressure on household incomes, transportation costs and prices of essential commodities.

While the Federal Government has defended its policy direction as necessary to address longstanding economic distortions, the scale of the immediate hardship has continued to generate public concern over the pace at which the benefits of the reforms would translate into improved living conditions.

Osinbajo’s lecture similarly drew attention to the wider democratic implications of persistent economic difficulties, particularly the possibility that citizens could lose faith in democratic institutions if governments failed to respond adequately to their expectations.

Barau, however, argued that bridging the gap between public expectations and government performance required political leaders to communicate more clearly, explain policy choices and provide credible information on the progress of ongoing interventions.

He called on public officials and other stakeholders to take collective responsibility for improving public understanding of government policies, stressing that effective communication should complement, rather than replace, tangible results.

For the Deputy Senate President, the challenge confronting Nigeria is therefore not only the implementation of policies to address economic and infrastructural deficits but also ensuring that citizens understand what the government is doing, why the interventions are necessary and how they are expected to improve their lives.

He maintained that sustained engagement between leaders and the electorate would be essential to rebuilding public confidence, strengthening democratic institutions and securing broader support for the country’s development agenda.

World.title: ADC PCC Alleges Plot To Shift Presidential Election, Insists on January 16
World.content:
Chuks Okocha in Abuja

The African Democratic Congress Presidential Campaign Council warned that reports of pressure on the Independent National Electoral Commission to shift the 16 January presidential election, just 80 days away, cannot be dismissed.

The ADC PCC said that plot to shift the presidential election was to be hinged on Ebola.

A statement by Phrank Shaibu, Director of Strategic Communication of the ADC Presidential Campaign Council, said, “If President Tinubu believes Nigerians want another four years of his government, he should face them at the ballot box, not seek more time through the back door.”

According to the ADC Presidential Campaign Council Director of of Strategic communications, “The Council has received information that the INEC Chairman is to be summoned to the Presidential Villa and instructed to shift the election.

“We are raising the alarm before that meeting takes place. President Tinubu must abandon any such attempt. Professor Joash Amupitan must refuse any instruction to change the timetable and immediately make any such approach public.

“The election date belongs to Nigerians. It must not be rewritten behind closed doors at the Villa”, the statement stated.

The ADC presidential campaign Council said that “Nigerians have endured three and a half years of soaring prices, shrinking incomes and relentless hardship.

“They have the right to judge this government at the ballot box on 16 January. A government that has made life this difficult for Nigerians must not be allowed to postpone its day of judgment.”

The ADC presidential campaign Council said that “Ebola is a serious public health concern. Health professionals must be free to contain it, and INEC must take every necessary step to protect voters and election workers.

“The NCDC Director General has said there is currently no reason to postpone the election. That position must not be twisted into a political excuse for delay.

“The Council puts INEC, domestic observers and international election monitors on notice: any proposal to change the timetable must be made openly, supported by published health evidence and subjected to public scrutiny. The Presidency must not use a health emergency to escape an electoral verdict.” Shuaib stated

World.title: No Shady Deal in Kwara Social Investment Programme, Says DG, Tejidini
World.content:
Hammed Shittu in Ilorin

Director General of the Kwara State Social Investment Programme (KWASSIP) Dr. Abdulwasiu Tejidini, has said that, there was no any shady deal in the financial operations of the agency.

He therefore said all the financial operations and approved funds disburshed to the beneficiaries were applied with the objectives of the mandate of the agency.

Dr. Tejidini in a statement issued in Ilorin, signed by the agency’s Press Secretary, Mrs. Yusuf Bola Shade, stated that the agency maintains records of beneficiaries across the 193 wards of Kwara State under programmes that includes Owo Isowo, Owo Arugbo, and the skilled and unskilled workers scheme.

Dr. Tejidini positions came on the sidelines of the recent called for a probe of the agency by the 52- youth coalition in the state that backed the call of the governorship candidate of the National Democratic Congress (NDC) for 2027 election, Professor Abdulmumin Yinka Ajia to look into the financial operations of the agency since its inception.

The statement read, “The Kwara State Social Investment Programme (KWASSIP) has taken note of recent allegations concerning the management and implementation of its programmes.

“KWASSIP assures the public that funds approved and released to the agency have been applied in accordance with the objectives of its mandate.

“The agency maintains records of beneficiaries across the 193 wards of Kwara State under programmes including Owo Isowo, Owo Arugbo, and the skilled and unskilled workers scheme.

“The Kwapreneur programme has also supported beneficiaries in establishing and expanding businesses, creating employment opportunities, and contributing to economic activity in their communities.

“These outcomes reflect the agency’s efforts to promote sustainable economic empowerment and support livelihoods across the state”.

The statement added, “In response to economic challenges, KWASSIP has, at various times, provided assistance to businesses, individuals, and households affected by difficult circumstances.

“This includes support provided to businesses affected by the #EndSARS protests at Palms Mall, which enabled affected operators to resume activities and rebuild their livelihoods.

“The agency also recently disbursed ₦90 million to 12 young entrepreneurs to support business expansion, strengthen enterprise development, and promote job creation across Kwara State.

“KWASSIP remains committed to transparency, accountability, and continuous improvement in the delivery of its programmes. Its activities and records are available for appropriate review, in accordance with applicable procedures and requirements.

“The agency welcomes constructive criticism and public scrutiny. It is important that public discourse remains guided by facts, evidence, and a genuine concern for the welfare of the people, rather than political considerations or unsubstantiated claims.

“KWASSIP therefore urges all stakeholders to assess its performance on the basis of verifiable information, documented programme outcomes, and credible evidence.

“KWASSIP will continue to work with relevant stakeholders to ensure that its interventions reach intended beneficiaries and contribute meaningfully to the social and economic development of Kwara State”.

World.title: Israel Election Count: Netanyahu’s Bloc Leads With 54 Seats, Eisenkot-led Bloc 49, Arab Parties 17
World.content:
Israel’s election count has revealed a political deadlock, with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud-led bloc leading with 54 seats, while the bloc led by Yashar party chief Gadi Eisenkot has secured 49 seats and Arab parties hold 17 seats.

According to Times of Israel reports, with more than 84 per cent of ballots counted, neither side has secured the 61 seats required for a parliamentary majority, leaving the formation of the next government uncertain.

The latest figures give the anti-Netanyahu bloc a combined 66 seats when the Arab parties are included. However, forming a coalition remains complicated by campaign promises from several party leaders not to partner with Arab-led parties.

The Joint List chief signalled readiness to support efforts to remove Netanyahu’s government, declaring: “We’re ready to pave the way to oust Netanyahu government.”

Despite the uncertainty, both Netanyahu and Eisenkot expressed confidence in their ability to form the next government following exit poll results released on Tuesday night.

The exit polls suggested that the election had produced a stalemate, with neither political camp able to form a coalition without making difficult political compromises.

The pro-Netanyahu bloc was initially projected to win between 51 and 52 seats, below the number it currently holds in the Knesset. Subsequent partial results increased its projected strength, although the latest count placed the bloc at 54 seats.

Meanwhile, reports indicate that Eisenkot’s bloc is exploring ways to use its votes, alongside those of the Arab parties, to replace Knesset Speaker Amir Ohana, a member of Likud.

No candidate has reportedly been agreed upon, but Yisrael Beytenu lawmaker Oded Forer and Yashar’s Elazar Stern have been mentioned as possible options.

Netanyahu’s Likud also performed strongly in Kiryat Shmona, Sderot and other communities severely affected by the war, according to reports by The Times of Israel.

Political parties across the spectrum celebrated their performances despite the inconclusive results, while several leaders urged patience until the final count is completed.

Although more than 84 per cent of ballots have been counted, the final outcome may take several days to emerge. Remaining votes include “double envelope” ballots cast by Israel Defense Forces soldiers, diplomats and other voters who did not vote at their assigned polling stations.

The final results will determine whether either camp can assemble a governing coalition or whether further negotiations will be required to break the political deadlock

World.title: Customs Hands Over N5.8m Seized Unregistered Drugs To NAFDAC In Sokoto
World.content:
Onuminya Innocent in Sokoto

The Sokoto/Zamfara Area Command of the Nigeria Customs Service (NCS) has handed over seized unregistered pharmaceutical products valued at N5,804,062.06 to the National Agency for Food and Drug Administration and Control (NAFDAC) for further investigation and necessary action.

The handing over ceremony was held on Wednesday , October 28, 2026, at the Command Headquarters in Sokoto, in line with existing inter-agency collaboration and the directive of the Comptroller-General of Customs, Bashir Adewale Adeniyi.

Speaking during the ceremony, the Acting Customs Area Controller, Sokoto/Zamfara Area Command, DC Haliru Isah Abdullahi, said the items were intercepted by gallant patrol teams along the Illela-Sokoto road, following credible intelligence and the commitment of officers of the Command.

He listed the seized items to include 360 packages of anti-cold containing 50 cards each with 4 tablets per card, 500 packages of Amodiaquine containing 25 cards each with 3 tablets per card, 140 packages of Paracetamol containing 100 cards each with 10 tablets per card, and 100 packages of Quinine containing 10 cards each with 10 tablets per card.

Abdullahi said the importation of the unregistered drugs contravened Section 55 of the Nigeria Customs Service Act 2023 and NAFDAC regulations, noting that the drugs posed great danger to the health of Nigerians as they were not certified for consumption.

He warned smugglers and dealers in unwholesome products that the Sokoto/Zamfara Command under his watch would not tolerate any form of smuggling, stressing that the Command remained vigilant and committed to safeguarding the health of citizens and the nation’s economy.

He commended the officers who made the seizure possible for their diligence and bravery, and appreciated NAFDAC for its continuous partnership with the Service.

“I hereby formally hand over these seized items to the NAFDAC team for further necessary action,” Abdullahi declared.

Responding, the Coordinator of NAFDAC, Sokoto State, Abdulsalam Lawan, commended the Nigeria Customs Service for the inter-agency collaboration that had helped in curbing the entry of fake drugs into the country.

Lawan noted that the agency and Customs had enjoyed wonderful collaboration which had led to the ridding of unwholesome products from the country, and urged the Customs Service to sustain the tempo.

He assured that NAFDAC would carry out further investigation on the seized products and take necessary action in line with its mandate to protect public health and ensure only certified drugs circulate in the country.

World.title: Religious, Media Leaders Mobilise Against Disinformation Ahead of 2027 Polls
World.content:
Yemi Kosoko in Jos

Religious leaders and media stakeholders have been urged to intensify efforts to combat misinformation, disinformation and Foreign Information Manipulation and Interference (FIMI) in order to prevent religious tensions, communal crises and electoral violence ahead of Nigeria’s 2027 general election.

The call was made at a two-day workshop organised by Alkalanci, a fact-checking and media literacy organisation, in collaboration with the Institute for Media and Digital Innovation (IMDIL), in Jos, Plateau State.

The workshop, themed ‘Scaling Faith-Based Resilience Against Disinformation and FIMI,’ brought together Christian and Muslim leaders to build their capacity to identify false information, promote responsible communication and strengthen community resilience against information threats.

Speaking at the opening session, Editor of Alkalanci, Alhassan Bala, warned that the proliferation of false information posed a serious threat to Nigeria’s security, social cohesion and democratic processes.

He noted that the growing use of artificial intelligence (AI) to create deceptive images, videos and audio recordings had made it increasingly difficult for citizens to distinguish authentic content from fabricated material.

According to him, malicious actors could exploit such technologies to inflame religious and communal tensions, provoke violence and undermine public trust, particularly as political activities gather momentum ahead of the 2027 elections.

Bala urged religious leaders to exercise caution and verify information before sharing it with members of their congregations, stressing that responsible communication remains critical to safeguarding peace.

“When in doubt, do not share,” he said, emphasising the need for verification before circulating information capable of misleading the public.

Also speaking, Cyber and Hybrid Threats Programme Lead at the UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office’s Integrated Security Fund (FCDO-ISF) West Africa, Oriola Odetoye, reaffirmed the United Kingdom’s commitment to supporting Nigeria in addressing foreign information manipulation and other hybrid threats.

He explained that the intervention, implemented under the UK-Nigeria Security and Defence Partnership, is designed to strengthen Nigeria’s capacity to detect, respond to and counter information manipulation campaigns that could threaten national stability.

Odetoye described religious and community leaders as critical stakeholders because of their influence in shaping public opinion and either preventing or escalating tensions within their communities.

He disclosed that the programme would be expanded to Plateau, Kano, Adamawa and Benue States to complement ongoing federal-level efforts aimed at promoting peace and countering information-related security threats.

Representing the Jama’atu Nasril Islam (JNI), Haruna Tanko cautioned against the deliberate spread of false information for political, religious or personal gain.

He warned that misinformation could create unnecessary fear, deepen divisions and trigger avoidable crises, especially during election periods.

Tanko called on both Muslims and Christians to uphold the values of truthfulness, peace and responsible communication while also advocating accountable leadership and improved governance.

Similarly, Chairman of the Christian Association of Nigeria (CAN), Plateau State Chapter, Rev. Dunka Gomwalk, urged religious leaders to strengthen interfaith dialogue and encourage their followers to verify information before sharing it.

He warned that unverified social media posts and impulsive public comments could fuel religious tensions and undermine ongoing peacebuilding efforts.

Gomwalk expressed optimism that the workshop would produce practical strategies and collaborative approaches through which faith communities could promote mutual coexistence.

Kalanci’s Programme Manager, Bamas Victoria, highlighted the organisation’s ongoing efforts to strengthen community resilience through fact-checking training, media literacy initiatives and public awareness campaigns.

She explained that the programme equips religious leaders, educators and other stakeholders with practical skills to recognise information manipulation, verify follow-up training sessions conducted in different locations have enabled participants to transfer knowledge to their communities, thereby expanding the reach of counter-disinformation efforts.

She expressed confidence in sustained collaboration among religious leaders, civil platforms, and techniques for identifying propaganda and manipulative narratives.

Organisers said the initiative aims to empower faith leaders to become stronger advocates for truth, peace and responsible information sharing as Nigeria prepares for another electoral cycle in 2027.

World.title: AFD, BoI Sign $30m Deal to Unlock Finance for Nigeria’s Creative Sector
World.content:
Michael Olugbode in Abuja

The French Development Agency (AFD) and the Bank of Industry (BoI) have signed a $30 million financing agreement to expand access to credit for Nigeria’s creative industry, with at least 90 per cent of the facility earmarked for micro, small and medium-sized enterprises (MSMEs).

The agreement, which includes a €500,000 technical assistance programme, is AFD’s first credit line dedicated to cultural and creative industries anywhere in the world, positioning Nigeria as the beneficiary of a financing initiative targeting one of the country’s emerging sources of jobs and economic diversification.

The facility, signed in Abuja during the visit of AFD Chief Executive Officer, Christophe Lecourtier, is designed to improve access to finance for businesses in fashion, design, textiles, music, film and audiovisual production, video games and visual arts.

Women-led and youth-led enterprises, as well as first-time borrowers, are among the priority beneficiaries of the programme, which seeks to address financing barriers that have constrained the growth of creative businesses.

The initiative comes as Nigeria’s cultural and creative industries account for approximately five per cent of the country’s Gross Domestic Product (GDP) and provide livelihoods for more than 4.2 million people.

Under the agreement, the BoI will deploy the credit facility to eligible businesses, while the technical assistance component will strengthen the bank’s capacity to finance the sector through staff training and the development of financial products tailored to the needs of creative enterprises.

The programme targets the training of at least 70 per cent of relevant BoI staff, alongside the development of specialised financing products to better serve businesses whose needs may differ from those of conventional industrial enterprises.

The agreement was signed by BoI Managing Director, Dr Olasupo Olusi, and Lecourtier, who represented AFD, reinforcing the longstanding partnership between the two institutions.

Beyond expanding access to credit, the initiative is expected to promote financial inclusion, support skilled employment and strengthen the contribution of the creative economy to Nigeria’s sustainable and inclusive growth.

Its focus on smaller businesses could prove particularly significant for entrepreneurs seeking to expand production, acquire equipment, develop new products or reach wider markets but who struggle to secure affordable financing.

The facility also aligns with the Federal Government’s Destination 2030 ambition for the creative sector, as Nigeria seeks to diversify its economy and harness industries capable of generating employment and business opportunities for its growing population.

The €500,000 technical assistance component is expected to complement the lending facility by improving BoI’s capacity to understand and meet the financing needs of creative businesses.

For AFD, the agreement represents an expansion of its development financing partnership with Nigeria, while the BoI is expected to use the facility to support enterprise development, job creation and economic diversification.

The two institutions said the programme would help remove financial and non-financial barriers to the development of Nigeria’s cultural and creative industries.

World.title: Parliament urged to push for R600 increase in SASSA old-age grant
World.content:
Parliament has been urged to motivate for a R600 increase in SASSA's old-age grant, which would take the monthly payment from R2 400 to R3 000. Image: Facebook @SASSANewsZA

Parliament has been urged to motivate for a R600 increase in SASSA’s old-age grant, which would take the monthly payment from R2 400 to R3 000.

The proposal was raised during public hearings on the Medium-Term Budget Policy Statement (MTBPS), hosted by Parliament’s Standing and Select Committees on Finance.

Financial pressure

The independent public interest initiative Math is not Mathing made the call, highlighting the financial pressure facing older South Africans as they attempt to cover essential living costs.



Presenting the proposal on behalf of the group, Geraldine Prinsloo questioned how pensioners were expected to make ends meet on the current grant.

“After food, electricity, accommodation, transport and medication, can we please explain to the South African elderly how they are expected to live on R2 400 per month?” Prinsloo asked.

She argued that while government budgets might balance on paper, the financial realities facing vulnerable people could remain unsustainable.

“A budget can balance perfectly on paper, while the lives it is supposed to sustain remains financially impossible,” she said.

Call for old-age grant to reach R3 000

The proposal would increase the monthly old-age grant by R600, representing a 25% increase from the R2 400 amount cited during the hearings.

Prinsloo called on Parliament to support the proposed adjustment, arguing that older people needed more assistance to meet their basic needs.



“Raise the older person’s pension from R2 400 to a mere R3 000 per month,” she said.

The request was made as part of public engagement on the MTBPS, which sets out government’s updated fiscal outlook and spending priorities.

Cost of living

The proposal places the cost of living facing pensioners in focus, particularly the need to cover food, electricity, accommodation, transport and medication from a limited monthly income.

However, any change to the old-age grant would depend on the relevant government budget and official announcements.

For now, the request from Math is not Mathing adds to the debate over whether social grants are sufficient to support older South Africans amid persistent household financial pressures.

Here’s how you can qualify for a SASSA Older Persons grant

The SASSA Older Persons grant, formerly known as the old age pension, is available to qualifying people aged 60 and older who need financial assistance during retirement.

But reaching the age requirement does not automatically mean an applicant will receive the grant.

Who qualifies for the Older Persons Grant?

Applicants must:

Be a South African citizen, permanent resident or recognised refugee

Live in South Africa

Be 60 years or older

Not receive another social grant for themselves

Not be cared for in a state institution

Pass the SASSA means test, which assesses income and assets

According to the SASSA criteria, applicants must not earn more than R86 280 a year if single (R7 190 a month) or R172 560 a year if married.

Their assets must also not exceed R1 227 600 if single or R2 455 200 if married.

World.title: SA’s water quality under scrutiny: Is Cape Town’s tap water safe to drink?
World.content:
Cape Town has released its latest annual water quality report, revealing how its drinking water performed over the past year.

With water contamination making headlines elsewhere in South Africa, the safety of municipal drinking water is (literally) under the microscope.

Covering the period from 1 July 2025 to 30 June 2026, the findings offer insight into the quality of Cape Town’s supply.



“Cape Town’s tap water continues to meet an excellent standard of drinking water quality,” the City said in a statement on Wednesday.

“This is according to the latest annual report published by the City’s Water and Sanitation Directorate.”

Siphesihle Magqazolo (Scientific Services) analyses a drinking water sample for nitrates, nitrites, sulphates, fluorides, chlorides and colour. Image: CoCT

Water quality: How Cape Town tests its taps

The report confirms that Cape Town’s municipal drinking water met the applicable quality criteria across all 11 assessed supply systems. Testing covered physical, chemical and microbiological parameters, measured against South African National Standard SANS 241:2015.

Water is purified at 12 treatment plants, where laboratories test samples every two hours. Scientific Services teams also collect about 200 drinking water samples weekly across the city’s 10 800km network.

“Maintaining excellent drinking water quality requires consistent leadership, skilled people and sustained investment across the entire water supply system,” said Zahid Badroodien, the City’s Mayco Member for Water and Sanitation.

Drinking water quality in Cape Town – percentage compliance 2021-2022 2022-2023 2023-2024 2024-2025 Quarter 1 (Jul – Sep) 99.1 99.5 99.1 99.3 Quarter 2 (Oct – Dec) 99.1 99.4 99.2 99.4 Quarter 3 (Jan – Mar) 99.0 99.3 99.2 99.6 Quarter 4 (Apr – Jun) 99.0 99.2 99.3 99.6

A tale of three cities

Cape Town’s results come amid a serious water contamination crisis in Tshwane.



The South African reported on Tuesday that the number of people who have fallen ill after drinking contaminated water in Bronkhorstspruit has climbed to 833, including 328 children aged four and younger.

Three patients remain in hospital.

Contaminated water supplied by the Bronkhorstspruit Water Treatment Works has been linked to hundreds of reported gastrointestinal illness cases. Investigators found that the water had not been chlorinated between 24 September and 14 October.

Water and Sanitation Minister Pemmy Majodina, however, insists there is no outbreak.

Meanwhile, in the East of Joburg, a precautionary alert has been lifted after a water quality scare in Bezuidenhout Valley.

“Johannesburg Water (JW) confirms that water samples collected on 23 and 25 October from the affected properties along 8th Avenue, at the corners of 4th, 5th, 6th and 7th Streets meet the required water quality standards for both microbiological and chemical parameters,” JW said.

Cape Town’s annual and quarterly water quality reports are available on the City’s website.

World.title: ‘For some it was cut off’: KZN caregiver questions how SASSA decides who keeps grant support
World.content:
Getrude Tshandu has nothing bad to say about how SASSA pays her. What she wants to know is how SASSA decides who keeps getting help.

The KwaZulu-Natal resident has received the Child Support Grant for more than five years. She shared her experience with The South African through our SASSA grant survey.

Reliable Grant payments, empty pockets

She said her grant has been straightforward from the start, with no problems, and rated SASSA’s communication with recipients as very good.



The money goes mainly towards school fees and her children’s needs. Tshandu rents privately and supports one to two dependants. She said her grant does not cover her basic needs and that she regularly struggles to make ends meet. By month end, nothing is left.

Even so, she has kept food on the table. She confirmed that no one in her household went without food in the past month.

Job hunt takes priority

Tshandu is unemployed and looking for work. She named unemployment as her biggest financial concern.

She has experience in admin and office work and is willing to relocate for the right job. That willingness shows how far many grant recipients will go for a steady income.

Tshandu has also tried to get extra government support beyond her grant, but she said she was declined or gave up during the process.

A question about fairness

That experience shaped the comment she shared with The South African. Tshandu wants to know why some people lost the Social Relief of Distress (SRD) grant while others kept receiving it.



“My comment will be based on why do other people get to be cut of from the R370 grant while others still receive the money, even those who gets it for children they still receive the money but for some it was cut off why is that,” she said.

Her question reflects confusion many South Africans have voiced about SRD grant approvals and cancellations. Some households report losing the grant without a clear explanation, while others in similar circumstances keep receiving it.

If you receive a SASSA grant and want to share your story, we want to hear from you.

Take part in our survey and stand a chance to win R2 000. Your responses help us tell the stories that matter.

World.title: Will SARB throw South Africans an early Christmas interest rate present?
World.content:
The SARB has warned the public about a fraudulent WhatsApp group falsely claiming to offer daily stock recommendations from Governor Lesetja Kganyago. Image: Facebook @SaReserveBank

South Africans face mixed signals over the prospect of an interest rate hike in November, with inflation risks keeping the door open to an increase while other indicators suggest the South African Reserve Bank (SARB) could leave rates unchanged.

The SARB’s final Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) meeting of 2026 is scheduled for Thursday, 19 November, with economists divided over whether further tightening is necessary.

A R10 billion fuel tax relief package announced by Finance Minister Enoch Godongwana during the Medium-Term Budget Policy Statement (MTBPS) has changed the inflation outlook, but uncertainty surrounding international oil prices and the rand continues to complicate the picture.



Fuel relief changes the inflation outlook

Before the announcement of the fuel relief package, expectations of higher petrol and diesel prices had raised concerns that inflation could climb sharply towards the end of the year.

The outlook has since improved, with the temporary reduction in fuel taxes expected to provide relief to motorists in November.

The latest forecasts cited in the market analysis suggest inflation could peak at around 5.7% in October before easing. This is lower than earlier expectations of a November peak of 6.4%.



However, the improved outlook has not eliminated the risk of an interest rate increase.

Persistently high fuel costs could feed into transport, production and other business expenses, eventually putting further pressure on consumer prices. Such second-round effects would make it more difficult for the Reserve Bank to bring inflation down to its 3% target.

Why the Reserve Bank could hold rates

Other market indicators suggest the Reserve Bank may have less reason to increase borrowing costs.



One view is that the recent inflation pressures could prove temporary, particularly if fuel prices stabilise and the impact of higher costs fades from annual inflation comparisons during 2027.

Under this scenario, inflation could move closer to the Reserve Bank’s 3% target as the year progresses, reducing the need for additional monetary tightening.

The rand’s recent weakness has also been linked to expectations that South African and US interest rate policies could move in different directions. A narrowing interest rate differential could put further pressure on the local currency, potentially complicating the inflation outlook.



Nevertheless, the argument for holding rates rests partly on the expectation that current price pressures will ease rather than become entrenched.

If inflation declines as anticipated, further rate increases could prove unnecessary and place additional pressure on households and businesses already facing high borrowing costs.

As a reminder, following the most recent Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) meeting in September, the repo rate stands to 7.25%, while the prime lending rate is 10.75%.



What happens next?

The SARB’s next Monetary Policy Committee meeting is scheduled for Thursday, 19 November 2026 and will be the final interest-rate decision of the year.

World.title: Gerda Steyn still waiting for Soweto Marathon prize money
World.content:
Gerda Steyn has revealed that she is still waiting for her R90 000 prize money almost a year after finishing third at the 2025 Soweto Marathon. Image: Instagram @gerda_steyn

South African running star Gerda Steyn has revealed that she is still waiting for her R90 000 prize money almost a year after finishing third at the 2025 Soweto Marathon, as the race’s wider R1.2 million payment crisis continues to affect elite athletes.

Steyn, one of the country’s most successful distance runners, finished on the podium at the 30th African Bank Soweto Marathon on 29 November 2025.

Despite her performance, the five-time Comrades Marathon and seven-time Two Oceans Marathon champion says she has received no payment and has been left without meaningful communication from the organisers.



“It’s almost exactly a year later, and there has been absolutely no communication about payments, and no payments have been made. I don’t even know if this is still something we are talking about,” Steyn said.

Gerda Steyn disappointed by lack of communication

Gerda Steyn said she had chosen to support the Soweto Marathon despite knowing the event was experiencing difficulties.

After the Cape Town Marathon was cancelled because of bad weather on 19 October 2025, she still wanted to take part in a marathon on home soil.

“I wanted to support them. I knew the race was not in a good position, but I still wanted to support them,” she said.

However, the prolonged delay has left her disappointed.

“When I look back 12 months later and see how we have almost been forgotten, it is incredibly disappointing,” Steyn said.



She also expressed concern about the impact on South Africa’s running community, which has traditionally rallied around major road-running events.

“We have such a community. When I look at the running community, we stand together. We support everything and everyone. We are proudly South African,” she said.

“This is not good for the community.”

Soweto Marathon prize money crisis affects winners

Gerda Steyn is not the only prominent athlete reportedly still waiting for payment.

Men’s race winner Joseph Seutloali, her Hollywood Athletics Club team-mate, is reportedly still owed R250 000. The outstanding payments form part of a wider prize-money shortfall estimated at approximately R1.2 million.

The dispute has raised questions about the management and financial accountability of the event, known as the People’s Race.

Title sponsor African Bank has confirmed that it fulfilled its contractual obligations and transferred the sponsorship fees and prize money to the Soweto Marathon NPO.

The organisers initially attributed the delays to outstanding doping test results. However, the South African Institute for Drug-Free Sport reportedly confirmed that the results had been finalised and delivered by mid-January 2026.

Despite that development, athletes have continued to wait for their money.

Government steps in amid mounting pressure

The crisis prompted further intervention in 2026.

In July, Central Gauteng Athletics announced that limited funds from the Gauteng Sports Confederation’s 2024 allocation would be used to make partial payments to affected athletes.

Sports, Arts and Culture Minister Gayton McKenzie subsequently announced government intervention, including plans for the outstanding prize money owed to the 2025 winners to be paid directly through government channels.

The department also undertook to oversee the organisation of the 2026 race.

The minister has further indicated that steps would be taken to pursue allegations of fraud and theft against the NPO organisers through the South African Police Service and the National Prosecuting Authority. Any criminal allegations would need to be investigated and established through the appropriate legal processes.

The proposed intervention has also raised governance questions, with provincial athletics bodies expressing concerns about a direct political takeover and the need to address the event’s structural problems.

World.title: Number Of The Day | 3.5% | 28 October 2026
World.content:
South Africa's AGOA Risk Is Bigger Than a 3.5% Tariff

The real danger of losing preferential access to the US market lies not only in higher duties, but in what those costs could do to South Africa's competitiveness.

A tariff of 3.5% does not immediately sound like an economic emergency. Compared with the much larger duties that have featured in recent international trade disputes, it appears almost manageable. But for a South African exporter competing against suppliers from across the world, even a relatively small difference in price can determine whether a contract is renewed, an order is reduced or a customer looks elsewhere.

That is why renewed uncertainty over South Africa's participation in the African Growth and Opportunity Act, commonly known as AGOA, matters well beyond trade negotiations between Pretoria and Washington.

AGOA allows qualifying products from eligible sub-Saharan African countries to enter the United States without the ordinary customs duties that would otherwise apply. Its

extension to the end of 2028 offers continued life for the programme, but does not automatically guarantee South Africa a place in it. Country eligibility remains subject to review.

This creates an uncomfortable distinction between the existence of a trade arrangement and the security of the businesses that depend on it.

How a small tariff becomes a bigger problem

The 3.5% figure discussed in eNCA's Number of the Day represents an approximate average tariff benchmark associated with the potential loss of preferential treatment. It should not be mistaken for a universal additional duty on every South African export. The actual impact depends on the product classification, the duties already applying and any exemptions or other trade measures.

That distinction matters because tariffs do not operate in isolation. An exporter must consider the complete cost of getting its goods into the destination market, including transport, insurance, compliance and customs duties. The importer, meanwhile, must decide whether the final price remains attractive enough to justify buying from South Africa.

Consider two producers selling comparable bottles of wine to an American retailer. If one supplier faces a higher landed cost, the retailer may ask for a discount, reduce its order or favour a competitor. The South African producer then faces an unenviable choice: absorb some of the additional cost and sacrifice margin, or maintain its selling price and risk losing business.

Neither outcome is particularly appealing. And the problem becomes more serious when similar decisions are repeated across numerous orders and customers.

Trade policy eventually becomes a business decision

Much of the public debate about US-South Africa trade relations focuses on diplomacy, political disagreements and the language of punishment or retaliation. These issues influence the trading environment, but they do not fully capture the commercial consequences.

The United States is simply too significant a market for South African businesses to disregard. According to the Office of the United States Trade Representative, US goods imports from South Africa totalled approximately $16.5 billion in 2025. Those purchases represent established commercial relationships that cannot be replaced overnight.

For exporters, finding a different buyer is not necessarily as straightforward as identifying another large economy. Products may need to meet different technical standards, packaging requirements or distribution arrangements. Producers may have spent years building relationships with importers, understanding consumer preferences and developing supply chains around a particular destination.

A decision to withdraw from that market would therefore carry costs of its own.

Nor would every South African export face identical exposure if AGOA preferences were withdrawn. Some products are covered by different tariff provisions or exemptions. The vulnerability of individual industries depends on their products, their competitive position and the treatment that applies at the US border.

A national debate framed around one percentage risks overlooking those differences.

The danger of treating market access as permanent

The deeper economic question is whether South Africa has become too comfortable relying on preferential access that it does not control.

Trade preferences can create opportunities for exporters to expand production, employ more people and enter markets that might otherwise be difficult to reach. Yet

those benefits are also exposed to policy decisions in another country. A change in eligibility requirements or political priorities can alter the commercial assumptions on which investment decisions were made.

The response should not be to abandon the American market. It should be to strengthen South Africa's position within that market while building credible alternatives.

That means pursuing new export destinations, improving domestic logistics, reducing avoidable production costs and helping businesses compete through reliability and product quality rather than tariff advantages alone.

Diversification is often discussed as though it means leaving one trading partner for another. In practice, it means ensuring that the loss of a particular advantage does not threaten the viability of an entire business.

South Africa's AGOA uncertainty is therefore about more than a possible 3.5% tariff difference. It is a test of how resilient the country's export economy would be if one of its most valuable trading privileges changed.

And that is a question worth answering before the next decision is announced.

World.title: Cuba wins UN vote against US embargo with weakest backing in 30 years
World.content:
WASHINGTON - The UN General Assembly on Wednesday adopted a new resolution calling for an end to the US embargo against Cuba, although support for the communist-ruled island fell to its lowest level in three decades.

Nearly every year since 1992 similar resolutions have been put to a vote and passed, but support for the measure this year was markedly lower.

The resolution, which has called for lifting the economic, trade and financial embargo against the island, received 130 votes in favor, with 17 against and 25 abstentions. It was the lowest level of support since 1995.

This year's Cuban resolution included a reference to the impact of restrictions on fuel supplies to the island imposed by the United States since January.

- 'Gangster coercion' -

In recent weeks, Havana accused Washington of mounting a diplomatic offensive to pressure countries into withdrawing their support for the Cuban resolution.

"The world has once again spoken out overwhelmingly against the blockade, even despite the most blatant pressure and blackmail from the US to change the course of this vote," Cuban President Miguel Diaz-Canel said in a celebratory post on X Wednesday, later adding that the US engages in "gangster-like coercion."

Speaking in New York, Cuban Foreign Minister Bruno Rodriguez accused Washington of seeking to "determine the nation's destiny" and "seize" its wealth.

In the minutes before the vote, US ambassador to the United Nations Mike Waltz denied that Cuba was under a blockade and said "the plight of the Cuban people is exclusively the fault of this corrupt communist regime."

"The reality is, today as we speak, there is no ring of US Navy warships around Cuba. Their ports are open. In recent months, data shows that shipments have arrived," from around the world, he added.

- Shouting match -

The vote came a day after a dramatic shouting match on the floor of the UN General Assembly that at one point saw Rodriguez approach Waltz and shout, "You are a liar!" as Waltz shouted for him to back away.

Amid the interruptions, the chair briefly suspended the session and instructed both countries' representatives to return to their places.

In his speech arguing against the resolution on Tuesday, Waltz held up pictures of Cuban leaders past and present, including Diaz-Canel, wearing luxury watches, prompting the Cuban delegation to repeatedly smack their desk in protest and interrupt.

Waltz later held up a satellite images and detailed luxury estates, boats and vacations that he claimed the Castro family and Cuban officials enjoy.

"The regime can never find enough fuel for Cuban ambulances. They can never find enough fuel for Cuban busses. But when the Castro family, the elites that are sitting at that table, want to go yachting, suddenly, it’s no problem." Waltz said.

Speaking on Fox News on Wednesday after the vote, Waltz said that the previous day's debate, "got a little spicy."
