World.title: Dozens are dead in a high-speed train crash in Spain
World.content:
Dozens are dead in a high-speed train crash in Spain

toggle caption i Juanma Jiménez/Europa Press via AP

URDA, Spain — One high-speed Spanish train slammed into another that had stopped on the tracks Wednesday, killing at least 68 people and shredding carriages in the country's second deadly rail collision this year.

The regional government for Castilla La Mancha confirmed the death toll and said another 58 people needed medical treatment in hospital. Rescue workers continue to search in the wreckage for survivors and bodies.

The accident comes with memories still fresh of another crash between high-speed trains in southern Spain in January involving trains from the same two companies.

Spain's rail system operator ADIF said the crash occurred Wednesday morning in the province of Toledo, involving two high-speed trains carrying hundreds of passengers and heading in the same direction from the capital Madrid to Seville in southwestern Spain.

Sponsor Message

One train, run by the state-owned RENFE company, ran into the tail of the other train owned by private company IRYO that had stopped, knocking two of its cars off the track in a rural area between two villages.

toggle caption i Guardia Civil via AP

David Gómez, a construction worker, was working with his brother and another colleague nearby when they heard the crash and ran to help, he told the newspaper El País.

"People were trying to get out through the windows ... We cut through some fences to access the area and treated people with the first-aid kits we had brought," until emergency services arrived, he said. "As I was trying to pull a young woman out, there was a piece of a leg."

Rail service was suspended between Madrid, Ciudad Real and Andalusia.

Until this year, there had been no fatal crash on Spain's dedicated high-speed lines since the network opened in 1992. It was a source of national pride.

Transport minister says crash was due to "inexplicable" decision

Spain's Transport Minister Óscar Puente said that the accident was caused by what he called the "inexplicable" order from a central command center for Spain's trains after a security system had failed. He said the train engineers were not to blame.

Sponsor Message

Puente said that at 8:30 a.m. the security system on a stretch of 63 kilometers (39 miles) stopped working due to a computer malfunction, causing all trains on that stretch to stop. But the central command told the RENFE train to start running again without any speed restrictions, and it ended up colliding with the stopped IRYO train at 8:53 a.m.

Puente said that the train should never have been told to start moving again since there was still a "stop signal" active that line. And if it had, at least it should have been told to go at reduced speed.

Puente said they were still studying information to see how fast the train was going, but it could have been at 200 kph (124 mph) for that stretch of the track.

"I am not attributing responsibility to anyone, I am just stating the facts," Puente said.

Everything went flying when the trains collided, a passenger said

The crash, which occurred in a flat stretch surrounded by olive fields in between the towns of Urda and Los Yébenes, left one car torn into bits of metal and other material, scattering debris down a gravel slope.

Spanish Health Minister Mónica García said that emergency workers were focusing on rescuing survivors and bodies from the two most damaged train cars. She said that the injured are being sent to different hospitals in the area.

"It was a high-speed impact, so we are expecting this to be a tragedy," García said.

Passenger Ignacio Relaño was traveling on the RENFE train. He told state broadcaster TVE that the train had stopped momentarily on the line before it started again and then crashed into the IRYO.

"We all felt the train abruptly slowing down and then the impact," he said. "The car leaned to one side like it was about to tip over. I hit my nose, everything went flying, luggage, cell phones. Everything shook."

Sponsor Message

Another passenger recounted to Cadena Ser radio how she felt the train slam on the brakes and was thrown forward in her seat, breaking the small table in front of her. She said she saw body parts and trapped people covered in blood.

Padilla said that 397 passengers were in the RENFE train and 147 passengers in the IRYO train.

IRYO, an Italian-owned company, said in a statement that it has "activated its security protocols and is closely working with authorities."

The mayor of the nearby town of Urda, Manuel Galán, said civil protection authorities had asked his officials to prepare a sports pavilion to receive injured passengers.

A military emergency brigade was deployed to help emergency services, firefighters and police. Ambulances and medical helicopters made trips to and from the site, while unscathed survivors were put on buses.

Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez canceled his agenda to focus on the crash. He wrote on X that he was "dismayed by the serious train accident in Toledo."

"Emergency services are working on site to attend to the affected passengers," wrote Sánchez, who faces a national election next month. "All my thoughts are with the victims and their families."

Spain's King Felipe VI visited the crash site. He and Queen Letizia said in a short statement on X that they were following news of the accident.

"We are deeply saddened and concerned by the train accident in Urda (Toledo)," the royal couple said. "We share in the grief of the families and loved ones of those who lost their lives, and we send our heartfelt support to the injured and all those affected."

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said "My heart goes out to the victims' families and loved ones. Today, Europe mourns with you."

Spain's soccer federation postponed all 24 Copa del Rey games scheduled on Wednesday.

Sponsor Message

Spain already suffered a devastating train crash this year

The wreckage of Wednesday's crash reminded many of the aftermath of another train collision in January, when 46 people died in southern Spain when a IRYO train jumped the track and hit an oncoming RENFE train. That sent the first two cars of the impacted train plummeting down a four-meter (13-foot) slope.

That crash was the deadliest in Spain since a 2013 crash that killed 80 people.

The January incident shook confidence in the European country's extensive high-speed rail service.

Spain is a leader in high-speed rail

Over recent decades, Spain has invested heavily in high-speed rail — which the country's railway union defines as rails for trains going 250 kph (155 mph) and over — turning it into a world leader.

Spain has laid some 3,900 kilometers (2,400 miles) of such tracks over more than three decades for its 49 million residents. Only China, with 45,000 kilometers (28,000 miles) for its 1.4 billion people, has more high-speed track, according to the International Union of Railways.

Only recently did Spain open its rail network to private companies to compete against RENFE. IRYO started operating in Spain in 2022.

A spokesperson for Spain's train workers' union, Joan Rodríguez, said that the increased traffic brought by privatization has put extra strain on rail infrastructure.

"We are not convinced that the liberalization of the high-speed passenger rail service was matched by the necessary upkeep of the lines," Rodríguez told TVE. "I am not saying it was a determining factor (in the crashes), but yes, the increase in use of the network is a factor to keep in mind."

World.title: How a lifelong Republican came to lead the data center battle in Ohio
World.content:
How a lifelong Republican came to lead the data center battle in Ohio

toggle caption i Andrea Hsu/NPR

Stay up to date with our Politics newsletter, sent weekly.

MT. ORAB, Ohio — The data center mystery in this rural exurb of Cincinnati has consumed Nick Owens.

The lifelong Republican and self-described small-town attorney has spent countless hours trying to figure out what's going on with 1,000 acres of farmland and trees that property records show were sold to a data center developer in 2024 and 2025.

In a few spots, the data center property runs right up against beautiful two-story homes.

"This is the Ohio that people brag about. This is the Ohio people love. This is the small town charm," he says. "Living in the rural area, but getting the benefits of a nice, lovely neighborhood."

Sponsor Message

Some of the most coordinated opposition to data centers anywhere in the country grew out of what happened in secrecy in this village of 4,300 people, a short drive up a country road from Owens' home.

Nondisclosure agreements have stymied Owens' efforts to learn more. But along his quest, he crossed paths with another local attorney and a real estate agent who were equally alarmed. Together, they mobilized a network of volunteers in nearly all 88 counties in the state. They are Democrats, Republicans and Independents. They called themselves Conserve Ohio.

"We all share the same ethos and the same passion for preserving our way of life, preserving the future of Ohio, frankly, from the hyperscale data center invasion," says Owens. "It's really beautiful."

This fall, the group is behind ballot initiatives in 10 communities that would amend local charters to prohibit the construction of large-scale data centers — the kind used to power artificial intelligence. It's an effort that goes beyond the temporary pauses that hundreds of municipal and county governments have embraced.

"All too often you hear from the politicians, 'Well, the community should have a say,'" says Owens. "We're going to find out in ten communities whether or not the communities want them."

Sponsor Message

Meanwhile, the grassroots group is working on a more ambitious undertaking: a petition for an amendment to the state constitution that would ban large-scale data centers statewide. Their goal is to put that to Ohio's voters in 2027.

Data centers bring economic benefits and angst

It's been more than a decade since tech companies first came to Ohio, drawn by the state's inexpensive and abundant land, its energy infrastructure and its generous tax breaks. That combination paved the way for some of the fastest data center growth in the country.

Now, despite the economic benefits — considerable tax revenue, money for schools, numerous construction jobs and a smaller number of permanent jobs — no one seems to want a computing campus in their backyard, especially one shrouded in secrecy.

toggle caption i Andrea Hsu/NPR

"Should the school have extra money or the local government have extra money so we have a constant hum and ridiculous amounts of emissions and pollution?" Owens says, pointing out that hyperscale data centers will require new power plants. "Our community is not for sale."

Pressed to consider whether the state should forgo all opportunities, Owens says he'd entertain the idea of putting data centers on old industrial sites, where they'd be buffered from people.

"If we're going to have data centers, those are the prime places," he says, while acknowledging that it'd be cheaper and easier for a developer to build on pristine farmland than on an old coal site. "I don't know if there are enough brownfield sites, but shouldn't we start with those first?"

A hot-button election issue

In recent months, candidates running for statewide office in Ohio have been trying to convince voters that they hear their concerns — even as they stop short of backing the kind of sweeping moratorium data center opponents are seeking.

Conserve Ohio has not endorsed any of them.

Sponsor Message

Until recently, data center projects weren't all that controversial, in part because they were smaller and weren't being built for AI.

But as the issue has gained traction, it's become a hot topic in the midterms, including in the tight race to fill a U.S. Senate seat. Former Democratic Senator Sherrod Brown has cast his opponent, the incumbent Republican Senator Jon Husted, as "the face of data centers." Brown has been reminding voters that as lieutenant governor, Husted welcomed tech companies to Ohio and championed their data center investments.

Meanwhile, Husted has accused Brown of hypocrisy, pointing to Brown's past support for data centers.

Husted has also introduced his own solution, pushing a bill in Congress aimed at getting data centers to pay for power grid upgrades and other costs associated with their massive energy use. Senate Democrats have blocked the bill, calling it toothless, prompting Husted to accuse the Democrats of not caring or helping.

Unconvinced that politicians will help

These political gestures have not persuaded Linda Moodie, an independent who's been volunteering with Conserve Ohio. She doesn't trust that any of the candidates running for statewide office "will do the right thing" if elected, which is to give the people a say in the data center buildout.

"It's really something that I think a lot of us didn't see coming, and all of a sudden there's just an influx of them," she says.

While Moodie wonders if all the talk on the campaign trail is simply to get votes, she says she will cast her ballot for Brown, who she thinks has been talking about data centers the longest.

toggle caption i Andrea Hsu/NPR

And meanwhile, between now and election day, she's seizing every opportunity to collect signatures to get the statewide ban on the ballot next year.

On a recent evening, she set up a booth at the "Halloween on the Green" celebration in the Cincinnati suburb of Fairfield. She handed out candy to kids and clipboards with the petition to parents. Both were enthusiastically received.

Sponsor Message

"The closer it hits to home, the more people that are going to want to do something," says Moodie.

A dampening of voter enthusiasm in a Republican stronghold

Two years ago, Owens served as a Trump delegate at the Republican National Convention. He won't say how he's voting this fall, but he says no doubt the data center issue, along with $6 diesel, have dampened Republican enthusiasm.

Throughout Mt. Orab, the absence of campaign yard signs is notable.

"Two years ago you would have seen Donald Trump signs left and right," says Owens.

This county, like much of rural Ohio, voted 80% for President Trump in 2024.

"You always have depressed votes in the midterms," says Owens. "But I think the enthusiasm gap for Republicans in particularly rural areas is going to be a lot more pronounced… than any type of enthusiasm gap for Democrats in the cities."

Trump's belittling of data center opponents isn't helping, he says, citing recent comments the president posted to his social media platform Truth Social.

"The only reason that communities throughout the U.S.A. should not want Data Centers is if they want to end up being backwards and poor. If they want to be successful and rich, with far lower taxes and jobs all over the place, let Data Reign," Trump wrote. "If we kill the Golden Goose, you will only have yourselves to blame."

Owens calls the president's statements "tone deaf."

"I mean, no one wants to be poor or backwards," he says. "I want our regular way of life."

Construction at the Mt. Orab site hasn't yet begun. It's not clear when it will. Owens says because of nondisclosure agreements, people who live here know nothing.

For now, standing at the edge of the data center property on a crisp fall day, it's nearly silent but for the birds.

World.title: Partnerships between ICE and local police surge, report finds
World.content:
Partnerships between ICE and local police surge, report finds

toggle caption i Charly Triballeau/AFP via Getty Images

The number of state and local officers working with Immigration and Customs Enforcement has doubled in size in the last eight months, according to a new report from the immigration reform advocacy group FWD.us.

The group analyzed the federal ICE program, called 287(g), that deputizes state and local police for immigration enforcement. It used the agency's public records and information requested by the Deportation Data Project, which is based at UC Berkeley and UCLA and collects U.S. immigration enforcement data.

More than 29,000 officers were deputized by ICE between January 2025 and October 2026. That's far more than the 11,600 deportation officers directly employed by ICE.

Sponsor Message

Felicity Rose, vice president of research and policy at FWD, says her organization's analysis highlights just how big a role these partnerships have played in the Trump administration's immigration enforcement work. The program was created in the 1990s under the Clinton administration but was little used — until President Trump returned to office.

"These state and local officers are a key lever in the administration's quieter approach to enforcement. They're trading what used to be splashy urban surges, which we saw in Chicago and Minneapolis, for just routine highway stops now under the 287(g) program," Rose told NPR ahead of the report's release.

The most common and most aggressive form of these 287(g) partnerships, the Task Force Model, allows police and sheriff's departments to make immigration arrests. And, in return, as long as these local agencies remain in "active and ongoing participation in 287(g) enforcement activity outlined" in the agreements signed with ICE , they get money to spend on new cars, equipment and other enforcement resources.

The Department of Homeland Security has said that 287(g) is a critical tool to cut down on crime and illegal immigration.

A more granular look

Law enforcement agencies in Florida and Texas, combined, accounted for about half of the more than 47,000 immigration arrests made nationally between January 2025 and August 2026 through 287(g), FWD found.

Sponsor Message

That is not such a surprise — governors in both of those states have mandated local police sign these deals. And aggressive enforcement by state and local police in Florida and Texas has made headlines.

Some states not usually known for aggressive enforcement also recorded a spike in immigration arrests made by deputized officers.

The FWD.us report showed that 287(g)-certified officers in Wyoming, New Hampshire and Oklahoma were responsible for huge shares of immigration arrests in each state in recent months.

In Wyoming, deputized officers made 77% of the total immigration arrests in the state in April 2026 and more than 60% every month since November 2025, the report found. Similarly, in New Hampshire, the program was responsible for 60% of immigration arrests there in June 2026.

In June, close to 50% of immigration arrests in Oklahoma were made by state or local police.

Oklahoma's Highway Patrol signed all of its troopers on to 287(g), giving their officers the power to stop a driver and potentially make an immigration arrest on state highways.

That has had a chilling effect on immigrant communities living in the state according to Gabriela Ramirez-Perez, the immigration and economic security policy analyst with the Oklahoma Policy Institute, a think tank that analyzes state policy.

"Even though Oklahoma may not be in the headlines, it's definitely a hotspot for immigration enforcement," Ramirez-Perez said. "We can say that it's definitely resulting in a lot of fear in immigrant communities. People are changing their day to day routines to try to avoid getting on the highway, to try to avoid driving as much as possible."

Financial incentives

The Justice Department earlier this summer offered $3 billion in funding for state and local agencies that join the program. The money can go toward staffing and new equipment in the coming years.

Florida has already given hundreds of millions of additional money to law enforcement agencies in the state in exchange for their participation in the program.

Rose, with FWD, says the promise of money appears to be a driving force behind the surge in 287(g) participation, and thinks it will lead to more partnerships in the future.

World.title: Government called its lawyers after U.S. steel CEO's 'confessions' over why he bought Stelco, Joly says
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Canada's industry minister says she called the department's lawyers after the head of Stelco's American parent company told CBC News that he only bought the Hamilton steelmaker to stop it undercutting his production facilities in the U.S.

"The last words by the president of Stelco definitely made us contact our lawyers to see what could be the consequences of such confessions," Industry Minister Mélanie Joly said Wednesday.

The minister's comments come after Cleveland-Cliffs CEO Lourenco Goncalves told CBC's Power & Politics Tuesday evening that the Hamilton company was "undercutting our prices in the United States."

"I bought Stelco because I could not afford anymore having Stelco flooding the market here in the United States to the detriment of my own company," he told host David Cochrane.

The CEO's comments come after Cleveland-Cliffs responded to Joly's recent demands that it reverse layoffs announced last month or face potential legal action for violating Investment Canada Act undertakings.

The government says the company agreed in those undertakings to keep the number of unionized Stelco employees at 2024 levels through to 2029 when the purchase was made.

In a letter to the company last week, Joly said if the company does not honour its agreement with the federal government it would pursue a remedy in the courts. That step, the letter said, could include asking that financial penalties be imposed or an order requiring Cleveland-Cliffs to divest from Stelco.

WATCH | Stelco in 'full compliance,' says CEO: Stelco in 'full compliance' with commitments to Ottawa, says CEO | Duration closed caption 14:18 With the federal government locked in a showdown with Stelco over its layoffs in Hamilton, Power & Politics speaks to the American owner of the steel plant about whether this standoff could wind up in the courtroom.

Goncalves's company maintains that it's in "full compliance" with the obligations it made under the Investment Canada Act when it bought the steelmaker in 2024.

In a letter to The Canadian Press, Goncalves said he hopes to bring back laid-off Stelco workers before Christmas if a plan to increase Canadian sales succeeds.

The CEO told Power & Politics that he "takes exception" with the notion that he should have to divest from Stelco, saying that, for now, "the company is not for sale," but that will change.

"I will sell the company after we operate the company for a while — and now that I know that I'm persona non grata in Canada, I will do that," he said.

He later said: "Give me another year. I'll make money, sell the company.… [The] minister of industry is not a realtor of companies, and if she is, go sell some other company. This company has an owner, it's Cleveland-Cliffs."

'On the surface it doesn't look good'

Sandy Walker, a lawyer who specializes in competition and the Investment Canada Act, says the Federal Court does have the power order Cleveland-Cliffs to divest itself of Stelco and impose financial penalties of up to $10,000 a day.

She also said Goncalves's comments on Power & Politics raise the question of whether the company signed the Investment Canada Act undertakings in good faith "if he was ultimately planning to shut the company down."

Walker said that while "on the surface it doesn't look good," it's not quite a slam dunk for the government.

Walker said Canada would still have to prove that Cleveland-Cliffs was not subject to conditions beyond its own control when it proceeded with the layoffs.

"I don't think this case is straightforward, that that confession last night is a complete gotcha," she said.

"But it does go to show the attitude of the signatory to these undertakings, assuming [Goncalves] was the one who signed them, and it may go to how hard he is trying to meet those undertakings."

Walker points out that a Canadian court has never made an order to a company under the Investment Canada Act.

In 2009, Ottawa filed a lawsuit against U.S. Steel, after the then owner of Stelco closed many of its Canadian operations when the 2008 financial crisis resulted in a decline in global steel demand.

Ottawa ultimately withdrew the suit in late 2011 when U.S. Steel settled out of court.

WATCH | Conservative MP urges government to sue: Conservative MP urges government to sue Stelco owner | Duration closed caption 1:15 Conservative MP Ned Kuruc for Hamilton East—Stoney Creek told reporters that 'if the government has an iron clad contract' with Stelco's American owner, Ottawa should take them to court over alleged violation of the company's agreements. 'Contracts are put in place to protect our interests and protect the workers,' Kuruc said. 'If we don't enforce them, then what do we have?'

Conservative MP Ned Kuruc, who represents Hamilton-East Stoney Creek, urged the government to sue.

"If the government has an iron-clad contract … file the lawsuit," Kuruc said. "We need action. Get to court, show them we mean business — because ultimately this shows weakness from our government."

World.title: EU dropping associate membership title for its closer alliance with Canada: sources
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The European Union is backing away from the idea of making Canada an associate member of the 27-nation bloc, sources tell CBC News.

A joint statement expected to be released at the 21st Canada-EU summit in Montreal on Friday will instead use softer language promising closer ties, according to sources who have seen the latest draft of the statement.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen surprised many last month when she announced the EU would begin the process of making Canada its first associate member — a status that does not exist within the bloc — raising questions among some members and Canadian politicians about what that would look like.

News that the summit's joint statement won't mention associate membership was first reported by Politico.

Sources with knowledge of the draft statement between Canada and the EU told CBC News the term "associate member" has been removed and the draft now calls for an "ever closer association."

They stressed the statement is still a draft and could change before the week's end.

A source speaking to CBC News on the condition they not be named because they weren't authorized to speak publicly added that this doesn't mean the substance of the agreement changes.

Another source said some EU countries opposed the term "associate member," particularly Germany who called it a red line.

WATCH | 'Names or nomenclature' don't matter, says Carney: EU agreement 'names or nomenclature' don't matter, says Carney | Duration closed caption 0:42 Prime Minister Mark Carney says what 'matters' at the EU summit set to take place later this week in Montreal is 'Canada as a whole becoming a more independent, more sovereign nation so we can live our lives as we choose.'

Speaking to reporters on Tuesday before a cabinet meeting, Prime Minister Mark Carney said the title of Canada's relationship to the EU shouldn't matter as long as it delivers for Canadians.

"The good news is it doesn't matter about specific names or nomenclature," he said.

"What matters is the difference that it will make to the lives of Canadians … and Canada as a whole becoming a more independent, more sovereign nation, so we can live our lives as we choose."

World.title: Arab parties offer Israel's political leaders a path to victory. Why does no one want to take it?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Israelis voted in record numbers yesterday, and ballot-counting continued through the night. Every official update triggered fresh bravado from the two front-runners, Benjamin Netanyahu and Gadi Eisenkot.

Prime Minister Netanyahu showed that his right-wing policies, while controversial in Israel and around the world, still appeal to a majority of Israeli Jews. Meanwhile, those hoping for change united around Eisenkot’s opposition coalition.

But neither has dared declare victory just yet.

They don’t have the parliamentary seats for a workable majority. They have only one choice to get that support, a choice considered politically distasteful among many Jewish voters — to join with Arab parties.

WATCH | Exit polls suggest no clear winner in Israeli election: No clear winner in pivotal Israeli election, exit polls suggest | Duration closed caption 4:38 Israeli exit polls show no clear winner in the national election widely seen as a referendum on Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's leadership. Neither Netanyahu nor his main rival Gadi Eisenkot appear to have secured a governing majority.

Flush with more seats than ever before after an 80 per cent turnout in their communities, the Arab parties have become potential kingmakers. There are two main groups: the Joint List, led by Yousef Jabareen, and the United Arab List, or Ra’am, led by Mansour Abbas.

As the spotlight turned to them on Israeli’s Channel 13 last night, Jabareen opened the door to joining any party offering a "genuine alternative to Netanyahu’s government of bloodshed" to create a "Jewish-Arab partnership."

That wasn’t the tone from Netanyahu, whose current coalition includes ideological hardliners, ultra-religious Jews and settlers eager to annex Palestinian territory in the Occupied West Bank and Gaza. His government has also been criticized for turning a blind eye to a "horrific" crime wave in Arab communities.

"We must form a strong right-wing national government," Netanyahu insisted, rejecting any co-operation with Arab parties, while claiming leadership of the country’s "Zionist public."

The anti-Netanyahu contingent

Eisenkot, a former military chief and retired general, is Netanyahu's main challenger and leader of the Yashar party.

Much of Eisenkot’s support comes from more centrist Israelis who blame Netanyahu for the devastating attack on Oct. 7, 2023 — for ignoring documented warnings that Hamas militants were about to cross from Gaza and for refusing to call an inquiry into security failures. About 1,200 Israelis were killed and 251 were taken hostage that day. Eisenkot has promised a commission to investigate.

His opposition coalition could oust Netanyahu and form a solid majority in Israel’s parliament, the Knesset, if it joined with the Arab parties.

An Arab-Israeli man casts his ballot during Israel's general elections on Oct. 27, 2026, in Umm El Fahem, Israel. (Amir Levy/Getty Images)

But two of his partners – Naftali Bennett, leader of B’Yachad and a former prime minister, and Avigdor Liberman of Yisrael Beytenu – have flatly rejected it. Eisenkot has resisted any formal coalition, though he has been less clear on the possibility of an informal arrangement of voting support in the Knesset.

Arab lawmakers were part of Bennett’s coalition government in 2021, but the Oct. 7 attacks on Israel changed the political landscape. Now, says Israeli political analyst and pollster Dhalia Scheindlin, the opposition parties’ "self-imposed" reluctance to include Arab parties is an "arbitrary, and, frankly, racist constraint."

A key barrier for Eisenkot seems to be the Arab parties’ reluctance to brand Hamas a terror organization, though Ra’am’s Abbas — a part of that earlier coalition — told Israeli media "we have condemned every act of terror and all the crimes that took place on October 7th" and reject the "loyalty test."

High turnout for Arab voters

The election results could put pressure on the opposition to reconsider, especially since political support of the Arab parties has surged among Arab citizens of Israel.

They jammed polling stations yesterday despite threats from hard-line Jewish Israelis, some of whom showed up armed.

In last-minute appeals that the opposition called "desperate," Netanyahu even went on social media to warn that Arabs would "steal the election" if his supporters didn’t vote.

That only seems to have encouraged more Arabs to turn out, including Osayadeh Makladeh in the Druze town of Daliyat Al-Karmel.

"We are now in a bad situation because of the government," she said. "We are here to demand change."

WATCH | Life inside Gaza, a year into the ceasefire: Life is brutal inside Gaza, one year into the ceasefire | Duration closed caption 2:41 Three years after the Oct. 7 attacks ignited the brutal Israel-Hamas war, Palestinians in Gaza continue to endure hunger, collapsing buildings and almost daily airstrikes — despite the year-old ceasefire agreement meant to bring peace to the territory.

The Arab parties' offer to help the opposition is an attempt to remove hardline settlers in Netanyahu’s cabinet from power. That includes politicians like National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, who has been convicted in the past of incitement to racism and boasted during the campaign of promoting harsher treatment of Palestinian prisoners in Israeli jails.

Arab politicians also want talks on a two-state solution or some other resolution in the Palestinian territories, an especially controversial issue in today’s Israel.

In Palestinian communities, issues are often more basic, like housing, infrastructure and crime.

A stalemate

But election math doesn’t seem to be adding up for either Netanyahu or Eisenkot at the moment, with no clear formula to create a majority.

The Knesset has 120 seats, elected through a national proportional representation system that relies on party lists to fill them. Since 1948, no single party has ever won the 61 seats needed for a majority. Both Netanyahu’s and Eisenkot’s coalitions are significantly short of that.

Netanyahu has found himself in similar situations in the past. As Israel’s longest-serving prime minister, he has often engaged in complex political manoeuvres to keep the top job over more than 19 years.

Israel’s Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu speaks during a ceremony commemorating Israel’s Remembrance Day for fallen soldiers, or Yom HaZikaron, at the Military Cemetery on Mount Herzl in Jerusalem on April 21, 2026. (Ilia Yefimovich/Pool/Reuters)

Throughout the campaign, he was seen as fighting for his political life, something that may be critical for his personal life as well. He is on trial for corruption, with charges of bribery, fraud and breach of trust. He has used his position as prime minister to delay hearings and seek a presidential pardon, all while proclaiming his innocence.

As the first exit poll results were announced, analysts like Amit Segal on Channel 12 news concluded that Netanyahu "suffered a major blow." Segal said the best he could do would be to "salvage a tie" by sharing government with Eisenkot or by facing a new election if no leader has a workable majority.

If that is the result once again, President Isaac Herzog will ask the leader with the best chance of forming a lasting majority to govern. If he fails, his opponent will have an opportunity.

It’s a process that could take months of negotiations and coalition building — and might still end with Israelis having to go through this all over again, with another election.

That is, unless the taboo on Israeli Jews and Arabs forming a Knesset coalition is lifted.

World.title: Canada not in a 'position right now' to agree to U.S. trade deal, Carney says
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Asked about the possibility of a trade deal ahead of the U.S. midterms, Prime Minister Mark Carney said Canada 'will only entertain' a deal that suits Canadians.

Canada's not in a 'position right now' to agree to a U.S. trade deal, Prime Minister Mark Carney says.

Prime Minister Mark Carney says his government is not yet in a position to agree to a trade deal with the United States, stressing that an agreement will only be possible "when it suits Canadians."

Speaking to reporters ahead of a Liberal caucus meeting on Wednesday morning, Carney said Ottawa is looking for "the right deal for Canadians."

"We think there's deals that are in the best interests of Canada, first and foremost, but also are in the interests of the United States. That's always been the case. We've been consistent," he said.

"If those deals present themselves, we will pursue them. But we're not at that position right now."

WATCH | U.S. teases progress on Canada trade deal: As midterms approach, U.S. teases progress on Canada trade deal | Duration closed caption 1:40:08 The Canada-U.S. trade war is dominating the final days of the U.S. midterm campaign — and now, the president and other senior U.S. officials are suggesting that progress is being made toward a deal. Power & Politics has the latest details from our reporters in Washington. Meanwhile in British Columbia, a snap election call backfires for the NDP as the Conservatives claim a resounding victory. The Power Panel weighs in.

With Canada-U.S. trade tensions emerging as a key issue ahead of the U.S. midterm elections, questions have swirled this week around whether a deal could be reached before the Nov. 3 vote.

U.S. President Donald Trump and other senior American officials have suggested in recent days that progress was being made.

"We'll have ​that settled pretty soon. They're willing to give us anything ​at this moment," Trump said during a rally in Michigan on Sunday.

But while trade talks have intensified, sources told CBC News earlier this week that the conversations didn't mean an agreement was imminent.

A source familiar with the discussions told Radio-Canada that "key elements" of the discussions remain unresolved, adding, "We are not on the verge of an agreement just yet."

Canada-U.S. negotiations fell apart in August and Washington imposed steep tariffs on a range of Canadian goods. Ottawa announced its own "dollar for dollar" levies in response.

Carney was also asked on Monday about the prospects of a deal, saying that his government is ready "to sign an agreement that is in the interests of Canadians."

"We have very clear bottom lines, red lines, which meant that we were not willing to sign what was offered in August," he said. "To the extent to which the U.S. is moving towards accepting those aspects, then there's a greater prospect of a deal."

World.title: N.S. premier's office criticizes Toronto professor over comments on AI data centre
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Nova Scotia Premier Tim Houston's office has criticized a Toronto professor for making "slanted comments" about a proposed artificial intelligence data centre in Cape Breton.

Sibo Chen, an associate professor of communication at Toronto Metropolitan University, researches the discourse around AI data centres. Chen said in an interview with CBC News last week that public concern over the proposed facility in Point Tupper, N.S., is valid.

Two days later, a communications adviser in the premier's office sent him an email that called his remarks "irresponsible" and "uninformed."

"Nova Scotians deserve facts, not speculation presented in a way that creates unnecessary anxiety," William Burns wrote in the email.

Nova Scotia NDP Leader Claudia Chender said last week her party has heard from thousands of people since EverWind Fuels announced its plan for an AI data centre that it plans to lease to artificial intelligence giant Anthropic.

Burns asserted in his email that Chen had not done sufficient research before commenting on the project. He pointed out Richmond County Warden Lois Landry, in a separate interview with CBC News , had addressed a number of the concerns Chen raised about local infrastructure, including water supply and the electrical grid.

WATCH | Prof 'clearly lacking in information,' Premier Tim Houston says: Premier Tim Houston defends data centre email to prof | Duration closed caption 2:36 Sibo Chen has been writing critically about the environmental impacts of resource extraction and AI growth. Houston says Chen was lacking in information, but speaking as an expert.

Premier Tim Houston addressed the email while speaking to reporters on Wednesday, saying Chen was "clearly lacking in information but yet speaking as an expert."

"The more people that have facts, the better on sensitive discussions like this. There's lots of people who spread misinformation knowingly, willingly. There's others who spread information that is wrong but just don't know it, they just didn't know the other side of it," Houston said.

"So I think when we see somebody who is speaking definitively and presenting themselves as an expert who is missing information, I think it's a good thing to share information."

WATCH | Why Nova Scotia's AI data centre feels like a surprise reveal: Why Nova Scotia's AI data centre feels like a surprise reveal | Duration closed caption 6:32 Construction of Nova Scotia's new AI data centre in Point Tupper is well underway, yet so many people were surprised to learn about it. The CBC's Tom Murphy pieces together the timeline.

Data centres have become a flashpoint across Canada, especially those that power AI, because they can have huge footprints and require vast amounts of energy and water for cooling.

Chen told CBC News on Monday that he was surprised by the response from the premier's office and said it's the first time he's had such a complaint levelled against his work.

"I have been writing actually critically about Alberta's oilsand extraction for a very long time, and I have never received a complaint from the premier's office of Alberta."

The email was copied to Chen's department chair at Toronto Metropolitan University, formerly Ryerson University, a step Chen interpreted as an attempt to exert institutional pressure. A reporter at CBC Nova Scotia who interviewed Chen was also copied.

The email also referenced Chen's "list of publications and research," noting that his work often focused on media perception rather than environmental expertise.

Chen said the response from the premier's office is an attempt to restrict who gets to make public comments, and he said it reinforces his belief in maintaining public engagement.

In his written reply to Burns, Chen defended his objectivity and shared published research on the environmental footprint of data centres. He said he had received no further reply.

World.title: New Vera C. Rubin telescope spots possible new dwarf planet beyond Pluto
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Scientists using a Chile-based telescope have identified an icy object orbiting beyond Pluto ‌that may join our solar system's small roster of dwarf planets.

Researchers said the candidate, named 2026 ED138, has a diameter estimated at between roughly 600 and 1,500 kilometres and is orbiting about 46 times farther from the sun than Earth. By way of comparison, ​Pluto orbits at an average of about 40 times farther from ​the sun than Earth.

The object was spotted using the new Vera C. Rubin Observatory, on the summit of the Cerro Pachón mountain in central Chile. The telescope is a joint ​initiative of the U.S. National Science Foundation and U.S. Department of Energy.

Further observations are ⁠needed to confirm that the ⁠object is a dwarf planet.

If confirmed, 2026 ED138 would ‌join five other dwarf planets recognized by the International Astronomical Union, the global authority on classifying celestial bodies. Those are Pluto, Eris, Haumea and Makemake, all of which orbit beyond the outermost planet Neptune, and Ceres, located in the main asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter.

WATCH | Dwarf planet candidate 2026 ED138's orbital arc:

Based on the current ⁠data, 2026 ED138 would be among the largest of the dwarf planets.

"For me, what this demonstrates is that many exciting discoveries remain to be made with the Rubin Observatory and other telescopes," said astrophysicist Matt Holman of the Center for ‌Astrophysics, Harvard & Smithsonian, who first spotted 2026 ED138.

Pluto long was considered the solar system's ninth and outermost planet, but was reclassified by the International Astronomical Union as a dwarf planet in 2006 because it did not meet the organization's formal definition of a planet. Pluto and the new dwarf planet candidate ​reside in a frigid region of the solar system populated by various icy bodies.

Questions remain

There are still questions about the size and composition of 2026 ED138. ⁠To be considered a dwarf planet, an object must possess sufficient mass for its own gravity to pull ⁠it into a round shape. 2026 ED138 appears to have sufficient mass for that, but more observations are ⁠needed.

"The ⁠main thing we need to do is ​to establish the physical size of 2026 ED138," Holman said.

WATCH | See a swarm of new asteroids: See a swarm of new asteroids | Duration closed caption 0:58 This video, released Monday by the team behind the Vera C. Rubin Observatory, shows images of more than 2,000 new asteroids.

"When we observe with Rubin, we are seeing the sun's ​light reflected from the object," Holman ⁠said. "A smaller, more reflective object would show the same amount of light as a larger, less reflective object. Fortunately, by looking at longer wavelengths, with an observatory like ALMA, we can detect the light emitted by the object itself," which is helpful in measuring an object's size.

ALMA, or the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array, is a powerful telescope also based in Chile.

The ⁠discovery was announced at a ‌scientific meeting in Spokane, Wash.

World.title: Most cougar deaths in Alberta study were caused by people
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Patrick Cummins once had a cougar cross his backyard, climb onto his deck and walk across the roof of his home.

Cummins, who lives near Bergen, Alta., didn't see the cougar. He only saw its tracks in the snow.

In 51 years living on the property, Cummins has never seen a cougar there with his own eyes, though he has caught the elusive predators on trail cameras.

"We always knew there was cougars there," Cummins said. "I suppose we were sort of always looking over our shoulder a little bit, but they've never bothered anybody around here that I know of."

But tracks can make an otherwise invisible predator vulnerable.

A cougar crosses Patrick Cummins's property near Bergen, Alta., on Feb. 7. New research examines how the human footprint affects cougar survival in west-central Alberta. (Submitted by Patrick Cummins)

New research from west-central Alberta suggests roads, homes and other human-made corridors cutting through cougar habitat may affect not only where the animals go, but their chances of survival.

Researchers tracked 80 GPS-collared cougars over five years and found their mortality risk was higher when the animals were closer to homes and secondary roads and when they crossed human-made clearings more frequently.

Of 37 documented deaths, 29 were caused by people.

"I think that's just all about access for hunters, really," said Carter Littlefair, lead author of the study, published Wednesday in PLOS One.

Littlefair, who completed the research while a graduate student at the University of Alberta, said secondary roads can provide hunters with easier access to cougar habitat. Clearings can also reveal where the animals have travelled.

"If a cougar was to cross the road, it's going to leave tracks."

Cougars often avoid trails used by people, which is why the province hopes to reduce trail density in key wildlife areas. (Submitted Delaney Frame/Alberta Environment and Parks)

Human footprint linked to mortality risk

The study followed cougars between 2016 and 2021 across a landscape that included secondary roads and human-made clearings such as seismic lines, powerline corridors and railways.

Hunting was the largest single cause of death, accounting for 16 of the 37. Another eight cougars died after being caught in traps intended for other animals. Five others were killed in vehicle collisions or removals involving problem animals or by a landowner.

Researchers also found a large seasonal difference in survival. Estimated survival was 96 per cent from April through October, but 62 per cent from November through March.

WATCH | Alberta cougar cubs find new home after mother killed by hunter: 2 cougar cubs found a home in Quebec. Now, they each need a name | Duration closed caption 2:06

Alberta's cougar hunting season during the study began Dec. 1 each year and ran through the end of February or until quotas were met.

The research found an association between cougar mortality risk and human-made features, but did not directly measure hunter activity. Littlefair said increased hunter access and the likelihood of detecting cougars could help explain the relationship.

CBC News requested comment from Alberta Forestry and Parks but did not receive a response by publication time.

What the findings mean for the population

Researchers estimated annual survival at about 60 per cent, which Littlefair said is similar to other hunted cougar populations. Hunting also accounted for a smaller share of mortality than in some other studies, he said.

The study did not estimate population size or reproduction, so researchers cannot say whether the population is growing, stable or declining.

Littlefair said the research provides insight into how cougars die, but cannot determine whether they are dying at an unsustainable rate.

For Cummins, the role people played in the deaths was unexpected.

"Yeah, that surprises me," he said.

"There's more people in the rural areas these days than there used to be," Cummins said. "So from that sense, maybe it's caused by more people being out in the bush."

World.title: Colombia’s opposition announces criminal charges against De la Espriella over ties to drug traffickers
World.content:
Colombia’s opposition leader, senator Ian Cepeda, accused President Abelardo de la Espriella of leading an agrarian counter-reform designed to benefit land-owning clans and convicted drug traffickers.

During a congressional debate, Cepeda claimed that De la Espriella put allies of drug traffickers and paramilitaries in charge of key state institutions responsible for land distribution and asset forfeiture.

The president and his appointees are part of a revolving door system of people who, before being appointed to government positions, defended the interests of drug traffickers and paramilitaries associated with De la Espriella and his businesses, according to the opposition leader.

For example, the president put Diana Patrica Bravo, a former prosecutor and partner at his law firm De la Espriella Lawyers, in charge of The Society of Special Assets (SAE), which controls assets that were seized from drug traffickers.

The leader of the leftist Historic Pact party showed financial statements of one of De la Espriella’s companies, Dominio De la Espriella, that would prove that in between 38% and 40% of its capital deposits came from the family and corporate network of Hugues Rodríguez, a.k.a. Comandante Barbie, a former paramilitary financier who was charged with drug trafficking in the US.

The SAE would control more than 130 properties of Comandante Barbie.

De la Espriella family construction firm, Cosenza S.A.S., made property purchases in the city of Monteria directly with individuals under investigation for money laundering and illicit enrichment, according to Cepeda.

The president’s ex-wife, Yoly Beatriz Illidge, was appointed Superintendent of Notaries, making her “directly responsible for inspecting and monitoring all land entries and records issued by restitution judges throughout the country,” according to Cepeda.

De la Espriella is an associate of drug traffickers, owns assets purchased from drug traffickers, and defends drug traffickers from within the national government. Senator Ivan Cepeda

Last but not least, Agriculture Minister Indalecio Dangond “arrived at this post to execute an agrarian counter-reform at the service of paramilitary land-grabbers, foreign capital, and agro-industrial partners” while blocking investments for small farmers and displacement victims, the opposition leader stated.

Cepeda vowed that he would give the dossier to the United States Department of Justcie and to “Congressmen of the Democratic Party, given that mister De la Espriella is a US citizen.”

The opposition leader additionally promised to file criminal charges against the president and his agriculture minister in Colombia.

World.title: Colombia’s government claims Petro exploited 48 women as president
World.content:
The administration chief of Colombia’s President Abelardo De la Espriella told Congress that former President Gustavo Petro hired at least 48 women who were “trapped and exploited” for presidential parties.

During a hearing, DAPRE director Carlos Andres Rios claimed that Petro had 48 women “working in the Presidency, who were unfortunately exploited through temporary work contracts.”

We’re going to prove this to the Colombian people: how, unfortunately, the Casa de Nariño was set up, organized, and designed not for governing, but for partying there every day, bringing women there and engaging in behavior we should not be engaging in—behavior that sets a bad example. DAPRE director Carlos Andres Rios

“Forty-eight women are already speaking with us about how, through a contract and an OPS, they were trapped and exploited in order to be with President Petro,” said Rios.

Former DAPRE director Angie Rodriguez, who was sacked by Petro in July, doubled down on her successor’s allegations and asked the former president to prove that the president managed a network of women, including child transvestites.

Were there transvestite children there? Answer me, Mr. President. Were there transvestite children there? I am asking you a question, and I have every right to ask it. Were there? And if there weren’t, uh… prove that what I am saying is a lie. Angie Rodriguez

Last but not least, far-right magazine Semana published an interview with a woman identified as Deicy Jimenez, who claimed she as hired by Petro after meeting him on an adult website.

Jimenez even told Semana’s former presidential candidate Vicky Davila she trafficked drugs for the former president when he was senator.

VD: What happened on the day you say you transported drugs for Petro? DJ: Yes, I was traveling, and he asked me as a favor to bring him some drugs. VD: Were you outside of Bogotá? DJ: Yes. VD: How do you recall that favor Petro asked of you? DJ: He asked me as the favor to bring him some drugs. VD: Did you buy them? DJ: Yes, I bought them somewhere. He gave me money. VD: Did he give it to you in cash or deposit it for you? DJ: In cash. VD: How much money? DJ: Three million pesos. VD: What kind of drugs did you buy? DJ: Cocaine. VD: Where did you buy it? DJ: I bought it from some people. I can’t say (publicly) their names or the location. VD: Is it a gang? DJ: Yes. VD: Did he know you were going to buy the drugs from that gang? DJ: Yes. VD: At that time, was he a senator or the president? DJ: A senator. VD: How did you bring that drug in? DJ: I brought it through the airport. VD: You mean, on a plane? DJ: Yeah. VD: Did you get on a plane with Petro’s drugs? DJ: Yes. VD: How were the drugs packaged? DJ: In bags. VD: Like individual doses? DJ: Yes. VD: And where did you hide the drugs? DJ: In my suitcase.

In a response, Petro denied having hired women for sex and claimed that the far-right attack were the result of authorities’ failure to sustain corruption allegations.

World.title: “Brazil and Colombia need each other,” says De la Espriella
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella recognized the election victory of his Brazilian counterpart Luiz Ignacio Lula, who defeated far-right candidate Flavio Bolsonaro on Sunday.

In a post on social media platform X, the Colombian President said that “in the Colombian presidential campaign, President Lula openly supported Ivan Cepeda, and I won. In the Brazilian campaign, I supported Bolsonaro, and Lula won.”

“Neither does Lula decide for Colombians, nor do I decide for Brazilians. THE PEOPLE DECIDE! And when the people speak at the polls, their will is respected because it is sacred,” the president added.

Lula and I have major and profound political and ideological differences, but we agree on one fundamental point: Brazil and Colombia need each other. No other consideration can take precedence over the interests of our nations. Colombia and Brazil are sister nations, facing enormous shared challenges and opportunities.

President Abelardo de la Espriella

De la Espriella stressed that “we have much to do and much work to carry out for the benefit of our peoples” an ought to “fight against narco-terrorism and illegal mining, the protection of the Amazon, and the well-being of our citizens.”

Lula was the first leftist candidate and critic of US President Donald Trump to win an election, triggering celebrations among leftists throughout the continent.

De la Espriella, a US citizen, has been among the most fanatic among Trump supporter in trying to align his domestic policies to US foreign policy.

World.title: De la Espriella sacks interior minister after Congress bungles Colombia’s 2027 budget
World.content:
Colombia President Abelardo de la Espriella sacked Interior Minister Rodrigo Lara hours after Congress found a procedural flaw in the passed 2027 budget, which makes the law invalid.

In a post on social media platform X, De la Espriella briefly thanked Lara and announced he would be replaced by the ambassador to the Organization of American States, Alejandro Ordoñez.

The news surprised the interior minister, who suddenly left a congressional debate on a law to facilitate the demobilization of illegal armed groups after receiving a message on his phone.

Lara was apparently held responsible for the blunder of Congress, whose two houses approved the 2027 budget but with conflicting versions of an article on financial risk-coverage mechanisms for the Ministry of Finance.

By the time the error was detected, the budget debate had passed its October 20 deadline, forcing De la Espriella to issue a decree that would convert an older version of the budget bill into law.

The interior minister was the administration’s primary political liaison responsible for managing legislative procedure and whip operations in Congress.

Lara’s job was already under pressure after he failed to convince Congress to cede its presidency to the president’s candidate.

While Ordoñez returns from Washington, Justice Minister Ivan Cancino will assume the role of interior minister.

The incoming interior minister is an ultra conservative Catholic with ties to the Society of St. Pius X, which considers the modernizing reforms of the Catholic Church heresies and errors, and was declared in a schism with the church in June.

In Colombian politics and particularly among the opposition, Ordoñez is mainly remembered as the inspector general who illegally removed former President Gustavo Petro from his post as mayor of Bogota in 2013.

Petro was ultimately reinstated and would become president of the country in 2022.

World.title: Colombia’s Congress approves De la Espriella’s 2027 budget
World.content:
Colombia’s Congress agreed to increase the government’s 2027 budget despite promises by President Abelardo de la Espriella to reduce public spending.

Next year’s budget will be COP634.9 trillion, almost $204 billion, which is 16% more than last year’s budget and 10% higher than the proposal made by former President Gustavo Petro.

According to Finance Minister Miguel Gomez, the budget seeks to bring the State’s finances in line with reality.

The budget was approved in both the Senate and the House of Representatives with the support of De la Espriella’s government coalition.

The Historic Pact, the only leftist opposition party, rejected the budget and boycotted the vote.

On behalf of the national government, I would like to thank you all for your work over the past few months in passing the budget. I would also like to thank the opposition for the strength with which they defended their views. The message that Congress has sent today regarding the government’s economic policy is very important. It is the first step toward putting the country’s economy back on track toward growth, fiscal responsibility, and addressing the nation’s needs. Finance Minister Miguel Gomez

The budget seeks to reimpose the neoliberal model that had been abandoned by Petro and reduce public debt.

According to Green Party representative Jaime Raul Salamanca, who opposed the budget, funding for free higher education was cut in half from COP800 billion ($254 million) to COP400 billion (127 million).

“This cut raises concerns about its potential impact on the continuity and scope of this policy, which has enabled thousands of young people to enroll in public institutions of higher education,” said Salamanca.

The budget also cut the budget for the war crimes tribunal JEP, which could endanger the future of the peace process with the FARC and is opposed by the government.

World.title: De la Espriella announces “open, resolute, and patriotic struggle against wokeism”
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella announced an “open, resolute, and patriotic struggle against wokeism” as part of his “cultural counterrevolution.”

During a visit to the Culture Ministry, De la Espriella described wokeism as “an ideological paradigm that aims to transform moral, cultural, and social foundations in the West, perverting values, family tradition, and national identity.”

According to the president, Culture Minister Paola Holguin was a general in the “cultural counterrevolution.”

Culture has an enormous capacity to shape society, and that is why the State has a moral, inescapable, and political duty to prevent cultural spaces from being taken over by social communism, which is atheist and an enemy to the fundamental values upon which the nation of Colombia is built. This is where that cultural counterrevolution will begin. President Abelardo de la Espriella

De la Espriella said that Holguin, the daughter of a reported money launderer, would lead the “Culture War” against the “extreme left,” which has “permeated all parts of society, particularly the cultural and academic spheres.”

I want to be clear about this: we are going to wage an open, resolute, and patriotic struggle against wokeism, which is nothing more than an ideological movement that aims to transform the moral, cultural, and social foundations of the West, corrupting values, family tradition, and national identity. President Abelardo de la Espriella

Earlier in the day, the National Museum removed all references to members of the exterminated Patriotic Union party, slain guerrilla leader and presidential candidate Carlos Pizarro, and the struggle for the rights of Colombia’s LGBT+ community.

References to Colombia’s former guerrilla movements was “terrorism apology, which is “exactly what we have come to confront” in an attempt to “recover pride for Colombian culture.”

Atheists, the Pizarro family and gay rights activists rejected the president’s attempts to remove them from mainstream culture.

World.title: Colombia’s first lady promises transparency over earthquake donations
World.content:
Colombia’s first lady, Ana Lucia Pineda, vowed to reveal how much money she collected and spent in response to the August 10 earthquake that affected hundreds of thousands of people.

Amid mounting public pressure about where the money had gone, Pineda went on the morning program of public television channel Nuestro Caribe to promise that her foundation, Luz y Sonrisas, will take its finances public on Friday.

Carrying a white folder, the wife of President Abelardo de la Espriella stressed that “in the foundation’s accounts rest all, absolutely all of the monies from the donations we received during the ‘Colombia One Single Heart’ campaign” that was announced on August 12.

“A lie is not going to tear down the truth of who I am or what I represent, or how my children recognize me,” said Pineda.

Luz y Sonrisas was one of three NGO’s that were promoted by the De la Espriella government to collect contributions for victims of the earthquake.

Pineda’s foundation was the only one that could receive contributions from abroad.

Earlier in the week, news program Noticias Uno revealed that her foundation that was founded on July 7 lacked the tax exemption that would allow it to accept donations, a process that usually takes months.

In a press statement, tax office DIAN subsequently said that it had granted the tax exemption to the first lady and that she could legally accept financial contributions.

Pineda did not say how much money she had received, but said that she stopped supporting the initial relief efforts “because the humanitarian aid was sufficient, it was huge.”

The first lady vowed she had saved the donations for the reconstruction phase “because I have also taken the initiative to build and return to the victims a house that is durable for the families who lost everything.”

World.title: Colombia’s opposition takes to the street to protest De la Espriella
World.content:
Despite intimidation attempts by the national government and the police, tens of thousands of people took to the streets throughout Colombia to protest the far-right government of President Abelardo De la Espriella.

The protest had been organized by social organizations, labor unions and the country’s largest opposition party, the Historic Pact.

Opposition leader Ivan Cepeda, who joined the protests in Bogota, told a reporter that the government is “exercising a mafia-style rule in the service of the worst elements of Colombian politics—the drug trade.”

Contrary to what De la Espriella is saying, this is not a government that opposes drug trafficking; it is a government that supports the drug trafficking cartels, the paramilitaries, and the ultra-conservative forces that want to destroy people’s rights, the democratic advances made by President Gustavo Petro, and the progress achieved by the popular movement over the past four years. Senator Ivan Cepeda

“That’s why we’re here; we won’t allow people’s rights to be violated or trampled upon,” said the senator.

Hours ahead of the protest, the president signed off on a decree that changed the police response to protests and accused the organizers of being “instigators of evil” who “seek to once again cause chaos.”

Human rights organizations denounced that the security forces put snipers on the roofs of buildings in Bogota and in Cali, a helicopter flew over the heads of the protesters.

The protests sought to test the waters for an even larger “national strike” that is set for November and shut down parts of the country in 2021.

“We are only warming up,” warned Cepeda, who has yet to recognize De la Espriella as Colombia’s legitimate president after losing the elections in July.

World.title: Falklands approves bill on oil pollution emergencies in relation to offshore installations, and responsibilities
World.content:
Falklands approves bill on oil pollution emergencies in relation to offshore installations, and responsibilities

28th Wednesday, October 2026 - 15:10 UTC Full article

The Director of Mineral Resources will be the competent authority – “Falkland Islands contingency plan” and “offshore installations” used in the OPRC Regulations.

The Falkland Islands Executive Council has approved a set of Regulations 2026 to amend the Maritime (Oil Pollution Preparedness, Response and Co-operation Convention) Regulations 2019 (“the OPRC Regulations”) to make provision for the preparation and maintenance of oil pollution emergency plans in relation to offshore installations and to require the persons responsible for offshore installations to report oil incidents where oil is discharged into the sea.

Regulations 1 and 2 provide for the title and commencement of the Regulations. Regulation 3 provides that these Regulations amend the OPRC Regulations and the following regulations provide for specific amendments to be made to those Regulations.

Regulation 4 amends regulation 3 of the OPRC Regulations, which sets out the objects of those Regulations, to include making provision for the preparation and maintenance of oil pollution emergency plans in relation to offshore installations.

Regulation 5 amends regulation 4 of the OPRC Regulations which contains definitions of words and phrases used in those Regulations. It adds new definitions for words and phrases used in the 17 amended provisions and replaces the definitions of “competent authority” – with the effect that in relation to ships, ports, harbours and oil handling facilities the Falkland Islands Maritime Authority (FIMA) is the competent authority, but in relation to offshore installations, the Director of Mineral Resources will be the competent authority – “Falkland Islands contingency plan” and “offshore installations” used in the OPRC Regulations.

Regulation 6 amends regulation 6 of the OPRC Regulations which is the application provision, to provide that the OPRC Regulations will apply to offshore installations.

Regulation 7 amends regulation 14 of the OPRC Regulations to require an operator of an oil handling facility to ensure that no activities that pose a risk of an oil pollution incident are undertaken unless the facility has an oil pollution emergency plan approved by the authority.

Regulation 8 inserts a new Part 3A into the OPRC Regulations which makes specific provision for the preparation and maintenance of oil pollution emergency plans in relation to offshore installations.

New regulation 15A requires the responsible person for an offshore installation to prepare and maintain an oil pollution emergency plan for each offshore installation for which they are responsible, although the Director of Mineral Resources may permit joint plans in specified circumstances.

New regulation 15B requires the person preparing an oil pollution emergency plan for an offshore installation to take into account guidance issued by the Director of Mineral Resources and for the plan to comply with the requirements contained in the new Schedule to the OPRC Regulations, which is inserted by regulation 13.

New regulation 15C sets out the procedure for the submission of an oil pollution emergency plan for an offshore installation to the Director of Mineral Resources for approval and the dates by which an application must be submitted.

New regulation 15D provides that an approved oil pollution emergency plan must be reviewed every five years or before then if specified events occur. The Director of Mineral Resources may require an oil pollution emergency plan to be reviewed at any time.

New regulation 15E sets out the consequences if a responsible person for an offshore installation fails to review, submit or amend an oil pollution emergency plan. These are that an oil pollution emergency plan ceases to be approved for an offshore installation and, as a result of new regulation 15G(1), this will mean that no oil or gas operations can be carried out.

New regulation 15F gives the Director of Mineral Resources power to direct, after consultation with a responsible person, that an oil pollution emergency plan be amended if it is not compatible with the Falkland Islands contingency plan or is not appropriate for dealing with oil pollution incidents in the area of the offshore installation.

New regulation 15G sets out the duties imposed on a responsible person for an offshore installation. These include: ensuring that no oil or gas operations are carried out unless the offshore installation is subject to an oil pollution emergency plan approved by the Director of Mineral Resources; maintaining relevant equipment; and undertaking exercises. In the event of an oil pollution incident, the oil pollution emergency plan must be implemented (new regulation 15G(3)).

New regulation 15H imposes duties on the licensee (defined as a person to whom a licence has been granted by the Governor under section 6 of the Offshore Minerals Ordinance 1994) to ensure that where it appoints responsible persons, those persons are capable of satisfactorily carrying out 18 the functions and discharging their duties and that they have access to adequate financial resources to discharge their duties.

New regulation 15I requires a responsible person for an offshore installation who observes or is made aware of any event involving a discharge of oil, or probable discharge of oil, or the presence of oil in the sea to report it to the Director of Mineral Resources. Regulation 9 amends regulation 17 of the OPRC Regulations to set out the steps FIMA and the Director of Mineral Resources must take in response to a report of a discharge etc of oil.

Regulation 10 amends regulation 18 of the OPRC Regulations to now contain provision for the inspection of ships, harbours, ports, oil handling facilities and offshore installations and the powers under which the respective inspectors may operate.

Regulation 11 amends regulation 19 of the OPRC Regulations to introduce offences where a person fails to comply with or perform duties introduced by these Regulations.

Regulation 12 introduces a new regulation 20 in the OPRC Regulations which empowers the Director of Mineral Resources, FIMA and Governor to share information obtained for the purposes of the OPRC Regulations with other agencies.

Regulation 13 inserts a Schedule in the OPRC Regulations that sets out the requirements for an oil pollution emergency plan in respect of offshore installations.

Regulation 14 makes transitional provision. Published by the Attorney General’s Chambers, Stanley, Falkland Islands
