We cannot do what we do without your support. A former colleague of Polish President Karol Nawrocki from when he worked as a security guard in a hotel two decades ago testified in court that he told her it was possible to “make some extra money by bringing in girls”. She says she saw him escort a woman onto the premises. The testimony was given after the president himself sued the owner of a website that, just before last year’s presidential election, published claims that Nawrocki had been involved in procuring prostitutes while working at the luxury Grand Hotel in the town of Sopot. The court case began in September but, until now, hearings have been held behind closed doors. However, the judge decided that today’s session would be open to the public, with two former colleagues of Nawrocki giving evidence. The president himself is due to appear before the court in January. 🗣️ "Moją automatyczną oceną było, że to prostytutka i alfons." Nowe zeznania w procesie Karola Nawrockiego z wydawcą Onetu. Przed sądem stanęła była współpracowniczka prezydenta z sopockiego Grand Hotelu. pic.twitter.com/Cn6KyMSjcv — tvp.info 🇵🇱 (@tvp_info) October 27, 2026 In May last year, less than a week before the second round of the election, in which Nawrocki was standing in a run-off against rival Rafał Trzaskowski, Onet, a leading news website, published an article titled “Karol Nawrocki and the secrets of the Grand Hotel”. It claimed, based on information provided by unnamed former colleagues of the future president, that he had “participated in bringing prostitutes for guests of the Grand Hotel in Sopot while working there as a security guard” almost 20 years earlier. Onet said that its interlocutors wished to remain anonymous for their own safety, but had expressed their willingness to testify in court if required. The revelations caused a major scandal, but were vigorously denied by Nawrocki, a conservative candidate aligned with the right-wing opposition, who called them a “pack of lies”. He then went on to narrowly defeat Trzaskowski in the election. Conservative presidential candidate @NawrockiKn says he will sue news website @onetpl for claims it published today that he procured prostitutes for clients at a luxury hotel when working there as a security guard. He called the report "a bunch of lies" https://t.co/WZ4rZWfFT1 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 26, 2025 Nawrocki then sued Ringier Axel Springer Polska (RASP), the Polish subsidiary of a German-Swiss media house that owns Onet, demanding an apology. RASP stood by Onet, saying that its reporting was “factual”. At today’s hearing, one of Onet’s sources, Natasza Geldon, who worked at the hotel in 2006 and 2007, was questioned. She said that, one evening, she had noticed Nawrocki leading a man and a woman into the hotel, before then taking only the woman into a lift and returning alone. This had struck her as unusual, because staff were not supposed to escort guests into the hotel, “let alone take them upstairs”, said Geldon, quoted by broadcaster TVP. “When Karol came back downstairs, I asked him what was going on,” continued the witness. “He said it was possible to make some extra money by bringing girls in, and asked if I wanted to join in.” Geldon refused the offer, telling the court that, “as a young girl, 19 years old, I had the impression that a pimp had been coming in with a prostitute”. However, when asked to confirm if she had seen prostitutes in the hotel, Geldon said: “I don’t know. It’s hard to say. It was just that one incident.” A second witness, Łukasz Franczak, described as a longtime friend of Nawrocki who worked alongside him in security at the Grand Hotel, also gave evidence on Tuesday after being called by Nawrocki’s legal team. He testified that there had been prostitutes in the hotel. However, he added that he had not heard of any organised operation to supply them to guests; nor had he witnessed Nawrocki procuring prostitutes or discussing payment for them, reported Onet from the hearing. Franczak’s testimony was welcomed by Nawrocki’s former national security advisor, Sławomir Cenckiewicz, who said that it showed that those making claims against the president have no evidence of his involvement in any wrongdoing. Oni się wszyscy teraz nakręcają jak szaleni, nie czytając tego co sami piszą na własnej stronie… No i dowiedzieli się dzisiaj, że w hotelach bywają prostytutki 🙂 A ja to wszystko czytam na bieżąco, a tam słynny Łukasz z Gdańska, ulubiony świadek-historyk Antka Dudka, i… https://t.co/9sKGZT4PpD — Sławomir Cenckiewicz (@Cenckiewicz) October 27, 2026 RASP’s lawyers have called for Nawrocki himself to testify in the case. The president’s legal team wanted him to provide his testimony in writing, according to Onet. But on Tuesday, judge Aleksandra Orzechowska ordered Nawrocki to give testimony directly – either in person or remotely – at the next hearing, which is scheduled for 18 January 2027, reports broadcaster TVN. World.title: Polish far-right leader charged over confrontation with abortion doctor and inciting hatred against Jews
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Polish far-right leader Grzegorz Braun has been charged with six alleged crimes, including inciting hatred against Jews and vandalising an LGBT+ exhibition. The other four allegations relate to an incident in which he confronted a doctor who performed a late-term abortion. The charges are the latest in a long line of legal cases against Braun, who is already on trial for attacking a Jewish ceremony in Poland’s parliament. However, his party continues to poll strongly, and may play a significant role in deciding what kind of government is formed after next year’s elections. Do sześciu razy sztuka. Grzegorz Braun dostał zarzuty, w tym za uwięzienie ginekolożki Gizeli Jagielskiej Wcześniej europoseł Grzegorz Braun pięć razy unikał przedstawienia zarzutów w Prokuraturze Okręgowej we Wrocławiu. Zainterweniował Prokurator Generalny Waldemar Żurek.… — Bartosz T. Wieliński 🇵🇱🇪🇺🇺🇦🇬🇱 (@Bart_Wielinski) October 26, 2026 As a member of the European Parliament, Braun enjoys legal immunity from prosecution. However, in November 2025, the EP stripped him of immunity to face the six charges. Subsequently, prosecutors tried five times to present Braun with the charges. However, he evaded those attempts by filing motions to have prosecutors excluded from the case or simply by leaving the prosecutor’s office before the charges were read. In July, Poland’s justice minister and prosecutor general, Waldemar Żurek, filed a motion to the EP for permission to forcibly detain Braun and present him with the charges. That application has not yet been considered but, on Monday, Braun finally attended the prosecutor’s office and heard the charges. Afterwards, Braun told a small group of his followers and the media outside the office in Wrocław that he was the victim of a “state lynching” carried out by “the prosecutor’s office of the Hanukkah cannibals, racists and genocide perpetrators”. Four of the charges against Braun relate to an incident in April 2025, when he entered a hospital and confronted a gynaecologist who had been involved in a late-term abortion that had drawn controversy and condemnation from right-wing groups. Braun claimed he was carrying out a citizen’s arrest, but is now charged with deprivation of liberty (for preventing the doctor from leaving her office), violating bodily integrity (by pushing her and holding her down), as well as insult and slander. The maximum sentence for those crimes is five years in prison. In separate proceedings, prosecutors later found that the doctor had not violated Poland’s strict abortion laws by terminating the pregnancy in the ninth month. The fifth charge Braun is now facing stems from an infamous incident in December 2023, when he attacked a Jewish Hanukkah celebration in parliament, putting out the candles with a fire extinguisher. Braun is already on trial over the incident itself. Now, however, prosecutors have charged him over a YouTube interview he gave shortly after the attack, in which they say he “described Hanukkah as a Satanic and racist celebration posing a threat to Polish Catholics, which should be counteracted”. For those remarks, he has been hit with a joint charge of inciting religious hatred and the obstruction of religious acts. The maximum penalty for those offences is a three-year jail term. Finally, Braun has been charged with destruction of property for an incident during his presidential campaign in March this year when he vandalised an exhibition about the local LGBT+ community in the city of Opole, spray-painting “stop the propaganda of perversion” on it. Police are investigating far-right presidential candidate and MEP Grzegorz Braun after he vandalised an LGBT+ exhibition. The city where it took place immediately cancelled a meeting he was due to hold there and is seeking compensation for the damage https://t.co/EbDpMzmpFw — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 20, 2025 Braun has pleaded not guilty to all the charges against him, as he has done with a string of other charges for various offences relating to his antisemitic, anti-Ukrainian and anti-LGBT rhetoric and actions. In September, he was stripped of immunity by the EP for the sixth time in order to hear charges of Holocaust denial for his claims that the gas chambers in the Nazi-German death camp of Auschwitz are “fake”. Braun’s high-profile stunts have seen his popularity surge among a section of the electorate. He finished a surprise fourth in last year’s Polish presidential election, with over 6% of the vote, and his Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP) party is now polling around 9%. If it manages to secure that level of support at next autumn’s parliamentary elections, KKP could become a key player in deciding what kind of government can be formed after what looks likely to be a very close contest between the ruling coalition, which ranges from left to centre right, and the right-wing and far-right opposition. Poland and Vietnam have upgraded their ties to a strategic partnership, pledging to deepen cooperation in trade and investment, security and defence, as well as education, science, technology and cultural exchanges. “Vietnam and Poland share a success story in terms of development,” declared Prime Minister Donald Tusk at a joint press conference with his Vietnamese counterpart Lê Minh Hưng in Hanoi on Monday. “The time has come to turn our successes into joint actions that will open up more opportunities.” The announcement comes amid a broader flurry of Polish diplomacy in Asia, with Tusk arriving in Hanoi following a visit to India and President Karol Nawrocki visiting the Philippines earlier this month. Poland also recently signed new strategic agreements with South Korea and Japan. 🇵🇱🤝🇻🇳 Polska i Wietnam wchodzą na poziom partnerstwa strategicznego! ✅ Podczas wizyty w Hanoi premier @donaldtusk oraz szef wietnamskiego rządu Lê Minh Hưng podjęli decyzję o podniesieniu wzajemnych relacji do rangi partnerstwa strategicznego, otwierając nowy rozdział we… pic.twitter.com/CCvHmc3eva — Kancelaria Premiera (@PremierRP) October 26, 2026 Tusk, who was making the first visit by a Polish prime minister to Vietnam in 16 years, pointed to the two countries’ rapid recent economic development. “Within a single generation, Vietnam achieved middle-income status”, while “Poland recently joined the ranks of the world’s 20 largest economies”. In fact, while Poland was forecast to join the world’s 20 largest economies last year, it eventually fell narrowly short. However, it is expected to soon overtake Switzerland, the current holder of 20th place. Tusk said that, during his visit, he had often heard people say that “Poland is the Vietnam of Europe and Vietnam is the Poland of Asia”. Last year, Hưng’s predecessor, Phạm Minh Chính, became the first Vietnamese prime minister in 15 years to visit Poland. The two countries first established diplomatic relations in 1950, and both leaders emphasised Poland’s large Vietnamese community, which dates back to students arriving around that time. Speaking on Monday, Hưng noted the two countries’ strong traditional ties, adding that Vietnam always remembers and is grateful for Polish support and assistance during his country’s struggle for independence and national reunification, reports the Vietnamese News Agency (VNA). The Vietnamese are Poland's largest non-European migrant group. Photographer Zula Rabikowska, through her images and interviews, offers an insight into their experiences, identities and the challenges they face https://t.co/tsRwHINapQ — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) December 27, 2019 The new strategic partnership agreement signed by Tusk and Hưng pledges to “bring tangible benefits to both nations and contribute to peace, stability, cooperation and prosperity”. It contains commitments to “maintain regular high-level contacts”, reduce non-tariff barriers to trade, and strengthen cooperation on defence, including trade in military equipment. On Sunday, Poland’s deputy minister for state assets, Konrad Gołota, told the Polish Press Agency (PAP) that negotiations are already underway for Vietnam to buy Polish Krab howitzers and Rosomak armoured fighting vehicles, among other hardware. Polish arms firm Mesko has announced the best financial results in its 100-year history. Record revenues and profits were driven in large part by international demand for Mesko's flagship Piorun air-defence system, which has proved successful in Ukraine https://t.co/Dx1yY54qCP — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) April 16, 2026 Tusk, pointing to Poland’s current trade deficit with Vietnam, said that Warsaw’s “priority remains a better balance in trade”. “The sectors in which the Vietnamese side is most interested, and in which we really have something to offer, are the arms industry, satellite and space cooperation, pharmaceuticals and food, especially dairy products,” he added. Tusk also announced that the number of annual Polish-Vietnamese student exchanges would rise by 250% and noted that Poland’s national carrier, LOT, would resume direct Warsaw-Hanoi flights in the first quarter of 2027. Poland is taking steps to attract more foreign students as universities face lower enrollment due to demographic decline. Turkey, South Korea, Vietnam and Uzbekistan are among the countries with which the government is cultivating stronger academic ties https://t.co/r878KqS5OV — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) April 25, 2026 The Polish prime minister acknowledged differences between Poland and Vietnam’s approach to Russia’s war in Ukraine. Vietnam, which has long maintained close ties with Moscow, has avoided condemning the Russian invasion. But he emphasised his belief that, “because of their history, wartime experience and international relations, both Vietnam and Poland can contribute a great deal to the peace process”. Tusk’s trip to Vietnam follows a three-day visit to India, where he and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi announced a goal of doubling bilateral trade by 2030. Poland and India's PMs have, after meeting in New Delhi, outlined aims to double bilateral trade by 2030 and expand cooperation in mining, shipbuilding, energy, space and defence technologies Polish-Indian relations are "gaining speed", said @narendramodi https://t.co/iIVIkCXnvr — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 22, 2026 In April, Tusk visited South Korea, upgrading Poland’s relations with the country he described as Poland’s “most important ally after the United States”, and deepened Poland’s strategic partnership with Japan on the same tour. Earlier this month, Tusk also announced plans to visit China before the end of the year. Meanwhile, President Nawrocki visited the Philippines this month as part of a bid to secure backing from Asian nations for Poland’s hoped-for membership in the G20. World.title: Two thirds of Poles support liberalising abortion law, finds new poll
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Just over two thirds of Poles support liberalising the country’s abortion law, which is among the strictest in Europe, according to a new poll. However, most do not favour introducing abortion on demand, as protesters called for during demonstrations last week. The findings come shortly after parliament approved legislation intended to ease access to abortion. But the measures face a potential veto from right-wing, opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki. 🔴 Sondaż dla @rzeczpospolita: Niemal 7 na 10 Polaków chce liberalizacji przepisów ws. aborcjihttps://t.co/f7mxwygIxz — Rzeczpospolita (@rzeczpospolita) October 25, 2026 In 2020, Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal (TK) outlawed abortions in cases where a severe defect is diagnosed in the foetus. That means pregnancies can now only be legally terminated in two cases: where they result from a crime (such as rape or incest) or if they threaten the mother’s life or health. In a new poll by SW Research for Rzeczpospolita, a leading newspaper, a total of 67.2% of respondents said that they want to liberalise that law. However, only 37.7% favoured introducing abortion on demand up to the 12th week of pregnancy. Meanwhile, 29.5% preferred the softer option of returning to the situation from before the 2020 TK ruling – often referred to the “abortion compromise” in Poland – in which terminations were only available in three cases. A further 16.2% supported maintaining the current abortion law; 6.0% wanted to make the rules even tougher (which would involve removing one or both justifications for abortion that currently exist); and 10.6% said they had no opinion. The poll found that support for liberalisation of abortion was stronger among women (73.8%) than men (60.3%). The latest findings are consistent with previous polling, which tends to show that a significant majority supports liberalising the abortion law but that there is not a majority in favour of abortion on demand (although some individual polls have narrowly found such a majority). One member of Poland's likely new ruling coalition, The Left, says polls show a majority in favour of abortion on demand. In fact, they do not. And this issue is likely to be one of the hardest for the incoming government to resolve, writes @danieltilles1 https://t.co/4Nze9wwEC3 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 20, 2023 The issue has caused significant political disputes in Poland, not only between the right-wing opposition and the more liberal ruling coalition, but also within the coalition itself. Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s centrist Civic Coalition (KO) and one of its partners, The Left (Lewica), favour introducing abortion on demand. However, more conservative elements of the government, especially the centre-right Polish People’s Party (PSL), prefer a return to the pre-2020 “compromise”. Much of the right-wing opposition, meanwhile, favours maintaining the status quo. However, some more moderate elements of the opposition have suggested it would be best to reverse the TK ruling and return to the “compromise”. Protests took place in towns and cities around Poland on Thursday evening, demanding that the government fulfil its promise to liberalise the country’s strict abortion laws https://t.co/q7eK7mV9zr — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 23, 2026 In 2024, due to disputes within his coalition, Tusk declared that it was unlikely there would be any abortion reform during the current parliamentary term due to differences within his coalition. However, last week the issue was revived, with the government’s majority in the Sejm, the lower house of parliament, approving a bill that would reverse the 2020 TK ruling (but not introduce abortion on demand). It also passed another bill decriminalising providing help to women in obtaining unlawful abortions. After both bills go through the upper-house Senate, which can suggest amendments but not block them, they will pass to President Nawrocki, who can sign them, veto them, or send them to the TK for assessment. Given that Nawrocki is aligned with the right-wing opposition, has declared his opposition to abortion, and has vetoed a record number of government bills, it is widely expected that he will seek to block efforts to liberalise the abortion law. World.title: Guitar Legend Carlos Santana to Return to Czech Republic in 2027
World.content:
Legendary guitarist Carlos Santana will return to the Czech Republic on July 22, 2027, for an outdoor concert in the Castle Gardens of Slavkov u Brna, near Brno.

The ten-time Grammy Award winner will perform as part of his Planet of Free Will Global Tour 2027, bringing more than five decades of music to the Czech audience.

Known for blending rock, blues, jazz and Latin rhythms, Santana has built a distinctive sound that has influenced generations of musicians and listeners.



His performance at the 1969 Woodstock festival helped establish him as an international star, while early albums such as Santana*(1969) and Abraxas (1970) produced classics including “Evil Ways,” “Black Magic Woman” and “Oye Como Va.”

Santana reached another career milestone with the 1999 album Supernatural, which featured collaborations with artists including Rob Thomas. The record became a global hit, spawning the singles “Smooth” and “Maria Maria” and winning nine Grammy Awards, including Album of the Year.

Over his career, Santana has received ten Grammy Awards and three Latin Grammy Awards. He was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 1998, received the Kennedy Center Honors and was ranked 11th on *Rolling Stone* magazine’s list of the 100 greatest guitarists of all time.

Despite his long career, Santana continues to release new music and perform internationally. His live shows are known for extended guitar solos, Latin-inspired rhythms and a mix of classic hits and newer material.

Tickets will cost CZK 2,000, plus booking fees.

General ticket sales start on October 30, 2026, at noon, through Ticketmaster and Ticketportal.

World.title: Prague Metronome Lets People Donate to Charity for Just 50 CZK
World.content:
Prague’s Metronome is taking on a charitable role through a new initiative that allows people to pay for a minute of illumination while supporting one of six nonprofit organizations.

The project, called Puls města (City Pulse), was launched by real estate company PSN, which operates the landmark on Letná Hill. Donations start at 50 Czech crowns, and participants can choose which organization they want to support.



The new initiative connects its lighting system with fundraising, allowing members of the public to contribute through the project’s website.

Six Colors, Six Charitable Causes

Each participating organization is represented by a different color. Red supports the Tereza Maxová Foundation for Children, while light blue represents the Kapka naděje (Drop of Hope) Endowment Fund.

Yellow is associated with Díky, že můžem, an initiative focused on civic engagement and democratic values. Pink represents Pink Crocodile, dark blue supports the AutTalk Endowment Fund, founded by Kateřina Sokolová, and green is dedicated to the Fund for Endangered Children.

Visitors can select a cause and make a contribution directly through the project’s website.

Donations Start at 50 CZK

Contributions range from 50 to 9,999 CZK. Regardless of the amount donated, each payment purchases exactly one minute of illumination. A larger contribution therefore does not extend the lighting time.

The website also displays the amount raised for each organization, allowing donors to follow the campaign’s progress. A virtual queue shows when each participant’s turn is scheduled, with the expected time provided after payment.

World.title: Prague’s Golden Eye to Host Japanese Brunch With Live Chef Demonstrations
World.content:
Prague’s Golden Eye bar at Fairmont Hotel is hosting a Japanese-inspired brunch combining traditional ceremonies, live sushi preparation, premium food and signature cocktails.

The afternoon will begin with Kagami Biraki, a traditional Japanese sake barrel-opening ceremony often associated with celebrations and new beginnings.



Guests will then be able to watch a live tuna carving, one of the event’s main attractions.

The programme will also include omakase bites, with chefs preparing sushi at a live station. Guests can pair the food with signature cocktails and a curated selection of wines throughout the afternoon.

A live DJ will provide the soundtrack, adding music to the Japanese-inspired dining experience.

The event is designed exclusively for adults, with tickets priced at CZK 7,900 per person. Full prepayment is required to secure a booking.

Reservations can be made through Golden Eye’s online booking page.

World.title: Hip-Hop Star Xzibit Coming to Prague’s Roxy on November 17
World.content:
West Coast rap legend Xzibit will perform at Prague’s ROXY on November 17, bringing his show featuring tracks from his latest album and some of his best-known hits.

Presented by Gotobeat and Enjoy Events, the show will feature music from *Kingmaker*, alongside career highlights including “X,” “Multiply,” “Paparazzi” and “What’s the Difference.”



Xzibit returns with new album Kingmaker

A major name in West Coast hip-hop since the 1990s, Xzibit built his reputation through his distinctive deep voice, forceful delivery and collaborations with some of the genre’s biggest artists.

His albums Restless, Man vs. Machine and Weapons of Mass Destruction helped establish him as one of the defining rappers of his generation. His work with Dr. Dre, Eminem, Snoop Dogg and Ice Cube further cemented his place in hip-hop, while his television career brought him to a wider audience as the host of MTV’s Pimp My Ride.

Released on May 16, 2025, Kingmaker marked Xzibit’s first solo studio album since 2012.

The 20-track record brings together established names and newer voices, with guest appearances from Dr. Dre, Ice Cube, Busta Rhymes, Ty Dolla $ign, Royce da 5’9”, Redman and B-Real.

The album combines the sound that made Xzibit famous with a more contemporary production style, reflecting on his decades in the music industry while introducing his work to a new generation of listeners.

World.title: From Takumi to Gonta, a New Chapter for Japanese Food in Prague
World.content:
For those craving a taste of Japan without leaving Prague, Takumi offers a chance to explore Japanese cuisine in the heart of the city.

Located behind Quadrio, near the moving head sculpture of Franz Kafka, the restaurant recently celebrated its first anniversary this September.

We spoke with co-owner Euntaek Kim about the restaurant’s history, his journey to Prague, and his latest project, Gonta, a Japanese tonkatsu restaurant.



From Korea to Prague

The Takumi franchise was founded in Düsseldorf, Germany, in 2007 by Haruhiko Saeki and Kenjiro Komatsubara. Kim and his business partner, Viet Hung Phung, later partnered with the founders to bring Takumi Ramen to Prague, opening their first branch on Senovážné náměstí in 2019.

Kim’s connection to the restaurant business began long before that. Before he moved to Prague, his uncle owned several Hanil restaurants in Vienna and planned to expand into the Czech market. This led Kim’s family to move to Prague in 2000, when he was just 12 years old.

Later, Kim and his sister took over the Hanil restaurant their parents had run. He eventually sold it to a Korean chef he had worked with for several years.

Over time, Prague became much more than a place to do business.

“Prague has become like my second home. After having lived here for almost 26 years, I feel connected to its culture as well as my own Korean culture. In business settings and everyday life, I always try to find a balance between both,” Kim says.

His decision to open a Japanese restaurant was driven by what he saw as a gap in Prague’s dining scene.

“I felt like something was missing in Prague. Previously, Asian cuisine was close to nonexistent here. I wanted to make a change,” he explains.

Since moving to Prague, Kim has noticed growing interest in Asian food and culture among local residents, reflecting the city’s changing culinary landscape.

Introducing Gonta, a Japanese Tonkatsu Restaurant

Kim’s latest project, Gonta, brings another Japanese specialty to Prague. Located at Jungmannova 750/34, near Můstek metro station, the restaurant focuses on tonkatsu, a Japanese dish made with breaded, deep-fried pork cutlets, typically served with rice and a tangy sauce.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Gonta Prague (@tonkatsugonta.prague)

“When people think about Japanese cuisine, most people tend to think of sushi or ramen. Tonkatsu is a delicious dish that has not yet reached Prague. I craved it a lot,” Kim says, explaining what inspired him to launch Gonta.

The restaurant is scheduled to open in October 2026, adding another option to Prague’s growing selection of Japanese dining spots.

World.title: Why October 28 Is a National Holiday in the Czech Republic
World.content:
October 28th is Czechoslovak Independence Day, marking the establishment of Czechoslovakia in 1918.

Although Czechoslovakia peacefully split into the Czech Republic and Slovakia in 1993, October 28 remains one of the most important dates in Czech history.

It commemorates the struggle for independence and the emergence of modern Czech statehood. It should not be confused with Czech Statehood Day, celebrated on September 28.



Why Czechoslovakia Declared Independence in 1918

Before 1918, the Czech lands and present-day Slovakia were part of the Austro-Hungarian Empire.

Bohemia, Moravia and part of Silesia belonged to the Austrian half of the monarchy, while Slovakia was part of Hungary. For decades, Czech and Slovak political leaders had sought greater autonomy and the right to determine their own future.

World War I, which began in 1914, weakened the empire and intensified nationalist movements. Food shortages, economic difficulties and growing public discontent increased support for an independent state.

Politicians working abroad played a crucial role in the independence movement. Tomáš Garrigue Masaryk, Edvard Beneš and Milan Rastislav Štefánik coordinated diplomatic efforts to win support from the Allied powers. France, Great Britain and the United States recognised the Czechoslovak National Council as a provisional government in 1918.

Czechoslovak legions also fought on several fronts during the war, including in France, Italy and Russia, helping draw international attention to the independence movement.

How Independence Was Declared

On October 18, 1918, Masaryk issued the Declaration of Independence of Czechoslovakia in the United States, known as the Washington Declaration. It outlined the ambition to establish a democratic state based on the right of the Czechs and Slovaks to self-determination.

The decisive events took place in Prague on October 28, as news spread that Austria-Hungary had agreed to armistice terms. Many people interpreted the reports as a sign that the empire was collapsing and gathered in public squares to celebrate.

The Czech National Committee took control and issued the first law establishing an independent Czechoslovak state. October 28 subsequently became the official date of its founding.

Who Founded the New State?

Masaryk became Czechoslovakia’s first president after independence. A philosopher, educator and politician, he had spent years persuading foreign governments to support the creation of a new state.

Beneš was instrumental in diplomatic negotiations and later served as foreign minister and president. Štefánik, a Slovak politician, astronomer and military officer, helped organise the Czechoslovak legions and strengthen cooperation between the Czech and Slovak independence movements.

Politicians working in Prague, including Alois Rašín, Karel Kramář and Antonín Švehla, also helped organise the transfer of power.

What Happened After 1918?

During the interwar period, Czechoslovakia became a parliamentary republic with one of Central Europe’s most developed industrial economies. However, tensions between its different national communities presented ongoing challenges.

In 1938, the Munich Agreement led to the loss of the Sudetenland. Nazi Germany occupied the Czech lands in March 1939, while Slovakia became a separate state aligned with Berlin. Czechoslovakia was restored after World War II but later came under communist rule.

The Velvet Revolution ended communist rule in 1989. On January 1, 1993, Czechoslovakia peacefully split into two independent countries.

World.title: Where to Celebrate Halloween in Prague: 6 Events for Children and Adults
World.content:
Prague will mark Halloween 2026 with events for children and adults, ranging from pumpkin carving and lantern parades to costume competitions and late-night club parties.

Here are some of the events planned across Prague, including admission prices where available.

Blackout Halloween Rave at SaSaZu

Blackout Events will hold its first Halloween rave on Tuesday, October 27, at SaSaZu, bringing hard techno, Halloween costumes and stage productions to the Prague club.

The lineup includes WYNTER at 9 p.m., HOOOR at 10:30 p.m., A.N.I. at midnight, NOTMYTYPE at 1:30 a.m. and KLAR at 3 a.m. The event is scheduled to finish at 4 a.m.

An afterparty will follow at Club Mecca in Holešovice from 3 a.m. The event is restricted to visitors aged 18 and over. Organizers say further program details will be published on Blackout Events’ Instagram account.

Halloween at Hybernia Theatre

Hybernia Theatre, near Náměstí Republiky, is also listed as a venue for a Halloween electronic music event. The program is set to combine electronic music, Halloween decorations and the historic theatre’s interior.

Italian DJ SPADA is announced as a special guest. Admission is listed at CZK 499, although the event date should be confirmed with the organizer before publication.

Spooks at Žluté lázně

Žluté lázně in Podolí will host a Halloween afternoon on Saturday, October 31, from 1 p.m. to 7 p.m.

Children can follow a spooky trail featuring a spiderweb tunnel, a mysterious castle and a series of challenges. The program will also include pumpkin carving, face painting and dancing.

The organizers will announce the winner of the best-costume competition at 6:10 p.m. Admission costs CZK 150, while children wearing costumes can enter for free. Pumpkins for carving will be available for CZK 100.

Halloween Among Dinosaurs at DinoPark Harfa

DinoPark on the rooftop of Galerie Harfa will offer Halloween activities on Saturday, October 31, including a trail where children can complete tasks among the dinosaurs.

The afternoon program will feature Stegoušek Kvído, a walking dinosaur character who will lead two lantern parades, at 4 p.m. and 5 p.m. Visitors should bring their own lanterns.

DinoPark will be open from 9 a.m. to 6 p.m. Children in Halloween costumes can enter for CZK 50.

Pumpkin Carving at the Public Transport Museum

The Public Transport Museum in Střešovice will combine Halloween activities with a look at Prague’s historic trams and buses on Saturday, October 31.

Visitors can carve pumpkins and explore the museum’s collection of historic vehicles. Those arriving in costume will receive a gift.

At 4:45 p.m., the carved pumpkins will be lit in the museum courtyard. The museum will be open from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m.

Bloody Sexy Halloween Returns to SaSaZu

Bloody Sexy Halloween will return to SaSaZu on Friday, October 30, and Saturday, October 31, for two nights of music, performances and themed productions.

Founded in 2009, the event has become one of the region’s established Halloween parties, attracting more than 4,000 visitors in previous editions, according to the organizers.

One of the weekend’s main attractions is the Bloody Sexy Costume Contest. Participants can register at SaSaZu between 9 p.m. and midnight. Costumes are judged on creativity, originality and presentation, with the winner selected by audience applause at midnight and awarded CZK 40,000.

World.title: Thirty Seconds to Mars to Play Prague in 2027 With Special Album Tour
World.content:
Thirty Seconds to Mars will return to Prague on May 18, 2027, for a concert at the O2 arena.

The Jared and Shannon Leto-led band will revisit two of its best-known albums, A Beautiful Lie and This Is War, as part of a special world tour.

The American rock band will perform without an opening act, with the show expected to last approximately two hours. Tickets start at CZK 1,500, excluding ticketing fees, and VIP packages will also be available.



The concert is part of the band’s A Beautiful Lie vs This Is War tour, which focuses on two records that helped establish Thirty Seconds to Mars as a major name in alternative rock.

Tickets will be available through Ticketmaster and Ticketportal from October 30, 2026, at 10 a.m. Fan club members will have access to a presale beginning October 27 at 10 a.m. Live Nation, Spotify and O2 presales will follow on October 29 at 10 a.m.

Two albums that defined the band’s sound

Released in 2005, A Beautiful Lie marked a turning point in the band’s career, bringing its music to a much wider international audience. The album features some of Thirty Seconds to Mars’ best-known songs, including The Kill, From Yesterday and the title track.

The follow-up, This Is War, arrived in 2009 and expanded that sound. Tracks such as Kings and Queens, This Is War and Closer to the Edge became signature songs, helping the band reach a broader audience.

From alternative rock to global tours

Led by brothers Jared Leto, the band’s vocalist, and Shannon Leto, its drummer, the group continued to develop its sound on Love, Lust, Faith and Dreams in 2013 and America in 2018. The latter included the singles Walk on Water and Rescue Me.

In 2023, the band released its sixth studio album, It’s the End of the World but It’s a Beautiful Day, exploring a different musical direction while maintaining its focus on melody and emotional themes.

The band has also received several MTV awards and a Billboard Music Award. Its touring history includes a Guinness World Records recognition for the longest concert tour.

The 2027 tour will take Thirty Seconds to Mars across Europe, the United Kingdom, South Africa and other destinations. Its Prague stop will bring the band’s anniversary celebrations and catalogue of established hits to the Czech capital for a show centred on two of its most influential albums.

World.title: European Commission approves Hungary’s EUR multi-billion defence plan
World.content:
The European Commission has approved Hungary’s EUR 5.4 billion defence investment plan under the European Union’s Security Action for Europe (SAFE) programme, paving the way for the proposal to be considered by EU member states.

Hungary to boost defence capabilities

Thomas Regnier, a spokesperson for the European Commission, announced the decision at a press briefing on Wednesday, confirming that Hungary’s plan was the last national proposal under the programme awaiting approval. The Commission’s decision endorses the EUR 5.4 billion allocation proposed for Hungary.

The plan will now be submitted to the Council of the European Union, which represents the bloc’s member states, for approval. Regnier added that, following the approval of the Hungarian governments’s plan, just over EUR 21 billion could remain available under the programme. The Commission is expected to contact member states at a later stage regarding the allocation of the remaining funds.

Stay up-to-date with Hungary Weekly Briefing: subscribe on Substack!

What is the SAFE programme?

The SAFE initiative is a EUR 150 billion EU lending scheme designed to strengthen Europe’s defence capabilities. It provides member states with access to favourable, long-term loans to finance defence investments and joint procurement projects. The programme aims to help European countries expand their military capabilities and support cooperation in defence procurement.

Hungary’s allocation is significantly lower than the EUR 16 billion in loans previously envisaged for the country. The government subsequently reduced its planned borrowing to EUR 5.4 billion, reflecting a more cautious approach to taking on additional debt. Hungary is not the only member state seeking less than its initially allocated amount. Other countries have also decided not to use their full potential allocations, leaving funds available for redistribution.

In case you missed it: Former service villa of Hungary’s defence minister cost EUR 1 million more than previously estimated

Further funding round expected

The European Commission is planning another application round for the unallocated funds later this year. The unused amounts must be offered again in 2026 or risk being lost under the programme’s timetable. Hungarian Defence Minister Romulusz Ruszin-Szendi said in September that decisions on SAFE borrowing should take account of the country’s economic capacity, stressing that the money would have to be repaid.

He also suggested the loans could be used to cover existing defence contracts or bring forward investments originally planned for later years. These could include projects related to transport infrastructure and cybersecurity, in addition to defence spending. Although the Commission has endorsed Hungary’s EUR multi-billion plan, the proposal must still pass through the Council before the next steps can proceed.

World.title: Hungary to tighten electric scooter regulations in new Highway Code reform
World.content:
Hungary is planning stricter rules for electric scooters, including minimum age limits, compulsory helmets and driving licence requirements for more powerful models.

Electric scooters will be regulated more strictly

Prime Minister Péter Magyar outlined the proposals in a video posted on Facebook on Wednesday. He said the government intended to submit the planned regulations to public consultation again before their formal adoption.

Under the government’s proposed Highway Code reform, e-scooters would become a separate vehicle category, with riding under the influence of alcohol and carrying passengers both prohibited. The changes follow growing concerns about accidents involving these type of vehicles.

According to figures cited in Hungarian reports, the number of e-scooter accidents resulting in personal injuries rose by 73 per cent between 2024 and 2025, increasing from 367 to 635.

Magyar said the government did not believe an outright ban was the answer, describing electric scooters as a potentially efficient and sustainable form of transport. Instead, the aim is to establish clearer rules and improve road safety.

Stay up-to-date with Hungary Weekly Briefing: subscribe on Substack!

Two categories based on speed

Under the proposed system, electric scooters would be divided into two categories according to their maximum speed. Low-powered scooters, capable of travelling at no more than 25 km/h, could be used from the age of 14. Riders under 18 would have to wear a helmet.

High-powered scooters, capable of exceeding 25 km/h, would be subject to stricter requirements. Riders would need to be at least 16 and hold a driving licence of at least AM category, which covers mopeds. Helmets would be compulsory for all users, and the vehicles’ maximum permitted speed would be 40 km/h.

Rental electric scooters would face a separate speed limit of 20 km/h. The proposed rules would also restrict where these vehicles can be ridden. High-powered models would be banned from pavements altogether. Low-powered ones could use pavements only where no alternative route, such as a cycle path, was available.

In case you missed it: Hungary’s new expressway opens – Drivers can use it for free for now!

Public consultation before adoption

The government says the reform follows public consultation and research into transport safety. According to Magyar, more than 360,000 people completed a road safety questionnaire launched during the summer, while a representative opinion poll was also conducted.

The prime minister said members of the public and transport experts broadly agreed that e-scooter regulation was urgently needed. The proposals have not yet become final law. The government plans to hold another public consultation before formally announcing the amended Highway Code.

If adopted as outlined, the changes would introduce a more structured legal framework for electric scooters in Hungary, placing greater responsibility on riders and imposing additional requirements on those using faster models.

World.title: Hungary reveals plan to revive economic growth and prepare for the euro by 2030
World.content:
Hungary’s government has unveiled a four-year economic and budgetary plan aimed at accelerating growth, cutting the budget deficit and preparing the country for eurozone membership by 2030. The Finance Ministry expects economic growth to pick up gradually, reaching 3.1% by the end of the decade, while promising to rein in wasteful public spending.

Government targets deficit reduction and eurozone readiness

The Finance Ministry published its medium-term economic and budgetary programme on Wednesday morning, setting out the government’s plans for the 2027–2030 period.

According to the document, the government is committed to responsible and sustainable fiscal policy. Its first major target is to bring the budget deficit below 5% of GDP in 2027, followed by establishing the conditions necessary for Hungary to join the eurozone by 2030.

The government says deficit reduction is essential to restoring stability and intends to achieve it primarily by cutting wasteful and overpriced operating expenditure across the state sector.

It also plans to replace corporate subsidies deemed inefficient with targeted programmes financed by EU funds. The government expects this approach to deliver budgetary savings while reducing incentives for rent-seeking and supporting a new growth model based on productivity.

If you missed it: Hungary’s euro ambitions face a major test: Why joining by 2032 could prove difficult

Economic growth expected to accelerate by 2030

The programme broadly matches the figures presented last week by Finance Minister András Kármán at a joint press conference with Prime Minister Péter Magyar.

The government forecasts that Hungary’s GDP will grow by 1.7% in 2026 before accelerating over the following years, reaching 3.1% in 2030.

Inflation is expected to rise from a forecast 1.7% this year to 3% in 2027, before easing to 2.5% in each of the following three years.

The ministry’s projections are somewhat more cautious than market consensus and slightly below the National Bank of Hungary’s earlier growth forecasts.

In its September inflation report, published before the budget plans were presented, the central bank forecast GDP growth of 2.9% in 2027 and 2.8% in 2028. It also projected inflation of 3.1% in 2027 and 2.6% in 2028.

Stay up-to-date with Hungary Weekly Briefing: subscribe on Substack!

Why Hungary needs a new growth model

According to Telex, the government argues that the economic model that powered Hungary’s rapid growth during the 2010s has run out of steam.

Growth during that decade relied heavily on bringing more workers and capital into production. By the 2020s, however, the pool of readily available labour had dwindled and investment had weakened. As a result, productivity growth has lagged significantly behind that of regional competitors since 2010.

Between 2015 and 2025, Hungary’s annual economic growth was more than one percentage point lower on average than Poland’s, according to the programme. The document attributes this entire gap to weaker domestic productivity growth.

It also identifies an uneven competitive environment and incentives for rent-seeking as factors that have undermined the efficient use of resources. Capital and other resources have not consistently flowed towards the most productive sectors and businesses.

Public spending is another area the government wants to reform. According to the ministry, running the state costs the equivalent of 1–1.7 percentage points of GDP more than in neighbouring countries in the region. State intervention in the economy also accounts for around three percentage points of GDP more than the regional benchmark.

At the same time, areas considered important for long-term growth, including social protection and healthcare, have been underfunded, the document argues.

Image generated by artificial intelligence.

Investment and exports expected to play a bigger role

Household consumption has been the main driver of economic growth in recent years. The government expects investment and exports to make a more substantial contribution from 2027 onwards.

EU funding is expected to support a recovery in investment, while fairer market competition and structural reforms should improve the productivity of Hungarian businesses.

The government’s strategy therefore aims to shift the economy away from a model driven primarily by expanding the workforce and consumption towards one in which productivity, investment and exports play a greater role.

Whether these targets can be achieved will depend on the pace of the planned reforms, the recovery in investment and the availability of EU funding. The programme sets out the government’s intended direction, rather than guaranteeing that Hungary will meet its 2030 eurozone objective.

World.title: Vučić allegedly considered a coup after election defeat – Did Orbán help stop him?
World.content:
Serbia’s leader Aleksandar Vučić, who conceded defeat on 28 October, was reportedly prepared to use force to cling to power after his election defeat, but backed down following calls from European leaders, according to British newspaper The Times. Unconfirmed reports have suggested that Hungary’s former prime minister Viktor Orbán may have been among those who persuaded him to concede.

Vučić’s political camp suffered a major defeat in Sunday’s snap parliamentary election, with the student-backed Student List securing a decisive victory. Vučić subsequently acknowledged the result, saying it was clear his side had lost. Preliminary official results put the Student List on 52.71% of the vote, compared with 39.17% for the list led by Vučić.

Thousands of police officers and alleged enforcers deployed in Belgrade

According to The Times, around 4,000 police officers and 3,000 alleged regime enforcers were deployed in central Belgrade on Sunday evening. The report claims that the men were expected to help the authorities retain control if the election result went against Vučić.

Spasoje Vulević, the former head of Serbia’s anti-terrorist police unit, told the newspaper he was convinced that Vučić had planned to reject the result.

“I am 100% sure he planned not to recognise the results,” Vulević said, according to The Times.

The report claims the situation changed at around 9.30 PM, approximately 90 minutes after polling stations closed. The men reportedly disappeared from streets that had been closed off, while Vučić subsequently conceded defeat.

However, the allegations have not been independently established. Vučić’s spokeswoman denied that there had been a coup plot, saying the heavy police presence was a response to threats of violence from protesters.

People celebrating on the streets of Belgrade after the Serbian elections on 25 October 2026. Photo: Anadolu Agency

European leaders reportedly intervened

Sandro Gozi, a Member of the European Parliament, told The Times that diplomatic sources had provided alarming information about the possibility of Vučić attempting to seize or retain power by force.

Radomir Saičić, a prominent candidate on the Student List, also claimed that the authorities had considered using force to invalidate the vote if the result was close. He said Vučić had received several phone calls from police officers and other individuals who warned him that carrying out such a plan would end badly.

Former police officer Spasoje Vulević suggested that the decisive calls had come from European governments at the highest level.

The identity of the people who allegedly intervened, however, has not been definitively established.

Did Viktor Orbán persuade Vučić to back down?

Speculation has circulated in Serbian media that Viktor Orbán may have played a role in persuading Vučić to accept defeat. The reports are unconfirmed, and there is no independently verified evidence establishing that Orbán stopped an attempted coup.

Vučić himself confirmed that Orbán had called him after the election defeat. Speaking to Serbian broadcaster Informer TV on Tuesday evening, the former Serbian leader also indicated that the two could meet in Belgrade within days.

“We will fight together, and we will succeed relatively soon,” Vučić said, according to Szeretlek Magyarország.

The planned meeting could attract attention given the close political relationship between the two leaders. Orbán lost power in Hungary in April 2026 after 16 years in government, while Vučić’s political camp has now suffered a major electoral setback in Serbia.

World.title: Hungarian forint pressured by US dollar, holds on against the euro
World.content:
The Hungarian forint remained relatively stable against the euro on Tuesday but weakened against the US dollar as the American currency continued to strengthen on international markets.

US dollar on a hot streak

Rising energy prices also weighed on the euro, while investors awaited key interest rate decisions from the US Federal Reserve and the European Central Bank. Late on Tuesday morning, the euro was trading at around HUF 367, broadly in line with Monday’s closing level. The forint managed a modest recovery during the morning, briefly strengthening towards HUF 366.7.

The picture was less favourable against the dollar. After starting the day at around HUF 328.6, the American currency climbed to approximately HUF 329. By early evening, the forint had recovered some ground against both currencies, with the euro trading at around HUF 366.7 and the dollar at approximately HUF 329.3. As Portfolio claims, the last time the Hungarian currency was this weak against the dollar was under the Orbán government.

Strong dollar puts pressure on European currencies

The dollar’s international rally was the main factor behind the forint’s weaker performance against the American currency. The US dollar index, which measures the greenback against a basket of major currencies, continued to rise following gains on Monday. The euro also lost ground against the dollar, falling by around 0.3 per cent to approximately USD 1.1138. Elevated energy prices may have contributed to the decline.

European natural gas prices approached EUR 100 per megawatt-hour at the start of the week, while Brent crude oil traded close to USD 120 a barrel. As the European Union relies heavily on imported energy, persistently high oil and gas prices increase import costs and can put pressure on the single currency.

Stay up-to-date with Hungary Weekly Briefing: subscribe on Substack!

Investors await central bank decisions

Currency markets could see renewed volatility this week as traders prepare for the Federal Reserve’s interest rate decision on Wednesday and the European Central Bank’s announcement on Thursday. Ahead of major monetary policy decisions, trading activity can ease as investors adjust their positions and wait for signals about the future direction of interest rates. The forint’s relatively narrow trading range on Tuesday may reflect this cautious mood.

Hungarian economic developments could also influence the currency. The government’s forthcoming 2027 budget proposal and the release of preliminary third-quarter GDP figures on Friday are among the domestic events investors will be watching.

In case you missed it: Hungary shuts down bank: What happens to customers’ money?

Fitch says euro adoption remains years away

Meanwhile, Fitch Ratings has suggested that Hungary could introduce the euro no earlier than 2032, provided it makes sustained progress in reducing its budget deficit and meets the necessary conditions. According to the ratings agency, Hungary would need to join the EU’s Exchange Rate Mechanism II in 2029, a key step towards adopting the common currency. Achieving the required fiscal targets and bringing inflation under control remain significant challenges.

Euro adoption could improve Hungary’s sovereign credit standing by removing exchange rate risk and reducing financing costs, Fitch argues. However, substantial fiscal adjustment and greater macroeconomic stability would be needed first. For now, the forint remains caught between a strengthening dollar and a euro facing economic headwinds, with central bank decisions likely to shape its next moves.

World.title: Shop closures in Hungary: what will be open and when?
World.content:
Shops across Hungary will largely close on Sunday, 1 November, for All Saints’ Day, while most retailers will operate as usual on Saturday, 31 October, and Monday, 2 November. Shoppers are advised to plan ahead to avoid finding supermarkets and shopping centre stores closed over the holiday weekend.

Closures due to public holiday

All Saints’ Day is a public holiday in Hungary, meaning most large supermarkets, hypermarkets and shopping centre shops will not open on Sunday. Saturday and the following Monday, however, are normal shopping days, with businesses expected to follow their usual opening hours.

The holiday falls on a Sunday this year, while All Souls’ Day, observed on 2 November, is a regular working day. Schools are also due to resume classes on Monday as the autumn half-term break ends.

Which shops can open on Sunday?

Although most retail outlets will close on 1 November, some businesses are permitted to operate on public holidays. These include petrol stations and their convenience shops, pharmacies operating on an on-call basis, independent florists, newsagents and confectioneries.

According to 24.hu, hospitality and entertainment venues, including restaurants, cafés and cinemas, may also remain open. Some smaller stores can open if the owner personally serves customers, while certain round-the-clock stores may continue trading.

Shopping centres will therefore not necessarily be entirely shut. While their retail units are generally expected to close, cinemas, restaurants and other leisure facilities may still welcome visitors. Customers should check individual businesses’ opening hours before setting out, as arrangements can vary.

Photo: Daily News Hungary

Stay up-to-date with Hungary Weekly Briefing: subscribe on Substack!

Cemetery visits and flower shops

The holiday weekend traditionally brings increased visits to cemeteries, where families remember deceased relatives and friends. Cemeteries and nearby florists may extend their opening hours to accommodate visitors.

Municipal public cemeteries in Budapest are scheduled to remain open from 7 AM to 8 PM between 30 October and 2 November. Opening arrangements elsewhere in the country may differ, so visitors are advised to check locally before travelling.

Independent florists are among the businesses that may open on the public holiday, making it possible to buy flowers and other items for cemetery visits even when supermarkets are closed.

If you have missed it: Budapest traffic restrictions announced for All Saints’ Day weekend – What drivers need to know

Plan shopping before the holiday

Anyone expecting to need groceries, household essentials or other everyday items on Sunday should consider buying them on Saturday. Petrol stations and other permitted retailers can provide alternatives for last-minute purchases, but their ranges may be more limited than those of supermarkets.

With most major stores closed on 1 November, checking local opening hours in advance can help avoid unnecessary journeys during the holiday.

World.title: Spain train crash kills at least 50 as two high-speed trains collide – UPDATE: Victim numbers rise, Magyar reacts
World.content:
Dozens of people were killed Wednesday when two high-speed trains collided in central Spain, according to Spanish public broadcaster RTVE.

Government sources told RTVE that at least 30 people had died. Spanish daily El Espanol reported at least 50 deaths, citing regional government sources.

UPDATE: As of 3 PM local time, El Espanol reports at least 64 victims.

Government sources initially told El Pais they feared the disaster could be “worse than Adamuz,” referring to a January high-speed rail crash in southern Spain that killed 46 people. Authorities have yet to announce an official death toll or injury count.

A view of the crash site after two high-speed trains collided in central Spain, killing dozens of people and injuring many others in Toledo, Spain on 28 October 2026.

Preliminary information from the Transport Ministry suggested a Renfe AVE train struck the rear of a stationary Iryo train. Two carriages derailed and fell down an embankment, according to emergency services.

The Iryo train was carrying 147 passengers and the Renfe train 397, according to a regional government spokesperson.

“There were dead people underneath the trains. So many people couldn’t get out, screams, … it was horrifying,” Eduarda, a passenger on the Iryo train, told Spanish radio station Cadena SER.

Wednesday’s crash occurred near the Urda station in the Toledo province at around 8.54 AM local time (0754GMT).

A view of the crash site after two high-speed trains collided in central Spain, killing dozens of people and injuring many others in Toledo, Spain on 28 October 2026.

Rail infrastructure operator Adif said both trains involved were serving the Madrid-Seville route. Services linking Madrid, Ciudad Real, and Andalusia were suspended.

Emergency crews, including firefighters and medical helicopters, were deployed to the scene. The Castilla-La Mancha regional government activated its emergency response plan, Anadolu Agency reported.

Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez cancelled his scheduled engagements to monitor the emergency. Regional President Emiliano Garcia-Page said he was heading to the crash site, and various political parties canceled campaign events scheduled for Wednesday.

A view of the crash site after two high-speed trains collided in central Spain, killing dozens of people and injuring many others in Toledo, Spain on 28 October 2026.

European leaders, including Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni and European Parliament President Roberta Metsola, have offered their condolences.

The cause remained under investigation, though initial reports point to “human error.”

UPDATE 2.0: PM Péter Magyar sends condolences

Prime Minister Péter Magyar, on behalf of Hungary, expressed his sincere condolences and sympathy to the people of Spain following the train accident on Wednesday morning. On his Facebook page on Wednesday, the Prime Minister wrote that at least 64 people had lost their lives in the tragedy and that there were a great many seriously injured.

European leaders express solidarity with Spain

European leaders have expressed solidarity with Spain following a collision between two high-speed trains in the province of Toledo on Wednesday, which killed at least 46 people, according to Spanish media reports.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said she was devastated by the news, extending condolences to the victims’ families and loved ones.

“Today, Europe mourns with you,” she said in a post on US social media platform X.

European Council President Antonio Costa said he had received the news with “deep consternation.”

Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said her government stood with Spain and the Spanish people during the difficult times.

French President Emmanuel Macron expressed France’s solidarity with Spain, saying his thoughts were with the victims, their families, the injured and rescue workers.

Belgian Foreign Minister Maxime Prevot said he was deeply shaken by the accident, extending condolences to the victims’ families and support to the injured and their loved ones.

He added that Spain could count on Belgium’s full solidarity.

Lithuanian President Gitanas Nauseda conveyed his condolences to Spanish King Felipe VI and Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez, wishing the injured a swift and full recovery.

Romanian Foreign Minister Dan Neculaescu also expressed sadness over the collision and offered condolences to the victims’ families, while wishing those injured a speedy recovery.

He added that Romania’s diplomatic and consular missions were in close contact with Spanish authorities and ready to provide assistance.

World.title: Ryanair expands Budapest base, but warns Hungarian government
World.content:
Ryanair has called on the Hungarian government to reduce airport charges, warning that rising costs could threaten further growth, even as the airline announces eight new routes from Budapest for the 2026 winter season.

Ryanair expands the number of destinations from Budapest

The Irish low-cost carrier will operate 54 routes from the Hungarian capital, adding destinations including Gdansk, Gothenburg, Kraków, Lamezia, Turin, Venice, Warsaw and East Midlands in England. It also plans to station an additional aircraft at its Budapest base, bringing its total there to 12.

According to Ryanair, the expanded winter schedule represents 6 per cent growth and will allow it to carry around six million passengers annually from Budapest. The company says its Hungarian operations support more than 4,800 jobs, including 360 positions for pilots and cabin crew.

Stay up-to-date with Hungary Weekly Briefing: subscribe on Substack!

Tax cuts boost growth, says the airline

Ryanair attributes its expansion partly to the Hungarian government’s decision to abolish the aviation-related windfall tax from January 2025. The airline says its traffic in Hungary has increased by 17 per cent since the tax was removed.

However, it argues that higher airport charges are undermining the benefits of the government’s tax policy. Ryanair claims that fees at Budapest Airport have risen by more than 10 per cent since 2024, making the airport less competitive than lower-cost alternatives elsewhere in Central and Eastern Europe.

Dara Brady, Ryanair’s marketing director, said the government should address airport costs as well as aviation taxes. As the majority owner of Budapest Airport, the Hungarian state has a significant role in shaping the airport’s cost competitiveness, the company argues. The airline has promised substantial further investment if charges become more competitive.

In case you missed it: Budapest Airport winter schedule brings 185 destinations, new routes and more flights

Promise of 10 million passengers

Ryanair says it could increase its annual passenger traffic in Hungary by more than 65 per cent, taking the total to over 10 million. It has also offered to station four additional aircraft in the country, invest USD 1.6 billion and create 120 new jobs in Budapest, around Lake Balaton and in Debrecen.

The announcement follows a wider pattern in which Ryanair links its capacity decisions across Europe to airport charges and aviation taxes. The airline has expanded in some markets following tax cuts, while announcing route and capacity reductions in others where costs have risen.

Its position is not universally accepted by airport operators, which have sometimes attributed capacity changes to Ryanair’s commercial strategy and the profitability of individual routes. The latest announcement therefore combines an expansion plan for Budapest with a clear message to the Hungarian government: further growth, the airline says, depends on keeping airport costs competitive.
