Transport and energy cooperation represent areas where OTS members have overlapping economic interests, particularly in developing the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route (TITR), also known as the Middle Corridor. Discussions increasingly focus on addressing infrastructure bottlenecks, simplifying customs procedures and improving coordination among participating countries.

“I would expect opportunities to advance the Middle Corridor through simpler customs procedures, electronic transport permits and better coordination of rail and Caspian shipping services,” said Abi.

“The Kazakhstan-Uzbekistan-Azerbaijan green energy corridor could also receive further political support. In my view, the main obstacles remain infrastructure bottlenecks, inconsistent regulations, financing and coordination. Ankara could help by securing clearer implementation commitments and timelines,” she said.

Zhumatay emphasized that the benefits of the Middle Corridor should not be assessed solely through its role as a transit link between Asia and Europe. Its contribution to export diversification, domestic manufacturing, logistics capacity and regional economic integration should also be considered when evaluating transport investments.

Abi similarly highlighted that Kazakhstan should prioritize easier market access, productive investment and stronger private-sector participation in identifying practical barriers to trade. Improved connectivity should support local businesses and regional supply chains rather than generate transit revenues alone, contributing to employment and skills development.

Security cooperation and institutional limitations

The OTS has also expanded discussions on security and defense-industry cooperation, although member states maintain different strategic interests and obligations under existing security arrangements.

Arynov noted that the organization’s security agenda has traditionally focused on nontraditional threats, including terrorism, organized crime and climate-related challenges.

Recent discussions have expanded to include defense industries and consultations among security officials, although the prospects for deeper military integration remain limited by members’ existing commitments.

“Türkiye is a member of NATO, and Kazakhstan and the Kyrgyz Republic are members of the Collective Security Treaty Organization. So those are two different institutional arrangements. I don’t think that the OTS will develop a very strong military or defense dimension,” said Arynov.

At the OTS informal summit in Turkistan in May, President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev also emphasized that the organization was not a geopolitical project or military alliance, placing greater emphasis on trade, technology, digital development and humanitarian cooperation.

According to Arynov, bilateral cooperation remains the more practical format for defense-related initiatives, including existing partnerships between Kazakhstan and Türkiye and arrangements involving Uzbekistan and Azerbaijan.

Defense-industry discussions could continue within the OTS, although member states remain cautious about developing a common military framework.

Zhumatay identified functional security cooperation as a more feasible direction, including cybersecurity, counterterrorism, border security, emergency preparedness and the protection of transport and energy infrastructure. He also highlighted opportunities for joint defense production, maintenance, technology transfer and workforce development, emphasizing the development of domestic industrial capabilities rather than increased arms procurement alone.

“The OTS should avoid becoming a vehicle for geopolitical polarization. Central Asian states generally seek to diversify their external partnerships without abandoning established economic and security relationships. An explicitly anti-Russian or anti-Chinese security agenda would therefore risk undermining the very cooperation the OTS seeks to promote,” said Zhumatay.

According to him, differences in strategic orientation make a unified defense doctrine or binding mutual-defense obligations difficult to envisage. The organization could instead facilitate information-sharing, consultations among security institutions and coordination on specific challenges without requiring members to change their existing commitments.

World.title: Vice President Erlan Karin: Strategic Decisions Will Shape Country’s Future
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan’s annual presidential address outlines strategic priorities that balance national interests with public well-being, Vice President Erlan Karin said, commenting on President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev’s address to the people of Kazakhstan.

“History is shaped not by time itself, but by strategic decisions made at the right moment. Today’s presidential address is proof of this. It takes into account both the interests of the state and concern for the well-being of the people,” Karin wrote on his Instagram.

He emphasized the strategic importance of Tokayev’s priorities, which aim to advance the country’s development.

In his address, Tokayev identified key areas for the country’s further development, with particular attention to strengthening sovereignty and domestic stability, developing the economy, and advancing science and modern technologies.

He also called for large-scale modernization of Kazakhstan’s infrastructure, allocating 6.5 trillion tenge (US$14.3 billion) to the initiative by the end of 2029.

Economic development was another major focus of the address. Tokayev called for a unified investment management system and instructed the government to develop a dedicated plan to support medium-sized businesses.

President Tokayev also outlined Kazakhstan’s strategic objectives for its next stage of development, emphasizing the responsibility to pass on a fundamentally renewed country to future generations.

World.title: Kazakhstan Records Sharp Increase in Transit Freight as Volumes Reach 36.3 Million Tons
World.content:
ASTANA – Transit freight volumes through Kazakhstan increased 5.6-fold over the past decade, rising from 6.5 million tons in 2015 to 36.3 million tons in 2025, according to the Bureau of National Statistics. The growth underscores Kazakhstan’s expanding role in transport links connecting China, Central Asia, Russia and Europe.

The increase accelerated in recent years, with transit freight volumes rising 70.8% in 2025 alone, adding 15.1 million tons. The figure exceeded 10 million tons for the first time in 2020, reaching 11.6 million tons, before climbing to 15.6 million tons in 2022 and 21.3 million tons in 2024. The upward trend continued in 2026. According to the government, 32.6 million tons of cargo passed through Kazakhstan in transit between January and September, up 13.1% compared with the same period last year.

The government aims to increase annual transit freight volumes to 100 million tons by 2035. To support this goal, Kazakhstan is building new railway lines and modernizing existing sections of its transport network.

However, official estimates for 2025 vary across government reports. While the Bureau of National Statistics recorded 36.3 million tons, a government report published on Oct. 15 put the figure at 39.1 million tons, representing an 18% annual increase.

Railways and road transport drive transit growth

Rail transport accounted for 18.7 million tons of transit freight in 2025, up from 13.3 million tons a year earlier. Another major category was vehicle combinations, including tractors with semi-trailers or trailers, which nearly tripled from 5.7 million tons in 2024 to 16.8 million tons in 2025. Together, these two categories accounted for the overwhelming majority of transit freight.

Meanwhile, transit shipments of vehicles moving under their own power as commodities declined from 1.8 million tons to 745,900 tons. Other transport categories accounted for relatively small volumes.

China remains a key source of transit freight

Routes originating in China dominated Kazakhstan’s transit freight flows in 2025. The largest route by volume was China–Uzbekistan, which carried 6.5 million tons. An additional 4 million tons consisted of consolidated cargo from China bound for Kazakhstan and other countries. The China–Russia route ranked third, with 3 million tons.

The top 10 routes also included Uzbekistan–Kazakhstan, China–Tajikistan, China–Belarus and Uzbekistan–China. The distribution highlights Kazakhstan’s role not only in freight transport between China and Europe but also in connections linking Central Asian countries with Russia and Iran.

Industrial goods make up a significant share of cargo

Industrial products accounted for a substantial share of transit freight through Kazakhstan in 2025. Cold-rolled iron and steel products topped the list, at 5.6 million tons. Motorcycles, mopeds and similar vehicles ranked second, with 2.2 million tons, followed by passenger cars at 619,200 tons.

Other leading categories included certain polymers, at 482,400 tons, and automotive parts, at 478,200 tons.

The top 10 product categories also included coated iron and steel products, vinyl chloride polymers, nitrogen and potassium fertilizers, and ceramic tiles. The figures indicate that Kazakhstan’s transit network carries both raw materials and finished goods, including vehicles and construction products.

Total freight transport falls under revised methodology

Beyond international transit, Kazakhstan’s transport sector handles domestic, export and import freight. The Bureau of National Statistics reported that all modes of transport carried 712.1 million tons of cargo between January and September 2026. This compares with 725.6 million tons in the same period of 2023, 782.4 million tons in 2024 and 853.5 million tons in 2025.

The latest figure appears to represent a 16.6% year-on-year decline. However, the comparison is affected by a change in statistical methodology: the bureau excluded empty rail wagons from freight transport calculations for January–September 2026 and the corresponding period of 2025.

When both periods are calculated using the same methodology, total freight transport instead increased by 0.9%.

Road and urban electric transport carried the largest volume during the first nine months of 2026, at 270.4 million tons. Railways transported 248.5 million tons, compared with 339.4 million tons a year earlier. On a comparable methodological basis, rail freight transport fell by 1.4%.

Pipelines transported 189.8 million tons, while maritime and coastal shipping carried 3 million tons. Inland waterways transported 265,000 tons, and air freight amounted to 20,000 tons.

Freight revenue rises despite changes in volumes

Revenue from freight, baggage and cargo-baggage transportation across all modes reached 4.5 trillion tenge (US$9.9 billion) between January and September 2026, increasing 5.3% year on year.

Rail transport generated the largest share, with revenue rising from 1.7 trillion tenge (US$3.73 billion) to 1.8 trillion tenge (US$3.95 billion). Revenue from road and urban electric transport increased from 1.1 trillion tenge (US$2.41 billion) to 1.2 trillion tenge (US$2.63 billion).

Pipeline transport revenue declined from 1.5 trillion (US$3.29 billion) to 1.4 trillion tenge (US$3.07 billion). Maritime and coastal transport generated 22.6 billion tenge (US$49.6 million), air transport 12.6 billion tenge (US$27.6 million), and inland water transport 1 billion tenge (US$2.2 million).

Despite the overall increase in revenue, freight transportation’s share of total transport enterprise revenue gradually decreased, from 79% in January–September 2023 to 77.9% in the same period of 2026.

The share varied considerably by mode. Freight accounted for 99.5% of revenue in maritime and coastal transport, 93.8% in rail transport, 76.1% in road and urban electric transport, and 52.4% in inland water transport. In aviation, where passenger services account for most revenue, freight contributed just 1.6%.

As international freight flows expand, Kazakhstan has an opportunity to derive greater economic benefits from its geographic position. Beyond developing transport corridors, the country will need to expand supporting services, including logistics, warehousing, vehicle maintenance and repair.

Strengthening this infrastructure could help domestic companies participate more actively in international supply chains, create jobs and increase the transport sector’s contribution to the national economy.

World.title: Kazakhstan’s Islamic Banking Market Faces Test Beyond Rapid Growth
World.content:
ASTANA – Islamic banking in Kazakhstan has grown significantly over the past years but still accounts for a small share of the financial system. Its long-term value will depend on whether it attracts new investors and channels additional funding into businesses and infrastructure, rather than redistributing existing resources, economist Ruslan Sultanov told The Astana Times.

“The main task in developing Islamic banking in Kazakhstan should not be to achieve a particular share of the banking market, but to create additional opportunities for financing the real sector of the economy,” he said.

Mastercard’s September 2026 report, titled Islamic Banking in Central Asia: A Window of New Opportunities, estimates the regional Islamic banking market at approximately $716 million and projects it could reach nearly $2.5 billion by 2028. For Kazakhstan, the challenge is to turn this growth into additional capital for businesses and long-term investment.

A growing market with limited reach

According to figures from the National Bank of Kazakhstan cited by Sultanov, the combined assets of ADCB Islamic Bank and Zaman Bank reached approximately 315.3 billion tenge (US$702.9 million) as of Sept. 1, representing around 0.42% of the banking sector’s 75.7 trillion tenge in assets (US$168.7 billion).

Sultanov said Islamic bank deposits stood at 39.3 billion tenge (US$87.6 million), or around 0.08% of total banking-sector deposits.

According to data from Ranking.kz citing the Islamic Financial Stability Report 2026, Kazakhstan’s Islamic banking assets increased almost 33-fold between August 2010 and August 2026. Despite this growth, the sector remains small relative to the wider banking system. Sultanov also said Islamic banking assets rose 4.7% between January and September, compared with 6.9% growth across the banking sector.

The limited market share reflects the small number of Islamic financial institutions, narrower product offerings and a more limited retail customer base.

Islamic finance is not automatically cheaper than conventional borrowing, Sultanov said, as costs depend on funding, operating expenses and credit risk. Some Islamic products can also be economically similar to conventional debt.

“If the development of Islamic banking results only in the redistribution of existing customers and financial resources between conventional and Islamic banks, the overall macroeconomic effect may remain limited,” he said.

New rules could widen access

Kazakhstan’s banking law, signed on Jan. 16, allows universal banks to conduct Islamic banking operations under their existing licenses, according to the Agency for Regulation and Development of the Financial Market. Banks should keep these activities separate from conventional operations, including through separate accounting and the segregation of assets and liabilities. Islamic products also require Sharia-compliance oversight.

The changes could allow established banks to offer Islamic products without creating separate Islamic banks, potentially expanding access. However, market development will also depend on product availability, specialist expertise and customer confidence.

Deposit protection remains a consideration. Kazakhstan’s Deposit Guarantee Fund says it does not cover deposits placed with Islamic banks, an exclusion that remains under the new banking framework.

A regional opportunity beyond banking

A May 2025 report by the Eurasian Development Bank, the Islamic Development Bank Institute and London Stock Exchange Group estimated Central Asia’s Islamic finance assets at around $699 million at the beginning of 2024. It projected Islamic banking assets could reach $2.5 billion by 2028 and $6.3 billion by 2033.

The report also projected the region’s sukuk market could reach $2.05 billion by 2028 and $5.6 billion by 2033, identifying energy, transport and logistics, industry, food security and social infrastructure as potential areas for financing.

Sukuk are financial certificates often described as Islamic bonds. Unlike conventional bonds, which typically pay interest, sukuk are structured to comply with Islamic finance principles and generally link investors’ returns to ownership interests in assets, projects or their economic performance. They could help Kazakhstan attract investors from the Gulf states and Southeast Asia and provide an additional source of funding for long-term projects.

Access to new financing instruments does not automatically reduce borrowing costs or guarantee investment. Investors will still assess creditworthiness, currency and country risks, governance and legal protections.

Measuring impact beyond market share

For Kazakhstan, the key question is whether Islamic finance can mobilize capital that would not otherwise enter the market and fund projects that might otherwise struggle to secure financing.

That could include expanding funding options for small and medium-sized businesses in agriculture and manufacturing, as well as supporting infrastructure and other long-term investments. Success would be measured not simply by asset growth or market share, but by new investors, additional savings, wider access to financing and projects made possible by these instruments.

As Sultanov said, Islamic banking’s significance will ultimately depend on how much additional economic activity it enables, rather than how much of the existing banking market it captures.

Islamic banking​ is a banking system that operates in accordance with the principles of Shari’ah law. It prohibits the payment or receipt of interest (riba) and emphasizes profit-and-loss sharing, asset-backed financing, and ethical investments.

World.title: Tokayev Calls for AI-Driven Digital Economy, Technology Push Across Industry
World.content:
ASTANA — Kazakhstan must build a digital economy, President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev said in his state-of-the-nation address on Oct. 28, calling for broader use of AI in industry and agriculture, modernized geological exploration and a shift from digital consumption to technology-driven production.

Tokayev said Kazakhstan had begun building infrastructure for its Digital Qazaqstan strategy, including launching two supercomputers, preparing to commission a third by the end of the year, and laying a fiber-optic trunk line across the Caspian Sea. Data centers are also under construction.

However, he acknowledged that the country still had to demonstrate results in digitalization, with the process sometimes reduced to automating existing procedures or purchasing expensive software without a clear understanding of its practical benefits.

“We must be realistic in assessing our capabilities and use the best that new technologies can offer for the well-being of our people,” Tokayev said.

He said Kazakhstan had only begun commercializing AI, asset tokenization, blockchain technologies and digital platform ecosystems. The government must develop a program to apply digital technologies across the economy.

“Our goal is to build a truly people-centered digital economy,” Tokayev said.

From digital consumption to digital work

Tokayev called for a shift in how people use digital technologies, noting that internet access should enable economic activity and employment rather than serve primarily as a space for consumption and entertainment.

“In public consciousness, the internet should be perceived not only as a space for consumption and entertainment, but also as a virtual territory for creation and work,” he said.

He said smartphones should become effective working tools rather than expensive distractions. The government is expected to establish a simplified legal regime for digital employment by the end of the year. Tokayev also stressed that access to digital opportunities should not depend on where people live.

“Our citizens, whether living in rural areas or cities, must learn to use smartphones as tools for earning a legitimate income,” he said.

To support this goal, the government should combine existing state business support measures with the capabilities of private marketplaces, banks, logistics companies and digital services. Beyond loans and subsidies, entrepreneurs need additional digital tools to produce and sell goods.

Next year, the government and the business community should launch pilot digital development projects in several regions to help rural producers market their products, with successful practices subsequently expanded nationwide. Tokayev also called for fully realizing the potential of asset tokenization, or transferring assets into the digital environment.

AI and the next phase of industrial development

Tokayev linked digital transformation to a broader push for industrial and technological development, including the modernization of geological exploration and the management of critical minerals. He said Kazakhstan needed to fundamentally change its approach to geological exploration, saying that outdated methods would not deliver the desired results.

“Today, we must recognize geology as a high-tech industry. It is extremely important for us to comprehensively study the country’s subsoil using advanced technologies and ensure transparency and accessibility of data. We should actively attract private investment in the search for and exploration of new deposits,” Tokayev said.

He called for a national system to manage critical metal reserves, supported by mechanisms for long-term financing of mining projects. The government should also consider off-take contracts to guarantee demand for products made by domestic enterprises in the sector.

Tokayev said Kazakhstan should consider establishing a national stockpile of nonferrous and rare earth metals and integrate the country into global production chains. He called on the government to build strategic partnerships with developed countries in this field.

At the same time, he warned against uncoordinated industrial investment that could create unnecessary competition for existing domestic producers. Tokayev cited Qarmet, an operating metallurgical enterprise, and plans to establish similar facilities in three other regions as an example, questioning whether the market would be able to absorb their output.

He said each region needed to identify its own priorities, while the government should strengthen coordination to prevent fragmented decisions and excessive dependence on a single industry or enterprise. Regional development should extend beyond core industries to encompass education, applied science, logistics, services, related manufacturing and technological entrepreneurship.

“There is confidence that the People’s Construction initiative will help create such a system in every region or, in modern terms, an ecosystem,” Tokayev said.

AI in agriculture

Tokayev also called for accelerating agriculture’s technological modernization, including increasing domestic production of advanced tractors and combine harvesters.

He cited a recent visit to Astana by NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang, who, according to Tokayev, said it was time to introduce AI technologies into Kazakhstan’s agriculture.

“In my view, this is a very timely proposal. We must begin implementing it as soon as possible,” Tokayev said.

According to him, adopting these technologies could strengthen Kazakhstan’s role in global food security.

“If our country overcomes this threshold, then, undoubtedly, in the event of a global food shortage, or the threat of world hunger, Eurasia could become one of the key centers for supplying food to the world,” he said.

Kazakhstan had extensive agricultural land near major water sources, and using these areas for irrigated farming could increase yields of traditional crops by 2 to 2.5 times.

President Tokayev called for applying advanced water-saving and agrochemical technologies when developing new agricultural land, noting that the country’s performance in this area remained low.

Digital tools should also be used to improve the accounting and management of water resources, enabling better-informed decisions when planning new industrial facilities. Tokayev called on the government to complete the National Water Resources Information System as soon as possible.

2027 as the year of nationwide construction drive

Tokayev said Kazakhstan’s next stage of development should combine an AI-based digital economy with investment in physical infrastructure. He proposed declaring the coming year the Year of Nationwide Large-Scale Construction, building on the current Year of Digitalization and Artificial Intelligence.

The initiative should include building and renovating civilian infrastructure in regional centers, districts and smaller settlements, including roads, airports, railway stations, health care facilities and rehabilitation centers for children with special needs.

Tokayev also called for new creative centers, sports complexes, libraries and scientific centers across the regions, while maintaining housing construction as a priority.

“Thus, our common, nationwide response to the approaching era of artificial intelligence is to build, and build again!” he said.

Tokayev said the initiative was intended to improve living standards and create opportunities for future generations.

“The Constitution defines improving the well-being of the people as a strategic priority of the state. I want to emphasize that all these initiatives are aimed at the benefit of the country and, above all, at securing the future of the younger generation,” he said.

World.title: Tokayev Urges Higher Taxes on Wealthy, Calls on Banks to Boost Business Lending
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan should consider raising taxes on wealthy individuals, revise parts of its new Tax Code to address business concerns, and encourage banks to provide more long-term loans to businesses, President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev said in his annual state-of-the-nation address on Oct. 28.

Tokayev outlined priorities for macroeconomic policy, including fighting inflation, improving public spending and increasing investment in the real economy. He stressed that economic policy should ultimately be measured by its impact on people’s prosperity and economic activity.

“Our main goal is therefore to increase household incomes. To achieve this, we must first systematically combat inflation,” he said, describing inflation as “a silent enemy that steadily undermines the well-being of our citizens.”

He called on the government and the National Bank to coordinate efforts to contain and reduce inflation, pursue balanced fiscal and tax policy, and create conditions for stronger production capacity and higher business productivity.

Higher tax rate for wealthy individuals

Tokayev also called for a discussion on introducing a higher tax rate for individuals with substantial wealth, framing the proposal as a matter of fairness rather than a restriction on private property.

“I believe the time has come to discuss introducing a higher rate for those with substantial wealth,” he said.

He stressed that the proposal would not involve restricting legally acquired assets, which he said would contradict the Constitution. Instead, he stressed that citizens should make a fair contribution to the country’s development in proportion to their means.

“This is about a proportionate and fair contribution by every citizen to the development of our country. This is about fairness,” Tokayev said.

The government and the Kurultai, Kazakhstan’s national legislature, are to examine the proposal and submit recommendations.

The president also linked fair taxation to transparency and digitalization. He called for advanced technologies, including artificial intelligence, to improve tax collection, reduce the shadow economy and lower corruption risks.

Banks urged to finance the real economy

Tokayev said Kazakhstan’s financial system remained resilient, with bank assets exceeding 75 trillion tenge (US$164.6 billion) and deposits reaching a record 52 trillion tenge (US$114.1 billion). About 78% of deposits are held in the national currency, which he cited as evidence of the tenge’s growing value.

The next priority, he said, is to channel these accumulated financial resources into the real economy.

“The most important task now is to direct accumulated financial resources toward the development of the real sector of the economy,” Tokayev said.

He called on the National Bank to play a more active role in initiatives supporting economic development while continuing to safeguard price and financial stability. President Tokayev also urged commercial banks to increase investment lending to businesses, describing it as their core responsibility. According to him, Kazakhstan’s demand for long-term financing exceeds the capacity of the state budget and development institutions.

“Banks must take the most active part in investment lending to businesses. This is their main mission,” Tokayev said.

He called for regulatory conditions that would encourage lending, including more effective management of excess liquidity in the banking system. He also proposed new mechanisms for long-term financing of key economic sectors involving banks, development institutions, international financial organizations and the Unified Accumulative Pension Fund.

According to him, the forthcoming Capital Market Law should provide concrete mechanisms to mobilize additional financing and strengthen investment discipline.

AI to help improve public spending

Tokayev identified better budget management as another priority for long-term macroeconomic stability. The Budget Code adopted last year has improved the management of public funds and strengthened financial discipline, he said. However, government expenditure continues to grow, making better budget planning and oversight increasingly important.

He proposed using artificial intelligence to identify unjustified or inefficient spending and called for the full digitalization of the state treasury system. The government should establish an automated system for managing public funds based on unified methods and standards, Tokayev said, adding that he expects concrete proposals from the government and the National Bank.

Targeted changes to Tax Code

Tokayev said Kazakhstan’s new Tax Code laid the foundation for a comprehensive overhaul of the tax system but acknowledged that implementing it created difficulties for businesses. Large-scale reforms inevitably reveal problems that are difficult to anticipate during drafting, he said, noting that companies were struggling to apply certain provisions.

“The Tax Code is not dogma, nor is it sacred scripture, and it must not be detached from reality,” Tokayev said.

“Our legislation has become so cumbersome and difficult to understand that it has turned into a real headache for entrepreneurs,” he added.

He instructed the government to address contradictions, eliminate ambiguous interpretations and remove disproportionate burdens on entrepreneurs. Tokayev emphasized that the government must carefully consider the changes to avoid repeatedly changing the rules for entrepreneurs.

World.title: President Tokayev Proposes SME Inspection Moratorium in State-of-Nation Address
World.content:
ASTANA — President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev proposed a new three-year moratorium on inspections of small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) and called for a more systematic investment policy in his state-of-the-nation address on Oct. 28.

“Investment efficiency should be assessed by the number and quality of commissioned production facilities, as well as their actual contribution to the economy,” Tokayev said.

He said priority should be given to projects involving deeper processing of products and higher labor productivity.

“This is the main requirement,” he said.

Tokayev also called for developing domestic production of construction materials, metal structures and engineering equipment needed for major infrastructure projects. He said these projects should form the foundation of the People’s Construction program.

“It is unacceptable to use National Fund resources to finance imports,” Tokayev said.

To give the economy fresh momentum, Kazakhstan should attract leading international companies with advanced technologies, expertise and access to global markets, including through cooperation with domestic companies, he said.

Tokayev proposes three-year moratorium on SME inspections

Tokayev proposed that the government and members of the Kurultai, Kazakhstan’s parliament, consider introducing a three-year moratorium on SME inspections starting Jan. 1, 2027. He said the proposal followed a mixed trend in enforcement. In the first half of the year, the number of violations by individual entrepreneurs fell by 34%, while the total amount of fines increased by nearly 11% and unscheduled inspections rose dozens of times.

“Meanwhile, an analysis of business activity shows that businesses simply need not to be obstructed,” Tokayev said.

He pointed to the 2020-2023 moratorium on inspections of micro and small businesses as an example of an effective measure, while stressing that the experience of the previous moratorium, including its positive and negative aspects, should be taken into account. Tokayev described the proposed measure as a strategic pause to reset the oversight system and transition to digital regulation.

Small and medium-sized enterprises account for 40% of Kazakhstan’s gross domestic product, while their share of investment in fixed capital is approaching 70%, he said. More than one-third of entrepreneurs in the sector are engaged in trade, underscoring the need to diversify small businesses.

The government must also develop a dedicated plan for medium-sized businesses, including mechanisms for long-term financing and technological modernization, as well as closer cooperation with large enterprises and opportunities for smaller companies to supply them with products.

Tokayev called for improving SME access to procurement by government agencies and quasi-public companies. He suggested reserving part of procurement volumes for small and medium-sized enterprises and easing requirements for suppliers.

“Most importantly, it is essential to ensure stable ‘rules of the game’ for entrepreneurs,” he said.

Alatau to establish investment court

Tokayev highlighted the importance of Alatau, the city planned as a center of accelerated development and an environment conducive to investment and entrepreneurship. He said effective justice was essential to maintaining the long-term attractiveness of any international jurisdiction and called for a judicial system in Alatau that would ensure high-quality justice.

“An investment court based on the English common law model will hear commercial cases,” Tokayev said.

A civil court would handle other matters related to the city’s special legal regime. The government is expected to submit amendments to the constitutional law on Alatau’s special legal regime to the Kurultai by the end of January 2027.

Tokayev stressed that the Constitution would protect investors and entrepreneurs.

“The investment interests of all respectable and honest entrepreneurs are guaranteed by the strongest and most reliable legal protection — the Constitution,” he said.

Calls for fair competition

Tokayev also called for further decriminalization of economic offenses and stronger safeguards for fair competition, particularly for SMEs. According to him, domestic producers, especially food manufacturers, sometimes faced deliberate obstacles. These included artificially lowering the prices of imported goods while restricting domestic products’ access to the local market.

Tokayev described such practices as corruption and called for them to be stopped, warning that they weakened the competitiveness of domestic companies and products. He said protecting businesses was directly linked to strengthening the independence of the national economy.

“It would not be an exaggeration to say that deliberately creating illegal obstacles for businesses is a crime against the state,” Tokayev said, calling for stronger mechanisms to support entrepreneurs, including through trade associations.

World.title: Armenian parliament ratifies framework agreement on Trump Route (TRIPP) project
World.content:
Armenia ratifies agreement on TRIPP project

The parliament of Armenia has ratified a framework agreement on strategic co-operation under the Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity (TRIPP) project. The parties initialled the document during Marco Rubio’s visit to Yerevan on 26 May 2026 and signed the final version remotely just a few days later.

TRIPP (Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity) is a road that will connect Azerbaijan with its Nakhchivan exclave through Armenian territory. The project also aims to reopen regional transport links. As a result, Armenia will gain access to third countries via Azerbaijan. For several years, Yerevan and Baku could not agree on this issue. Azerbaijan demanded a road that it called the “Zangezur corridor”. Armenia’s authorities said they were ready to reopen all transport routes but rejected the term “corridor”, arguing that it implied a loss of Armenian control and sovereign rights over the territory. The two sides reached an agreement only on 8 August in Washington. Under the deal, the road will remain under Armenia’s sovereign control, while the US will join the project as a business partner. The initiative took the name “Trump Route” after the US president, who mediated the agreement.

Parliament ratified the agreement with 63 votes in favour and 32 against. Only MPs from the ruling faction supported it.

The parliamentary opposition had announced in advance that it would vote against ratification of the framework agreement. Opposition MPs argued that the document took US and Azerbaijani interests into account but failed to protect Armenia’s interests.

MPs from the ruling faction, by contrast, believe the project will reopen regional transport links on the basis of reciprocity. In their view, this would benefit Armenia economically. The opposition disagrees, pointing to the lack of any financial assessments.

Debates on ratifying the TRIPP project began in parliament the previous day. MPs had only two hours for the discussion. However, opposition lawmakers managed to raise all their concerns and put forward several proposals.

Opposition MP on the interests of the US, Armenia and Azerbaijan

Anna Grigoryan, head of the opposition Armenia faction, noted that Armenia and the United States had signed a bilateral document concerning the implementation of TRIPP. However, she said, the document also refers to a third party — Azerbaijan.

“Azerbaijan’s interests are actually reflected in this document more directly and clearly than the interests of the Republic of Armenia.”

Grigoryan also outlined what she believes each side stands to gain from the project.

“The US gains a direct presence in the region, particularly along the border with Iran, in a strategically crucial area. Azerbaijan secures a link between Nakhchivan and the rest of the country — a goal that both Azerbaijan and Turkey have long pursued.”

When asked what Armenia stands to gain, she said the question was harder to answer.

“When the political majority tries to answer this question, the first word they use is ‘unblocking’. But on the ground, no transport links are being reopened and no borders are opening. So that part of the answer does not reflect reality.”

Should the launch of TRIPP be linked to the signing of a peace treaty?

Narek Karapetyan, leader of the opposition Strong Armenia faction, is concerned that Azerbaijan may lose its incentive to sign a peace treaty once the Trump Route begins operating.

“Azerbaijan gets what it set out to achieve, while what we are supposed to get — peace — could be postponed for five to ten years. Why would they sign a peace treaty with Armenia if they are already getting a link to Nakhchivan?”

Official Yerevan has not ruled out the possibility that the Trump Route could begin operating before Armenia and Azerbaijan sign a peace treaty.

The MP argues that the two important issues should not be treated separately. He proposes linking the implementation of the Trump Route to the signing of a peace treaty.

Deputy Speaker of the National Assembly Ruben Rubinyan disagreed. In his view, it is a positive development that TRIPP can proceed without depending on the signing of a peace treaty.

“If you argue that we should not implement this project in order to secure the signing of a peace treaty, you are saying that TRIPP is a bad initiative for Armenia. But TRIPP is by no means a bad initiative for Armenia.”

The ruling party representative welcomed the prospect of “elements of peace taking shape on the ground” independently of the peace treaty. By “elements of peace”, Rubinyan means both the launch of the Trump Route and the ongoing process of delimiting and demarcating the border between the two countries.

Background to the Trump Route project

The Trump Route offers Armenia a real opportunity to reopen regional transport links. For Azerbaijan, it provides the shortest route connecting the country with Nakhchivan.

The project envisages using the railway along a stretch of about 43km through Armenian territory. A motorway, energy infrastructure and digital communications links will also run through the area.

All infrastructure located on Armenian territory will remain under Armenia’s sovereignty and jurisdiction.

The ratified framework agreement provides for the establishment of TRIPP Development Company, which will oversee the project’s development and implementation.

Initially, the US will own 74% of the company’s shares and Armenia will hold 26%. After 49 years, if the parties extend their co-operation for a further 50 years, Armenia’s stake will rise to 49%. Armenia will grant TRIPP Development Company exclusive rights to use and develop land, along with other necessary powers within the areas allocated to the project, for 49 years.

Armenia and the US still need to agree on and adopt the company’s charter and shareholder agreement.

It also remains unclear what border-crossing arrangements will apply to Armenian citizens travelling through Nakhchivan.

Foreign Minister Ararat Mirzoyan said the two sides had yet to agree on the technical details of travel through Azerbaijani territory.

“We still need to discuss these issues with Azerbaijan. They fall within the framework of Armenia–Azerbaijan relations.” Armenia–Azerbaijan relations.”

Armenia ratifies agreement on TRIPP project

World.title: “Like a black cat in a dark room”: Georgia’s opposition ban case enters sixth day of hearings
World.content:
What happened at Georgia’s opposition ban hearing

On 28 October, Georgia’s Constitutional Court held the sixth day of hearings on a lawsuit filed by the ruling Georgian Dream party seeking to ban five opposition parties. The court is currently hearing submissions from the parties involved. On Tuesday, it heard arguments from representatives of the Coalition for Change.

The lawsuit names the United National Movement, Coalition for Change, Lelo – Strong Georgia, Gakharia for Georgia and the Federalists. Georgian Dream argues that these parties have violated Article 23 of the Constitution, which prohibits political parties whose aims include overthrowing or forcibly changing the country’s constitutional order. One of the arguments is that the parties refuse to recognise the legitimacy of the current authorities. The lawsuit also accuses them of organising attempts to overthrow the government. The United National Movement faces additional accusations of undermining Georgia’s independence and violating its territorial integrity. The lawsuit holds the party responsible for the August 2008 war with Russia over South Ossetia, when it was in power. All five opposition parties reject the accusations. Hearings are scheduled to continue through 30 October. The court must deliver its final ruling by 24 June 2027. A simple majority is required to uphold the claim, meaning at least four of the seven judges must vote in favour.

The Coalition for Change is represented in court by Nika Gvaramia, Tengo Tevzadze, Maia Kopaleishvili, Giga Lemonjava and Marika Arevadze. None of their motions was granted.

Constitutional Court President Revaz Nadaraia clashed twice with the coalition’s representatives, over their citation of a European Parliament resolution and their reference to the “Russian doctrine”.

The hearings will resume on 29 October at 11 a.m.

Judge Nadaraia: “European Parliament resolution is irrelevant to this case”

Giga Lemonjava presented an 8 October 2026 European Parliament resolution at the hearing. The resolution compared the Georgian ruling party’s bid to ban opposition parties with the Russian and Belarusian models, describing it as part of a strategy to eliminate political pluralism and turn Georgia into a one-party state.

Constitutional Court President Revaz Nadaraia interrupted the presentation and asked how the resolution was relevant to the proceedings. Lemonjava replied that it was not directly relevant to the case but that the public should be informed about it.

Nika Gvaramia commented: “Public hearings mean that participants are speaking not only to the court but also to the public.”

Nadarაიa responded: “Public hearings mean that everyone can follow the proceedings, not that someone can make political statements here.” He also reprimanded Gvaramia, saying: “You are interrupting me and disrupting the proceedings.”

Judge Nadaraia says comparison with Russia’s new doctrine is irrelevant to court proceedings

Constitutional Court President Revaz Nadaraia raised a similar objection for a second time during Giga Lemonjava’s address.

The opposition representative drew attention to two claims in the lawsuit against the opposition: that the previous government, when the United National Movement was in power, artificially restored the borders of the former South Ossetian Autonomous Region in 2007 and started the war with Russia in 2008.

Lemonjava argued that these claims closely matched Russia’s new foreign policy and security doctrine. If the court accepted them, he said, a Georgian state institution would be giving legal legitimacy to Russia’s version of events for the first time. “You need to be aware of this danger,” he told the judges.

Lemonjava also argued that giving legal force to these claims would contradict Article 78 of Georgia’s Constitution, which obliges state institutions to take all measures to ensure the country’s full integration into the European Union and NATO.

Nadaraia did not allow Lemonjava to continue with this line of argument, describing his remarks as “demagoguery” and saying he had gone beyond the scope of the proceedings. The judge again told him not to interrupt.

Judge Gotsiridze: “Do not look for a black cat where there is none”

Maia Kopaleishvili, representing the Coalition for Change, and Constitutional Court judge Eva Gotsiridze previously served together on the court’s panel. At the hearing, they clashed over a section of the lawsuit concerning an alleged attempt to enter parliament.

Kopaleishvili questioned whether Gotsiridze had studied the ruling party’s lawsuit thoroughly enough. The judge called the remark inappropriate.

“Perhaps this issue simply needs clarification. Do not look for a black cat where there is none,” Gotsiridze replied.

Opposition representative Kopaleishvili tells ruling party lawyers: “You were my students”

Maia Kopaleishvili addressed Archil Gorduladze and Tornike Cheishvili, who are representing the ruling party in court.

“You said opposition parties should be banned to protect future generations from a threat. You were my students. What threat do my colleagues and I pose to the country’s future?” Kopaleishvili asked.

Gvaramia warns of return to Soviet-style one-party elections

Nika Gvaramia noted that 28 October marked 36 years since Georgia held its first multiparty elections in 1990, as the Soviet Union was breaking apart.

“And now we are going back to where we started,” he said.

Gvaramia also described as a “distorted reality” the attempt to remove Lelo opposition party leader Badri Japaridze from politics, despite his being one of the signatories of Georgia’s 1991 Act of Restoration of State Independence.

Opposition assesses court hearing

Tornike Artkmeladze, a member of Lelo, said after the hearing that banning opposition parties in a single move would destroy what had been painstakingly built over the past 35 years.

“This is preparation for the first stage of clearing the political field — first of parties, and then they will move on to banning any active political activity. Georgian Dream wants to be the only force on the political scene. But they fail to understand that there are at least a million people in this country who will not give up their freedom,” Artkmeladze said.

News in Georgia

World.title: Azerbaijan’s former powerbroker sentenced to 14 years, suspended, for treason
World.content:
Mehdiyev, former powerbroker, sentenced in Azerbaijan

Ramiz Mehdiyev was a man who could influence who became a member of Azerbaijan’s parliament, which newspaper was shut down and who received a pardon. He headed the presidential administration for 24 years, first under Heydar Aliyev and then under Ilham Aliyev, chaired the pardons commission and was widely regarded as the country’s unofficial second-in-command.

He has now been found guilty of treason.

A Baku court sentenced Mehdiyev, 88, to 14 years in prison.

However, the sentence was suspended due to his age and health.

Despite being found guilty of attempting a coup, Mehdiyev will not go to prison.

Mehdiyev was convicted on four charges:

Actions aimed at the violent seizure of power;

Treason;

Money laundering;

Accepting a bribe on an especially large scale.

The court also ordered his property confiscated by the state and recommended that he be stripped of his state awards.

The verdict was delivered on 22 October, but became public only five days later, on 27 October. The trial was held behind closed doors, and the verdict has not been published. The list of confiscated assets and their value have also not been officially disclosed.

The verdict brings the criminal case to a close, but leaves unanswered the main question that has fuelled debate for the past year: why did Mehdiyev come under scrutiny, and why now?

In recent months, government officials, pro-government media, independent commentators and the opposition have offered different, sometimes contradictory, explanations.

Official version shifts from hints of Kremlin involvement to accusations against opposition

In the early days of the investigation, pro-government news agency APA presented its own account of events.

According to the agency, in early 2025, amid rising tensions between Baku and Moscow, Mehdiyev proposed a plan to Russia to overthrow Azerbaijan’s government and establish an interim State Council, which he intended to lead.

The agency claimed that Russian President Vladimir Putin informed Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev of the plan during a meeting in Dushanbe on 9 October.

However, a detailed statement issued by Azerbaijan’s State Security Service on 12 February 2026, followed by the indictment, presented a different timeline.

According to investigators, in August and September 2025, Mehdiyev drafted a document in a foreign language entitled “Proposals for Reorganising the System of Public Administration” and passed it through his aide, Eldar Amirov, to Ali Karimli, chairman of the opposition Azerbaijan Popular Front Party (APFP).

The final version of the document was sent on 3 October.

The indictment also refers to the Union of Russian Azerbaijani Organisations, a group registered abroad and known as the “Union of Billionaires”.

The State Security Service claims the organisation was established by foreign intelligence services and was led by Abbas Abbasov, a former first deputy prime minister, and screenwriter Rustam Ibragimbekov.

According to the investigators’ account, Mehdiyev, Abbasov and the APFP leadership were part of a group that conspired to seize power by force.

The focus of the case has therefore shifted significantly over the past year.

While the Kremlin was initially portrayed as the main player behind the alleged plot, the opposition took centre stage by the time the investigation concluded.

In February, the State Security Service released an audio recording in which Mehdiyev can be heard speaking in Russian with a woman believed to be a foreign intelligence officer. He tells her that he has proposals for reorganising the system of public administration.

The woman replies: “That is your own business.”

Judging by the published excerpt, the woman believed to be an intelligence officer appears to distance herself from Mehdiyev’s proposals rather than show interest in them.

In September, a bribery charge was added to the case. However, authorities did not disclose who allegedly paid Mehdiyev, what the payment was for or how much money was involved.

The official statement on the verdict also refers to a “foreign state” but does not identify the country.

Official rhetoric casts Mehdiyev as traitor, oligarch and schemer

The day after the verdict was announced, the presidium of Azerbaijan’s National Academy of Sciences decided to expel Mehdiyev from its membership. The decision must now be approved by the academy’s general assembly.

Academy president Isa Habibbayli described Mehdiyev’s actions as “a betrayal unworthy of a scholar”.

The central message at the meeting was that betrayal was unforgivable from someone who had enjoyed every privilege the state could offer for many years.

Meanwhile, pro-government websites focused on Mehdiyev’s assets.

They published lists of villas, plots of land, stakes in shopping centres and bank shares allegedly belonging to him, as well as information about the Sharq-Gharb publishing house.

Lawyer Chingiz Ganizade told Modern.az that once the verdict comes into force, the confiscated property could be sold at auction, rented out or partly transferred to war veterans and families of fallen servicemen.

He noted, however, that the verdict had not yet taken legal effect and that there was a 20-day period for appealing it.

Another aspect of the case involves personal grievances.

After the verdict, television presenter Khoshgadam Hidayatgizi published a lengthy post on social media. She alleged that Mehdiyev had pressured the authorities to close her newspaper in 1999–2000 and blocked her candidacy in the 2005 elections.

She also said she had learned of an alleged plot to kill her by staging a car accident.

These claims could not be independently verified. Hidayatgizi also highlighted what she described as a striking change in attitudes towards Mehdiyev: people who once called him “father” and “aksakal” – a respected elder – were now among his fiercest critics.

Eldar Namazov, a political analyst and former head of the presidential administration’s secretariat, testified as a witness in the case. He recalled warning in 2020 that the network Mehdiyev had built posed a threat to the state.

Namazov told Oxu.az that Mehdiyev attended all court hearings remotely, was fully conscious and did not object to Namazov’s testimony.

A common thread running through this rhetoric is the attempt to portray Mehdiyev as an outsider to the political system.

Yet official discourse has largely avoided a central question: why was a man who shaped personnel policy, the ideological course of the country and the system of media control for 25 years allowed to remain untouchable throughout that period?

Critics question verdict delivered behind closed doors

Independent sources have focused less on the substance of the charges against Mehdiyev than on the lack of transparency surrounding the trial.

The Turan news agency says the closed-door proceedings make it impossible to independently assess the prosecution’s evidence or the defence’s arguments. It is also unclear why the verdict was announced only five days after it was delivered, or whether Mehdiyev intends to appeal.

According to the agency, political interpretations of the case in the context of Azerbaijan’s relations with Russia also remain speculation rather than established fact.

Turan columnist Tapdig Farhadoglu highlights another contradiction:

The first official document to reveal the income and assets of a man who headed the presidential administration for 24 years was not a declaration of assets, but a criminal verdict.

Even the information released about the verdict does not disclose the scale of the asset confiscations.

Lawyer Akram Hasanov offered a brief and pointed reaction on social media: “If Mehdiyev had died a few years earlier, he would have been buried in the First Alley of Honour.”

For the opposition, the most sensitive aspect of the case concerns Ali Karimli.

Karimli, chairman of the opposition Azerbaijan Popular Front Party (APFP), and Mammad Ibrahim, a member of the party’s leadership, are being held in connection with the same criminal case, although the charges against them are being handled in separate proceedings.

Both are accused of attempting to seize power by force. The relevant article of the Criminal Code carries a sentence of 12 to 20 years in prison or life imprisonment. A preliminary court hearing is scheduled for 3 November.

The APFP rejects the charges as politically motivated. In a statement issued in September, the party said Karimli had refused to testify from the outset of the investigation and denied claims that he had co-operated with Mehdiyev.

Against this backdrop, it is significant that Mehdiyev was convicted before proceedings against Karimli had begun.

Legally, the conviction of one defendant does not predetermine the outcome of proceedings against others in the case.

Politically, however, the situation looks different: the alleged central figure in the plot has already been found guilty, casting a shadow over the forthcoming trial of Karimli.

Why was the sentence suspended?

The court cited Article 70 of Azerbaijan’s Criminal Code, which allows a suspended sentence if the court concludes that the convicted person can be rehabilitated without serving time in prison.

Lawyer Ramil Suleymanov explained that a suspended sentence is not the same as house arrest. If the convicted person breaches the conditions imposed by the court, the suspended sentence can be revoked and the person sent to prison to serve the term.

The Turan news agency notes that the probation period under the law ranges from six months to five years. The length of the period imposed on Mehdiyev has not been disclosed.

The political significance of the verdict, however, appears to be independent of the form of punishment. Mehdiyev has been officially found guilty of treason, his assets are to be confiscated, and he could lose his state awards and membership of the National Academy of Sciences.

The authorities have secured this outcome without exposing the 88-year-old to the risk of dying in prison.

A suspended sentence also leaves open the possibility of tougher punishment in future. Any breach of the court-imposed conditions during the probation period could lead to the suspension being revoked and Mehdiyev being sent to prison.

This means the sentence could still be enforced through actual imprisonment at a later date.

At the same time, the verdict presents an obvious contradiction.

The state portrays Mehdiyev as a man who attempted to overthrow the constitutional order by force, yet considers it acceptable to leave him at liberty.

This leaves two possible explanations: either the threat was not as serious as the charges suggest, or the main purpose of the verdict was not so much to neutralise a threat as to send a political message.

News in Azerbaijan

World.title: Abkhaz businesses to be required to install solar panels amid energy crisis
World.content:
Businesses in Abkhazia will be required to install solar panels. The government sees the measure as one way to tackle an energy shortage that has affected the region for years during the autumn and winter.

The initiative aims to reduce peak demand on the power grid and give commercial properties a more independent electricity supply. Under the proposal, newly built commercial premises and businesses would have to meet part of their electricity needs through alternative sources, such as solar panels.

The authorities are currently discussing the electricity consumption threshold above which businesses would have to use alternative, self-contained power sources.

Some businesses in Abkhazia have been using solar panels for several years. For them, installing the panels was a necessity, as they had no other way to secure an uninterrupted electricity supply. However, they received no assistance or incentives from the authorities for doing so.

It remains unclear whether the government will help businesses install solar panels now that the measure is set to become mandatory. This issue is also still under discussion.

Abkhazia relies on the Inguri hydropower plant as its sole source of electricity. Under an agreement with the Georgian side, with which Abkhazia jointly operates the plant, the region receives 40% of the electricity it generates. However, this has not been enough for the past decade, particularly in autumn and winter, when water levels at the plant fall.

Abkhazia’s budget has recently begun to include funding for electricity imports from Russia, but this money is also insufficient to cover the shortfall fully.

As a result, the region faces scheduled power cuts every year from November to March.

The main, though not the only, cause of the shortage is uncontrolled cryptocurrency mining, which consumes huge amounts of electricity. Authorities have managed to reduce the scale of mining significantly in recent years, helping to ease the problem. However, they have yet to resolve it completely.

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

World.title: Six-fingered ‘trolls’ working for Georgia’s authorities: Myth Detector identifies 445 fake accounts
World.content:
Fake pro-government accounts in Georgia

The organisation Myth Detector has identified a new network of so-called “trolls” comprising 445 fake accounts. The findings follow monitoring of the Facebook pages of TV channels Imedi and Rustavi 2, whose editorial policies align with the government’s agenda.

The accounts operate in a co-ordinated manner, liking posts by Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze, Parliament Speaker Shalva Papuashvili, Tbilisi Mayor Kakha Kaladze and pro-government philosopher Zaza Shatirishvili.

The posts cover topics including bans on opposition parties, Western interference in Georgia’s domestic affairs and threats to the country’s sovereignty. Myth Detector believes the aim is to create the impression of widespread public support for the government’s rhetoric.

In an earlier investigation, the same organisation identified 434 similar profiles. Myth Detector concludes that the emergence of new accounts indicates that the practice is continuing.

Monitoring revealed several common characteristics across the network of fake accounts: identical profile pictures; anatomical and geographical inconsistencies typical of AI-generated images; recurring first and last names; and similar patterns of behaviour on social media.

According to Myth Detector, most of these accounts were created within a two-day period. A total of 329 profiles were registered on 25 August 2026 and another 109 on 26 August.

Of the 445 accounts identified, 316 use AI-generated profile pictures. The remaining 129 feature images of public figures, landscapes, posters or photographs belonging to other social media users.

The organisation says some of the newly discovered accounts overlap with profiles identified in October by the non-governmental organisation ISFED.

What do the fake accounts like?

According to Myth Detector’s analysis, the suspicious Facebook accounts were mobilised around posts published by TV channels Imedi and Rustavi 2. Their activity focused primarily on political statements by Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze, Parliament Speaker Shalva Papuashvili and Tbilisi Mayor Kakha Kaladze.

Co-ordinated likes were particularly noticeable under posts about a possible ban on opposition parties, Western interference in Georgia’s domestic affairs and alleged threats to the country’s sovereignty from Western institutions.

The fake accounts actively liked posts by Irakli Kobakhidze and Kakha Kaladze concerning a lawsuit against opposition parties filed with the Constitutional Court. Co-ordinated activity was particularly evident under a Rustavi 2 post in which Georgia’s Foreign Ministry described critical comments by EU representatives about a possible ban on opposition parties as interference in Georgia’s domestic affairs and an attempt to put pressure on the Constitutional Court.

Accounts mobilised around statements by Shalva Papuashvili supported the argument that foreign interference threatens freedom and democracy in Georgia.

Co-ordinated likes were also recorded under posts criticising the methods used to disperse protests in France and other European cities, drawing parallels with the situation in Georgia.

The accounts’ activity is not limited to engaging with posts by senior officials.

According to Myth Detector, co-ordinated likes also appeared under posts by pro-government philosopher Zaza Shatirishvili. He is one of the leading ideologues of the ruling team and the anti-Western platforms associated with it. His rhetoric closely echoes the narratives of the ruling party and its affiliated People’s Power movement.

Co-ordinated likes were also recorded under a post showing Bidzina Ivanishvili attending a party event, as well as under material covering a statement by Georgia’s Foreign Ministry.

AI-generated images and identity theft

According to the investigation, a significant proportion of the fake accounts attempt to imitate real people’s profiles.

They use photographs and biographical details of people with different ages, professions and interests, creating the impression of a diverse group of government supporters.

The profiles list a wide range of employers, including municipal and government institutions, banks, insurance companies, microfinance organisations and major media outlets such as Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty and even the Pirveli TV channel.

In some cases, the stated place of employment does not match other information in the profile. For example, an account registered under the name Levan Kavtaradze features a photograph of a man standing beside a car during the grape harvest, yet lists the perfume and cosmetics retailer Voulez-Vous as his employer.

Keti Giorgadze’s profile lists Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty as her employer, while the accounts of Temo Khitarishvili and Nutsa Simonia name the news service of Pirveli TV.

According to Hive Moderation, there is more than a 90% probability that the photographs found in the 445 accounts were generated using artificial intelligence. In some cases, the probability reaches 100%.

The images contain anatomical defects, inconsistencies in the surrounding environment and distorted text — all characteristic signs of AI-generated content. In some pictures, the number or shape of fingers looks unnatural, while others show altered architectural details, logos and national symbols.

A photograph posted by an account under the name Simoniko Janashia shows a person holding a cup with their left hand, which has six fingers instead of five. A mark associated with images generated by the Gemini AI model is also visible in the bottom-right corner of the picture.

In other examples, a hand holding a wine glass is missing its little finger, while hands appear unnaturally fused together or blended into clothing.

A photograph shared by Tako Dvalishvili shows a person holding a book. However, the text on its cover is distorted: instead of the words “History of Georgia”, it displays something illegible.

The organisation also identified geographical inconsistencies. Comparisons with genuine images of well-known locations in Georgia show that AI alters architectural details and surrounding landscapes, sometimes even adding structures that do not actually exist.

Reproducing the visual appearance of old profiles

The investigation found that some of the newly identified accounts use profile pictures that had previously appeared on accounts uncovered by Myth Detector and later removed by Facebook.

In some cases, these visual similarities include identical anatomical flaws characteristic of AI-generated images. For example, photographs used in personal profiles under the names Tako Chagelia and Nia Gamkrelidze show the same finger defect previously observed in the profile picture of an account attributed to Maiko Vibliani.

The investigation also identified other common patterns in the behaviour of some accounts. A total of 196 profiles had liked the Tbilisinews.ge page, 14 had liked Ai Politika and three had liked Rustavi 2. Fake accounts identified by the organisation in previous investigations had also liked the Ai Politika page.

Most of the suspicious profiles have no friends at all, while some have only one or two. The investigation also uncovered accounts created in 2024 with friend lists ranging from 169 to 4,800.

Fake pro-government accounts in Georgia

World.title: Five baobab trees destined for Georgia seized in South Africa
World.content:
South Africa blocks shipment of baobabs to Georgia

Authorities in the South African city of Durban have blocked the shipment of at least five baobab trees. The trees were reportedly destined for a landscaping project in Georgia. A criminal investigation into the case is now under way.

According to Daily Maverick, officials discovered the baobabs at a warehouse in Durban owned by Africa Global Logistics (AGL), a subsidiary of Paris-based transport giant MSC Group.

Bidzina Ivanishvili, Georgia’s informal ruler, is known for his passion for collecting rare trees and plants. His name has featured in several cases involving the import of exotic trees into the country. In 2022, an attempt to bring eight baobabs from Kenya to Georgia attracted international attention. However, all eight trees eventually dried up and died.

What happened

According to South Africa’s Department of Forestry, Fisheries and the Environment (DFFE), those involved in exporting the trees failed to produce valid permits authorising their possession and removal from the country.

The baobab is one of Africa’s most recognisable tree species and can live for up to 2,000 years. In South Africa, it is among 50 endemic tree species that receive special protection. Without the appropriate official permits, it is illegal to cut down, damage, move, possess, sell, transport or export these trees.

The identities of the Georgian buyers and their representatives have not yet been disclosed.

Candy Botha, AGL’s regional marketing manager, told Daily Maverick that the company had provided logistics services only. It was neither the owner of the cargo nor the exporter, and it did not hold the required permits.

After learning that the trees were in Durban, Daily Maverick visited the AGL warehouse and photographed at least five baobabs. The trees lay on their sides on a paved surface. They appeared to have been left there in direct sunlight for two to three months.

Asked about the trees’ legal status, the company said such matters fell outside its responsibilities as a logistics provider. AGL also refused to disclose the client’s identity or contact details, citing confidentiality.

After Daily Maverick sent further questions to the DFFE, it emerged that no valid export licence had been issued for the trees. There was also no permit authorising their removal and relocation. According to available information, the baobabs came from the Waterberg District in Limpopo province.

Based on photographs, Jeff Nichols, a specialist in endemic plants, suggested that the trees could be more than 50 years old if they had been taken from the wild. If they had instead been grown under artificial conditions with irrigation, he estimated their age at 20 to 30 years.

The DFFE said the exporter applied for the required licence on 27 July 2026. The application covered the removal, possession, collection, transport, export and acquisition of five protected trees. However, the department rejected it on 31 July. “The application was rejected because a criminal investigation into the matter is under way. The department will not issue a licence retrospectively to legitimise actions that appear to have been unlawful,” the department said.

On 8 August, the exporter appealed against the decision. The department said the appeal was currently under review by the official responsible for such matters.

Asked whether the applicants had complied with the relevant regulations, the DFFE said they had failed to meet the requirements of the National Forests Act. According to the department, the trees came from the local municipality of Lephalale in Waterberg District, Limpopo province, and were intended for export to Georgia.

The department has launched criminal proceedings in the case. Under the law, the offence carries a fine or a prison sentence of up to three years.

The DFFE has not disclosed the names of those facing criminal proceedings, nor has it identified the owner of the trees or the exporter. The department explained that possessing, collecting, removing, transporting, exporting, buying or selling protected trees constitutes a Category 1 offence.

The plan to transport the baobabs to Georgia has also raised concerns among environmentalists. Dr Sarah Venter, founder of the Baobab Foundation, said that although it was technically possible to uproot baobabs and transplant them elsewhere, the record of their survival in Georgia was discouraging.

“Unfortunately, the survival rates of these trees in Georgia leave much to be desired,” Venter said.

The Kenyan case: eight baobabs transplanted to Georgia dried up and died

The investigation currently under way in South Africa echoes an earlier attempt to transport baobabs from Kenya to Georgia, an incident that attracted international attention in 2022.

On 24 October 2022, The Guardian reported that Kenyan farmers had sold baobabs growing on their land to a group led by Georgian national Giorgi Gvasalia. The plan involved uprooting eight trees and transporting them to Georgia.

In November that year, Kenya’s Ministry of Environment suspended a foreign company’s licence to uproot baobabs, citing several violations. The ministry also instructed the Kenya Forest Service to stop the trees from being moved.

The ministry said uprooting baobabs required the appropriate permit and a transparent process demonstrating how relocating the trees would benefit the public. It concluded that the established requirements had not been met in this case. In April 2023, the Environment Committee of Kenya’s National Assembly, the lower house of parliament, launched an investigation into the circumstances surrounding the export of baobabs from the Kilifi region to Georgia.

The eight uprooted trees remained in that condition for almost two years and eventually died.

According to Georgia’s Dendrological Park, workers had uprooted the trees in 2021, but various obstacles delayed their transport to Georgia until October 2023. They planted the baobabs in the ground on 8 November 2023.

“These African giants spent almost two years uprooted, in natural conditions entirely unsuitable for them and without proper care. Unfortunately, the stress took its toll: six to seven months after they were planted in Georgia, all eight baobabs had died,” the park said.

Investigators in South Africa must establish who owned the trees and who arranged their removal from the country, under what circumstances these protected plants were uprooted, and who bears responsibility for the attempt to transport them to Georgia.

South Africa blocks shipment of baobabs to Georgia

World.title: Amnesty International, GYLA urge independent probe amid rising Georgian prison abuse claims
World.content:
Violence in Georgian prisons

International human rights organisation Amnesty International and the Georgian Young Lawyers’ Association (GYLA) issued a joint statement calling on the Georgian authorities to ensure an independent investigation into reports of torture and other forms of ill-treatment in prisons, as well as to establish effective mechanisms to prevent violence.

According to the organisations, reports of torture and other forms of ill-treatment in Georgian penitentiary institutions have increased, including allegations of sexual violence, beatings and threats.

The organisations also expressed serious concern about the risk of reprisals against prisoners who speak out about such abuse.

In their joint statement, the organisations cited the cases of Giorgi Davitadze, Giorgi and Davit Peikrishvili, Lasha Chachanidze and other prisoners.

The authors of the statement also noted that the authorities’ hasty denials, in the absence of proper investigations, raised serious questions. The organisations urged the authorities to “break the vicious cycle of impunity and establish an oversight mechanism capable of effectively and independently preventing violence”.

Giorgi Davitadze case and allegations of sexual violence

On 2 October 2026, a recording of a court hearing emerged in the media in which prisoner Giorgi Davitadze alleged that he had been subjected to sexual violence by penitentiary service staff. According to him, on 21 December 2025, in a de-escalation room at Prison No. 6 in Rustavi, one of the officers inserted a finger into his anus.

The Special Penitentiary Service rejected the allegations and released CCTV footage. The service said that a forced search had been carried out in accordance with established procedures after the prisoner refused to undergo a search and began insulting staff.

The footage, which has no audio, shows several officers restraining Davitadze, placing him face down on a bed and positioning themselves behind him. As the officers partially obstruct the view of the prisoner, it is impossible to fully assess their actions.

According to his lawyers, the penitentiary service released only a short excerpt from footage lasting approximately 20 minutes. A second camera was installed in the room, but prosecutors did not obtain its recording.
