According to the Public Defender’s Office, Davitadze’s lawyers reported the alleged abuse on 26 December 2025, and prosecutors launched an investigation on 29 December. Prosecutors say dozens of witnesses have been questioned, while Davitadze refused to undergo a forensic medical examination on 12 January 2026.

His lawyers explained that the proposed examination was aimed solely at identifying physical injuries and did not involve investigating the alleged rape itself.

Amnesty International and GYLA said the published footage did not clarify what had happened in the room. The human rights organisations stressed that, in cases involving allegations of sexual violence, the authorities were obliged to promptly arrange independent medical and psychological examinations.

According to his defence team, Davitadze was repeatedly subjected to humiliation and threats: half of his hair was shaved off, the heating in his cell was deliberately switched off, and threats were made against him and his family members. On 13 October, his lawyers reported that two officers had verbally abused the prisoner and confiscated his television.

According to representatives of the human rights organisations, the prison administration had not restricted access to Davitadze for the officers he accused of abuse. They demanded that the investigation examine not only the events of December but also all allegations of repeated threats and humiliation.

Alleged reprisals against prisoners

The organisations also highlighted the cases of prisoners at Prison No. 6 in Rustavi who expressed solidarity with Davitadze. According to reports, after Davitadze’s allegations became public, some prisoners staged protests, including by making noise in their cells. They were reportedly subsequently subjected to beatings, placed in de-escalation cells (isolation cells) and transferred to other penitentiary institutions.

On 5 October, the lawyer representing Lasha Chachanidze said prison officers had physically assaulted his client and four other prisoners in response to their protest. According to the lawyer, Chachanidze was beaten with batons on 2 October, with officers striking his arms and legs. Visible injuries were documented on his body when he was transferred to Prison No. 3 in Batumi.

On 16 October, another prisoner, Beka Tsertsvadze, reported that prison officers had beaten and verbally abused him while transferring him to a de-escalation cell, after which he was moved to another facility.

The Special Penitentiary Service rejected the allegations of beatings. The service said that placing at least four prisoners in de-escalation cells was a lawful security measure. According to the service, the measure was taken in response to attacks on prison staff on 2 and 4 October and was unrelated to the protests.

The service also released video footage showing two incidents in which prisoners attacked prison officers.

Amnesty International and GYLA noted that prison authorities were obliged to protect both staff and prisoners from violence. However, they stressed that alleged misconduct by prisoners did not justify the use of violence in retaliation.

The use of force is permissible only when strictly necessary and must be proportionate to the situation. Furthermore, restrictive measures must not become a means of punishing prisoners who file complaints or express solidarity with others.

The statement also cited an assessment by the European Committee for the Prevention of Torture (CPT). In a report published in February 2026, the committee expressed concern about the frequent and sometimes prolonged use of de-escalation cells in Georgian prisons. The CPT warned the authorities that, in practice, placing prisoners in such cells could amount to punishment. According to the committee, de-escalation cells should be used exclusively for prisoners who are agitated or displaying aggressive behaviour, for the shortest possible period and under medical supervision.

Davit Peikrishvili beating case

The case of Davit Peikrishvili has raised further concerns. On 20 October 2026, his lawyer, Paata Gogiashvili, reported that Peikrishvili had been repeatedly subjected to physical violence by fellow inmates at Gldani Prison No. 8 since 16 October.

According to the lawyer, the prisoner had been diagnosed with four fractured ribs, injuries to his skull and facial bones, and numerous bruises across his body. On 19 October, Peikrishvili was transferred to hospital, where medical staff confirmed that he had sustained multiple injuries.

On 19 October, the Special Penitentiary Service initially denied that Peikrishvili had been beaten. The following day, amid media reports and public criticism, the Justice Ministry announced the launch of a criminal investigation into his injuries. On 22 October, the Public Defender said that, according to Peikrishvili, prison officials had also participated in the beating. The Public Defender called on prosecutors to conduct an independent investigation.

On 26 October, prosecutors told journalists that the case had been transferred from the Justice Ministry’s General Inspectorate to the investigative department of Georgia’s Prosecutor General’s Office. Prosecutors also recommended the suspension of Giorgi Pataridze, director-general of the Special Penitentiary Service under the Justice Ministry.

Following the recommendation, Pataridze left his post, and a new head of the service was appointed.

According to human rights organisations, the developments surrounding Peikrishvili’s case have once again highlighted problems with the effective investigation of allegations of torture and other forms of ill-treatment in Georgia, as well as holding those responsible to account. They linked these concerns, in particular, to reports of violence against protesters detained since 2024.

Rights’ groups urge authorities to establish independent oversight mechanism

Amnesty International and GYLA insist that all credible allegations of torture and other forms of ill-treatment must be subject to prompt, thorough, independent and impartial investigations. They argue that the authorities must ensure that all relevant evidence is collected, victims of alleged abuse are protected, and those against whom there is sufficient evidence are held accountable.

The organisations also called on the authorities to review practices in penitentiary institutions, complaints procedures and mechanisms for protecting prisoners from ill-treatment.

“The Georgian authorities must break this vicious cycle of impunity by establishing an oversight mechanism genuinely capable of effectively and independently preventing violence, creating truly independent complaints procedures, and guaranteeing victims access to justice and compensation,” the organisations said in their joint statement.

World.title: Aliyev discusses peace, external threats and ‘double standards’ at Baku forum
World.content:
Aliyev’s speech at Baku Dialogue Forum

Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev spoke at the opening of the 7th World Forum on Intercultural Dialogue in Baku on 27 October. In his speech, he addressed peace efforts with Armenia, the role of international organisations, Azerbaijan’s foreign policy and security.

Aliyev said the country faced no internal threats, criticised “double standards” in international politics and proposed using Azerbaijan’s experience of transitioning from war to peace to help resolve other conflicts.

The World Forum on Intercultural Dialogue brings together representatives of governments, international organisations and experts from different countries to discuss intercultural and interfaith dialogue. The forum was first held in Baku in 2011 as part of the Baku Process initiative launched by Azerbaijan in 2008. It was originally intended to take place every two years. After a break caused by the COVID-19 pandemic, the forum resumed in 2024. This year’s seventh edition takes place from 27 to 29 October under the theme “Dialogue for a Shared Future”.

Intercultural dialogue and national unity

Aliyev described Azerbaijan’s geographical position between Europe and Asia as an important factor in fostering intercultural ties. He said religious and ethnic tolerance, as well as traditions of multiculturalism, were among the foundations of the country’s stable development.

The president said members of different ethnic and religious groups in Azerbaijan enjoyed equal constitutional rights and lived in an atmosphere of mutual understanding. According to him, the idea of Azerbaijani identity united different ethnic groups, and this unity had been evident even during the most difficult periods in the history of independent Azerbaijan. As an example, he cited the participation of members of different ethnic and religious groups in the Second Karabakh War.

Aliyev recalled that October marked the 35th anniversary of the restoration of Azerbaijan’s independence. He stressed that, despite changes in political systems, the Azerbaijani people had managed to preserve their language, traditions and national identity. The president said the country’s achievements since independence were the result of the Azerbaijani people’s efforts and that its development had taken place without international assistance.

“All potential threats come from beyond our borders”

In the part of his speech devoted to security, Aliyev said Azerbaijani society demonstrated unity on all issues. In his assessment, the country faced no internal threats, while all potential risks came from abroad.

“All potential threats come from beyond our borders,” the president said.

He compared ideological risks to physical threats and stressed the need to remain vigilant to protect national identity, statehood, independence and the country’s way of life. However, Aliyev did not specify which countries or organisations might pose such threats.

Karabakh negotiations and military operations

Aliyev said that restoring Azerbaijan’s territorial integrity had been the country’s main goal for most of its independence. The president criticised the years of negotiations over the Karabakh conflict, saying they had been aimed not at resolving the conflict but at freezing it.

He justified Azerbaijan’s military actions by citing the right to self-defence under the UN Charter.

According to the president, Azerbaijan restored its territorial integrity and sovereignty as a result of the 2020 war and the 2023 military operation, independently securing the implementation of UN Security Council resolutions adopted in 1993.

Peace with Armenia and experience of ending war

Speaking about relations with Armenia, Aliyev said that Azerbaijan had initiated peace efforts after the end of hostilities. According to him, the draft peace agreement initialled in the summer of 2025 had also been prepared by Baku.

The president stressed that Azerbaijan had not sought a protracted war and had decided not to continue the confrontation after achieving its military objectives. He noted that the desire for revenge could make war endless. In Aliyev’s view, it was important not only to achieve victory but also to know when to stop and offer peace.

The president suggested that parties involved in armed conflicts study Azerbaijan’s experience. He acknowledged that every conflict had its own characteristics but noted that ambition, aggression, the pursuit of superiority and a sense of impunity all played a role in their emergence.

UN resolutions, sanctions and “double standards”

Aliyev called for special attention to be paid to establishing a mechanism to ensure the implementation of UN Security Council decisions as part of discussions on UN reform. He criticised the failure to implement four resolutions on the Karabakh conflict for many years and the absence of sanctions against Armenia.

The president recalled that numerous sanctions had been imposed on countries to Azerbaijan’s north and south, describing the different approach towards Armenia as an example of “double standards”. He accused Armenia of occupying around 20% of Azerbaijan’s territory, carrying out ethnic cleansing and destroying religious and historical monuments. According to him, one million Azerbaijanis had been forced to flee their homes, while 65 mosques had been destroyed in Karabakh.

In criticising “double standards”, Aliyev addressed not only the international community’s response to wars. He also described attempts by other countries to dictate how Azerbaijan should live and what decisions it should make as unacceptable.

The president said Azerbaijan did not interfere in the internal affairs of other countries and expected the same treatment in return. According to him, displays of disrespect towards Azerbaijan and attempts to impose outside demands on the country had always met with firm resistance and would continue to do so. Aliyev also noted that relations based on mutual respect could help reduce the number of international conflicts.

Partnerships with US, China and Europe

Speaking about foreign policy, the president described Azerbaijan as a pillar of stability in an unstable region. He attributed the country’s stronger international standing to its independent policies, economic potential and role in the energy and transport sectors.

Aliyev highlighted strategic partnerships with China and the US, as well as strategic partnership agreements with ten EU member states. The president said Azerbaijan would host a summit of the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation in 2027 and a summit of the European Political Community in 2028.

He also recalled the summit of the Conference on Interaction and Confidence Building Measures in Asia, held in Baku in October. According to him, Azerbaijan’s chairmanship of the organisation had been extended for another two years, and the country had been invited to become a full member of the Central Asian Consultative Format. Aliyev described these decisions as recognition of Azerbaijan’s growing role on the international stage.

External debt, energy and transport routes

Turning to economic issues, Aliyev said Azerbaijan’s external debt stood at just over 5% of GDP. He highlighted energy exports and international transport links as factors strengthening the country’s position.

In his view, Azerbaijan’s infrastructure and political ties, as well as its geographical location, played an important role in the development of international transport routes.

The president stressed that developing international transport links required maintaining good relations not only with neighbouring countries but also with their neighbours.

Peace agreement initialled in Washington and region’s future

Concluding his speech, Aliyev noted that both positive and negative developments had taken place around the world since the previous forum. He cited the outbreak of new wars in neighbouring regions as negative developments and the peace process with Armenia as a positive one.

The president recalled that the text of a peace agreement had been initialled in Washington in August 2025, with the participation of Donald Trump. Aliyev stressed that, at that stage, the agreement had only been initialled, not signed. The US president had, however, signed a trilateral declaration as a witness. According to Aliyev, this process marked a new chapter for the South Caucasus.

World.title: Chronicles of Victory: October 29, 2020
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 29. The Azerbaijani Army launched a counter-offensive operation, later called the "Iron Fist," on September 27, 2020, in response to the large-scale provocation of the Armenian armed forces along the frontline.

The 44-day second Karabakh war ended with the liberation of Azerbaijan’s territories from nearly 30-year Armenian occupation and the restoration of territorial integrity.

Trend presents the chronicle of the 33rd day of the Second Karabakh War:

- President Ilham Aliyev approved a law on renaming the Vang village of Khojavand district into Chinarli village.

- President Ilham Aliyev called Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan.

- The Azerbaijani Defense Ministry released information on the latest situation on the frontlines. A list of destroyed military equipment of the Armenian Armed Forces was announced.

- A video of the liberated villages of the Gubadli district was released.

- The territory of Goranboy and Tartar districts came under fire. The Armenian troops, who were forced to retreat, opened fire on the civilian population.

- High-ranking Armenian officers were killed. Footage of equipment and ammunition left by the Armenian troops on the battlefield was released. Two Armenian Su-25 planes were destroyed.

- The territory of the Tartar district, including diplomatic representatives, came under fire. Another civilian was killed as a result of the Armenian fire.

- Armenian servicemen, who fired at civilians in Azerbaijan’s Barda, were killed on the battlefield. Equipment of Armenia's troops was destroyed.

World.title: India’s Rossari registers as gas purification reagent supplier in Azerbaijan (Exclusive)
World.content:
ASHGABAT, Turkmenistan, October 28. The Indian company Rossari Biotech Limited has registered as a supplier of MDEA, a chemical reagent used for gas purification, and is exploring opportunities to expand its cooperation with the State Oil Company of Azerbaijan (SOCAR) and other oil and gas companies in the country, a representative of Rossari Biotech Limited, Ketan Gadhiya, told Trend on the sidelines of the 31st International Conference and Exhibition "Oil and Gas of Turkmenistan" (OGT 2026) in Ashgabat.

"In Azerbaijan, our company has already registered as a supplier of MDEA, a chemical reagent for gas purification. We are also exploring potential cooperation with SOCAR and other oil and gas companies operating in the country," he noted.

According to Gadhiya, the company intends to focus primarily on supplying chemical products for all segments of the oil and gas industry: upstream (exploration and production), midstream (transportation and storage), and downstream (refining and marketing).

He explained that the company’s manufacturing specialization enables it to offer oil and gas enterprises products of the required quality at competitive prices.

"We focus on national oil companies and refineries, as we are manufacturers ourselves. This allows us to supply high-quality products at competitive prices to oil and gas companies operating in Azerbaijan and Turkmenistan," the Rossari Biotech representative said.

Rossari Biotech Limited is an Indian manufacturer of specialty chemicals, founded in 1997. The company produces chemical solutions for the oil and gas and textile industries, as well as for the production of household chemicals, agricultural products, and other sectors. According to the company, its product portfolio includes over 4,300 items, and its operations span more than 65 countries.

Meanwhile, Indian External Affairs Minister Subrahmanyam Jaishankar said at a joint press conference with Azerbaijani Foreign Minister Jeyhun Bayramov that Indian companies are interested in investing in Azerbaijan’s oil and energy sectors.

According to Jaishankar, there are good opportunities to further expand bilateral trade and investment.

"We agreed that we should explore the possibility of further deepening investment in the oil and energy sectors, as well as expanding cooperation in other areas," the minister added.

World.title: Azerbaijan, OIC discuss ways to expand cooperation (PHOTO)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 28. Azerbaijan and the Organization of Islamic Cooperation (OIC) discussed ways to expant bilateral cooperation during a meeting today in Baku.

This was reported by the press and public relations department of the Azerbaijani Parliament.

The discussions were held during the meeting between Speaker of Azerbaijan’s Parliament Sahiba Gafarova with a delegation led by Organization of Islamic Cooperation (OIC) Secretary-General Hissein Brahim Taha, who is visiting Azerbaijan.

Congratulating Taha on his election as OIC secretary-general, Gafarova wished him success in his new role. She noted that Azerbaijan was among the first countries he had visited since taking office, describing this as a reflection of the strong ties between Azerbaijan and the OIC. She expressed confidence that the visit would help strengthen bilateral cooperation.

Gafarova highlighted the discussions held during Taha’s meeting with President Ilham Aliyev, as well as his participation in the 7th World Forum on Intercultural Dialogue and the third high-level meeting of heads of law enforcement agencies responsible for combating corruption in OIC member states, both held in Baku.

She said the World Forum on Intercultural Dialogue aims to promote dialogue, mutual trust and understanding, build bridges between different cultures and religions, and foster respect for the values of others. Gafarova noted that, since its inception at the initiative of President Ilham Aliyev, the forum had become one of the leading global platforms for intercultural and interfaith dialogue.

The meeting also highlighted Azerbaijan’s important role in the OIC. Participants noted the organization’s consistent support for Azerbaijan both during the period of occupation of its territories and in the post-conflict period, with numerous OIC resolutions and decisions reflecting this support and solidarity.

Gafarova briefed the guest on the history, modern structure and international activities of the Parliament. She noted that the Azerbaijani parliament actively participates in the work of numerous international parliamentary organizations and currently chairs three of them.

The speaker also highlighted the 20th session of the Parliamentary Union of the OIC Member States (PUIC), held in Baku in June, during which she served as chair. She shared her views on prospects for cooperation between the PUIC and the OIC.

Taha thanked Azerbaijan for its support for the OIC’s activities and for successfully hosting the World Forum on Intercultural Dialogue in Baku. He shared his impressions of his meeting with President Ilham Aliyev, the president’s address at the forum and the development he had witnessed in Azerbaijan.

He said Azerbaijan was setting an example for the world in preserving peace and stability. Taha also highlighted the significance of Azerbaijan hosting the 16th session of the Islamic Summit Conference and chairing the OIC in 2027. He expressed confidence that Azerbaijan’s chairmanship would further strengthen the organization’s work.

Speaking about the importance of parliamentary diplomacy, Taha reaffirmed the OIC’s consistent support for Azerbaijan’s territorial integrity and sovereignty. He also conveyed his congratulations on the upcoming Victory Day and praised the work carried out in Azerbaijan’s liberated territories.

The meeting included an exchange of views on strengthening Islamic solidarity, promoting intercultural dialogue, further expanding cooperation between Azerbaijan and the OIC, and other issues of mutual interest.

World.title: Azerbaijan and NATO discuss development of military cooperation (PHOTO/VIDEO)
World.content:
Photo: Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Azerbaijan

BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 28. Deputy Commander of Azerbaijan Air Force – Air Combat Commander, Major General Zaur Rustamov met with Assistant Chief of Staff for Military Cooperation at Supreme Headquarters Allied Powers Europe (SHAPE), Brigadier General Theodoros Stefou.

This was reported by the press service of the Ministry of Defense of the Republic of Azerbaijan.

At the meeting, held within NATO Evaluation Level-2 (NEL-2) for a pair of Mi-17-1V helicopters of the Azerbaijan Air Force, conducted under NATO’s Operational Capabilities Concept (OCC) Programme, the sides discussed current state and prospects for the development of Azerbaijan-NATO military cooperation.

The meeting featured presentations on the joint activities, the units’ training level, and the assigned tasks.

It was emphasized that such events are of great importance in enhancing training level for peacekeeping operations, strengthening interoperability, and expanding the exchange of experience.

Then an extensive exchange of views on issues of mutual interest was held.

At the end of the meeting, the sides exchanged gifts and a photo was taken.

Following the meeting, the guests visited the training area, reviewed the units’ equipment and evaluated its compliance with NATO standards and requirements.

World.title: Live: US Fed holds rates unchanged, chance of local rise more than 75pc
World.content:
So, the result of the Fed's meeting overnight was expected.

But that doesn't mean interest rates are on hold forever in the world's biggest economy.

The outcome of this week's meeting was widely expected after top Fed ​officials indicated they saw no rush to ​raise rates again following the quarter-percentage-point increase ⁠approved last month, despite inflation data in the meantime that was stronger than forecast and concerns that price pressures are broadening across the economy.

Energy costs remain high, including for diesel fuel, which is a key input for shipping, agriculture, and other industries. Inflation and the cost ​of living in general have been central to the political races that will determine whether Trump's Republican Party remains in control ​of both houses of Congress on ⁠November 3, or whether Democrats move into leadership positions and gain more robust oversight powers, including over the Fed.

Financial markets are still pricing in a couple of additional rate hikes in the coming months, though with slightly less conviction than before Fed Chair Kevin Warsh spoke.

Pricing shows about an 80% chance of a rate hike at the Fed's December 8-9 meeting, with another ⁠likely by March.

Inflation, ​which is currently around a percentage point above the Fed's target, has shown little progress in recent ​months.

The US central bank has missed its inflation target for five and a half years, a fact that has left some officials worried that businesses and households are becoming accustomed to faster price increases and may plan ​for them in ways that will make inflation harder to control.

- with Reuters

World.title: Trump expands hunt for voter fraud ahead of midterms
World.content:
Hello! Welcome back to our US midterms briefing.

Click here to see how popular Trump is today, and click here for a quick breakdown on what the midterms are all about.

Here's what you need to know today

Presidents hit the trail: Republican President Donald Trump and Democratic former president Barack Obama are heading to Ohio and Georgia respectively to shore up votes as the US enters its last week before the midterms. These states are the sites of critical contests that could decide which party could control the US Senate for the remainder of Trump's term. Obama kept a low profile for most of this election cycle, but has hit the campaign trail in recent days to deliver some fiery speeches against his successor.

Republican President Donald Trump and Democratic former president Barack Obama are heading to Ohio and Georgia respectively to shore up votes as the US enters its last week before the midterms. These states are the sites of critical contests that could decide which party could control the US Senate for the remainder of Trump's term. Obama kept a low profile for most of this election cycle, but has hit the campaign trail in recent days to deliver some fiery speeches against his successor. Hunt for non-citizen voters: The Trump administration has issued more than 100 subpoenas demanding records on tens of thousands of voters in at least 13 states, Reuters reports. It's the latest in an effort to uncover evidence of voter fraud. Election officials and lawyers worry the investigations could undermine confidence in election systems, and be used to attack the legitimacy of narrow races. Since Trump returned to office, prosecutors have accused at least 147 people of illegally voting, Reuters reports, but the cases amount to fewer than one for every million people who voted in 2024.

It's the latest in an effort to uncover evidence of voter fraud. Election officials and lawyers worry the investigations could undermine confidence in election systems, and be used to attack the legitimacy of narrow races. Since Trump returned to office, prosecutors have accused at least 147 people of illegally voting, Reuters reports, but the cases amount to fewer than one for every million people who voted in 2024. The tale of two Dans: If you missed it, Republican senator Dan Sullivan is defending his Alaska seat from independent candidate … Dan Sullivan. It's been a point of ire for Republicans for months, with (unsuccessful) challenges to throw the newcomer off the ballot making it all the way to the Alaska Supreme Court. They argue the second Sullivan (AKA, Dan J Sullivan) is running just to confuse voters. Dan J Sullivan has maintained he's running for legitimate reasons. But a New York Times exclusive has put a new twist in the tale, reporting that campaign aides for Democratic candidate Mary Peltola sought a spoiler candidate by the name of Dan Sullivan to undermine the senator back in 2025.

A deeper dive

I messaged North America correspondent Kamin Gock about the Republican Party's standing in states that are typically conservative. Here's what he had to say.

E Elissa Fitzgerald Trump is off to Ohio after a campaign blitz in Texas yesterday. That's a lot of time spent on what are usually safe Republican areas. Is he worried about losing ground here? K Kamin Gock Absolutely — this will be his third visit to the state this month! Ohio has been reliably Republican in Senate races. But it could now be a crucial battle ground, with polls showing a very competitive race between Republican Jon Husted and Democrat Sherrod Brown. If the Democrats pick up four Senate seats across the country, they'll retake control of the upper house. In Ohio, Democrats also hope they can pick up a seat in the House of Representatives and none of that spells good news for Trump. E Elissa Fitzgerald You spent some time in Nebraska — another typically red state — not long ago. What did you learn there? K Kamin Gock Some farmers are really feeling rising costs linked to tariffs and the Iran war, particularly fuel and fertiliser price hikes. One farmer told me he is paying an extra $US1,400 ($1984) a day for diesel to operate his farm. Those are extra costs the farmers I spoke to say they did not vote for. K Kamin Gock There was a lot of disquiet and disappointment among Republicans, but just because they are unhappy with Trump doesn't mean they will vote Democrat. As one man told me, he probably just won't vote.

You can read more about Kamin's trip to Nebraska here.

How popular is Donald Trump today?

US President Donald Trump might not be up for election at the midterms, but his popularity will have a strong influence over the outcome.

The president's party almost always loses House seats in midterm elections and that trend gets steeper when the president is unpopular.

Historic polling data collated by analytics firm Gallup shows presidents with approval ratings below 50 per cent have seen their party lose an average of 37 House seats.

Presidents with approval ratings above 50 per cent have netted smaller loses, with an average of 14 seats.

World.title: Concern as Queensland port plans sea dump in coral spawning season
World.content:
The Port of Townsville in north Queensland is planning to dump silt and sediment at sea within days of coral spawning.

The timing has residents of nearby Magnetic Island concerned that poor water quality will compromise local reef reproduction.

Corals simultaneously release egg and sperm bundles during spawning. (Supplied: SCU/Peter Harrison)

James Cook University coral ecologist Andrew Baird said Queensland inshore reefs were expected to begin spawning within days.

"Coral spawning is a very important part of reef recovery," Professor Baird said.

"If reefs get disturbed, the main source of recovery will be sexual recruits from the coral spawning."

The Port of Townsville said it was planning not to dredge, due to coral spawning, until November 4.

It said it would then dump naturally occurring sediment build-up from shipping channels at sea 6 kilometres offshore of Magnetic Island's Florence Bay.

A drone image of sediment in waters off Magnetic Island in 2025. (Supplied: Lawrence Scheele)

Community concern

Diving instructor Chad Bertram, who lives and runs a scuba and snorkel business on the island, said dredge spoil muddied the local waters.

"Easterly winds and the currents that we do have generally brings [the spoil] to the shores of Magnetic Island and on our fringing reefs," he said.

"There are times we have to cancel for safety when there is visibility of next to nothing."

Chad Bertram is a dive instructor who lives and works on Magnetic Island. (ABC News: Chloe Chomicki)

He said he feared that dredge spoil in the water, particularly during coral spawning, could have long-term implications for the reefs.

"I think anything we can do to minimise our human impact can only be a good thing, so concerned is an understatement."

The Magnetic Island Nature Care Association, led by Gethin Morgan, has spent years raising concern about the port dumping spoil at sea.

The port dumps sediment in a dredge material placement area (DMPA). (Supplied: Port of Townsville)

The area in Cleveland Bay, between Townsville and Magnetic Island, is excised from the Great Barrier Reef Marine Park and has been an approved disposal site for decades.

"It is a real shock to hear that they are going to do dredging and dumping in the middle of the spawning season," Mr Morgan said.

"We all know that October and November are months in which corals spawn, and they can also be very windy months."

Silt and sediment affect spawning

Australian Institute of Marine Science coral ecologist Katharina Fabricius said coral larvae were sensitive to poor water quality well after the initial spawning.

"They are looking for clean reef surfaces and that could be up to two weeks after the spawning event, sometimes longer," she said.

"During those times the larvae are searching for places that are free of sediment, then they settle and become baby corals.

"Any type of silt and sediment is affecting coral spawning, no matter where it comes from."

Katharina Fabricius is a coral ecologist with the Australian Institute of Marine Science. (ABC News: Chloe Chomicki)

Port says dredging is essential

The Port of Townsville said it had voluntarily planned for no dredging during the main predicted spawning window in October as a precaution.

"Maintenance dredging of the port's main shipping channels and harbour is scheduled to recommence from November 4 for 10 days to remove naturally occurring sediment build-up," a spokesperson said.

"Maintenance dredging is an essential and routine activity that supports the safe movement of vessels, which is a statutory responsibility for the port.

"The dredging program is being undertaken some kilometres from sensitive coral reef habitats, and environmental modelling does not predict impacts on those reefs."

The spokesperson said the port had undertaken maintenance dredging and sea placement at this time of year previously, most recently in 2024.

World.title: Breaking: Man arrested after woman dies in Armidale stabbing

World.title: Quick hits: Green survives Rorschach test as Aussies put Cape Town to sleep
World.content:
Cam Green has fallen on the right side of a line-ball call and "that annoying number three" has collected another unwanted record as the Aussies sent Cape Town to sleep on a dominant second day.

Here are the quick hits from the third Test at Newlands.

1. Unwanted record for 'annoying number three'

The South Africans were eagerly awaiting Labuschagne's entrance on day two. (Getty Images: Grant Pitcher/Gallo Images)

The Aussies were cruising.

Starting their innings at the beginning of day two, the tourists raced out of the blocks in glorious mid-morning sun, just as South Africa's openers had done 24 hours earlier.

But things changed with Simon Harmer's entrance into the attack, with the off spinner promptly removing Travis Head for 41 and exposing the under-pressure Marnus Labuschagne.

The South Africans had been clearly looking forward to welcoming Labuschagne to the middle all morning, with the stump mic having earlier picked up an unknown fielder encouraging his bowler to "get that annoying number three in here".

Loading Instagram content

But the hosts did not get much of an opportunity to enjoy Labuschagne's company, with the Queenslander spending four deliveries trying to work a single before edging to slip to be out for a five-ball duck.

Harmer wheeled away in celebration, joined by a horde of ravenous teammates, as Labuschagne's career crisis continued.

The Queenslander's latest failure was his 48th Test innings without a century, making it the longest run without a ton for a top-four batter in Australia's history.

2. Green survives third umpire's Rorschach test

The Proteas were convinced they had their man.

Cam Green had made his way to 22 when he pushed tentatively to a Gerald Coetzee length ball, with his thick edge flying to a stooping Harmer at second slip.

At first glance, it looked to be a regulation grab, with the off-spinner rising then roaring in celebration, but Green was not going anywhere.

After a brief consultation, the umpires decided to send the decision upstairs, where the footage was combed over frame-by-frame.

It was close, with the two camera angles telling two different stories.

The two angles told two different stories. (Fox Cricket)

Straight on, it could be argued the ball had kissed turf as it nestled into Harmer's hands, but side on, the ball looked to have been collected cleanly.

It was something of a Rorschach Test for the third umpire, and unfortunately for the hosts, he saw the image that kept Green out in the middle.

Only a matter of moments later, it was Renshaw's turn to survive a very close call, with a line-ball LBW decision going the Aussies' way.

3. Sandpaper in the stands

The only remaining member of the trio that was punished for the Sandpapergate scandal in 2018, Steve Smith's 11th hour withdrawal robbed cricket fans of one of the most eagerly anticipated returns in Test history.

But if the Australians thought that meant they wouldn't be reminded of one of their darkest days, some in the Cape Town crowd have ensured they were mistaken.

Video emerged of Nathan Lyon taking his place on the boundary at fine leg on day one, with a cackling spectator leaning forward while holding out a sheet of what looked to be sandpaper.

Lyon declined the offer.

Another fan, wearing a shirt with Smith's sobbing face emblazoned across it, told the Herald Sun he was disappointed the batter wasn't playing, and that he had been looking forward to some "banter".

4. Magic Marco joins rare air

With both Renshaw and Green set and with the luck appearing to go their way, South Africa was in need of something special.

Marco Jansen provided it.

South Africa vs Australia third Test, day two live Alex Carey and Josh Inglis put together a handy partnership late on day two in Cape Town to put Australia in firm control of the third Test against South Africa.

The world's number one ranked bowler provided a fearsome spell in the shadows of tea, dismissing both batters to swing the momentum once again.

Renshaw stood his ground as he just about middled one through to Ryan Rickelton behind the stumps, but was rightly given out for 74 on review, and Green (65) was caught — this time fairly — by Harmer at second slip.

With neither the ball nor pitch appearing to offer very much, it was a seriously impressive five-over spell, and one that saw the 26-year-old take his 100th Test wicket.

In terms of balls bowled, Jansen's 3,864 deliveries saw him become the fifth-fastest bowler to claim a century of scalps, and the third fastest since the 19th century.

5. Carey and Inglis put Cape Town to sleep

Coming together after that Jansen double strike and with Australia's innings at a crossroads at 4-185, Alex Carey and Josh Inglis were composed and circumspect in building their partnership.

The pair were for the most part untroubled in pushing their stand past 100, playing only the shots that were presented to them and offering up few opportunities to the increasingly desperate South Africans.

Not even the second new ball could interrupt their rhythm, with Jansen and Kagiso Rabada unable to emulate Mitchell Starc's stunning spell from late on day one.

But where Starc had low clouds and fading light, the South African spearheads had a placid pitch and still sparkling evening sun.

And in the dying embers of a taxing, 90-over day, some in the Newlands crowd couldn't help but nod off.

Carey and Inglis pushed Australia into a lead and put some in the Newlands crowd to sleep in the process. (Fox Cricket)

Carey (51*) and Inglis (85*) will resume on day three having batted the entire final session and with Australia one run in front.

World.title: Dozens of trees poisoned along valuable and beloved Sunshine Coast beachfront
World.content:
Dozens of native trees, including at least one towering Norfolk pine, are dying after being illegally doused with poison along a beachfront walkway on Queensland's Sunshine Coast.

A 300-metre stretch along Dicky Beach in Caloundra was the target of the chemical attack, which has the potential to permanently contaminate the soil.

The Sunshine Coast Council is investigating a tree poisoning that stretches about 300 metres along a popular beachfront walkway at Dicky Beach. (ABC News: Owen Jacques)

Sunshine Coast councillor Terry Landsberg said council teams had been scouring the area "with a fine-tooth comb" to remove any remaining traces of the poison.

"It's so distressing to see the amount of dieback that we're actually witnessing, as well as potentially the loss of one of our iconic Norfolk pines," he said.

"This is probably one of the largest in terms of poisoning that we've witnessed [on the Sunshine Coast].

"To see it on this scale is really distressing."

Dicky Beach on Queensland's Sunshine Coast has become popular for property investors and tourists. (ABC News: Owen Jacques)

Cr Landsberg said the council was testing the samples collected from the area to determine the exact poison used, in the hopes of saving the affected trees.

"It appears as though this poison may be affecting the photosynthesis, and maybe their ability to attract sunlight," he said.

"We can see that it's extremely aggressive".

'We've got to follow due process'

The councillor declined to speculate about why anyone would want to poison a long line of beachfront trees.

"You can take your own assumptions in regards to why people do this on this scale," he said.

Sunshine Coast councillor Terry Landsberg says the poisoning may be one of the largest to occur in the region. (ABC News: Owen Jacques)

"We've got to make sure we respect the process before we start singling out any property owner or individual.

"We've got to follow due process and make sure we deal with it in an appropriate manner."

If a culprit is found and prosecuted, environmental vandalism can carry fines of more than $130,000.

Caloundra resident Chloe Christopher, 28, has lived in the area her entire life, and said she was hurt to see the damage done.

Caloundra woman Chloe Christopher, 28, has lived in the area her entire life and says it's sad to see the flowers and greenery slowly disappear. (ABC News: Owen Jacques)

She said the area was usually "luscious" and dotted with flowers.

"It's sad to see because we live in such a beautiful part of the coast, so it's really sad to come past and see all of our beautiful plants dying," she said.

" I'm not sure what the point of poisoning it was, but it's just really disappointing because it just ruined a beautiful place on the coast. "

Dicky Beach resident Brittany Guy, with son, questioned why anyone would poison the same trees that make the area so beautiful and valuable. (ABC News: Owen Jacques)

Brittany Guy, who lives nearby, spends a lot of time in the area with her young son and said she was furious to learn trees had been poisoned.

"What was the point? Do you live around here? Do your children grow up around here?" she said.

"There's people paying millions and millions of dollars to live here for the environment that we live in and that nature we're around.

"I don't understand why they would do that."

Couple fined over Noosa clearing

The Sunshine Coast council is not the only one grappling with illegal destruction of trees and greenery.

In September, Noosa couple Heidi Meyer and Kim Carroll were ordered to replant almost 1,600 trees and pay court fees of almost $50,000 for illegally clearing their private land.

The cleared and subdivided land on Picture Point Crescent in Noosa Heads was listed for sale online for $25 million last year.

A Noosa council spokesman said he hoped the costs and orders would serve as a warning to others.

World.title: Breaking: Police fatally shoot woman allegedly armed with axe in Adelaide's east
World.content:
Police have shot and killed a woman who was reportedly armed with an axe during a confrontation at Firle in Adelaide's eastern suburbs this morning.

The incident happened about 2am when police were called to Gwynne Street.

Police said they were responding to reports "that a woman was armed with an axe" and that when they arrived they were confronted by the woman, who allegedly threatened them.

Police said a taser was used, but it was ineffective, and that they then "discharged a firearm, striking the woman".

Officers attempted first aid before ambulance paramedics arrived, police said, but the woman died at the scene.

"Major Crime Investigation Branch detectives, Forensic Response Section officers and investigators from Internal Investigation Section are at the scene and will examine the circumstances surrounding the incident," police said.

Police said an officer sustained minor injuries.

Gwynne Street is closed, and police said they would provide further information later this morning.

Police will prepare a report for the coroner.

World.title: Child safety caseworkers 'on the brink of collapse' and leaving in droves
World.content:
Youth justice union delegates say caseworkers are "on the brink of collapsing", with highly experienced staff leaving in droves amid crushing workloads and less resources.

Together Union members, across youth justice and child safety are set to walk off the job today, in what will be their longest stop action since 2018.

Workers in the south-east corner will walkout from midday and bus to parliament house, after bargaining negotiations over agreements collapsed.

The Together Union has been negotiating with the state government on a new child safety and youth justice agreement since March. (Supplied)

Mount Isa union delegate, Karlie Markham said the Youth Justice Service Centre has lost a collective 50 years of experience in the last 12 months, as highly skilled caseworkers left for better paying, and better resourced jobs.

"We're continuously being told that we have to do more with less and we're at the end of working with less. We can't sustain ourselves," she said.

"We're on the brink of everything collapsing and we just need the support from the government to be able to give us the funding and the resources and the staff to be able to do our jobs."

Mount Isa union delegate, Karlie Markham said workers continue to leave the industry. (ABC News: Tim Little)

Ms Markham said not only were caseloads increasing, but they were becoming more complex.

"It's just expanded significantly and we're struggling to keep up," she said.

" We just cannot get the work done within our hours. It's impossible. "

The Together Union said at its worst, the Mount Isa centre was operating with four less caseworkers and for a prolonged period without a team leader.

Assistant Secretary for the Together Union, Dee Spink said there was "critical workforce shortages in frontline roles".

"This government loves to talk about community safety, but they're not resourcing the workers to actually do the job on the front line," she said.

Dee Spink is the Together Union's Assistant Secretary. (Supplied)

The Union said the government's breach bail, go to jail laws, set to be passed in parliament tonight, would only put further pressure on caseworkers.

Ms Markham said it was another reason why the government needed to channel more resources towards youth justice workers.

"If this government is serious about addressing youth crime and community safety, they actually need to start to get serious about supporting their staff," Ms Markham said.

"And that starts with more staffing and more resources, so we're actually able to do the minimum of our jobs and keep ourselves and communities safe."

Queensland child safety workers strike Employees are set to bring air mattresses to local members of parliament's offices to highlight cases in which children have spent the night in government offices waiting for suitable placement to be found.

In a statement, a Crisafulli government spokesperson said contingency plans were in place to minimise the disruption of the stop action.

"The Crisafulli Government values the incredible commitment of its youth justice staff and is continuing to negotiate in good faith, and we urge the Labor unions to do the same," it said.

Ms Spink also said three experienced caseworkers in Hervey Bay had left for jobs with Education Queensland in the past 12 months, citing higher pay, lower caseloads and better resources.

"You can't replace that overnight," Ms Spink said.

The Union is currently in reconciliation with the Queensland government in the Industrial Relations Commission.

World.title: Spain train crash live updates: At least 68 killed in high-speed train crash with death toll set to rise as nation’s PM says ‘all of Spain is in mourning’
World.content:
A key question about this horrific crash is whether the Iryo train should have been moving, or moving faster, when it was struck from behind on the high-speed line heading south from Madrid to Seville.

The Spanish government’s early statements indicate that as many as six trains on the same line had been stopped at some point on Wednesday morning due to problems with the signalling system.

The trains crashed on a high-speed railway, killing at least 68 people and injuring dozens more. AP Photo/Manu Fernandez

Transport Minister Óscar Puente said an order had been given for some of the six trains to resume their journeys.

Iryo is now flatly contradicting that statement. The company has told El Mundo, one of the major media outlets in Spain, that its train driver did not receive an order to resume movement.

World.title: Fed keeps rates on hold despite inflation surge; ASX set to rise, Wall Street advances
World.content:
Updated BusinessMarketsWorld markets Fed keeps rates on hold despite inflation surge; ASX set to rise, Wall Street advances Stan Choe Updated October 29, 2026 — 7:24am ,first published 5:16am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Wall Street held firm and the bond market swung after the Federal Reserve announced it will keep interest rates on hold. It was a widely expected move, with the central bank opting to delay any changes to borrowing costs until after next week’s US midterm elections and awaiting further data on the path of inflation. Fed chair Kevin Warsh said the central bank has “started to see some changes in financial and credit conditions. They have tightened for some businesses and households.” Bloomberg The S&P 500 rose 0.3 per cent, the Dow Jones Industrial Average added 0.2 per cent and the Nasdaq composite rose 0.3 per cent. In the bond market, the two-year Treasury yield initially jumped after the Fed held its main interest rate steady. It then reversed course after traders pared expectations for coming hikes to rates. The Australian sharemarket is set to rise, with futures at 6.59am AEDT pointing to a rise of 40 points, or 0.5 per cent, at the open. The ASX closed flat on Wednesday. The Australian dollar was trading at US70.35¢.



Related Article Casinos ‘Profit over compliance’: Star says it can afford $260m money-laundering fine In a 10-2 decision, the Fed said it would maintain its benchmark interest rate within the current 3.75 per cent-4.00 per cent range while acknowledging that inflation “remains elevated,” upgrading its assessment of the economy, and hinting that further rate hikes may be coming depending on the performance of inflation. “The accumulation of more information will help the Committee determine the policy stance appropriate to ensure a timely return of inflation to the Committee’s 2 per cent goal,” the rate-setting Federal Open Market Committee said in its latest policy statement. “The Committee will deliver price stability.” At a news conference following the announcement, chair Kevin Warsh said the Fed has “started to see some changes in financial and credit conditions. They have tightened for some businesses and households.” The Fed raised its benchmark rate last month for the first time in three years, defying President Donald Trump’s demands for rate cuts, in an effort to get inflation back to its 2 per cent target in a “timelier” manner. The Fed is tasked by Congress to combat inflation, and it does so by lifting rates to slow borrowing and spending and cool price increases. The statement leaves the Fed’s next moves unclear, even though officials last month penciled in another rate hike for this year. Wall Street investors have also priced in a rate hike in December, according to futures markets.



Fed Governor Lisa Cook, currently targeted by President Donald Trump for removal from the central bank, dissented in favour of a quarter-percentage-point rate hike, as did Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack, a consistently hawkish voice who also dissented in July for the same reason Wall Street cares so much about interest rates because they are one of the main levers that set prices for stocks. The other big variable is how much profit companies are making, and several companies rallied Wednesday after joining the list of those beating analysts’ expectations for the summer. Wall Street held its gains after the widely-expected decision and Warsh’s press conference. Bloomberg GE HealthCare Technologies jumped 6.6 per cent after delivering both profit and revenue for the summer that surpassed analysts’ expectations. It also raised its forecasts for revenue growth and other financial measures for the full year. Etsy climbed 5.5 per cent after its profit for the latest quarter blew past analysts’ forecasts. CEO Kruti Patel Goyal said the online marketplace saw growth in active buyers from prior-year levels for the first time in two years, while its active seller base grew at its fastest rate in two years.



Stocks in the artificial-intelligence industry were also relatively solid. They’ve stabilised this week following big swings on worries that high borrowing costs caused by high interest rates will undercut the boom in AI data centres largely built with borrowed money. AI stocks got an additional boost after a major player in the industry, South Korea’s SK Hynix, soared 13.3 per cent in Seoul following its latest profit report. The seller of memory chips said it’s in the midst of a virtuous cycle of rising AI usage, and it expects demand to continue to outpace supply through 2030. On Wall Street, Micron Technology rose 5.9 per cent and was the strongest force lifting the S&P 500. It also sells memory for computers. Outside of tech and earnings, Wendy’s soared 15.2 per cent to $US7.07 after Trian Fund Management, run by investor Nelson Peltz, offered to buy the chain for $US7.35 per share in cash. That helped offset a drop for Boston Scientific, which fell 5.9 per cent even though the seller of medical devices reported a milder drop in profit for the latest quarter than analysts expected. It gave a forecast for profit in the current quarter that fell short of analysts’ expectations.



Related Article Opinion

Trade wars Thank you, Mr President: BlueScope gets a windfall from Trump’s tariffs Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist Robinhood Markets sank 3.3 per cent after reporting weaker profit and revenue for the latest quarter than analysts expected. Rising oil prices pushed upward on Treasury yields as uncertainty continues about what will happen in the Middle East and the global energy industry. The price for a barrel of Brent crude, the international standard, climbed 2.7 per cent to $US112.39. In stock markets abroad, South Korea’s Kospi jumped 6.6 per cent following SK Hynix’s leap. Japan’s Nikkei 225 rose 1.1 per cent, while France’s CAC 40 rose 0.1 per cent. AP with Reuters The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. Get it each weekday afternoon.

World.title: Apple unveils its first-ever touchscreen laptop
World.content:

Apple after two decades of spurning the idea, unveiled an overhauled MacBook Pro that includes a touch screen, giving its flagship laptop a feature that has become a must-have in the personal computer industry.

The thinner and vastly lighter machine, which comes in 14-inch and 16-inch sizes, is also the first Mac with OLED — short for organic light-emitting diode — a display technology used on recent iPhones, iPads and other Apple devices. It’s also the first Mac with a Dynamic Island, the screen element familiar to iPhone users.

Apple has given its flagship laptop a feature that has become a must-have in the personal computer industry. Apple

The computer has a redesigned interface optimised for touch and is offered with the M5 Pro and M5 Max chips. The 14-inch version is priced from $4599 in Australia and is available for pre-order. It will be released on November 6 (US time).

Johny Srouji, Apple’s chief hardware officer, called the new machine a “monumental step forward for the Mac.” It was introduced on stage by new chief executive officer John Ternus, who took the reins from Cook last month.

World.title: The most common special exemptions in Queensland year 12 exams
World.content:
NationalQueenslandHigh school The most common special exemptions in Queensland year 12 exams Catherine Strohfeldt October 29, 2026 — 6:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Thousands of Queensland senior students are sitting a different test to their classmates this exam season, as special conditions and allowances rise, and educators voice doubts about whether the testing format remains fit for purpose. Across the 17-day external assessment block last year, the Queensland Curriculum and Assessment Authority approved adjustments on at least one exam for 5056 students, or 12 per cent of the cohort. These allowances included alternative format papers such as black-and-white materials, braille, and enlarged typeface, rest breaks, readers, scribes, or additional time. The number of students receiving special adjustments on their external year 12 exams has grown by 1 per cent of the cohort each year since 2022. Dominic Lorrimer The proportion of students receiving adjustments has risen by 1 per cent of the testing cohort each year since 2022.



In 2025, this amounted to almost 10,300 special condition allowances, although a student may be granted multiple adjustments for a single exam. Dr Matthew White specialises in inclusive education at the Australian Catholic University. Australian Catholic University Dr Matthew White, an expert in inclusive education at the Australian Catholic University, said the trend highlights shortcomings of the exams themselves, rather than students’ abilities. “A lot of universities have early entry now,” he said. “We’re still wedded to a final exam … what’s the purpose of that exam?” Between 2022 and 2025, the overall number of adjustments grew by 49.1 per cent, and alternative formatting for papers increased by 89.5 per cent.



White said a similar range of adjustments had been offered across states since the late 2000s, but the options were “too narrow”. “So much has changed since then with regard to technology and health,” he said. “Our way of looking at exams and the whole way of looking at adjusting for young people with disability and things like that has advanced since then, but this hasn’t. It’s remained exactly the same.” A QCAA spokesperson said the assessment authority awarded adjustments for long-term or chronic conditions, mental health diagnoses, temporary injuries or short-term conditions, and illness or misadventure. The latter applied for students taught the wrong ancient history topic in 2025.



These four eligibility categories had remained the same since the new Queensland Certificate of Education system was rolled out in 2020, the spokesperson said. Related Article High school How students are picking vocational and trade subjects to boost their ATAR The most common special condition was additional time, granted for 4781 exam papers, followed by rest breaks, which were applied for 2513 external assessment sittings. Students used, on average, about 40 per cent of their approved extra minutes, and between 9 and 11 per cent of their rest breaks. White said the arrangements were frequently given for students with anxiety, so the most important part was just knowing a time or break was available.



“When you have a rest break, you’re usually in a separate room, you usually have someone sitting close by you, you’re not in a big exam room, and it’s that just that psychological safety net,” he said. “You don’t have that same time pressure … [but] more often than not, students are just keen to get through the exam.” Over the next three weeks, 43,277 Queensland students will sit at least one general subject external exam. World.content:
Exclusive SportAFLAFL 2026 AFL bets on Sunday nights as overlapping matches are scrapped Peter Ryan October 29, 2026 — 6:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Sunday night football will become a feature of the AFL fixture in 2027, with a match to be played in the timeslot in each of the first 13 rounds for the first time. The overlapping of Sunday matches that impacted viewer satisfaction at times this year will be removed, giving fans the chance to end their weekends watching three AFL matches back-to-back-to-back. Josh Fraser and Will Hayward celebrate their win over Essendon in this year’s King’s Birthday eve clash. It was Fraser’s fourth win as coach after replacing Michael Voss mid-season. AFL Photos In all but rounds one and six, the first game each Sunday will start at 12.30pm, leading into a 3.15pm match and then finishing with a night game, which is defined as starting after 6pm. Next year’s fixture marks an increase from eight Sunday night matches in the first 13 rounds in 2026, with four of the matches to be played at Marvel Stadium and one at the MCG.



When possible, the AFL has attempted to anchor the Sunday night fixtures to public holidays in the states where they are played, with two of the biggest such games reserved for Easter Sunday and the night before the King’s Birthday public holiday. The extension of Sunday night football means nine matches will be broadcast each round on four nights of the week from Thursday to Sunday. Related Article Exclusive

AFLW The Magpies’ CEO said they didn’t need outside help for an AFLW review. They’ve backflipped Marvel Stadium co-tenants the Western Bulldogs and St Kilda will clash at Marvel Stadium on Easter Sunday in round two, presenting the Saints with a tough opening to their critical 2027 season (matches against Collingwood and the Bulldogs). Luke Beveridge’s men will also be coming off a tough round one clash against the Dockers in Perth. Essendon and Carlton will again meet on King’s Birthday eve in a match that has been locked into the fixture since 2023. Each of the four previous matches in that timeslot have attracted crowds of more than 70,000 to the MCG.



In round one, the Sunday night clash will occur when West Coast host Gold Coast in Perth in the afternoon local time, a game that will be beamed back into the eastern states on a Sunday evening. Related Article AFL 2026 Double Dreamtime: Tigers and Bombers to take their rivalry to Perth in 2027-28 Port Adelaide will host the Western Bulldogs as Zak Butters returns to Adelaide Oval in the red, white and blue on Sunday night during Gather Round. Six of the eight matches played on Sunday nights in the opening 13 rounds in 2026 were played outside Victoria, but the removal of Opening Round means that nine matches will occur in each round during most of the early rounds of the season. The AFL’s first attempt to regularly lock Sunday nights into the fixture stalled after a night match in the middle of winter in 2014 between Carlton and Collingwood attracted just 40,939 fans.



The backlash to the six-match trial made the league gun shy about adopting the timeslot, particularly in Victoria, but they have been slowly building the number of games played then since 2025 – with careful programming in place to ensure attendances at the matches reflect the enthusiasm of television viewers. The addition to the competition of the Tasmania Devils in 2028 could lead to each team playing 24 matches each home-and-away season, up from 23.
