World.title: What Lula’s win in Brazil means for the Amazon and the warming world
World.content:
Analysis EnvironmentClimate changeParis Agreement What Lula’s win in Brazil means for the Amazon and the warming world Nick O'Malley October 29, 2026 — 5:50am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

The world dodged a bullet on Monday morning (AEDT) when a Brazilian electoral court declared that President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva had an insurmountable lead over challenger Flávio Bolsonaro and had won a fourth term in office. Lula, as he is known, had secured 51.76 per cent of votes against Bolsonaro’s 48.24 per cent. President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva has been declared the winner of Brazil’s election. Getty Images It is impossible to overstate how much is riding on that small margin. For Brazil, it is the difference between the continued defence of the democracy it achieved following the end of its military dictatorship in 1985. Flávio, son of jailed former president Jair Bolsonaro, had campaigned on a promise to pardon his father, and clear his allies for their involvement in the coup attempt that followed Jair’s election loss to Lula in 2022.



For the world, it means that hopes to stabilise the planet’s climate have not been dashed. The Amazon rainforest, which sprawls across 6 million square kilometres, 60 per cent of which lies inside Brazil’s borders, produces between 6 and 9 per cent of the world’s total oxygen and acts as a carbon sink, absorbing more carbon dioxide than it emits. That’s changing. Under Bolsonaro’s rule, clearing and burning for agriculture, beef production and mining had reached record highs, pushing it towards the point at which it may start to emit more carbon than it absorbs. In large sections that point has already been breached. This was no accident. In 2019, Jair Bolsonaro rejected data from Brazil’s National Institute for Space Research that detected a surge in deforestation since his election, telling foreign reporters, “You have to understand that the Amazon is Brazil’s, not yours,” and declaring: “If all this devastation you accuse us of doing was done in the past, the Amazon would have stopped existing – it would be a big desert.” It is estimated that Lula’s efforts to preserve the forest over the past fours years has saved 20,000 square kilometres of the Amazon. As a result of his efforts, Brazil’s emissions fell 13 per cent in 2024 and a further 6 per cent last year.





Flavio won the first round of elections, before a surge of voters mobilised by a massive turnout effort to put Lula over the top in the second round, the first time such a reversal has happened. This suggests that to many voters this was as much a battle over democracy as it was over climate. When it appeared that Bolsonaro had an unassailable lead after the first round of voting, illegal clearing fires tripled, suggesting some farmers believed that conservation efforts and fines for illegal clearing would soon be abandoned. Lula will now confront a national congress in which Bolsonaro’s far-right Liberal Party (PL) forms the biggest block in both houses. It holds 121 of 513 seats in the lower house, and 29 of 81 in the Senate, while Lula’s PT-coalition holds 88 and nine respectively. The PL is expected to use its numbers to continue its efforts to open Indigenous lands to mining and undermine environmental safeguards. According to analysis by Brazil’s Climate Observatory, nearly 70 per cent of lower house MPs have low or very low alignment with environmental protection policies, a figure that rises to 79 per cent in the Senate. “The executive branch will have a crucial role to play in preventing setbacks in environmental and social legislation and ensuring that progress on environmental protection continues,” said Maurício Voivodic, executive director of WWF-Brazil. Loading



Nonetheless, the climate movement is breathing a sigh of relief this week, while multilateral institutions consider how the world might better help finance the protection of rainforests. “Science shows that we can still prevent the irreversible transformation of vast areas of the Amazon, but time is running out,” said Carlos Nobre, professor at the University of São Paulo and co-chair of the Science Panel for the Amazon, of Lula’s victory. “The next four years will be decisive for the future of the world’s largest tropical rainforest and for climate stability in Brazil and around the world.” Get to the heart of what’s happening with climate change and the environment.

World.title: Another cookie-cutter comedian game show? Yep, and we’re sick of them.
World.content:
★★ CultureTV & radioReview Another cookie-cutter comedian game show? Yep, and we’re sick of them. Bridget McManus October 29, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Celebrity Escape ★★ Some things are more fun to do than watch, and yet still make passable television. Just think of all the programs about fishing, cooking and renovating. There’s even a reality show involving knitting. But Australian-New Zealand collaboration Celebrity Escape, which puts seven comedians into escape rooms to solve puzzles and unlock doors, manages to make this popular activity awkward and boring, and even more awkward and boring to watch. The cast of Celebrity Escape (from left) Frank Woodley, Abby Howells, Hayley Sproull, host Rove McManus, Josh Thomson, Chris Parker, Celia Pacquola and Luke McGregor. Originally launched in New Zealand to mixed reviews in June, Celebrity Escape is the latest in a wearingly long line of comedian-stacked game and panel shows. Hosted by Rove McManus in the role of games master, it purports to be a new concept, but it is really just another tired idea relying on a props department for visual gags, and comedians for improvised slapstick and wordplay. McManus is jestingly sadistic, chortling from a surveillance chamber at the players’ ineptitude, while explaining the rules and pointing out the clues. However, the villainous power afforded his position doesn’t sit as comfortably on this perennial nice guy as it does on Taskmaster Australia overlord Tom Gleeson.



Assembling in “the void”, a corridor lined with doors leading to themed chambers, four New Zealanders (Josh Thomson, Hayley Sproull, Abby Howells and Chris Parker) and three Australians (Luke McGregor, Celia Pacquola and Frank Woodley) resort to cartwheeling when the banter runs dry. Related Article Streaming The 14 most anticipated TV shows still to come this year Once inside the first room, a “witch’s cabin” named after a real woman hilariously executed during the Salem witch trials, the comedians descend into dithering confusion. This task requires analytical thinking, not so much a quick wit, and rather than this resulting in the uproarious spectacle of celebrities out of their comfort zones – like we need any more of that – it feels pointless. It’s not as if they don’t try, but unfortunately the group dynamics yield neither humour nor drama. McGregor and Pacquola are the nice besties from Rosehaven, while whimsical fool Woodley becomes uncharacteristically serious. The Kiwis work their self-deprecating shticks, except for Wellington Paranormal’s Josh Thomson, who makes a valiant effort to stoke competition with deadpan trash talk. At least Taskmaster, on which many of these performers have appeared, has scope for physical silliness. There, the comedians largely work alone, bouncing off a skilled fall-guy (Tom Cashman is superb in the local version).



The comedians, including Luke McGregor and Celia Pacquola (left), find keys in the Mechanics Workshop in episode two of Celebrity Escape. Even more worryingly, Celebrity Escape is just another in a seemingly endless line of comedian-stacked panel and game shows. Julia Morris’ Class Clowns is currently testing our patience for this kind of low-budget comedy, but at least that format is open-ended enough to give its players room to move. While Julia Zemiro’s Crime Night! doesn’t need to try quite as hard, but it’s also guilty of shoving comedians from an ever-shrinking casting pool into a themed setting and expecting them to find the funny – in that case, in the grisly details of true crimes. Related Article ★★★★

Review ‘No one was burning for me’: Tina Arena tells her story with grace, fire and wit Please, for the love of Thank God You’re Here, can we return to the ingenious simplicity of theatresports? And properly invest in our funny folk, so that more sitcoms such as Kath & Kim and Fisk, and sketch shows such Full Frontal and Aunty Donna’s Big Ol’ House of Fun and Black Comedy might be developed. We have too proud a history of homegrown comedy, and way too much talent that is needed now, more than ever, to make sense and light of a darkening world, to waste our finest comedians on cookie-cutter entertainment. Celebrity Escape premieres at 9pm on Thursday, November 5, on ABC Entertains and ABC iview.

World.title: Spain train crash live updates: At least 68 killed in high-speed train crash with death toll set to rise as nation’s PM says ‘all of Spain is in mourning’
World.content:
A key question about this horrific crash is whether the Iryo train should have been moving, or moving faster, when it was struck from behind on the high-speed line heading south from Madrid to Seville.

The Spanish government’s early statements indicate that as many as six trains on the same line had been stopped at some point on Wednesday morning due to problems with the signalling system.

The trains crashed on a high-speed railway, killing at least 68 people and injuring dozens more. AP Photo/Manu Fernandez

Transport Minister Óscar Puente said an order had been given for some of the six trains to resume their journeys.

Iryo is now flatly contradicting that statement. The company has told El Mundo, one of the major media outlets in Spain, that its train driver did not receive an order to resume movement.

World.title: Fed keeps rates on hold despite inflation surge; ASX set to rise, Wall Street advances
World.content:
Updated BusinessMarketsWorld markets Fed keeps rates on hold despite inflation surge; ASX set to rise, Wall Street advances Stan Choe Updated October 29, 2026 — 7:24am ,first published 5:16am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Wall Street held firm and the bond market swung after the Federal Reserve announced it will keep interest rates on hold. It was a widely expected move, with the central bank opting to delay any changes to borrowing costs until after next week’s US midterm elections and awaiting further data on the path of inflation. Fed chair Kevin Warsh said the central bank has “started to see some changes in financial and credit conditions. They have tightened for some businesses and households.” Bloomberg The S&P 500 rose 0.3 per cent, the Dow Jones Industrial Average added 0.2 per cent and the Nasdaq composite rose 0.3 per cent. In the bond market, the two-year Treasury yield initially jumped after the Fed held its main interest rate steady. It then reversed course after traders pared expectations for coming hikes to rates. The Australian sharemarket is set to rise, with futures at 6.59am AEDT pointing to a rise of 40 points, or 0.5 per cent, at the open. The ASX closed flat on Wednesday. The Australian dollar was trading at US70.35¢.



Related Article Casinos ‘Profit over compliance’: Star says it can afford $260m money-laundering fine In a 10-2 decision, the Fed said it would maintain its benchmark interest rate within the current 3.75 per cent-4.00 per cent range while acknowledging that inflation “remains elevated,” upgrading its assessment of the economy, and hinting that further rate hikes may be coming depending on the performance of inflation. “The accumulation of more information will help the Committee determine the policy stance appropriate to ensure a timely return of inflation to the Committee’s 2 per cent goal,” the rate-setting Federal Open Market Committee said in its latest policy statement. “The Committee will deliver price stability.” At a news conference following the announcement, chair Kevin Warsh said the Fed has “started to see some changes in financial and credit conditions. They have tightened for some businesses and households.” The Fed raised its benchmark rate last month for the first time in three years, defying President Donald Trump’s demands for rate cuts, in an effort to get inflation back to its 2 per cent target in a “timelier” manner. The Fed is tasked by Congress to combat inflation, and it does so by lifting rates to slow borrowing and spending and cool price increases. The statement leaves the Fed’s next moves unclear, even though officials last month penciled in another rate hike for this year. Wall Street investors have also priced in a rate hike in December, according to futures markets.



Fed Governor Lisa Cook, currently targeted by President Donald Trump for removal from the central bank, dissented in favour of a quarter-percentage-point rate hike, as did Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack, a consistently hawkish voice who also dissented in July for the same reason Wall Street cares so much about interest rates because they are one of the main levers that set prices for stocks. The other big variable is how much profit companies are making, and several companies rallied Wednesday after joining the list of those beating analysts’ expectations for the summer. Wall Street held its gains after the widely-expected decision and Warsh’s press conference. Bloomberg GE HealthCare Technologies jumped 6.6 per cent after delivering both profit and revenue for the summer that surpassed analysts’ expectations. It also raised its forecasts for revenue growth and other financial measures for the full year. Etsy climbed 5.5 per cent after its profit for the latest quarter blew past analysts’ forecasts. CEO Kruti Patel Goyal said the online marketplace saw growth in active buyers from prior-year levels for the first time in two years, while its active seller base grew at its fastest rate in two years.



Stocks in the artificial-intelligence industry were also relatively solid. They’ve stabilised this week following big swings on worries that high borrowing costs caused by high interest rates will undercut the boom in AI data centres largely built with borrowed money. AI stocks got an additional boost after a major player in the industry, South Korea’s SK Hynix, soared 13.3 per cent in Seoul following its latest profit report. The seller of memory chips said it’s in the midst of a virtuous cycle of rising AI usage, and it expects demand to continue to outpace supply through 2030. On Wall Street, Micron Technology rose 5.9 per cent and was the strongest force lifting the S&P 500. It also sells memory for computers. Outside of tech and earnings, Wendy’s soared 15.2 per cent to $US7.07 after Trian Fund Management, run by investor Nelson Peltz, offered to buy the chain for $US7.35 per share in cash. That helped offset a drop for Boston Scientific, which fell 5.9 per cent even though the seller of medical devices reported a milder drop in profit for the latest quarter than analysts expected. It gave a forecast for profit in the current quarter that fell short of analysts’ expectations.



Related Article Opinion

Trade wars Thank you, Mr President: BlueScope gets a windfall from Trump’s tariffs Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist Robinhood Markets sank 3.3 per cent after reporting weaker profit and revenue for the latest quarter than analysts expected. Rising oil prices pushed upward on Treasury yields as uncertainty continues about what will happen in the Middle East and the global energy industry. The price for a barrel of Brent crude, the international standard, climbed 2.7 per cent to $US112.39. In stock markets abroad, South Korea’s Kospi jumped 6.6 per cent following SK Hynix’s leap. Japan’s Nikkei 225 rose 1.1 per cent, while France’s CAC 40 rose 0.1 per cent. AP with Reuters The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. Get it each weekday afternoon.

Independent MP Dai Le has encouraged Pauline Hanson to rein in party brass after it distributed controversial colouring books to children at shows in Brisbane and Mount Gambier.

The colouring books contained illustrations that appear to show Bluey and Robert Irwin being held at knifepoint, along with unflattering depictions of rival politicians. World.title: Apple unveils its first-ever touchscreen laptop
World.content:
You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month.

Apple after two decades of spurning the idea, unveiled an overhauled MacBook Pro that includes a touch screen, giving its flagship laptop a feature that has become a must-have in the personal computer industry.

The thinner and vastly lighter machine, which comes in 14-inch and 16-inch sizes, is also the first Mac with OLED — short for organic light-emitting diode — a display technology used on recent iPhones, iPads and other Apple devices. It’s also the first Mac with a Dynamic Island, the screen element familiar to iPhone users.

Apple has given its flagship laptop a feature that has become a must-have in the personal computer industry. Apple

The computer has a redesigned interface optimised for touch and is offered with the M5 Pro and M5 Max chips. The 14-inch version is priced from $4599 in Australia and is available for pre-order. It will be released on November 6 (US time).

Johny Srouji, Apple’s chief hardware officer, called the new machine a “monumental step forward for the Mac.” It was introduced on stage by new chief executive officer John Ternus, who took the reins from Cook last month.

World.title: The most common special exemptions in Queensland year 12 exams
World.content:
NationalQueenslandHigh school The most common special exemptions in Queensland year 12 exams Catherine Strohfeldt October 29, 2026 — 6:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Thousands of Queensland senior students are sitting a different test to their classmates this exam season, as special conditions and allowances rise, and educators voice doubts about whether the testing format remains fit for purpose. Across the 17-day external assessment block last year, the Queensland Curriculum and Assessment Authority approved adjustments on at least one exam for 5056 students, or 12 per cent of the cohort. These allowances included alternative format papers such as black-and-white materials, braille, and enlarged typeface, rest breaks, readers, scribes, or additional time. The number of students receiving special adjustments on their external year 12 exams has grown by 1 per cent of the cohort each year since 2022. Dominic Lorrimer The proportion of students receiving adjustments has risen by 1 per cent of the testing cohort each year since 2022.



In 2025, this amounted to almost 10,300 special condition allowances, although a student may be granted multiple adjustments for a single exam. Dr Matthew White specialises in inclusive education at the Australian Catholic University. Australian Catholic University Dr Matthew White, an expert in inclusive education at the Australian Catholic University, said the trend highlights shortcomings of the exams themselves, rather than students’ abilities. “A lot of universities have early entry now,” he said. “We’re still wedded to a final exam … what’s the purpose of that exam?” Between 2022 and 2025, the overall number of adjustments grew by 49.1 per cent, and alternative formatting for papers increased by 89.5 per cent.



White said a similar range of adjustments had been offered across states since the late 2000s, but the options were “too narrow”. “So much has changed since then with regard to technology and health,” he said. “Our way of looking at exams and the whole way of looking at adjusting for young people with disability and things like that has advanced since then, but this hasn’t. It’s remained exactly the same.” A QCAA spokesperson said the assessment authority awarded adjustments for long-term or chronic conditions, mental health diagnoses, temporary injuries or short-term conditions, and illness or misadventure. The latter applied for students taught the wrong ancient history topic in 2025.



These four eligibility categories had remained the same since the new Queensland Certificate of Education system was rolled out in 2020, the spokesperson said. Related Article High school How students are picking vocational and trade subjects to boost their ATAR The most common special condition was additional time, granted for 4781 exam papers, followed by rest breaks, which were applied for 2513 external assessment sittings. Students used, on average, about 40 per cent of their approved extra minutes, and between 9 and 11 per cent of their rest breaks. White said the arrangements were frequently given for students with anxiety, so the most important part was just knowing a time or break was available.



“When you have a rest break, you’re usually in a separate room, you usually have someone sitting close by you, you’re not in a big exam room, and it’s that just that psychological safety net,” he said. “You don’t have that same time pressure … [but] more often than not, students are just keen to get through the exam.” Over the next three weeks, 43,277 Queensland students will sit at least one general subject external exam. World.title: AFL bets on Sunday nights as overlapping matches are scrapped
World.content:
Exclusive SportAFLAFL 2026 AFL bets on Sunday nights as overlapping matches are scrapped Peter Ryan October 29, 2026 — 6:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Sunday night football will become a feature of the AFL fixture in 2027, with a match to be played in the timeslot in each of the first 13 rounds for the first time. The overlapping of Sunday matches that impacted viewer satisfaction at times this year will be removed, giving fans the chance to end their weekends watching three AFL matches back-to-back-to-back. Josh Fraser and Will Hayward celebrate their win over Essendon in this year’s King’s Birthday eve clash. It was Fraser’s fourth win as coach after replacing Michael Voss mid-season. AFL Photos In all but rounds one and six, the first game each Sunday will start at 12.30pm, leading into a 3.15pm match and then finishing with a night game, which is defined as starting after 6pm. Next year’s fixture marks an increase from eight Sunday night matches in the first 13 rounds in 2026, with four of the matches to be played at Marvel Stadium and one at the MCG.



When possible, the AFL has attempted to anchor the Sunday night fixtures to public holidays in the states where they are played, with two of the biggest such games reserved for Easter Sunday and the night before the King’s Birthday public holiday. The extension of Sunday night football means nine matches will be broadcast each round on four nights of the week from Thursday to Sunday. Related Article Exclusive

AFLW The Magpies’ CEO said they didn’t need outside help for an AFLW review. They’ve backflipped Marvel Stadium co-tenants the Western Bulldogs and St Kilda will clash at Marvel Stadium on Easter Sunday in round two, presenting the Saints with a tough opening to their critical 2027 season (matches against Collingwood and the Bulldogs). Luke Beveridge’s men will also be coming off a tough round one clash against the Dockers in Perth. Essendon and Carlton will again meet on King’s Birthday eve in a match that has been locked into the fixture since 2023. Each of the four previous matches in that timeslot have attracted crowds of more than 70,000 to the MCG.



In round one, the Sunday night clash will occur when West Coast host Gold Coast in Perth in the afternoon local time, a game that will be beamed back into the eastern states on a Sunday evening. Related Article AFL 2026 Double Dreamtime: Tigers and Bombers to take their rivalry to Perth in 2027-28 Port Adelaide will host the Western Bulldogs as Zak Butters returns to Adelaide Oval in the red, white and blue on Sunday night during Gather Round. Six of the eight matches played on Sunday nights in the opening 13 rounds in 2026 were played outside Victoria, but the removal of Opening Round means that nine matches will occur in each round during most of the early rounds of the season. The AFL’s first attempt to regularly lock Sunday nights into the fixture stalled after a night match in the middle of winter in 2014 between Carlton and Collingwood attracted just 40,939 fans.



The backlash to the six-match trial made the league gun shy about adopting the timeslot, particularly in Victoria, but they have been slowly building the number of games played then since 2025 – with careful programming in place to ensure attendances at the matches reflect the enthusiasm of television viewers. The addition to the competition of the Tasmania Devils in 2028 could lead to each team playing 24 matches each home-and-away season, up from 23. World.title: What Lula’s win in Brazil means for the Amazon and the warming world
World.content:
Analysis EnvironmentClimate changeParis Agreement What Lula’s win in Brazil means for the Amazon and the warming world Nick O'Malley October 29, 2026 — 5:50am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

The world dodged a bullet on Monday morning (AEDT) when a Brazilian electoral court declared that President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva had an insurmountable lead over challenger Flávio Bolsonaro and had won a fourth term in office. Lula, as he is known, had secured 51.76 per cent of votes against Bolsonaro’s 48.24 per cent. President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva has been declared the winner of Brazil’s election. Getty Images It is impossible to overstate how much is riding on that small margin. For Brazil, it is the difference between the continued defence of the democracy it achieved following the end of its military dictatorship in 1985. Flávio, son of jailed former president Jair Bolsonaro, had campaigned on a promise to pardon his father, and clear his allies for their involvement in the coup attempt that followed Jair’s election loss to Lula in 2022.



For the world, it means that hopes to stabilise the planet’s climate have not been dashed. The Amazon rainforest, which sprawls across 6 million square kilometres, 60 per cent of which lies inside Brazil’s borders, produces between 6 and 9 per cent of the world’s total oxygen and acts as a carbon sink, absorbing more carbon dioxide than it emits. That’s changing. Under Bolsonaro’s rule, clearing and burning for agriculture, beef production and mining had reached record highs, pushing it towards the point at which it may start to emit more carbon than it absorbs. In large sections that point has already been breached. This was no accident. In 2019, Jair Bolsonaro rejected data from Brazil’s National Institute for Space Research that detected a surge in deforestation since his election, telling foreign reporters, “You have to understand that the Amazon is Brazil’s, not yours,” and declaring: “If all this devastation you accuse us of doing was done in the past, the Amazon would have stopped existing – it would be a big desert.” It is estimated that Lula’s efforts to preserve the forest over the past fours years has saved 20,000 square kilometres of the Amazon. As a result of his efforts, Brazil’s emissions fell 13 per cent in 2024 and a further 6 per cent last year.





Flavio won the first round of elections, before a surge of voters mobilised by a massive turnout effort to put Lula over the top in the second round, the first time such a reversal has happened. This suggests that to many voters this was as much a battle over democracy as it was over climate. When it appeared that Bolsonaro had an unassailable lead after the first round of voting, illegal clearing fires tripled, suggesting some farmers believed that conservation efforts and fines for illegal clearing would soon be abandoned. Lula will now confront a national congress in which Bolsonaro’s far-right Liberal Party (PL) forms the biggest block in both houses. It holds 121 of 513 seats in the lower house, and 29 of 81 in the Senate, while Lula’s PT-coalition holds 88 and nine respectively. The PL is expected to use its numbers to continue its efforts to open Indigenous lands to mining and undermine environmental safeguards. According to analysis by Brazil’s Climate Observatory, nearly 70 per cent of lower house MPs have low or very low alignment with environmental protection policies, a figure that rises to 79 per cent in the Senate. “The executive branch will have a crucial role to play in preventing setbacks in environmental and social legislation and ensuring that progress on environmental protection continues,” said Maurício Voivodic, executive director of WWF-Brazil. Loading



Nonetheless, the climate movement is breathing a sigh of relief this week, while multilateral institutions consider how the world might better help finance the protection of rainforests. “Science shows that we can still prevent the irreversible transformation of vast areas of the Amazon, but time is running out,” said Carlos Nobre, professor at the University of São Paulo and co-chair of the Science Panel for the Amazon, of Lula’s victory. “The next four years will be decisive for the future of the world’s largest tropical rainforest and for climate stability in Brazil and around the world.” Get to the heart of what’s happening with climate change and the environment.

World.title: Another cookie-cutter comedian game show? Yep, and we’re sick of them.
World.content:
★★ CultureTV & radioReview Another cookie-cutter comedian game show? Yep, and we’re sick of them. Bridget McManus October 29, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Celebrity Escape ★★ Some things are more fun to do than watch, and yet still make passable television. Just think of all the programs about fishing, cooking and renovating. There’s even a reality show involving knitting. But Australian-New Zealand collaboration Celebrity Escape, which puts seven comedians into escape rooms to solve puzzles and unlock doors, manages to make this popular activity awkward and boring, and even more awkward and boring to watch. The cast of Celebrity Escape (from left) Frank Woodley, Abby Howells, Hayley Sproull, host Rove McManus, Josh Thomson, Chris Parker, Celia Pacquola and Luke McGregor. Originally launched in New Zealand to mixed reviews in June, Celebrity Escape is the latest in a wearingly long line of comedian-stacked game and panel shows. Hosted by Rove McManus in the role of games master, it purports to be a new concept, but it is really just another tired idea relying on a props department for visual gags, and comedians for improvised slapstick and wordplay. McManus is jestingly sadistic, chortling from a surveillance chamber at the players’ ineptitude, while explaining the rules and pointing out the clues. However, the villainous power afforded his position doesn’t sit as comfortably on this perennial nice guy as it does on Taskmaster Australia overlord Tom Gleeson.



Assembling in “the void”, a corridor lined with doors leading to themed chambers, four New Zealanders (Josh Thomson, Hayley Sproull, Abby Howells and Chris Parker) and three Australians (Luke McGregor, Celia Pacquola and Frank Woodley) resort to cartwheeling when the banter runs dry. Related Article Streaming The 14 most anticipated TV shows still to come this year Once inside the first room, a “witch’s cabin” named after a real woman hilariously executed during the Salem witch trials, the comedians descend into dithering confusion. This task requires analytical thinking, not so much a quick wit, and rather than this resulting in the uproarious spectacle of celebrities out of their comfort zones – like we need any more of that – it feels pointless. It’s not as if they don’t try, but unfortunately the group dynamics yield neither humour nor drama. McGregor and Pacquola are the nice besties from Rosehaven, while whimsical fool Woodley becomes uncharacteristically serious. The Kiwis work their self-deprecating shticks, except for Wellington Paranormal’s Josh Thomson, who makes a valiant effort to stoke competition with deadpan trash talk. At least Taskmaster, on which many of these performers have appeared, has scope for physical silliness. There, the comedians largely work alone, bouncing off a skilled fall-guy (Tom Cashman is superb in the local version).



The comedians, including Luke McGregor and Celia Pacquola (left), find keys in the Mechanics Workshop in episode two of Celebrity Escape. Even more worryingly, Celebrity Escape is just another in a seemingly endless line of comedian-stacked panel and game shows. Julia Morris’ Class Clowns is currently testing our patience for this kind of low-budget comedy, but at least that format is open-ended enough to give its players room to move. While Julia Zemiro’s Crime Night! doesn’t need to try quite as hard, but it’s also guilty of shoving comedians from an ever-shrinking casting pool into a themed setting and expecting them to find the funny – in that case, in the grisly details of true crimes. Related Article ★★★★

Review ‘No one was burning for me’: Tina Arena tells her story with grace, fire and wit Please, for the love of Thank God You’re Here, can we return to the ingenious simplicity of theatresports? And properly invest in our funny folk, so that more sitcoms such as Kath & Kim and Fisk, and sketch shows such Full Frontal and Aunty Donna’s Big Ol’ House of Fun and Black Comedy might be developed. We have too proud a history of homegrown comedy, and way too much talent that is needed now, more than ever, to make sense and light of a darkening world, to waste our finest comedians on cookie-cutter entertainment. Celebrity Escape premieres at 9pm on Thursday, November 5, on ABC Entertains and ABC iview.

World.title: Killer admits double murder, six years after wife's honeymoon death
World.content:
A man who killed his wife six years ago has admitted murdering two men and attempting to murder another.

Rodney Fallowfield appeared in the High Court at Christchurch on Thursday.

The 58-year-old pleaded guilty to murdering Glen Allan Tukaki and Nigel John Robinson following an incident at a property in Phillipstown on October 10.

Fallowfield also admitted of wounding with reckless disregard and wounding with intent to cause grievous bodily harm.

Do you know more? Email sam.sherwood@rnz.co.nz

RNZ can now reveal Fallowfield was jailed in October 2021 for four years and three months after being found not guilty of murder, but guilty of manslaughter after killing his wife Shirley Reedy while on their honeymoon.

He was released on parole in September 2023.

Shirley Reedy and Rodney Fallowfield. supplied

The Parole Board's decision said Fallowfield had been undergoing individual psychological sessions for about three months and his statutory release date was about one year away.

The Board said a relative of Reedy's conveyed to the Board that they had forgiven Fallowfield but they wanted to know why he committed the killing, not just the details of the offending.

The Board said they posed that question to Fallowfield.

"He said there are no words he can say that will alleviate the distress he has caused and it will also haunt him for the rest of his life what he has done. His expressions of regret and apologies are seen as genuine."

He said the sessions with the psychologist had been good for him, and that he had learnt what he could do in the future to be able to "remove himself from any kind of highly stressful situation".

"Mr Fallowfield very much wants to move on with his life if he is able to and after his stay with [withheld] wants to find his own housing and employment."

A Principal Corrections Officer gave him an "excellent report", the Board said.

"In consideration of everything that was heard today Mr Fallowfield will be released on parole," the Board ruled.

"This Board considers he is no longer an undue risk considering the work he has done in the prison, his presentation today, his future planning and the support he will have in the community and the conditions which are to be imposed. It is noted he is considered as low risk of re‑offending."

World.title: Could the public bankroll a third supermarket competitor?
World.content:
Audio player for " Crowdfunded supermarket raises nearly $2 million " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/business/2211894%2Fcould-the-public-bankroll-a-third-supermarket-competitor

Crowdfunded supermarket raises nearly $2 million Morning Report Download MP3 3m

While pressure grows for someone to challenge the supermarket duopoly, the people are putting their money behind Plenty Foods in Upper Hutt.

The family-owned company has raised over $1.8 million through crowdfunding, with over 600 investors.

The funds will go towards expanding the brand, and customers say they can see potential for it to become the country's highly anticipated third competitor.

Video player removed for printing https://players.brightcove.net/6093072280001/default_default/index.html?videoId=6407258629112

In return, investing customers become "founding owners" with equity shares, and grocery discounts.

Manager Quan Yang said the company was looking for new sites to expand, with possible branches in Wellington or Porirua.

The manager made the switch to Plenty Foods after working at Pak'nSave Petone for 30 years.

"I see the future in this."

Yang claimed the shop's prices were cheaper than duopoly supermarkets.

Special signs around the store marked a 12 pack of eggs for $4, two cucumbers for $3, and a whole hot chook for $5.50.

Yang said over a 1000 people had applied to work at the store when it opened a year ago, which they'd carved down to 40 staff.

And new stores would bring more jobs, Yang said.

Special signs around the store marked a 12 pack of eggs for $4, two cucumbers for $3, and a whole hot chook for $5.50. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

'We're supporting a smaller entity' - locals

Local Michael Buchanan has shopped at Plenty Foods since it opened, going back each week for the meat and veges.

"I like the fact that we're supporting a smaller entity, as opposed to a huge monopoly.

"It's just about supporting someone who's making an effort to do something different."

He said the crowdfunding was a great idea: "People like to make a buck along the way so I mean if you can invest in something like this, why wouldn't you?"

A Plenty Foods staff member serving a customer. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

The prices were a main difference for customers, who said they found meat and vegetables were cheaper at Plenty Foods.

This was especially helpful for parents to seven kids, Trinity and Sheldon Morehu.

Their trolley was filled with bulk items like pasta, cereal, noodles, and baking supplies.

"We usually have to buy - cause we have so many kids - at least a good few kgs of each meat. So, the affordability here's good."

Independent Upper Hutt supermarket Plenty Foods. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

Thomas George Colson worked around the corner, and went over to the shop a couple times a week for coffee and snacks.

"You used to be able to go to different supermarkets for cheaper prices, but it seems quite streamlined now across them.

"So a third supermarket, or something like this, is great for finding little deals."

Colson, having previously worked at New World checkouts, said there was a real sense of community at Plenty Foods.

He liked seeing a younger crowd of workers, who recognised him each time he went in.

Customers said there was a sense of community at Plenty Foods. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

Meanwhile, parents Josh and Emma weren't convinced having a third competitor would change prices. They said options like Plenty Foods were just a nice-to-have.

World.title: Samoa replaces World Cup qualifying coach with former Mystics coach Winikerei
World.content:
Netball Samoa has replaced its winning coach who led Tifaimoana Samoa to qualify for the 2027 Netball World Cup.

Tia Winikerei, a career policewoman and Northern Mystics head coach ahead of the 2023 ANZ Premiership season, takes over from Natalie Mathews.

Mathews term had expired at the end of the Oceania Netball Championship in Nuku'alofa last month.

Winikerei spent 16 years in the New Zealand Police.

Netball Samoa said with the Netball World Cup as their primary international objective, Winikerei will lead the team's technical preparation and contribute to player identification, squad development and performance planning as Samoa builds towards the tournament.

"We welcome Tia to this important role and look forward to working with her, our players, coaches, partners and the wider netball community as we take this next step for Samoa netball," Netball Samoa's CEO Justine Wilson-Ata said.

"The appointment marks an important step in our preparations for the Netball World Cup.

"As a nation, we recognise the significance of this opportunity and the responsibility of preparing a team that can represent Samoa with pride, discipline and determination on the world stage."

Wilson-Ata said Winikerei's appointment reflected Netball Samoa's commitment to identifying eligible talent, developing a competitive squad and ensuring our players receive the guidance and preparation needed for international competition.

"While the World Cup remains our primary focus, we are also committed to providing our players with valuable opportunities to compete internationally, strengthen their combinations and gain experience against quality opposition."

Winikerei also served as the inaugural head coach of the Mystics men's team in 2022, before progressing to the franchise's senior coaching role.

She said her coaching approach places emphasis on team unity, individual contribution, strong team culture and creating an environment in which players can contribute to collective performance.

She described coaching Samoa as a "tremendous honour".

"I feel privileged to be part of this journey and to help bring Samoa's talent, passion and potential to the world stage at the Netball World Cup Sydney 2027.

"Over the years, I have coached many Samoan players and have seen first-hand their exceptional talent for reading our game, competing with strength and dominating the sport.

"I have followed Tifaimoana through the Oceania series and in overseas competitions for many years.

"Last week I was excited by the opportunity to observe players in the local tournament in Samoa. There is genuine potential within the Samoan netball community, and together, we have an opportunity to build a team that believes in its ability to compete on the world stage."

Assistant coaches

Also named this week are two assistant coaches: Anita Keelan AM and Pelesa Semu.

Netball Samoa sais Keelan AM brought more than 32 years of coaching and development experience across Australian netball.

She currrently serves as Netball Australia's pathway head coach, leading the national programmes across the Under-17 to 21 categories.

Semu is a former Samoa international and Capital Shakers captain, alongside a distinguished coaching career in New Zealand spanning grassroots, school, age-group, National Netball League and ANZ Premiership environments.

Netball Samoa said together, Keelan and Semu bring complementary strengths in high-performance preparation, talent identification, athlete development and coaching leadership to Tifaimoana Samoa's journey towards the world stage.

Former Tifaimoana head coach Mathews Netball Samoa

Mathews devastated

Mathews said she was devastated when she recieved the news that would no longer be coach.

She told RNZ Pacific over the weekend that she was disappointed she would not continue in the role as it was something she had invested a lot of time in.

After the qualifier in Tonga, she said she was proud of the team's achievement and was confident that the current squad would do well at the world meet.

Speaking to Samoa Observer this week, Mathews said the team achieved so much together.

"We achieved significant milestones together, including the Pacific Aus Sports Netball Series title, qualification for the 2027 Netball World Cup and a record of eight wins from nine matches during my tenure," she said.

She said she saw Samoa moved from 18th to 13th in the world rankings and winning the Pacific Aus series last year came after Tonga had dominated that competition since 2022.

"I have never doubted the potential of Samoan netball or the talent that exists within our communities," she told the Samoa Observer.

World.title: OCR surprise a mixed bag for retailers
World.content:
Audio player for " Nicola Willis discusses Reserve Bank’s OCR decision " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/business/2211361%2Focr-surprise-a-mixed-bag-for-retailers

Nicola Willis discusses Reserve Bank’s OCR decision Morning Report Download MP3 8m

A retail industry group says keeping the official cash rate (OCR) at 2.75 percent will be a mixed bag for many shops.

The Reserve Bank surprised economists on Wednesday when it narrowly voted not to increase the OCR, which immediately caused the New Zealand dollar to drop 1.3 percent, landing at 56.1 cents against the US dollar.

Retail NZ chief executive Carolyn Young said that would tighten margins for stores that imported their products from overseas.

"In New Zealand we don't manufacture a lot, so if you think about the retail environment anything including groceries, apparel, footwear, DIY stores, a lot of the products are imported from overseas, books come in from overseas, stationery, all of those items are going to be at a higher price because of the exchange rate, and so that has an impact right now," she said.

Different sectors within retail would be impacted differently, she said.

"If you're a car dealer, for example, if you're placing orders, because a lot of car purchases now are done on order rather than having stock on hand, would you want to hold off a couple of days and see what happens to the exchange rate?" she asked.

"Most retailers will have their stock in, that'll be ordered and paid for now, but if you're ordering your autumn stock then that could have a further impact."

But she said a stable OCR could give customers more confidence heading into the holiday season.

"From a consumer perspective, they'll be thinking 'okay well that's good, I know my mortgage rate isn't going to increase', or 'my rent should stay stable', so that could create confidence for consumers," she said.

"Consumer confidence is, of course, directly impactful into a positive outcome for retailers, so there are some upsides, potentially, to not increasing interest rates right now."

That confidence may be short lived, with many economists now predicting an OCR increase in early December.

Kelvin Davidson. SUPPLIED

"We'll probably get an OCR increase at the next meeting, so it's probably only a temporary reprieve," Cotality's chief property economist Kelvin Davidson said.

The good news, Davidson said, was that fixed mortgage rates were unlikely to spike, because they had already been adjusted under the assumption the OCR would increase in October.

"Financial markets are forward looking, fixed mortgage rates tend to reflect that future so they move ahead of the OCR anyway, and so this possible further tightening we've got to go has probably already, to an extent, been priced in, so I don't think mortgage rates are going to spike in the next little while," he said.

Avoiding big surprises

Audio player for " Former Reserve Bank economist on surprise OCR decision " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/business/2211361%2Focr-surprise-a-mixed-bag-for-retailers

Former Reserve Bank economist on surprise OCR decision Morning Report Download MP3 6m

Former Reserve Bank economist Michael Riddell said the "overwhelming weight of market opinion was expecting a move".

"When you're the Reserve Bank, while you never want to be driven entirely by what the market's expecting, you also want to avoid big surprises like that."

He said the bank appeared "gun shy" when it came to tackling persistent inflation.

"I was just looking back at some statements that were made by the Reserve Bank back in 2021 when inflation first became a problem, and they were talking about trying to get core inflation - strip out oil prices - back to 2 percent. Five years on, we're still not there.

"And there was nothing in yesterday's statement as to how they think that once the oil shock passes… inflation is going to drop back to that 2 percent."

He said because the decision not to move the OCR caused a drop in the value of the dollar, higher import prices would result in more inflation.

"I think yesterday's statement, even if it was the right decision - and I'm not sure it was - it wasn't particularly compellingly made. There was a lot of emphasis, for example, on the fact that the AI bubble might burst overseas. Well, it might, and it probably will at some point, but you react to that when it happens. What you need to be focusing on now is actual inflation pressures here in New Zealand."

National finance spokesperson Nicola Willis said the government's financial discipline was partly the reason for the OCR staying where it is. Riddell said that was "just pure politicising", with the only references to fiscal policy in the Reserve Bank's statement being to foreign fiscal policy, not domestic.

World.title: Why your car might be losing value faster than it used to
World.content:
Audio player for " When does my property become relationship property? " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/personal-finance/2211479%2Fwhy-your-car-might-be-losing-value-faster-than-it-used-to

Your car may be losing value more quickly than it might have done 10 years ago.

Trade Me had compared like-for-like vehicle age cohorts in 2016 and today.

It found petrol vehicles were losing value more quickly than equivalent models did a decade ago.

Audio player for " Trade Me data shows petrol cars depreciating faster " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/personal-finance/2211479%2Fwhy-your-car-might-be-losing-value-faster-than-it-used-to

Trade Me data shows petrol cars depreciating faster Morning Report Download MP3 2m

"It is a market-wide trend for petrol, not a specific impact on older vehicles."

Diesel vehicles in both age groups were holding their value better than they did in 2016.

Hybrids and plug-in hybrids were steady.

"Conventional hybrids and plug-in hybrids show near-zero price drops within the year, insulated by steady demand.

"The takeaway isn't that older cars are disproportionately affected; there is simply a modest signal that petrol models in general are seeing softer price retention than they did 10 years ago, while hybrids and diesels are holding their ground."

AA spokesperson Terry Collins was not surprised and said it was part of a wider market move.

Battery-electric and plug-in hybrid vehicles accounted for 25.2 percent of new light vehicle registrations in September, up from 9.1 percent a year earlier, according to Drive Electric's analysis of NZTA data.

"If you think about electric vehicles, what you had to pay for five years ago and what you pay for today… I'll give the example of a Tesla. When they first came out they were $78,000 or $76,000. Now they're $60,000-something. So if they drop $10,000 off the new market what do you think it does to the secondhand value? The sharp prices and discounting for brand new ones drives down the second-hand market."

He said it was not just that model that was affected by other vehicles as well. 'If you've only got to spend a few extra grand or $10,000 extra to get a new car, why would you spend a lot on a secondhand one?"

He said as modern cars with new features became more affordable it pushed down the values of every other vehicle in comparison to where they were a decade ago.

It was a trend that was likely to continue, he said. "I really think the electrification of our fleet will finally start really taking off meaningfully… the running cost savings are just about a no-brainer.

"With sustained high fuel prices for a while, we buy about $12.1 billion worth of fuel into the country every year, that's the total value of our exports. If we were even to save 20 percent of our fuel by going and moving to electric… that's the whole value of our wine exports. I just think if we can get some ideas around the government, when the penny drops… and people go, 'my God, this is going to work', that's going to change our fleet."

That would create some "weird" vehicle values for a while, he said.

"Go back to the 70s, our last massive oil shock, and how long that went, that created efficiency standards for cars, that got rid of all the pollution in LA, it created efficient fridges, products, everything about storage, it just had a significant long term impact. This, I think, could be of an equal seismic kind of wake up call."

He said it was likely that big V8 vehicles and inefficient six-cylinders were likely to have lower values.

Collins said diesel was a different market because many of the buyers were purchasing for commercial fleets.

Consumer NZ spokesperson Jessica Walker said even before fuel prices increased, 18 percent of owners of cars that were not electric said they were likely to buy an EV as their next car and 25 percent said they were somewhat or extremely likely to buy a plug-in hybrid.

"That same survey found that 96 percent of EV owners would buy another EV - and lower running costs was a key driver for over half of people who had already switched to driving an EV. Since that research was undertaken, we have seen financial concerns about the cost of fuel reach record-highs.

"The cost of fuel is likely to be making electric vehicles and hybrids even more popular now than our December research indicated. That will be a significant factor in what's happening with car values."

Simplicity chief economist Shamubeel Eaqub said it was to be expected that increasing petrol prices would change the desirability of vehicles and make EVs more appealing.

"Their prices are holding, while petrol car prices are falling. This is consistent with lots more hybrid and EVs being imported - both new and used."

World.title: Auckland mayor Wayne Brown's election plea: 'Sod off'
World.content:
Audio player for " Wayne Brown wants government to back Auckland or step aside " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/politics_election-2026/2213698%2Fauckland-mayor-wayne-brown-s-election-plea-sod-off

Wayne Brown wants government to back Auckland or step aside Morning Report Download MP3 8m

"Keep out of it" and "sod off" are Wayne Brown's messages to government politicians at this election.

The Auckland mayor on Wednesday unveiled his manifesto for the election - a document laying out his priorities and hopes for the next government's stance regarding the city.

He agreed that he'd had a "gutsful" of thing being imposed on Auckland where the useful benefits were not as useful as the cost would suggest.

"That's pretty much it, really," he said.

He spoke about roading, complaining that in a country short of money for roading the transport authority was spending "ridiculous sums" on motorways in Auckland "without even telling me where they are".

"There is a $3.2 billion - which apparently they're thinking it might be $3.6b - set of 25 kilometres of highway going in between Warkworth and Te Hana which they've never even shown me what the route is.

"You can build a nice hotel for less than that, and that's for a road. And what is that going to do? It's seven minutes quicker ... I can only get one truck down and back in a day, anyhow."

He wanted a rational 30-year plan built on the best ways of delivering people and goods across the district with the money available.

"That doesn't allow for somebody to say, 'oh, let's put a motorway in somewhere or other, so we might get elected' - that's not a reason. Roads are there for the transport of people and goods, not for re-election purposes."

On housing, he decried the intervention over Auckland's unitary plan, and the Medium-Density Residential Standards that allowed three three-storey homes on each section, and the flip-flopping on that.

"They discovered all the people in the leafy suburbs, and the member for Epsom [David Seymour] suddenly thought 'oh, I might not get re-elected, so I don't like this'.

"Just sod off. We know how to have a rational way of developing, or we want to develop the city, and we do have multi-storey we've spent a whole lot of money putting trains and bus routes in."

He said New Zealand was the move centrally managed country in the world - "in other modern cities we would be running the police and the schools" - but Auckland was essentially a state government given it accounted for 40 percent of the population.

There had been some areas where the council and the government had worked well together, he said, "a long list".

"But then the election comes along, and they've got a seven-pronged attack on the public and they're each announcing more and more unaffordable things knowing full well that they can say 'oh, we would have done that but Winston or David or someone else wouldn't let me do it'.

"So I want them to say 'Wayne is not going to let you do it'. Think about me. Because I represent the city, and ... I had something which none of them will experience, it's a landslide."

World.title: Surge in people injecting peptides prompts Health NZ needle exchange kits
World.content:
Audio player for " New needle exchange kits target people injecting peptides " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/health/2213308%2Fsurge-in-people-injecting-peptides-prompts-health-nz-needle-exchange-kits

New needle exchange kits target people injecting peptides Morning Report Download MP3 5m

Health New Zealand has started providing pharmacies with peptide-injecting kits as part of its needle exchange programme for people injecting peptides without a prescription.

In the six weeks since the programme began, 2300 kits have been handed out to 190 participating pharmacies - and it has been suggested users include parents administering peptides to their children.

But Medsafe has warned many of the unapproved peptides are illegal, untested and potentially dangerous.

"Peptides are small substances made naturally in the body that act as signals, helping to regulate things like growth, healing, hormones and our metabolism," Bronwyn Petrie, Health NZ group manager of population health as part of the needle exchange programme, told Morning Report on Thursday.

"I don't think we know the size and scale of the unapproved peptides in New Zealand, but what we do know is that internationally and here in New Zealand, there has been a huge spike in people injecting peptides."

She said unapproved peptides were being promoted "widely" on social media, with claims they could slow ageing and help with muscle-building and losing weight.

There had been a massive rise in the number of people approaching needle exchange services - set up in the 1980s to help drug users get their fix in a safer way - to inject peptides. It is funded by Health NZ, and considered one of the country's most successful harm reduction initiatives.

"And so they have [pulled] together a free pack for those providers and for our pharmacies to provide for those people," Petrie said.

"But critically, I really want to point out that this shouldn't be seen as an endorsement of unapproved peptides. It's about supporting our providers, responding to the demand, meeting people where they are, and ultimately preventing potential harm."

In May 2026, Medsafe warned against anyone using them if they were not prescribed or sourced from a pharmacy.

"There is a very real risk that these products may be of poor quality, not contain the substance claimed on the label (if they are labelled), contain other harmful substance not on the label or not be sterile (and so may contain substantial quantities of germs or mould).

"These products... are illegal and potentially harmful. Using them can cause serious and potentially life-threatening reactions."

Specific products mentioned by Medsafe included BPC-157, CJC-1295, GHRP-6, Ipamorelin, Kisspeptin, KLOW, melanotan II, retatrutide, sealank, seamax, TB-500 and thymosin.

"Even if these products actually contain the advertised ingredient, there is no good scientific evidence that they work as advertised or that they are safe. Neither is there any evidence that these products are sterile, and because they are injected, it means there is a high risk of a life-threatening infection from using them."

Petrie said that warning was "pretty clear".

"I guess our role from Health New Zealand was really supporting our providers, making sure that they had information and the packs to provide. And really our key messages are if you are injecting peptides, you know, speak to a health professional, but also please use sterile equipment, never share needles and dispose of it safely."

Petrie said needle exchanges offered confidentiality to encourage their use, so records of who accessed the services were not kept.

"But anecdotally we have heard you know, whether it be a gym user or whether it be a mother coming in wanting something for their child, it's a really wide range of people and I think that's what makes it even more challenging in many ways."

She said she did not know the specifics in the case of a mother needing peptides for her child, but it "could be associated with growth or muscle healing or a whole range of different things".

World.title: The 'stigma' of being a non-disabled player in elite wheelchair sport
World.content:
There are few athletes in world sport quite like Bayley McKenna.

Shaggy-haired and expressive, he is the kind of player highlights packages are built around, and at 26, he is the youngest-ever captain of Australia's wheelchair rugby league team.

But what really sets him apart is his status as a non-disabled athlete in elite wheelchair sport, with international wheelchair rugby league allowing participation from both people with disability and non-disabled players.

Leading out the Wheelaroos at the Wheelchair Rugby League World Cup, starting tomorrow in Wollongong, will undoubtedly be a pinch-me moment for the Townsville world-beater.

McKenna is widely regarded as one of the world's best players. (Supplied: Wheelchair Rugby League Australia)

But it is also an occasion he approaches with some trepidation.

McKenna received a flood of online abuse during his breakout World Cup in 2022 and is now bracing for more negativity from outside the sport.

"There is such a f***ing stigma around able-bodied athletes playing in wheelchairs," McKenna told ABC Sport.

"It is ridiculous … I'd be lying to you if I said I was going into this World Cup not expecting it."

McKenna's journey as a non-disabled player

McKenna's journey towards the Wheelaroos began in 2006, when his father was involved in an accident and became a wheelchair user.

It was a tough period of transition for Darren McKenna, grappling with the realities of his disability and what it meant for his career, family and independence.

He was reluctant to accept assistance from anyone, but his six-year-old son gave him little choice.

"I pretty much said, 'I'm helping you no matter what,'" Bayley McKenna said.

"We did everything together. I was the only person allowed to push him in his wheelchair because I didn't really give him the option.

McKenna began playing wheelchair sport alongside his disabled father.

"I've been his little offsider ever since."

And it was not long before the father-son duo entered the sporting arena, first competing together in wheelchair basketball before finding wheelchair rugby league, which Darren McKenna was integral to growing in both Queensland and Australia-wide.

Participation from non-disabled players is vital to wheelchair sport at a grassroots level, allowing for more teams and competitions for disabled athletes, but wheelchair rugby league is unique in allowing international sides to field up to two non-disabled players at any given time.

This policy ensures that teams at every level of the sport can attract enough players to compete, while also fostering a unique kind of inclusion that flows from grassroots all the way to elite competition.

And the sport is full of stories like the McKennas' — including Australia's Cory Cannane, who shared the field with disabled father Craig at the 2022 World Cup, and non-disabled England legend Jack Brown, who only began playing the sport because of his disabled brother.

The McKennas enjoyed serious success while representing Queensland. (Supplied: Bayley McKenna)

Having experienced the benefits of the policy firsthand, McKenna said it was that "inclusion" that provided the game much of its magic.

"I really, really didn't think that anything could have brought us closer together," McKenna said.

"But it did."

Wheelchair rugby league is also a mixed gender sport, although there are no women in the Wheelaroos' squad for the tournament.

Dealing with the 'stigma' of being a non-disabled player

McKenna burst onto the international scene at the 2022 World Cup in England, where his playmaking exploits earned him a spot in the team of the tournament as well as significant attention online.

Aged 22, McKenna's shaggy mullet, uncompromising hits and exceptional chair skills made for ideal social media fodder, with the Australian making regular appearances across the tournament's official channels.

McKenna was taken aback by the vitriol in the online correspondence he received as a result.

"I would have copped about a dozen messages from people all around the world saying, 'you're a fraud, you shouldn't even be in the chair, this is a sport for disabled people,'" McKenna said.

"These guys were coming at me, like, 'you're lucky you're not out there on the street by yourself.'"

It was only after an early-morning conversation with teammate and longtime friend Pete Arbuckle that McKenna began to feel at peace with the abuse.

Pete Arbuckle is a longtime family friend of the McKennas. (Getty Images for Rugby League World Cup: Pat Elmont)

"Me and Pete were at the gym over in the UK and I got one of these messages and Pete said, 'Don't worry about that bud, don't even stress. You're here representing your country and he's probably at home on the couch,'" McKenna said.

"That put me back in my stride a bit, and it helped me out a lot."

Recalling the conversation, Arbuckle said he reassured McKenna his journey to international competition was a "natural progression" from his early years playing alongside his amputee father.

"I said, 'You don't have to justify anything, you only have to justify yourself to us, your teammates. You don't have to justify yourself to anyone else on the planet,'" Arbuckle said.

"And he didn't let it affect him, and he had a really good World Cup."

Arbuckle, who lost a leg in an accident in 2016, said the contributions of non-disabled players have been vital to the growth of the sport in Australia.

"If it wasn't for the able-bodied players, I don't think we'd have the game here in Australia," Arbuckle said.

"We just wouldn't be feasible … there'd be no Wheelaroos to speak of, or certainly not at the level we're at currently."

McKenna enjoyed a breakout tournament at the 2022 World Cup in England. ( Henry Browne: Getty Images)

McKenna said the rules of the game ensure it is a "level playing field" for all athletes, while both he and Arbuckle described their wheelchairs as equipment needed for the sport, analogous to cricket bats or baseball mitts.

"What people don't realise is this is a wheelchair sport; it's not a disability sport as such," Arbuckle said.

"We play a sport in wheelchairs, and our rules define what can and can't happen."

Wheelchair rugby league's looming watershed moment

The upcoming tournament will provide wheelchair rugby league the kind of exposure most non-mainstream sports could only dream of.

Bundling the wheelchair competition with the men's, women's and physical disability events allows for the World Cups to be marketed as one cohesive product, and for the Wheelaroos to benefit with free-to-air, prime-time coverage.

Wheelaroos out for breakthrough World Cup title The Wheelaroos will have prime-time exposure this Wheelchair Rugby League World Cup, and they are aiming to use it to take their rough-and-tumble, uniquely inclusive sport mainstream.

Well aware of the looming watershed moment, Arbuckle said he hoped the attention would bring more disabled players into the fold.

"It's really going to open our game to people that haven't heard of it before and people that want to choose a physical sport," Arbuckle said.

"I think there's an untapped resource out there."

But the Wheelaroos, and McKenna in particular, are also bracing for the spotlight's burn.

The Australian captain is certain his inbox will once again turn ugly.

But this time, knowing he can call on the support of his teammates and loved ones, he said he will be ready.

"It's just going to be one of those things we move past and move forward, and don't let it get in the camp," McKenna said.

"I've got some f***ing damn good mates, bud.

"And they will support me until the cows come home."

World.title: 'We haven't got it right': Collingwood to review AFLW
World.content:
Collingwood has pledged to thoroughly review the wreckage of its AFLW program, admitting "we haven't got it right".

The day after announcing that women's coach, Sam Wright, is about to leave, the Magpies said they would bring in a consultant to help with the strategic review.

Collingwood is a perennial AFLW under-achiever, winning only one game so far this season to be second-last.

Including the last two seasons, their record is five wins and 29 losses.

With Wright about to leave and captain Ruby Schleicher about to return home to WA, there are also reports of a mass player exodus once the season ends.

Collingwood AFLW coach to step down Coach Sam Wright becomes another casualty in Collingwood's horror season, saying he will leave the AFLW club.

"Our AFLW program is an integral part of Collingwood, and we are committed to ensuring it is positioned for sustained success," president Barry Carp said in a club statement.

"The board, together with the executive team, acknowledges that we haven't got it right — we take responsibility for that and are committed to getting better, both on and off the field.

"Engaging an expert outside Collingwood is important for us to provide a broader perspective, challenge our existing approaches and identify what needs to improve or change."

He added the expert would work with their AFLW sub-committee to ensure the women are set up for long-term success.

Collingwood's woeful AFLW season Former AFLW player and coach Lauren Arnell has criticised the standard of Collingwood, while emphasising the responsibility of coaches to "put on a show" to grow the game.

"We have a responsibility to our players, coaches, staff, members, supporters and the wider game to listen to feedback and be prepared to make meaningful, considered changes across the club to build a stronger AFLW program for everyone at Collingwood," Carp said.

Wright will coach Collingwood for the last time on Sunday against Essendon at Windy Hill. It will also be Bombers coach Natalie Wood's last game.

St Kilda are also looking for a new AFLW coach after Nick Dal Santo's departure, and expansion team Tasmania are the fourth team in the market.
