World.title: Diamonds avoid clean sweep in Constellation Cup
World.content:
The Diamonds have defeated the Silver Ferns 68-58 in front of a sold-out crowd of 9,471 at John Cain Arena to avoid a Constellation Cup clean sweep.

Despite falling to an overall 3-1 series defeat, the victory gives Australian fans hope ahead of the team's title defence at the 2027 Netball World Cup.

Both sides were only separated by a single goal at the half-time break, 32-31, before the hosts outscored the Commonwealth Games gold medallists in the second half, 37-26.

The result extends the Diamond's 11-year undefeated record against New Zealand in Melbourne.

Ferns coach Noeline Taurua and captain Karin Burger hold the Constellation Cup. (Getty: Daniel Pockett)

New Zealand head coach Noeline Taurua made 19 changes to her team throughout the game to try and slow down the Diamonds in attack.

Australia, meanwhile, were unchanged for the entire 60 minutes.

A new shooting combination between Sophie Garbin and Georgie Horjus looked promising for the Diamonds. Together, the pair finished with an overall accuracy of 91 per cent.

It was the first time Horjus has got a proper chance at goal attack. She was named in that position on Sunday for game three but quickly had to slot back into wing attack following a finger injury to Kate Moloney on the first centre pass.

Horjus was named Player of the Match for her efforts inside the circle on Wednesday night.

Despite being 12cm shorter than her direct opponent Karin Burger, and 20cm shorter than goal keeper Kelly Jackson, she was not spooked by their wingspan or height.

Georgie Horjus shoots during game four of the Constellation Cup. (Getty: Kelly Defina)

There were points where Garbin was sandwiched between the Silver Ferns defenders and Horjus had to step up, sharing the shooting load and scoring a total 26 goals.

Speaking with the media after the match, Horjus conceded she was nervous to start the game but grew in confidence as the minutes wore on.

"There was a lot of talk about Kelly's long arms and the defence over the shot, but after the first quarter I got a little more relaxed," Horjus said.

"Having the support from Liz and Sophie around me just to shoot it.

"I train against the best in the world every week [in Super Netball] so I think my mindset just changed a little bit and I was more confident to go to post."

Diamonds centurion and captain Liz Watson has been scrutinised in recent times, as fans call for a changing of the guard. (Getty Images: James Fearn)

Liz Watson had a much improved game at her preferred position.

Taking back the wing attack bib, the Australian captain shrugged off criticism that has followed her performances this series to finish the match with a huge tally of 50 feeds.

Jackson topped the gain stat, but newcomer Jessie Grenvold wasn't far behind. The goal keeper has been a star in her first appearances for the Diamonds at 23 years old.

Her stats sheet read: one intercept, seven deflections and one rebound.

Grenvold was the only Australian defender to consistently ruffle Kiwi powerhouse Grace Nweke's feathers throughout the Constellation Cup.

Grenvold and Amy Parmenter (three gains) helped to turn the screws in the back half of the match. They hunted ball with a sense of urgency and disrupted the flow of the Silver Ferns.

Jessie Grenvold wins the ball during the Constellation Cup. (Getty Images: Mark Metcalfe)

Head coach Taurua said her team looked tired and weary, and the Diamonds were simply too good on the night.

They may yet take out the number one ranking when World Netball does its calculations and updates its list on December 1st.

"It was a bittersweet feeling," New Zealand captain Karin Burger said.

"We still won the Cup and according to statistics we're actually equal first [in the rankings], so we'll take that for what it is and then we'll work really hard for next year."

"As I understand when we came in, we needed to win 4-0 to be number one outright, three [wins] we'd be drawn and anything less, we'd be in the same position," Taurua added.

Norma Plummer presents Grace Nweke with the Plummer-Aitken medal. (Getty: Daniel Pockett)

"We've been looking at that for six weeks which is why this series has been massive for us, to try and get that ranking."

Look back at all the action in our live blog of game three.

World.title: Monster Carey-Inglis stand puts Australia in driver's seat in Cape Town
World.content:
An unbeaten 145-run partnership between Josh Inglis and Alex Carey has put Australia in firm control of the third Test against South Africa in Cape Town.

Inglis finished day two unbeaten on 85 while Carey finished 51 not out as Australia took a first innings lead into stumps, finishing the day's play on 4-330, one run ahead of South Africa's first innings total.

Carey and Inglis counterattacked sensationally in the final session, keeping South Africa wicketless after tea while also successfully negotiating 10 overs of the second new ball before stumps.

It was a stark contrast to South Africa's efforts against the second new ball late on day one.

The day's play began with Australia's inexperienced batting line-up needing to prove itself after the bowlers' terrific response to end day one.

Australia's new opening pair of Travis Head and Matt Renshaw looked assured against the new ball, putting together 58 for the first wicket before Head was bowled for 41 after an inside edge onto his stumps off the bowling of Simon Harmer.

Head's dismissal brought the under-fire Marnus Labuschagne to the crease and his torturous innings lasted just five deliveries before he nicked Harmer to slip for a duck.

Simon Harmer came on to bowl and blew the innings open with a double wicket maiden. (AP Photo: Halden Krog)

Harmer's double-strike brought about fears that South Africa might once again run through the Australian batting line-up, but the opposite ensued.

Cam Green, batting at number four in Steve Smith's absence, showed just what his absence had denied Australia in a crucial stand alongside Renshaw.

The pair each survived scares en-route to a 126-run partnership that spanned the majority of the middle session.

Gerald Coetzee thought he had Green caught at slip on 22 but the third umpire deemed that the ball had not carried to Harmer, much to South Africa's dismay.

Matt Renshaw's innings came to an end when he edged an attempted uppercut through to Ryan Rickelton. (AP Photo: Halden Krog)

Six overs later, Harmer had a massive LBW shout against Renshaw, which was given not out on the field when Renshaw was on 49.

South Africa reviewed and the on-field decision was upheld with ball tracking showing the ball would've only clipped the bails.

Renshaw looked nailed on for a century before he tried to uppercut Marco Jansen and was caught behind for 74, with that decision also bizarrely given not out on the field before being overturned following a successful South African review.

Jansen then doubled up by removing Green for 65 as a part of a devilish five-over spell before tea that saw him register figures of 2-3.

Follow the live blog below for a recap of all the action from day two as it happened.

World.title: Beale called up for Wallabies Spring Tour ahead of Rugby World Cup
World.content:
Veteran playmaker Kurtley Beale has been summoned for the Wallabies' spring tour of the UK in a big development ahead of next year's Rugby World Cup in Australia.

Beale on Wednesday answered an SOS call from coach Les Kiss to join the squad for next month's three Tests against England, Scotland and Wales before the inaugural Nations Championship finals in the UK from November 21-23.

The 95-Test-capped Beale will replace midfielder Hunter Paisami, who is unavailable due to personal reasons, while James Ramm and Kalani Thomas were also named to join the touring group.

No Wallabies call yet for Nawaqanitawase The Wallabies are confident star code-crosser Mark Nawaqanitawase wants to play for Australia at next year's Rugby World Cup, but he still has a choice of three nations.

But the 37-year-old's inclusion will be the major talking point as Kiss seemingly considers biting the bullet and ending Australia's revolving door of flawed five-eighths by backing a proven number 10 to steer the wobbly ship ahead of next year's global showpiece.

Kiss's predecessors Joe Schmidt, Eddie Jones, Dave Rennie and Michael Cheika have used almost a dozen different playmakers since Bernard Foley guided the Wallabies — under Cheika — to the 2015 World Cup final in England.

But none of the likes of Noah Lolesio, Ben Donaldson, Carter Gordon, Tane Edmed or Harry McLaughlin-Phillips has been able to hold down the spot.

Fellow stalwarts James O'Connor, Quade Cooper and Matt Toomua have also had cracks without commanding the role.

Cheika has turned to Foley to rejoin the NSW Waratahs from Japan, more than a decade after the duo masterminded the club's one and only 2014 Super Rugby premiership.

Now it appears Kiss is seriously considering Beale to revive the Wallabies' fortunes after Australia slipped to number seven in the world rankings after losing the Bledisloe Cup for a 23rd straight year this month.

Kurtley Beale last played for the Wallabies against Wales in 2021. (Getty Images: Stu Forster)

Beale last appeared in a Wallabies squad in 2024 before an Achilles injury prematurely ended his season. His most recent appearance in the gold jersey was against Wales in Cardiff in 2021.

But the silky-skilled talent and former World Player of the Year nominee boasts three World Cup experiences from 2011, 2015 and 2019 since first being called up by Wallabies coach John Connolly as a schoolboy prodigy.

"With Hunter's unavailability, we're excited by what Kurtley can bring to the group," Kiss said of the super versatile talent.

"He's got 95 caps worth of Test experience, and whilst he will primarily cover inside centre, he has the versatility to play a number of positions across the back line.

"Kurtley's also been in great form for the Western Force in Super Rugby Pacific and Super Rugby AUS and is excited to contribute to the environment."

AAP

World.title: FA expecting Socceroos friendlies in Middle East to go ahead
World.content:
The Socceroos are set to forge ahead with plans to play friendlies in the Middle East next month in the face of the increasingly volatile conflict in the region.

Australia is scheduled to face Qatar in Doha on November 14 before taking on Jordan in Amman on November 17 in what will be the Socceroos' final hit-outs before coach Tony Popovic names his squad for January's Asian Cup.

But there are security concerns following violence this month, including a Houthi strike at the Riyadh airport in Saudi Arabia, which is hosting the cup.

Socceroos dates November 14: Friendly vs Qatar (Doha)

November 17: Friendly vs Jordan (Amman)

January 9: Socceroos first group match at Asian Cup finals, vs Singapore (Khobar, Saudi Arabia)

Last week nine people were gunned down by Syrian militants at an orthodox church in Jordan, one of the more stable countries in the Middle East.

The Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade advises Australians to reconsider their need to travel to Jordan. Qatar is rated as a much safer destination.

As things stand Football Australia (FA) is expecting the games with Qatar and Jordan to go ahead as scheduled.

"Football Australia is closely monitoring the situation in the Middle East ahead of the Socceroos' matches against Qatar and Jordan in November," an FA spokesperson said in a statement to AAP.

"The safety and wellbeing of our players, staff and supporters remains paramount.

"Our experienced security team is actively monitoring developments and providing regular updates, and we will be guided by the advice of our head of security.

"Risk assessment is part of our planning for every national team camp, and it will be a key focus of our preparations for November."

Popovic knocked back extension Socceroos coach Tony Popovic has revealed he turned down a four-year contract offer from Football Australia (FA) to take the team through to the 2030 World Cup.

While FA's decision to push on is encouraging, there is still no clear decision on what will happen with January's Asian Cup.

Saudi Arabia has been forced to move a friendly with South Korea to Qatar as part of the flow-on effect of the Riyadh attack, and several Asian Champions League games involving Saudi club sides have been postponed.

A decision is yet to be made as to whether the Asian Cup, which is expected to kick off with the hosts taking on Palestine in Riyadh on January 7, will still take place as scheduled.

Australia's is scheduled to take on Singapore in Khobar on January 9 for its first group game of the tournament.

There is growing concern that the Asian Cup would be delayed by 12 months, with AFC president Sheikh Salman bin Ebrahim Al Khalifa saying a decision may not be made until the end of November.

"If we need to make a decision then we will, but we could move back a year to 2028 if we need to," he said in Zurich this month.

"But at the moment we are monitoring the situation and everything is on schedule."

AAP/ABC

World.title: Fox axing from Devils VFL not due to single incident, club says
World.content:
Tasmania Devils have strongly defended their club culture after axing VFL skipper Robbie Fox following an off-field indiscretion.

The Devils also said the decision to part ways with their inaugural captain was not based on an isolated incident.

The team confirmed yesterday that Fox would not be offered a contract for the 2027 season, citing, in part, the club's "expectations regarding player behaviour and adherence to our standards".

Yesterday, the ABC revealed Fox had been involved in an incident at a Hobart pub, the Granada Tavern, where he was ejected from the venue after becoming drunk and disorderly, and acting belligerently toward some staff.

It is also understood a bottle was thrown and smashed during the incident.

Nobody is believed to have been injured, and there was no police involvement.

Kath McCann says Fox had "some areas for improvement and for growth, and he's dealing with the consequences of that". (ABC News: Ashleigh Barraclough)

The ABC can also reveal Fox had earlier played in a charity golf event at the nearby Claremont Golf Club with several Devils teammates.

Fox's foursome included vice-captain Jye Menzie and reigning best-and-fairest Hugh Dixon.

There is no suggestion those players were involved in the later incident at the Granada Tavern.

Robbie Fox (left) pictured during his tenure with the Swans. (Getty Images: AFL Photos/Michael Willson)

Chief marketing officer Kath McCann told local media today that the decision not to offer Fox a contract was, in part, the culmination of several "situations".

"I want to be really clear that there was no particular one incident that led to this decision", she said.

"There have been situations where Robbie probably had some areas for improvement and for growth, and he's dealing with the consequences of that.

"I think it's fair to say that not everybody gets everything right," she said

Fox has been contacted for comment.

McCann said the Devils's culture was strong, and that their swift decision to cut on-field ties with Fox was indicative of that.

"Our club has really high standards, and we're really proud of that," she said.

"We've said from the start that our club is focused on ensuring we work with the very best people, and the highest of standards.

" It's been a part of our success to date and will continue to be in the future. "

But McCann also confirmed that Fox would continue in his role as the club's Strategic Projects Lead, and defended the decision to keep him on as a club employee.

McCann said the club was "very comfortable" with where it had landed regarding his playing contract and that it would not divulge details around its internal processes.

"Robbie's a member of our staff, he's been an important part of our inaugural year, and he's a really great person," she said.

Fox played 13 games for the Devils in an injury-affected year, after being recruited back to his native Tasmania following his delisting by the Sydney Swans.

Under his captaincy, the Devils finished in the VFL top four and earned a finals double chance.

World.title: Former Australian Open champ Stan Wawrinka ends illustrious career
World.content:
Stan Wawrinka's illustrious tennis career finally came to an end at his home tournament in Basel.

The three-time grand slam winner was beaten by eighth-seeded Jiří Lehečka in the first round of the Swiss Indoors, losing 7-5, 7-6(2).

The 41-year-old Wawrinka's last shot as a professional tennis player was a backhand that landed wide — to the audible disappointment of the vociferous home crowd.

Wawrinka, who turned pro in 2002, had announced last December that 2026 would be his last year on tour and "Stan the Man" had received warm send-offs throughout his farewell season.

"For me, all I wanted in my career was to give everything, to have no regrets, to always fight, to always give 100 per cent in every match — out of respect for myself, for the opponent, for the tournament, for the fans, for everybody," Wawrinka told the ATP Tour website ahead of his final match.

"That was always the most important thing for more than 20 years, and that's the only way you can leave the sport: without any regrets."

Wawrinka won his three grand slam titles after defeating the then-world number 1 player in each final. He beat Rafael Nadal to win the 2014 Australian Open and downed Novak Djokovic for the French Open title in 2015 and the US Open the following year.

Wawrinka, who reached a career-high world ranking of number three in 2014, won 16 tour-level titles.

He also paired with Roger Federer to win the doubles title for Switzerland at the 2008 Beijing Olympics. The duo helped Switzerland win its first Davis Cup title in 2014.

AP

Tech.title: Foreign gadget bans: all the news about the FCC’s clampdown on Chinese tech
Tech.content:
What do drones, routers, and Roombas have in common? The US government wants to keep Chinese ones from entering the country. They’re the first consumer gadgets that are facing de facto import bans because of the US government’s xenophobic stance — and they might not be the last.

Originally, the US government was just worried about US networks. It’s been distrustful of Chinese telecom equipment providers Huawei and ZTE for well over a decade, eventually requiring telecom providers to “rip and replace” their gear. (Many telecoms have still failed to do so.) It established an “Entity List” for companies whose gear should be banned from import, marketing, and sale.

But under the second Trump administration, that list has been weaponized against entire home consumer gadget categories too — starting in December 2025 when Trump and Brendan Carr’s FCC banned all future foreign drones unless their companies obtained a waiver.

Next was a ban on all future foreign routers, all future foreign robots and power inverters, and within the robot ban, all future foreign robovacs. In each case, the government claims it’s because those gadgets fundamentally pose an unacceptable threat to US national security. But in each case, the US has provided zero public evidence of a threat, has done nothing about existing drones and routers and robots that might pose such a threat, and hasn’t given us any reason to trust that its waivers have anything to do with security.

Besides, there are rarely any US companies to fill the gaps left by foreign ones. Consumer gadgets are largely made overseas, including practically all routers and practically all drones — just like how your Apple, Dell, and HP laptops are not made in the US.

Tech.title: Hands-on with the new OLED iPad Mini
Tech.content:
Apple announced a new iPad Mini with a larger OLED display this week, and we’ve just gotten to try it out at Apple’s “Pro and tell” event.

It’s an iPad for sure, but the new OLED on the Mini looks exceptional, and the optional nano-texture matte finish is awesome. The “Pro and tell” event venue has soft lighting that’s not the most conducive to blinding glare on displays, but the matte finish pretty much squashes it entirely.

Moving the front-facing camera to the long edge is also a welcome change, matching other recent iPad models. (The shift means that the whole iPad line has the camera that way.) The reliance on Touch ID instead of Face ID is still a bummer, though.

Previous Next













1 / 8 The back of the iPad Mini. Photo by Antonio G. Di Benedetto / The Verge

The eighth-generation iPad Mini, revealed on Monday, has an 8.5-inch OLED screen, thinner bezels, and a higher peak brightness of up to 1,200 nits. The display still tops out at a 60Hz refresh rate instead of hitting 120Hz. It’s equipped with an A20 Pro chip, though the 128GB and 256GB models have five CPU cores, while the 512GB model gets six. Apple has also touted the new iPad Mini’s “Acoustic Display,” which includes woofers “paired through the display to produce punchier bass and more volume.”

The new iPad Mini starts at $699 and comes in two colors: starlight and midnight. It’s available to preorder now ahead of its launch on November 6th.

Tech.title: Brendan Carr plans to let prisons jam cellphone signals
Tech.content:
As the Commission takes this historic step to improve public safety, eligible entities pursuing either of the two licensing paths will be subject to technical standards and testing requirements. This includes initial testing pursuant to an experimental license to prove that the jamming solution does not cause harmful interference outside of the designated geographic areas, as well as post-license grant testing at the subject correctional facility prior to beginning operations.

Jamming may occur only within a Commission-authorized “jamming containment area” where wireless device operation is prohibited, and it must not cause harmful interference outside that area.

Additionally, relevant carriers, FirstNet, public safety coordinators, and 911 authorities would receive advance notice of the on-site testing, and nearby communities would receive notice before deployment.

Tech.title: Microsoft is ending Copilot support on smart TVs
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter who’s been covering and reviewing the latest gadgets and tech since 2006, but has loved all things electronic since he was a kid.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Nearly two years after LG and Samsung announced at CES 2025 that their latest smart TVs would include access to Microsoft’s Copilot, the company is ending support for the AI assistant’s functionality on all TVs this year, according to a report by Windows Central.

The news comes not from an official announcement from LG, Samsung, or Microsoft, but from an on-screen notification that appeared on Windows Central’s Zac Bowden’s webOS-powered LG TV earlier today. “Microsoft has recently decided to end support for Copilot functionality on all TVs, including the Copilot-enabled feature available on our LG TVs. As a result, the Copilot-enabled feature on your TV is no longer available and may stop functioning shortly,” the notification explains. It doesn’t specify exactly when Copilot will stop working on smart TVs, but says the feature is “scheduled for discontinuation during 2026” and a specific date is “subject to Microsoft’s timeline.”

Last December, LG faced backlash after an update to webOS added an unremovable Microsoft Copilot shortcut to their TVs that opened the AI assistant’s web app in a browser. LG eventually decided to allow the shortcut to be deleted following many users expressing their frustration online with it being added without their approval.

Microsoft Copilot primarily served as a friendly AI-powered companion on Samsung and LG smart TVs that users could chat with, ask questions about what was currently on screen, or get recommendations for TV shows and movies. But earlier this year, Microsoft introduced a new Copilot “super app” that bundled multiple AI capabilities including chat, agents, and coding into a single interface as part of a push towards positioning Copilot more as a business and productivity tool, and less as a digital companion.

Tech.title: Surprise: The Google Xreal glasses debut at a Meta-beating $1,099
Tech.content:
is a senior editor and founding member of The Verge who covers gadgets, games, and toys. He spent 15 years editing the likes of CNET, Gizmodo, and Engadget.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

In this economy, how often does a product get less expensive before its debut? That just happened with the Google / Xreal Aura, the lightweight 95-gram glasses with a tethered Android XR compute puck and multiple virtual screens that just went on sale today. Xreal and Google have just announced the headset costs $1,099 through the end of the year, down from the $1,279 that Xreal was charging for early preorders last month.

I expect that’s because at $1,279, they were going head to head with Meta’s VR Glasses, and that’s tough competition for Google and Xreal’s new product. The Xreal Aura has one of the widest fields of view for transparent glasses yet at 70 degrees diagonal, but that’s still not huge and transparent glasses have other tradeoffs.

Perhaps just as importantly, you no longer have to navigate a maze of reservations, preorders, and Founder’s Editions if you want to buy the new Google glasses (so long as you live in a launch country). You can just order the 12GB RAM + 256GB storage model for $1,099 in the US, Canada, and South Korea, or the 16GB + 512GB for a discounted $1,299, with “units expected to begin shipping in mid-November.” It’ll go on sale November 2nd in Japan, with broader availability next year.

And if you did preorder at the original price, Xreal GM and spokesperson Ralph Jodice tells The Verge that the company will automatically and instantly refund you the difference.

Xreal and Google say that the headset will launch with over 150 “made-for-XR experiences,” some of which you can see in Google’s blog post and read about in Xreal’s press release, as well as new immersive films like Andy Serkis’s Nevatars and Galapagos: the Last Eden. You’ll be able to plug a computer or handheld game console right into the USB-C compute puck to mirror it to the glasses, alongside your virtual windows, and you can ask Google’s Gemini AI about what you’re seeing.

Google also writes that Google Photos is getting an XR update: “This year, Google Photos will include a new spatial gallery that wraps your library around you. You can pan from an entire year down to a single day with your hands, then open a favorite memory in 3D.”

Xreal is also partnering with GameSir to offer a wireless gamepad with a dedicated Gemini key (and a charging dock, and swappable D-pads) and is announcing a folding portable wireless keyboard; we don’t have price, release date, or other details for those.

The GameSir gamepad for Xreal. Image: Xreal The folding wireless keyboard. Image: Xreal

Tech.title: Here’s where to preorder the new MacBook Pros
Tech.content:
is a tech journalist and commerce writer based out of Portland, Oregon. He’s contributed to sites like Digital Trends, Business Insider, and WIRED.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

As expected, Apple finally showed off its 14- and 16-inch MacBook Pros at its recent “Pro and tell” event. The long-awaited laptops feature a Tandem OLED display with full touch capabilities, while also cutting some weight and bringing back the glowing Apple logo. While less exciting, there’s also an updated 14-inch MacBook Pro that features Apple’s M6 chip, along with improved wireless connectivity. It’s a small, somewhat iterative update of the prior generation, with no substantial new features beyond performance gains.

Alongside the MacBook updates, Apple also announced an M6-equipped iMac that starts at $1,499, with the same color variants as the previous generation. Lastly, the iPad Mini got some love, with a larger OLED display, smaller bezels, water resistance, and a slimmer, lighter design.

Preorders for the 14-inch MacBook Pro are available at Apple and Best Buy, while the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR display is currently only available for preorder from Apple, although we expect Best Buy to follow suit soon. For anyone looking to get their hands on either laptop before its November 6th launch, we’ve compiled information on configuration options, pricing, and retailer availability below.

Where to order the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display

The forthcoming MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display starts at $2,899 for the 14-inch model, or $3,399 for the 16-inch version, and begins shipping on Friday, November 6th. Two CPU options are currently available, each with an optional upgrade to add more cores. The base 14-inch M5 Pro model starts with 24GB of memory and 1TB of storage, and the upgraded $4,499 14-incher with the M5 Max starts with 36GB of memory and 2TB of storage, with maximum memory and storage options depending on CPU choice. It comes in space black and silver, and you can upgrade to nano-texture glass for $150.

The biggest new feature here is the PROLED XDR display. In addition to finally adding touch capabilities to the macOS lineup, the screen features a Tandem OLED panel, which Apple says can reach an impressive 2,000 nits at peak brightness, with a 120Hz refresh rate. This update also brings back the glowing Apple logo on the back of the shell, a feature that disappeared when the system slimmed down years ago.

Where to order the latest 14-inch MacBook Pro

The updated 14-inch MacBook Pro ships on Friday, November 6th, and comes in three CPU options. The M6 version with 16GB of memory and 1TB of storage starts at $1,999; the model with the upgraded M5 Pro chip and 24GB of memory and 1TB of storage starts at $2,499; and the top-end model with the M5 Max chip with 36GB of memory and 2TB of storage starts at $4,099.

Memory and storage upgrades are also available, with up to 32GB of memory and 4TB of storage on the M6 version, or 48GB of memory and 4TB of storage on the M5 Pro. The M5 Max has more limited options, but you can configure it with up to 128GB of memory and 8TB of storage if you also opt for the upgraded CPU. It’s available in both space black and silver, with the option to upgrade to the nano-texture display for an extra $150.

Additionally, Best Buy is currently including a $100 e-gift card with the purchase of any M6-powered MacBook Pro. The card will automatically appear in your cart under the “Complete your purchase” section.

Tech.title: You can see every red flag in Theranos 2.0
Tech.content:
This is Optimizer, a weekly newsletter sent from Verge senior reviewer Victoria Song that dissects and discusses the latest gizmos and potions that swear they’re going to change your life. Opt in for Optimizer here.

From afar, it’s easy to look back at the Theranos debacle and scream at Nathan Fielder that, obviously, Elizabeth Holmes is lying in You Can See Everything. In the weeks since the movie’s release, journalists and whistleblowers alike have rushed to remind moviegoers of Holmes’ numerous documented lies. Chief among the facts: The Theranos device never worked as advertised. But Fielder’s aim with this film wasn’t relitigating Theranos. Even the most mind-bending of three-hour documentaries doesn’t have enough time to fully tackle the quagmire that was the secretive biotech startup.

It’s worth remembering that Theranos was a prime example of overinflating what technology can do. It sure would be nice if a single droplet of blood could be run in a magical machine and beep boop — you’ve got accurate results for over a hundred diagnostic tests. It’s a compelling concept, but the existing science doesn’t support the idea. As I wrote in last week’s Optimizer, you simply can’t test for every disease from blood alone. Sometimes, a blood test is merely part of a multistep process to rule out what you don’t have. A finger prick carries a higher risk of rupturing blood cells, which can skew test results. Your finger is more prone to surface contamination because hands are dirty by nature. Compared to drawing blood from a vein, a finger prick may not be purely blood — it often mixes with interstitial fluid, diluting the sample. Different biomarkers can require wholly different testing procedures, making the small volume collected difficult to work with. These are just some of the practical challenges Theranos had to solve to be better than the clinical gold standard. It couldn’t, and that’s why they had to fake it by bringing in Siemens devices that used traditional blood testing methods.

That makes it even more astonishing that Holmes and her partner Billy Evans spend a chunk of the film actively working on what Evans casually calls Theranos 2.0.

This new venture, Haemanthus, involves a similar diagnostic device that uses… lasers. The official line is that Holmes is not helming the effort, but Evans refers to it as “getting the band back together.” The film purposefully blurs the lines between truth and lies. But with nascent health tech, it’s genuinely hard for the average person to distinguish promising medical advancements from snake oil.

If you left You Can See Everything wondering if there’s any truth to using lasers to diagnose conditions — you don’t have to watch microbiology videos at twice the speed to find out. Instead, here are a few extra tips when it comes to spotting shenanigans straight out of the wellness grifter playbook.

Technology is not magic

In the documentary, Fielder likens Holmes to a magician. Technology, no matter how powerful or well crafted, is never magic.

But going along with Fielder’s metaphor, magicians succeed through misdirection. Evans presents lasers in the film as though they’re a little-known marvel — a key technology Theranos was missing — and that Haemanthus will be the first to make them truly useful. Based on a patent published by The New York Times, Haemanthus uses Raman spectroscopy. For the record, Raman spectroscopy does involve lasers, but it’s not a new technology. It was first discovered in 1928.

In a nutshell, this laser tech is used to identify chemical structures in a molecule. There are myriad biological and medical uses for it, including noninvasively studying tissue samples. But will it, as a New York Times report describes, “identify and qualify biomarkers such as glucose and hormones” and then use AI to “detect cancer and infections”?

With Theranos, Elizabeth Holmes often spoke of technology like it was some magical force that would usher in a new era. Photo: AFP via Getty Images

Researchers are exploring using this tech to diagnose early-stage cancers. They’re also looking into using it for glucose monitoring. Does that mean this is a better method than what currently exists? Maybe for certain cases, but probably not in every scenario. In medicine, it’s common to require multiple tests for diagnosis. Similarly, there are often multiple ways to treat the same condition. It’s often a game of weighing pros and cons for various approaches. There are too many unknown factors to accurately comment on Haemanthus, but it’s concerning that Evans zeroes in on lasers like they’re a panacea for everything that plagued Theranos.

When investors, journalists, and the public ask hard questions, founders love to sprinkle technology into their rhetoric like it’s fairy dust. You can see it happening right now with AI. But tech is a tool. Any tool will have pros and cons, situations it excels in and scenarios it’s ill suited for. It’s not always a grift, but anytime an executive shows signs of magical thinking or inflates what technology can do, your bullshit alarm should be ringing.

Tech likes to move fast, medicine really doesn’t

In recent history, I can think of exactly one time the public health sector truly hauled ass to make something happen: the covid-19 vaccine. The vaccine took roughly 10 months to develop, compared to the typical five-to-15-year timeline. But even then, it was a Herculean effort requiring global coordination and tens of billions of dollars, largely from the government. (That’s not including the billions invested in researching mRNA vaccines during the three decades prior to the pandemic.) It was a heartening feat of human ingenuity — but again, it took 10 months built on 30 years of foundational research and several billion dollars.

So it’s an immediate red flag when Evans says in the documentary that Haemanthus would have a novel, revolutionary prototype working in about a year. Case in point, he said that in 2023, and it’s already 2026. But even if lasers were the key to everything, there’s no way in hell something like this would breeze through the regulatory process.

Not much is known about Haemanthus. It has no website, unless you count a sparse LinkedIn page that says the company has two to 10 employees and is working on “AI-native sensors for health,” a technology that “captures thousands of biomarkers.” The bulk of what’s publicly known comes from You Can See Everything and a 2025 New York Times article, which states Haemanthus is building a device that uses a “laser to scan blood, saliva, or urine from pets and analyze the sample on a molecular level.” (The startup is apparently aiming to do veterinary tests first before perhaps eventually graduating to humans.) Its “long-term goal” is a “stamp-size, wearable version” of its product for humans, which will “require three years and $70 million.”

Researchers are already using Raman spectroscopy. In this photo, it’s being used to identify dosage and chemical makeup in a sample. Image: Bloomberg via Getty Images

This is an incredibly expeditious timeline for any medical device, let alone a novel one. Not least because the biggest names in wearable technology right now can only detect — not diagnose — signs of perhaps two or three conditions. The holy grail is considered noninvasive continuous glucose monitoring, an endeavor that started in 1975 and that Apple has been rumored to be working on for over 15 years now. In 2023, I did a deep dive into why you shouldn’t expect this to arrive on smartwatches anytime soon. The reasons ranged from weak signals and regulatory mazes to skin color impacting how light reflects and battery life. In 2026, not much has changed on this front.

Meanwhile, take the continuous glucose monitor. Attempts to monitor glucose levels started in the mid-1800s, but a portable way to monitor glucose didn’t emerge until the 1960s. The first FDA-approved CGM was the Medtronic MiniMed in 1999, but it could only be worn for three days, and data couldn’t be viewed live. A clinician had to review it and inform the patient afterward. The first real-time CGM wasn’t available until 2004, the first over-the-counter CGMs didn’t hit the market until 2024, and only this year did Abbott announce a CGM that can measure two biomarkers.

AI advancements could theoretically help remove some technological roadblocks that may, in turn, speed up the overall process. But you know what AI doesn’t really replace? The absolutely labyrinthine regulatory approval and clearance process. You can have a product made and ready to go, only to have it held up in regulatory limbo for years. It’s happened to several Withings products. The infamous wearable taint zapper took six years, an untold number of testing bunnies, and at least a million dollars to hit the market. It’s why wearable companies are currently lobbying in Washington, likely spending mountains of cash to lower these hurdles.

So the next time a biotech startup promises something revolutionary relatively fast, it’s usually a pretty good sign they’re either delusional or not telling you the whole truth.

Beware anyone who doesn’t show their work

Another red flag with Theranos was that the company never published its research or submitted it for peer review. Haemanthus’ pseudo-secrecy — if you really wanted to build in stealth, why would you talk about it at length in a documentary? — is another concerning sign.

Perhaps because of Theranos, health tech companies have begun publishing more of their science. Oura, Apple, and Google are all great examples of companies that have published clinical and peer-reviewed research in reputable journals, as well as white papers explaining their features.

The act of publishing doesn’t get you a hall pass from scrutiny. Science-washing in the wellness and health sectors is rampant, with some companies using consumer perception studies as “evidence” instead of more rigorous studies. Or, if clinical studies are done, they’re often more of a vanity project than a groundbreaking revelation. Lastly, not all peer-reviewed papers are created equal. You have to be able to read and analyze the fine print to tell if the study itself was done well.

However, the absence of any reviewable research should sound the alarm for anyone who values science. In early 2015, months before the damning Wall Street Journal report, Stanford University professor John P.A. Ioannidis penned a critique of Theranos’ lack of peer-reviewed research in JAMA. Theranos responded by siccing its lawyers on Ioannidis in an attempt to get him to retract his opinion. That’s sketchy as hell — especially for any biotech or health tech company.

Based on these criteria, Theranos and Haemanthus set off a cacophony of obvious warning bells. But they’re not the only ones. Every year at CES, there are plenty of health tech startups peddling dubious concepts and vaporware right next to people genuinely doing the work. Health is the most valuable thing anyone has, so it’s not always easy to see false promises when your eyes are clouded by hope. No one wants to be sick, and technological miracles are an easier pill to swallow than the protracted ups and downs of real science. But if there’s one thing I took away from You Can See Everything, it’s that Theranos’ playbook is still, unfortunately, alive and well.

Tech.title: Here’s how macOS is changing for touchscreens
Tech.content:
is a senior reviewer with over a decade of experience writing about consumer tech. She has a special interest in mobile photography and telecom. Previously, she worked at DPReview.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Touchscreen laptops are nothing new in the Windows world, but Apple has only just announced its first MacBook with a touchscreen. Apple isn’t rushing to change a bunch of things in macOS to optimize for touch, though: Most of the touch action will be in the apps themselves, it seems.

As far as major macOS changes go, iOS’s Dynamic Island will debut on the new MacBook Pro, and Apple touts the added touch controls as particularly useful for interacting with the interface to accept AirDrops and pause music playback.

Otherwise, Apple gives some pretty predictable ways that the touch input will work with the new MacBook Pro. Gestures you could use with the trackpad, like swiping from the right edge to show the notification center, have been translated to the touch display. The system will also magnify drop down menu options and the traffic light window controls when you tap them to create bigger targets. Other than that, you’ll be able to pinch and zoom in on photos, drag and drop slides between two different presentations, and swipe to scroll through webpages. Which, yeah. That’s how touchscreens work.

Previous Next

1 / 2 Some UI elements will be magnified when you touch them. Photo: Antonio G. Di Benedetto / The Verge

The more interesting stuff will probably happen in individual apps. Unsurprisingly, Apple’s apps will already be “optimized” for touch, and the system will automatically translate touches into clicks. Apart from that, Apple lists a handful of third-party apps that will take advantage of the new touch controls, including Notion, Canva, Zoom, Word, Excel, PowerPoint, Lightroom, and DaVinci Resolve. Adding the possibility of multitouch to some of these pro creator apps is interesting, but for the most part, it seems that touch will merely be a secondary input mechanism rather than a whole new way of interacting with the entire system. You’ll be able to double tap to make a window full screen the way you can with a double click, and you can drag the corner of a window to resize it.

Multitouch could be an interesting addition to certain apps. Image: Apple

Update October 28th: Added more details about interacting with window resizing controls and drop down menus.

Tech.title: Anthropic just launched tools to show companies what their AI spending is buying
Tech.content:
The financials Anthropic shared with investors this week suggest that its AI coding tool, Claude Code, is every bit the business success the frontier lab wanted. The company recorded an operating profit in the second quarter, and 900% net revenue retention — that is, spending from the same customers in Q3 2025 grew nine times in Q3 2026.

Anthropic has focused on getting enterprise users to stick around and Wednesday announced a new suite of reporting tools designed to give those customers a more granular understanding of the value they get from their token spend.

Using internal analytics and employee surveys, managers can view a team’s work over a given date range, what the team produced, how much it cost, and where its workflows broke down. Anthropic says it won’t use this data for model training by default. The reports will also offer recommendations on how to improve the results.

Image Credits:Anthropic Image Credits:Anthropic Image Credits:Anthropic Image Credits:Anthropic Image Credits:Anthropic Image Credits:Anthropic Image Credits:Anthropic

This is a clear attempt to demonstrate the return on investment of Anthropic’s tools and to show customers how to improve it — a major concern among large customers. Anthropic is also creating pooled group budgets to allow teams to better manage token spending.

Businesses have been hunting for that kind of information as they figure out how best to deploy AI tools. While usage among venture-backed firms is driving token spend, most of the Fortune 500 are not seeing major gains from deploying AI.

Jellyfish, a company that makes tools for software developers, released a new report yesterday based on the use of agentic coding tools by 276,000 of its customers. Claude Code and other tools built on Anthropic models remain the most widely used in the survey, responsible for nearly a third of all proposed code changes submitted for review. More importantly, spending on those tools has grown 10x since the beginning of the year, with their cost now equal to about 2% of total engineering cost.

“Even if you’re saying 2% is still small, that 10x growth is growth that most CFOs didn’t plan for,” Nicholas Arcolano, the chief scientist at Jellyfish, told TechCrunch. We’re certainly getting to the point where people are realizing, okay, it’s not enough to just spend a bunch. You now have to optimize it, make it work.”

Anthropic’s new reports speak to that challenge. Anthropic leads among enterprise customers, but what makes an agentic coding tool truly sticky is difficult to identify. The release of OpenAI’s Astra model this summer seemed like a potential threat to Anthropic, but so far it hasn’t slowed Anthropic’s adoption numbers.

“It took a long time for us to see Codex really pop in our data at all, and it has come up with Astra [OpenAI’s latest model],” Nikolas Albarran, the AI product lead at Jellyfish, told TechCrunch. Looking at X, he continued, you’d get the distinct impression that the competition is more heated. “Everyone in the Valley is like, ‘Oh, Codex is better.’” In reality, Albarran continued, “Anthropic was just there with great enterprise motions, and they had an incumbent weight of their own — this stuff just worked and worked well, and a lot of people just put a lot of effort into standardizing workflows around it. And there’s not a big enough reason to switch.”

It’s not just a question of models and workflows, either. The realities of business mean that once a frontier lab has gotten its hooks into a customer, switching is harder than it is compared to an individual programmer or small organization. Albarran points to the investment all the major AI labs are making in forward-deployed engineering (FDE) organizations, teams that embed AI consultants inside customer organizations to help them get off the ground. These new reporting tools can be seen as a kind of FDE-lite, a lighter version of that hands-on help, for Anthropic customers.

“We’re at a point now where it’s mature enough, where once you’re in, it’s going to be harder and harder to switch because you’ve spent the effort,” he said. “Even if they’re all mostly the same, they’re all going to be slightly different, have their own slight quirks of how they handle agents to ND files, etc., and so that cost to switch is not zero.”

Tech.title: Wiz’s CTO on PHP2Shell and the coming ‘vulnpocalypse’
Tech.content:
Loading the player…

The PHP scare may have faded from your feed, but the cleanup is far from over. Last week, two critical bugs in the open source language behind roughly 70% of websites left organizations scrambling to fix their systems, with some taking sites offline until the vulnerabilities could be patched. According to researchers who found the bugs, this is only the beginning, as AI changes how quickly novel vulnerabilities can be uncovered and exploited.

On this episode of TechCrunch’sEquity podcast, Rebecca Bellan talks with Tomer Schwartz, CTO of Exposure Management & AppSec at Google-owned Wiz, who was part of the scramble — alongside OpenAI, research group Calif, and the PHP team — to fix the bugs. On the show, Schwartz and Bellan get into what the race looked like from the inside, how early-stage startups can build with security in mind, and why patching by hand won’t scale.

Subscribe to Equity on YouTube, Apple Podcasts, Overcast, Spotify, and all the casts. You can also follow Equity on X and Threads, at @EquityPod.

Tech.title: Apple launches its new touchscreen MacBook Pro
Tech.content:
After years of resisting, Apple today launched a MacBook Pro with a touchscreen starting at $2,899. The release comes nearly 10 years after the company first tried integrating touchscreens on its laptops, with its Touch Bar on a MacBook Pro, which it later went on to remove.

The new MacBook Pro more fully embraces the touchscreen, offering a new PROLED XDR Display in both 14-inch and 16-inch screen sizes. The device is powered by M5 Pro and M5 Max chips as options to choose from, along with up to 128GB of unified memory and up to 16TB of storage. The display has 2,000 nits peak HDR and SDR brightness and a 10,000,000:1 contrast ratio.

To make the new MacBook easy to use, Apple designed a hinge that stabilizes the screen when users touch it. This also helps to stabilize the camera when you are on a video call and trying to access content on the display.

In addition, the screen will include a Dynamic Island-style cutout instead of the notch that’s present on most of the current MacBooks. Plus, the new MacBook features a six-speaker array with a new woofer design for better sound.

The 14-inch Pro weighs 3.0 pounds (1.38 kg), and the 16-inch Pro weighs 4.0 pounds (1.82 kg) — lighter than its non-touch predecessors.

Both feature three Thunderbolt 5 ports, an HDMI port, an SDXC card slot, MagSafe, and a headphone jack. Users can hook up three external displays on the M5 Pro variant and up to four displays on the M5 Max variant.

The Touchscreen MacBook Pro 14-inch starts at $2,899, and the 16-inch version starts at $3,399.

Consumers can place a preorder for the new touchscreen MacBook Pro from October 30, and the device will be available starting November 6.

The new Touchscreen MacBook marks two marquee product launches for new CEO John Ternus, who also introduced the company’s first foldable, the iPhone Duo, in September. Various Apple executives, including Steve Jobs and Tim Cook, have scoffed at the idea of a touchscreen Mac in the past. Jobs famously called the idea “ergonomically terrible” at one point. However, rumors of the company working on such a variant started circulating nearly three years before today’s introduction.

The launch follows yesterday’s unveiling of a new standard MacBook Pro with the M6 chip in 14-inch size starting from $1,999.

Tech.title: Xreal Aura is a new wired headset powered by Android XR
Tech.content:
At the Android Dev Summit on Wednesday, Google’s smart glasses partner Xreal launched its new Xreal Aura wired smart glasses, powered by the Android XR and Qualcomm’s Snapdragon Reality Elite platforms. The companies had teased the glasses earlier in the year at Google’s I/O developer conference.

As Meta expands its push into smart glasses, competitors like Apple and Google are keen to release their own devices. Much like it did with Android smartphones, Google is relying on an assortment of partners, including Samsung and Xreal, to bring devices powered by its Android XR platform to consumers.

The new Xreal Aura smart glasses are tethered to a smartphone-like device for processing power, rather than handling all the computing themselves. The glasses then display the content in the wearer’s field of view.

The device’s design, meanwhile, is closer to Meta’s smart glasses than Apple’s Vision Pro, which is a larger headset.

Xreal Aura uses Sony’s Micro-OLED display with 1200p resolution at 120 Hz and a 95-degree field of view — screen specs that put the glasses above the Ray-Ban Meta Display on paper. However, Xreal’s smart glasses are heavier at 95 grams compared to Meta’s 69 grams, and you have to carry the puck.

At launch, the Aura supports many popular Google Play apps and games along with specific XR experiences, including the NBA App for Android XR; Nevatars; Fallout: Factions; Project Hail Mary: Journey Among the Stars; the NASCAR XR App; and the San Francisco Ballet Company’s “The Nutcracker.”

Users can opt to plug a computer or handheld gaming console directly into the Xreal Aura via USB-C to make it an augmented display. The device can also allow for various entertainment and productivity use cases by spinning up a multimonitor setup or a big virtual screen.

For audio, the Xreal Aura uses Bose’s tech to power its sound while watching videos or listening to music.

Given that the new smart glasses are powered by Android XR, Gemini is available to users as a Q&A assistant and can help them understand on-screen context.

The Xreal Aura is available to order starting today in the United States, Canada, Japan, and

South Korea. The 12GB + 256GB version costs $1,279 with a limited launch price of $1,099 through December, and the 16GB + 512GB version is priced at $1,499 with a launch price of $1,299 through December. The company said it will start shipping by mid-November.

In May, Xreal CEO Chi Xu told TechCrunch that building a smart glass business is hard and everyone is losing money. He also said that the Aura glasses will have a wide range of use cases, and the industry has reached an inflection point of having the right hardware, software, and design smart glasses to reach scale.

“You need all the key pieces ready — you need the hardware ready, the operating system needs to be ready, and then you need a great user interface,” Xu said at that time.

Tech.title: As AI agents reshape the web, Google opens Gemini and Search to more apps
Tech.content:
Google is making it easier for businesses to connect their apps to its AI experiences across Search and Gemini with the debut of its Connected Apps Platform.

Introduced in Gemini and Google Search earlier this year, connected apps let users securely link and interact with popular third-party services, then use them to take specific actions. For instance, you could connect to Canva to design a flyer, or to YouTube Music to build a playlist.

We’ve seen varying takes on the idea by other consumer-facing AI services like ChatGPT and Meta’s Muse. The premise is that such integrations could ultimately shift consumer behavior away from launching and using individual apps to instead using their favorite services through their preferred AI provider.

However, to successfully capture and retain consumers’ attention, there have to actually be a wide range of connected apps to explore.

Google’s idea is to open its doors to any business or developer that wants to reach users through Search or Gemini by allowing them to submit their own connected apps and monitor their performance.

The platform preview is currently available in beta to developers in the U.S., and will allow developers to build and submit apps that can be used across Google’s products.

To get started, developers would integrate with a cloud-hosted MCP (Model Context Protocol) server or Android MCP using the AppFunctions APIs, then use the Google Connected Console to register, test, and submit their app, Google explains.

Essentially, this process lets devs connect their app to Google’s services so it can be used with the search giant’s AI features. Developers can also choose whether they want their app to be available via Search, the Gemini app, or both.

After the app is live, developers can track traffic, latency, and error rates, and maintain control over their brand identity, such as their verified logos and authenticated accounts.

Similar to how SEO allowed companies and websites to show search engine rankings, this could well be one of the initial steps for businesses that want their services to be more visible to users on the agentic web.

Google already has over 50 Connected Apps available in Gemini, including from partners like Adobe, Experian, Localiza, Peloton, and others, in addition to its own expansive set of services, from Workplace and Photos to YouTube Music and Google Home.

These apps will now come to Google Search over the next few weeks. Search today has fewer integrations, featuring apps like Instacart, Canva, YouTube Music, Yahoo Fantasy Football, and others.

Google said meditation app Calm is another new partner on this effort, and that its app will soon launch on both Gemini and Search.

Tech.title: Chrome’s AI-powered Autofill can now dig through your Gmail to fill out forms
Tech.content:
In Brief

Google’s Chrome browser is getting an update that will improve its autofill capabilities using AI. On Wednesday, the company said that Chrome will get an advanced version of autofill that will help users fill out online forms with suggestions pulled from their Gmail.

That means Chrome could suggest things you might need to know, like a flight confirmation number, membership ID, tracking information, order number, address, phone number, or credit card number by referencing your email.

The update is an expansion of Google’s Personal Intelligence, which already allows users to connect their Google Apps to its AI assistant, Gemini, to retrieve certain details and then use them to answer complex questions.

Though seemingly minor, the update could make Chrome easier to use, which could give users another reason to continue to use Google’s browser and stay in its AI ecosystem. It’s reminiscent of one of Apple’s most appreciated features: the ability to automatically detect verification codes sent via text and display them above the keyboard, allowing users to enter them with a single tap.

As with other Personalized Intelligence features, users can decide whether or not to enable enhanced autofill from their Chrome settings. Sensitive data is encrypted, Google notes.

The feature is rolling out to U.S. users on the desktop, and in the iOS and Android apps for Gemini in Chrome.

Tech.title: Reddit is the latest platform to embrace the ‘For You’ feed
Tech.content:
Reddit is the latest social platform to adopt the “For You” feed popularized by TikTok. The company announced on Wednesday that users will now see two options when opening the platform: “For You” and “Following.”

The “For You” feed combines posts from communities users have joined with recommendations tailored to their interests. Reddit says the feature will help users discover relevant communities and conversations they might not have otherwise come across. The “Following” feed only displays posts from communities they have joined.

The company says the change is designed to foster connection, participation, and belonging.

Reddit is likely hoping that the redesigned feed experience will nudge users to engage with content beyond the communities they already follow. It also brings Reddit more in line with the recommendation-driven experience that’s become standard across social media, where algorithms play a significant role in shaping what users see.

With the launch, Reddit joins a number of popular platforms that have adopted “For You”-style feeds, including Instagram, X, Threads, and Facebook.

Of course, not everyone will welcome the change, as some users may prefer the more focused feed experience of only seeing posts from communities they’ve joined, rather than having recommended content mixed into their home feed. Some users who encountered the new feed during its initial testing phase have already expressed their frustration with the change.

Reddit says users can switch between feeds and return to the one they last viewed the next time they open the platform.

It’s worth noting that although Reddit has long recommended posts from outside users’ subscribed communities, the new layout gives those recommendations their own feed on the homepage.

“This new feed experience is a first step in helping drive discovery that leads to something novel and relevant – an idea, a connection, a unique perspective, or even a new interest,” the company wrote in a blog post. “A more human internet is not just something you sit back and watch, it is something you find value in and want to participate in.”

The new feed experience is rolling out globally over the next few weeks, the company says.

Tech.title: AI execs may be too out of touch to build for the general public
Tech.content:
Former Yahoo CEO and early Google engineer Marissa Mayer is catching a lot of flak for how she uses AI. In an interview about her new app Dazzle, an AI assistant that learns from your camera roll, Mayer poses what she believes is an impressive flex for the product: It helped her come up with three bullet points about her 10-year-old daughter for a birthday presentation at school, describing her as “empathetic, creative, and an animal lover.”

It’s a vague description, like a generic horoscope — it could probably describe a lot of 10-year-olds.

Some onlookers, like progressive activist Leah Greenberg, marveled that “the fact that Marissa Mayer would voluntarily disclose this to a reporter is a pretty good demonstration of how deeply the culture of Silicon Valley has diverged from the rest of humanity.”

Perhaps Mayer drew so much backlash because we have repeatedly observed sheltered billionaires suggest that we outsource child-rearing — one of life’s greatest tests of patience, humility, and kindness — to a computer that is incapable of understanding human emotion.

We’ve been primed for this frustration. Last year, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman told Bored Ape owner and late night host Jimmy Fallon on national television, “I cannot imagine … figuring out how to raise a newborn without ChatGPT.” The public didn’t love that comment, either, but Altman wasn’t fazed by the negative feedback. A few months ago, he said on X that a “cool use case” of ChatGPT Work would be creating a podcast that talks about your kids’ upcoming birthdays or soccer games and “explain[s] your kids’ interests.” (He was brutally ratioed with comments like, “What if you just talked to your children?”)

After publication, Mayer defended herself in a long X post. She claims she was not relying on Dazzle to explain her child to her, but rather, she was testing what her prototype could do — it resurfaced photos of “forgotten kindergarten projects,” like a “snake devenomer” or “sandcat playground,” illustrating her daughter’s creativity and care for animals.

Fair enough. But Mayer remarks in the same interview that people could also use her AI to outsource the mental load of “figuring out the theme for your child’s birthday party.” She says she’s used her app to plan a playdate for her daughter, book family activities on vacation, and decide what to be for Halloween. She even proposes that her AI assistant could coordinate plans with her husband’s AI assistant. When the reporter asks her if it’s depressing to imagine this “frictionless future … planned by AI,” Mayer replies, “I haven’t really thought that through.”

These leaders seem to write off the naysayers as part of a small, angry fringe group. Yet a Pew Research Center study reports that 50% of U.S. adults think that AI will reduce people’s ability to form meaningful relationships. Only 5% of respondents said AI would make it easier to build these connections.

Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, however, joins his Silicon Valley kin in envisioning a world where our social needs are met via AI.

“The average American I think has, it’s fewer than three friends, three people they’d consider friends, and the average person has demand for meaningfully more, I think it’s like 15 friends,” Zuckerberg said last year on a podcast. “The average person wants more connectivity, connection than they have.”

Zuckerberg predicts that it will become more socially acceptable to outsource our emotional needs to AI therapists or even AI romantic partners. “There are all these things that are better about physical connections when you can have them,” he added. “But the reality is that people … feel more alone a lot of the time than they would like.”

Zuckerberg goes on to explain how virtual-reality embodiments of AI avatars are only growing more realistic. Meta seems to be more keen on improving our relationships with these approximations of humans, rather than between the actual billions of humans who use its platforms each day.

Maybe part of this stems from the culture of the tech industry, which prizes efficiency. People try to biohack their own bodies by optimizing their sleep schedules with health trackers or injecting unregulated “peptide stacks” to maximize their productivity.

If you’re building electric vehicles or computer chips, then sure, efficiency is a clear north star. But our relationships with other people are not a tech product that we’ve been challenged to ship with as little capital as possible. Human relationships are inherently messy, but our connections with one another can be what gives our lives meaning. When we delegate those interactions to computers, we surrender the difficult, yet fulfilling experience of being people.

Tech.title: The New M6 MacBook Pro Has a Serious Price Problem
Tech.content:
Just yesterday, Apple refreshed its 14-inch MacBook Pro with the new M6 chip inside, and it’s currently available for preorder. This is the first MacBook to get the chip (but certainly not the last), and I look forward to testing this thing out myself. But I do already have a good sense of how well it’ll perform, as I already tested this same chip in the latest Mac Mini. And it points to an issue with the current state of the Mac lineup.

The 14-inch M6 MacBook Pro currently costs $1,999. That gets you 16 GB of RAM and 512 GB of storage. Even for as good as these laptops are, that feels like too much money for those specs. Apple raised prices across all Macs earlier this year, but the base 14-inch MacBook Pro got hit the hardest, with a $300 bump. It was already an awkward configuration, as it used the same M5 chip as the much cheaper MacBook Air models. It was such bad pricing that it ended up on my “do not buy” list. The addition of the M6 seems like it’ll add some value, especially with the improvements to GPU performance I saw in the M6 Mac Mini. It also has the dual Neural Engine, which can speed up certain AI tasks in creative applications, especially for content creators. I won’t pretend to make a final evaluation until I’ve thoroughly tested the machine myself.

The Smarter Buy

But consider this. The M6 Mac Mini is on sale for $779 right now, $120 off its retail price. The 13-inch M5 MacBook Air is similarly $150 off its retail price right now. You could buy both for the same price as one M6 MacBook Pro. That’s kind of insane when you think about it. You miss out on the MacBook Pro’s excellent Mini-LED display and powerful speakers, but to me, it’s a tempting alternative for a $2,000 budget.

It’s even more compelling when you consider how many people are using Mac Minis these days—more as always-on AI agent boxes that you can control remotely with any old MacBook. Pairing the M6 Mac Mini and M5 MacBook air together is a recipe for AI goodness (especially if you configure the Mac Mini up to 32 GB or 64 GB of memory).

Another alternative is the M5 MacBook Pro with an M5 Pro chip inside for only $200 more. It looks identical on the outside, and has better performance on the inside.

I’m still interested to see how the new M6 MacBook Pro performs, but the price alone makes me wonder if there aren’t better ways of spending your money—even while staying within the Mac lineup.

Tech.title: I Put a Bunch of AI Agents in Charge of a Fantasy Soccer Team. They’re Not Better Than Humans—Yet
Tech.content:
I have consulted my AI-powered crystal ball, and it’s telling me that frontier models are going to get a lot better at making predictions in the near future. Just ask my Premier League fantasy team.

A few weeks ago, I deployed a small horde of AI agents to craft and manage an experimental roster. Given the proliferation of AI agents into pretty much every aspect of our lives, I wanted to know if a swarm of bots could put together a winning team.

I first looked at the potential for AI here a few years ago, playing around with a tool from the UK’s Turing Institute that selected teams after modeling previous fantasy league data. Its suggestions were remarkably bonkers—it didn’t incorporate real-world information, like a player’s injury or a team’s change in management.

This time, while on a flight to visit family, I asked Codex for help. First, I fed the model a couple of relevant research papers. Then, I asked it to build a harness—instructions and code that guides different agents through various steps—that would check recent news and run a model to make predictions.

It quickly came up with a setup that seemed to collate and analyze way more information than I ever would have. And yet I was surprised by how dumb the initial team suggestions were. Leaving Erling Haaland on the bench? Really, Codex?

Tech.title: The Inside Story of Why Apple Finally Brought a Touch Display to the Mac
Tech.content:
Ternus doesn’t endorse that take, but he doesn’t object when I suggest it. “We’ve been working on these products for quite some time,” he says. “It feels like everyone here is just kind of riding high right now, enjoying it.”

I ask if Apple is about to break a long-imposed taboo and introduce a Macintosh with a touch screen.

Ternus beams. “Who knew?”

We are referring to the new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display that Apple is releasing today at an event in Los Angeles. It’s got a mighty M5 Pro or M5 Max chip and a show-stopping tandem OLED screen. (A tandem screen has multiple light-emitting layers, producing more dramatic contrasts.) But its most conspicuous feature is one that’s been deeply woven into iPhones, iPads, and even Apple Watches for years but not Apple’s laptops: a touch display. After years of resistance, a Mac screen has finally gone digital. As in fingers.

This turnaround is a big deal to Apple fans. Ternus shrugs off the drama. “The Mac is first and foremost an indirect input device, built around the trackpad and keyboard. But I think there’s times when it’s comfortable and handy to have touch.”

Ternus and Apple want to make sure that the Mac faithful don’t panic that the 42-year-old franchise is losing its identity to Apple’s gangbusters mobile products. “We needed to get to a point where adding touch didn’t make the product lesser in any way. It didn’t make it heavier. It didn’t make it thicker. That came together with the OLED screen, the best display we’ve ever put into a Mac,” Ternus told me. “All of these things, and, oh yeah, it has touch as well.”

Apple has a long history of refusing to implement certain desirable features, only to pivot when it feels the time is right. Steve Jobs once proclaimed iPods would never do video, until they did. He also once said “no one’s going to buy” a jumbo-size phone—and then Apple released a supersized iPhone 6. Then there was that time Jobs declared styluses inappropriate for tablets. Now the Apple Pencil works with iPads and the brand-new Duo.

The 2026 MacBook Pro instantly qualifies as the canonical example of this switcheroo. Apple executives had been on record regarding touch on PCs as a misbegotten idea. Never mind that just about every PC maker not headquartered in Cupertino has implemented touch on their laptops. And customers of Microsoft, Dell, Acer, Lenovo, and HP have snapped them up. Clearly, people wanted touch on their laptop displays. Even toddlers knew it—put some rugrats in front of a computer and their little arms shoot straight to the screen in futile attempts to swipe and scroll as they do on their iPads. People were baffled why Apple—the pioneer in touch displays since the iPhone—was so steadfast in its rejection.

Tech.title: Sony Wants You to Forget About Discs With Its Gorgeous Transparent Controllers
Tech.content:
Sony has a collection of colorful, translucent cosmetics for its PlayStation consoles and controllers. Announced Wednesday, the Prism collection brings three new, gorgeous color options that conjure a nostalgic, transparent tech feel.

They come in Flare Orange, Emerald Green, and Graphite Gray. (Based on the pictures, the gray looks more like a blue to me.) You can get Sony’s DualSense PlayStation 5 controllers in the Prism design or opt for PS5 console covers. On the controllers, translucent plastic wraps around almost the entire device’s frame, letting you view the components inside. On the console cover version, the transparency is more limited—you can see only the fan and a few other components.

The Prism Collection DualSense wireless controllers cost $85, while the console covers cost $75. Preorders start on November 10, but the collection won’t ship until February 4. Those are roughly the same prices as existing controllers and covers, though on the higher end. Basic color controllers start at $74 on the PlayStation website. Covers start around $59. The more colorful options on both products go up from there.

Tech.title: Senators Demand to Know if Dr. Oz Collaborated With Election Denial Groups
Tech.content:
With a week to go before the midterms, a group of Democratic senators are demanding that Mehmet Oz, the administrator for the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS), share communications his department may have had with far-right groups promoting a baseless conspiracy theory about left-wing groups stealing votes from residents of nursing homes.

In July, Oz’s agency issued a memo rescinding previous guidance on how staff at nursing homes could help residents to vote by assisting with mail-in voting or transporting residents to polling locations. The memo replaced that guidance with threats of prosecution if staff “engage in inappropriate coercion or other violations of residents’ rights.” Referring to this memo, election denial groups last month began to boost claims that voter fraud was happening inside care facilities.

That campaign was spearheaded by the Election Integrity Network, a group led by Cleta Mitchell, a former adviser to president Donald Trump. “These left-wing groups go into the nursing homes, and they go into the group homes, and they basically steal the votes of these most vulnerable,” Mitchell said in a recent appearance on Steve Bannon’s War Room show.

Now, citing WIRED’s reporting on the nursing home conspiracy theories, a group of senators that includes Elizabeth Warren, Richard Blumenthal, Alex Padilla, Mazie Hirono, Ron Wyden, Kirsten Gillibrand, Jeff Merkley, and Cory Booker wrote in a letter to CMS to ”urgently request that CMS rescind its July 2026 memorandum and reinstate its 2020 and 2024 nursing home voting guidance.”

“This is as low as it gets,” Warren tells WIRED. “The Trump administration’s unfounded allegations of election fraud are inspiring election denial groups to harass nursing home residents and staff. With less than a week until Election Day, every lawmaker in America should be standing up for fair elections and pushing back on this attack on seniors’ voting rights.”

A CMS spokesperson did not respond to questions about the agency’s communications with election denial groups but instead referred WIRED to the July 2026 memo.

Tech.content:
