Honorable Mentions

Photograph: Nena Farrell

There's no bad Kindle, in my opinion, but I don't recommend buying all of them. Here's the rest of the current Kindle lineup and my thoughts.

Kindle Aluminum (2026) for $190: The 6-inch Kindle got its first 32 GB version this year with the 2026 Kindle Aluminum, which has an aluminum body that comes in two beautiful colors. It also has the new AI features we've seen in newer models, Story So Far and Ask This Book (the latter is still to be released, though). While it's a beautiful device—everyone who's seen me reading on it has commented that the color is a huge temptation to invest in one—it's a bummer you're not getting much for the price. The lack of a warm option for a front light is a big downside for me as a nighttime reader (especially at this price point), but I love the size and feel of this aluminum e-reader otherwise.

Kindle Scribe (2025) for $500, Kindle Scribe Colorsoft (2026) for $680, and Kindle Scribe Without Front Light for $430: These are all essentially the same device with the same physical design and software experience, with some key differences: the Colorsoft version has a color screen and shorter battery life, and the Without Front Light has (obviously) no front light, so you can't use it in a dark room without an external light. All three models of the latest Kindle Scribe have a new, taller design with an 11-inch screen, a slightly slimmer form factor, and an updated stylus. They also have a quad-core chip and a new homepage, and will support a variety of AI features, including AI search (along with some AI tools for summarizing books you’re reading without giving spoilers, though those won’t arrive until next year). Users can connect to Google Drive and Microsoft OneDrive to mark up documents, which the older model can’t do. Overall, I’d say they’re good devices, but as long as the cheaper second-generation Kindle Scribe is available, I think it’s the better buy.

The New Kindle Accessories

Amazon launched new accessories along with its 2026 lineup of Kindles: the Kindle Click ($35) Bluetooth page-turner remote, the Kindle Page-Turn Cover ($80), and Amazon Wireless Charging Stand ($60), plus a variety of new covers from Amazon, including ones that will magnetically attach to the aluminum-backed versions of each Kindle. I've tested a few of these accessories so far, and while I've been happy with the experience, there's a clear winner for existing Kindle users. Here are all my thoughts on Amazon's range of new Kindle accessories so far.

Courtesy of Amazon Save to wishlist Save to wishlist Amazon Kindle Click $35 Amazon

This is the best new accessory for a Kindle. It's backward compatible with 2024 Kindles, so you don't need the latest model to use it. The Kindle Click connects via Bluetooth to your device and has buttons on the front to turn the pages forward and back. The two small buttons on the side adjust the screen brightness. For the price, it's a great buy, and you won't need an extra dongle to attach to your Kindle like many third-party page turners require.

Photograph: Nena Farrell

Photograph: Nena Farrell Chevron Chevron Save to wishlist Save to wishlist Amazon Kindle Page Turn Cover $80 Amazon This cover works great if you want page-turn buttons on your device, but it only pairs with the new Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition or Kindle Colorsoft Signature Edition, so it'll cost you $330 for the cheapest combination. At that point, you might as well get the Kobo Libra Colour instead. It does come in pretty colors to match the colorful variants of these Signature Editions. Photograph: Nena Farrell

Photograph: Nena Farrell

Photograph: Nena Farrell Chevron Chevron Save to wishlist Save to wishlist Amazon Kindle Slim Cover with Magnetic Attach $50 Amazon (Kindle) $70 Amazon (Kindle Paperwhite/Colorsoft) This is another option for the Signature Editions or the Kindle Aluminum. It attaches magnetically to the back of your Kindle's aluminum body and uses a plant-based leather to wrap around the cover's exterior. The inside has a microfiber interior that's safe to press against your e-reader's screen (and feels nice on your hand).

More Kindle Accessories

Looking for more accessories to use with your Kindle? Here’s a handful of my favorite cases, grips, stands, and more. Check out my full guide to the Best Kindle Accessories for more recommendations. Most of these were tested on the older 2024 Kindles unless otherwise noted.

Photograph: Nena Farrell

Photograph: Nena Farrell

Photograph: Nena Farrell Chevron Chevron Save to wishlist Save to wishlist Lamicall Tablet Pillow Stand Holder $46 Amazon This pillow stand holder can sit freely on your lap, bed, or any nearby surface while holding up your Kindle. There are two receptacles built into it, one of which is big enough for my larger mugs. I usually drop a snack or my phone into the other one. Photograph: Nena Farrell

Photograph: Nena Farrell

Courtesy of Strapsicle Chevron Chevron Save to wishlist Save to wishlist Strapsicle E-Reader Hand Strap $20 Amazon (Kindle Gen 4-11/Kobos) $20 Amazon (Kindle Paperwhite/Colorsoft) $20 Strapsicle (All Sizes) This soft silicone strap hooks onto the ends of a Kindle (or other e-reader) without any adhesive needed. It was nice and secure when I slid my hand into it. It comes with two straps, but a single strap was plenty of security for me.

Photograph: Nena Farrell Save to wishlist Save to wishlist PopSockets PopCase Kindle and PopGrip $40 PopSockets (Kindle Case) $30 PopSockets (PopGrip) PopSockets came out with its own line of Kindle cases that have a built-in MagSafe adapter, so you can more easily add your PopSockets grip of choice. There are matching sets of cases and grips you can shop for, or you can mix and match as you please. Photograph: Nena Farrell

Photograph: Nena Farrell Chevron Chevron Save to wishlist Save to wishlist PopSockets PopGrips $30 PopSockets (Bookish Collection) $35 PopSockets (Custom MagSafe) The PopSockets PopGrips are handy to add to Kindles so you can easily grip your device, but you will need to attach them with an adhesive, a MagSafe adapter, or a MagSafe Kindle case. There are a ton of fun designs, and you can even customize your own, like my custom WIRED PopGrip.

Why Are Kindles More Expensive Now?

Amazon raised its prices across its product categories, including Kindle devices. The price increases hit several current Kindle models, leaving only Kindle Scribe models with their original price tags. Amazon declined to comment to WIRED, but a spokesperson told CNET the price hikes were due to rising costs in memory and storage components. Interestingly, none of the more powerful Scribe models needed a price update, but it’s also a relief since all three of those models are significantly more expensive than a regular Kindle.

Here are all the increases, including for the Signature versions. The new 2026 models all reflect this new pricing.

If you have your eyes on one of these Kindles, I’d wait until Black Friday to shop, as they'll likely be on sale.

If You’re Interested in Older (and Cheaper) Kindles

Amazon usually takes a few years between new Kindle models; we just saw a new lineup launch after two years, and it's likely we'll see the 2024 model availability start to dwindle soon. But the 2022 (and earlier) models are also still around if you want a better deal. I only suggest buying these if they're on sale for the right price, though.

Before making your purchase, cross-check the price against the latest model to make sure you’re paying a fair amount less for the older device.

Kindle (2022): This is the smallest of the lot at 6.2 inches tall and 4.3 inches wide, with a 6-inch screen. If you find tablets too cumbersome to hold with one hand, consider this one, with 16 GB of storage and a 300 pixels per inch (PPI) resolution. It’s tough to find, and I usually don’t see it for less than $75 these days.

Kindle Paperwhite (2021): This is the next step up from the basic model. It has a bright 6.8-inch screen with adjustable warm lighting, a fast page-turn rate, a USB-C port, and 16 gigs of storage. It’s waterproof, too. I like the Signature Edition, which also includes auto-adjust brightness and 32 GBs of storage. I don’t recommend spending more than $100 on this one.

Kindle Scribe (1st Generation): The original Scribe is a great option for note-takers. It has a giant 10.2-inch screen for taking notes, marking up PDFs, or drawing, and numerous paper formats you can choose, like college-ruled or dotted. It also comes with the Basic Pen, which feels natural to write with and attaches to the side of the Scribe magnetically. It’s only worth it for $230 or less, and I often see it for below $200 on eBay.

Kindle Kids (2022): This is an older kid-friendly model. It comes with a cover, a year’s subscription to Amazon Kids+, parental controls, and a two-year warranty, but the fact that it’s only available secondhand means you’ll likely miss out on the subscription window and may or may not still have a cover. Ideally, you won't spend more than $70 on this one.

Kindle Paperwhite Kids (2021): This older Paperwhite version is a step up from the previous basic Kids models. It has a high-resolution 300-ppi display with an adjustable warm screen and is also waterproof. You shouldn’t spend more than $110 on this one if you can find it at all. (I couldn't find any resellers for this older model at the time of writing.)

If you’re trying to figure out which model you're dealing with, this Amazon page includes photos, specs, and release years for the entire lineup. Once you know which one you have, you may be able to trade it in for credit toward a newer model. Most old Kindles probably still work, just with fewer bells and whistles. It’s best to avoid Kindles with keyboards or any other physical buttons other than page-turn buttons. Some older models lost the ability to browse, purchase, or borrow new books directly from the device. However, you may still be able to do this via Amazon on your computer or phone and have it sent to your Kindle, which is a better experience anyway. How Do You Get Free or Cheap Ebooks on a Kindle? AccordionItemContainerButton LargeChevron If you buy every single book you want to read on a Kindle, it can add up! But there are ways to save some money while reading as much as your heart desires. You may want to subscribe to Kindle+ (previously called Kindle Unlimited) for $12 a month. You can only choose from the Kindle+ catalog, but it features millions of titles, including audiobooks and magazines. Start out with the 30-day free trial. If you already pay for a Prime account, you’re eligible for some free ebooks through Prime Reading. It doesn't include as many options as Kindle+, and in a lot of cases, you’ll see both the Kindle+ and Prime options lumped together; you’ll have to look closely to find the free ebooks. It’s still something, though, and there are even a few magazines. If you don’t want another monthly subscription and don’t want to continue giving your money to Amazon, take advantage of the ebooks available with your library card. Browsing a digital catalog is not as magical as spending an afternoon looking over every shelf in a library, but such is the ebook life (no one says you can’t read both!). We have a detailed how-to on this that you should check out, but here are some of the takeaways: Get a library card for your local branch.

Check your branch’s website for its ebook offerings. Many libraries use a service called OverDrive.

Download directly to your Kindle library. The titles in question will automatically be removed when they’re due back. What Else Can a Kindle Do? AccordionItemContainerButton LargeChevron Kindles have other helpful features you may want to use. Long-press a word or phrase to see its definition, highlight it, or take notes. You can also search the entire book for that particular word or phrase or translate it to or from other languages. Word Wise shows short definitions in small text within the lines. Unfortunately, it’s not available for all books, but when it is, you can turn it on or off and choose more and fewer hints. Clicking the short definition opens a longer one from Word Wise and the New Oxford American Dictionary or Oxford Dictionary of English (you can switch between the two), plus translations and a Wikipedia page, if applicable. While reading, tap the top of the screen and click “Aa” to change font size or type. There’s a font called OpenDyslexic that helps make reading easier for people with dyslexia. You can control margin sizes and line spacing from that menu, too. When a Kindle connects to a Bluetooth speaker or headphones, VoiceView Screen Reader (accessed through Settings > Accessibility) allows you to use gestures to navigate your device and reads aloud what you’ve pressed. It can also read a book aloud, though it doesn’t sound nearly as nice as an audiobook. Amazon owns Goodreads, so it syncs seamlessly to Kindles (press the three-dot menu > Goodreads). If you have a Goodreads account, you can review the Kindle books you’ve read or browse your bookshelf and recommendations. Long-pressing a word or phrase, in addition to what is mentioned above, opens up an option to share quotes directly to Goodreads. There’s also a web browser if you’re connected to the internet (three-dot menu > Web Browser). It’s not the best, so I’d reserve it for emergency searches. What Do I Do If My Kindle Colorsoft Has a Yellow Bar? AccordionItemContainerButton LargeChevron Following customer complaints in 2024 of a yellow bar at the bottom of the Colorsoft Signature’s screen and discoloration along the edges, an Amazon spokesperson confirmed to WIRED that "customers who notice this can reach out to our customer service team for a replacement or refund.” The company also said it’s “making the appropriate adjustments to ensure that new devices will not experience this issue moving forward.” We haven't seen any recent complaints about this issue, and haven't had any issues with a yellow bar appearing on any Colorsoft device WIRED has tested, including the new second-generation model. Is Now a Good Time to Buy a Kindle? AccordionItemContainerButton LargeChevron The best time to buy a Kindle is during a major sale event like Amazon Prime Day, Prime Big Deals Days, Black Friday, or Cyber Monday, when Amazon often offers steep discounts on its products. Are Kindles Good for Students? AccordionItemContainerButton LargeChevron Kindles are great for students, though the model that's best for each student depends on how they'll use it. If they want to pair it with a stylus for highlighting and be able to take notes, they should consider a Kindle Scribe model. These have long battery life, making them great for students to use for weeks on end without worrying about charging. Some textbooks are also available on Kindles. For students who love to read but don’t want to take a ton of notes, a regular Kindle or Kindle Paperwhite will work well.

It's worth noting that while the price of these new models is the same as the 2024 editions, it's because Kindle raised the prices of its 2024 versions back in August. And it's a valid move: These models will be my new picks, because if you're spending the same amount, why wouldn't you want the latest model?

But that doesn't necessarily help you decide if it's worth upgrading. It might be worth it if you're desperate for page-turner buttons, which is easily my favorite part of this new line of Kindles. If you don't have a Kindle already and are on a mission to select your first one, this latest version of the Paperwhite remains a good choice unless you're determined to splurge on a color screen. The warm light is a big benefit for anyone who reads in the evening, and you'll have to choose one of these two models from Kindle's lineup to get it anyway.

The Base Lineup

The 2026 Kindle Paperwhite (left) and 2026 Kindle Colorsoft (right). Photograph: Nena Farrell

The Kindle Paperwhite and Kindle Colorsoft are, to some degree, the same device. You'll see a similar laundry list of features: a 7-inch screen, a front light with adjustable brightness and warmth, and 16 GB of storage in the base models. Both have the same new look of a flush-front screen and ever-so-slightly-smaller body when compared to the 2024 Paperwhite and 2025 Colorsoft (the first Colorsoft in 2024 was later renamed the Signature Edition, and a cheaper base model came out in 2025).

Tech.title: Amazon Adds an Alexa Photo Frame and a Bedside Clock to Its Echo Family
Tech.content:
Panos Panay, Amazon’s senior vice president of Devices and Alexa, says a couple hundred million people now use Alexa+, the revamped version of the decade-old voice assistant, on its Echo devices. He says people talk to Alexa+ two to three times more than before its AI glow-up, cook with it five times more, listen to music three times more, and create routines twice as much.

To keep that momentum going, Amazon has new Echo products to deliver a richer Alexa+ experience, including minor refreshes on existing hardware and entirely new categories. Announced Wednesday and available for purchase now, they include the Echo Dot ($100), Echo Studio With Home Camera ($250), Echo Show 16 ($500), Echo Time ($200), and the first Alexa Photo Frame ($200).

“I don’t think anyone’s really doing AI at all in the home, and if they are, they aren’t doing it well,” Panay says at an intimate media-only event in New York City. As people have “deeper” conversations with Alexa+, Panay says devices need to be in premium shape—a strategy Amazon has been focusing on after announcing more premium Kindles and Alexa Tablets in early October.

You can see that premiumization in the hardware pricing: The Echo Dot—once the affordable, entry-level $50 smart speaker—now starts at $100. That’s higher than the marked-up prices on existing Amazon devices from this summer, which the company blamed on the memory shortage.

Echo Dot

The new Echo Dot costs $100 and comes in four colors. Photograph: Julian Chokkattu

Panay says Amazon has sold more than 100 million Echo Dots, and in 2026 alone, people spent more than a trillion minutes listening to music on the diminutive orb. So, the main goal for the new Dot? Boost the sound. The full-range driver reportedly delivers 50 percent stronger bass performance and crisper vocals.

With four beamforming microphones (up from three) and Amazon’s AZ3 chip, Alexa can isolate your voice in a noisy environment and track your commands more effectively. It also has Omnisense like last year’s Echo Dot Max, which can sense the environment to, say, detect when you walk into the home and turn on the lights.

The Dot now supports the Matter standard and works as a Thread border router, turning it into a hub for setting up and controlling smart home devices. If you have an Eero router, it can also turn into a Wi-Fi extender.

Tech.title: New iPhone Duo? Here are 4 Cool Features to Try
Tech.content:
If you’ve managed to snag a shiny new iPhone Duo, congratulations on surviving the scramble to get one. Now the fun begins.

I’ve spent two weeks with Apple’s first foldable phone, and it has several features that make it feel like a genuinely practical and intuitive device — and with a $1,999 starting price, I’d sure hope so.

What stands out about the Duo is its versatility. Similar to other passport-size folding phones like the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 and the Xiaomi 18 Fold, you can hop between a more compact, 5.4-inch cover screen when sending a text or checking a notification and a wider, 7.6-inch inner display when watching videos, multitasking or scrolling through social media. It’s like a phone-tablet hybrid that fits neatly into a pocket or the palm of your hand.

Details like the matte inner display, which minimizes glare and makes the crease less noticeable, along with seamless software integration across screens give the Duo a distinct character of its own.

Here are four features worth checking out to get the most of your new iPhone Duo. And if you’re still in the market for one, it’s worth checking out carrier and trade-in deals to help bring down the cost (and maybe get the phone earlier than January).

Use Duo Preview and Smart Take for photos

Smart Take and Duo Preview can make taking photos a little easier. Abrar Al-Heeti/CNET

The iPhone Duo’s foldable design and dual screens open up more ways to take pictures. A few handy features let you easily use the 48-megapixel rear cameras for better shots than you’d get with the 12-megapixel cover-screen selfie camera.

If someone is taking a picture of you or you want to snap a selfie with the rear camera, use Duo Preview to get a glimpse of what the shot will look like. With the phone open, you’ll see an image preview on the cover screen as you or your photographer snaps away, so you can ensure the framing and poses look exactly how you want.

To turn on Duo Preview, unfold the Duo and open the Camera app. Then tap the control in the top left corner (when the phone is in landscape) that looks like a mini Duo. Tap Duo Preview and snap away.

If you’re trying to take a group photo and there’s no one around to snap it for you, you no longer have to awkwardly prop your phone against a surface and then race against a timer — or make do with a lackluster selfie. Place your Duo on a flat surface when it’s half-folded and point the camera at your subjects. A feature called Smart Take will use AI to detect when everyone is in-frame and ready, and then automatically take a photo. As people change their poses, Smart Take will register that there’s a fresh scene to snap. You can also use Duo Preview to check framing via the cover screen.

To enable Smart Take, open the camera app while the Duo is either opened or closed. Then tap the photo options in the corner (six little dots), and tap Smart Take. A button with a yellow circle will then appear to the right of the shutter; tap that to start the process.

Smart Take will keep snapping pictures for around two minutes or until it captures about 20 images as people readjust their poses. You’ll then be able to sift through the options in Photos.

Lastly, Kid Cue can make it easier to hold a child’s attention when snapping photos. With the Duo open, a Snoopy animation will play on the cover screen to draw attention toward the camera. To turn on Kid Cue, unfold the Duo, open the Camera app and tap the Duo icon in the upper left corner. There, you’ll see the option to turn on Kid Cue.

StandBy mode gets more handy

StandBy on the iPhone Duo works even when the phone isn’t charging. Abrar Al-Heeti/CNET

Apple launched StandBy in 2023, which turns the iPhone into a smart display of sorts, with access to widgets like the clock, calendar and weather. But unlike other iPhones, the Duo doesn’t have to be charging to launch into StandBy.

Just set the Duo down while it’s locked, either slightly unfolded and on its side in tent mode, or while standing upright. Then you’ll see your favorite widgets, as well as Live Activities. That way, you can track the status of a food delivery, sports score or approaching rideshare at a glance.

To ensure StandBy is enabled, go to your iPhone’s Settings, then tap StandBy and check that the toggle is on.

Marathon watch as you like

Netflix is optimized for the Duo’s displays — from the cover screen to the main display to this half-open configuration with controls on the bottom half. Celso Bulgatti/CNET

Streaming video really shines with the iPhone Duo’s dynamic design. Open the phone to watch on the tablet-like, 7.6-inch display. Minimal black bars at the top and bottom of the screen allow for more immersive viewing.

You can also fold the Duo halfway and set it down, essentially making it look like a mini laptop. With apps like Netflix and Apple TV, your movie or TV show will play on the top half, while controls appear on the bottom for skipping forward, rewinding, pausing, playing and turning on closed captions. Netflix also has an added flair: You’ll see what appears to be a reflection of the upper-screen’s content playing down by the controls, as if it’s subtly mirroring that footage. It makes for a nifty immersive effect.

You can also prop your iPhone Duo into tent mode and watch content on the 5.4-inch cover screen. I do this when I’m moving around my apartment tidying up. That way, I can easily see what’s happening without needing a phone stand. Even though the Duo’s cover screen is significantly smaller than the main display, it’s just big enough to still comfortably watch most content (perhaps not as Christopher Nolan intended, but it’ll do).

Lock a pair of apps when multitasking

You can lock an app pair when multitasking. Celso Bulgatti/CNET

The iPhone Duo can run up to two apps simultaneously in its open horizontal orientation, so you can watch a YouTube video on one half of your screen while texting your friends on the other, for example. Some other foldable phones support running three apps side-by-side, but I find that feels too crowded.

On the iPhone Duo, you can save an app pair, so that if you swipe away, you can quickly pull up that same combination without having to drag the apps side by side again. It’s a quick time-saver that lends itself to the intuitive nature of iOS 27 on the iPhone Duo.

To create an app pair, tap the divider between two apps that you’ve already dragged side by side. This will lock in that combination, so you can easily restore that dual-window card when you’re scrolling through the App Switcher. Just select the still-paired window and carry on with your multitasking (or doomscrolling).

Tech.title: Live Now! We’ve Folded the iPhone Duo 100,000 Times – Watch Us Fold It Thousands More
Tech.content:
The iPhone Duo wowed us as Apple’s first foldable phone, but it’s time to test out how its first-gen hinge holds up. We’re now testing the $1,999 iPhone Duo using our custom-made folding machine, the Fold-a-Phone, which has been diligently opening and closing the phone since we bought the Duo on Friday. We just passed 100,000 folds, and we’re not stopping until the Duo breaks.



CNET is livestreaming our iPhone Duo long-term folding test on our YouTube channel, which you can watch embedded here. Our robust in-house machine will open and close the foldable around 20,000 times per day to simulate years of wear and tear on the hinge. You can watch this testing on a livestream from our CNET Labs location in Louisville, Kentucky.

More from CNET

Product Quiz

Powered by Digioh

The livestream isn’t just for watching a phone open and close — you’ll also be able to chat with CNET editors who will be available to answer your iPhone Duo questions live in the chat. Will Apple’s first foldable live up to the likes of the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 and Google Pixel 11 Pro Fold? Will its neat opening animation remain slick over thousands of folds? Join us and find out.

Our iPhone Duo folding test is ongoing, with our Fold-A-Phone machine running since Friday. Screenshot by David Lumb/CNET

This long-term test will join our iPhone Duo review, which provides a snapshot of what it’s like to be among the first to use Apple’s first foldable phone. If you’re sold on it, check out the best iPhone Duo deals. And if you want to compare even further, you can check out our roundup of the best foldable phones currently available if you want help deciding between the Duo and other folding and flip-style phones from Samsung, Motorola and Google.

Tech.title: Apple’s ‘Pro and Tell’ Event: Everything Announced This Week
Tech.content:
Apple’s Pro and Tell experience week is here, with the new iPad Mini unveiled on Monday, a new MacBook Pro and iMac on Tuesday and a long-anticipated touchscreen laptop on Wednesday morning.

Apple’s had a busy few months, launching the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max in September alongside the Apple Watch Series 12, Apple Watch Ultra 4 and the AirPods 5, followed by the iPhone Duo going on sale at the end of last week. Apple’s refreshed smart home lineup, revealed during its recent Welcome Home event, is up next: the HomePod Mini 2 will launch on Friday; the Apple HomeView and Apple TV 4K on Nov. 13; and availability for the Home Collection products begins in December.

This week culminated with Apple hosting a special event on Wednesday, and CNET was on the ground capturing all the latest details.

More from CNET

Apple’s new iPad Mini

One of the two new iPad Mini colors: midnight. Apple

Announced on Monday, Apple’s new iPad Mini is available to preorder on Wednesday and will go on sale Nov. 6. It starts at $699 for 128GB of storage, $799 for 256GB and $999 for 512GB.

Setting it apart from the last iPad Mini, which came out two years ago, the new tablet has an 8.5-inch OLED screen (versus an LCD), IP67 water and dust resistance, an Apple A20 processor, a repositioned front-facing camera and a through-screen speaker system called Acoustic Display, as well as being thinner and lighter than before.

A new iMac

Apple’s new iMac M6 comes in a choice of seven colors.

The latest iMac, announced Tuesday, features Apple’s M6 processor with a CPU and a GPU each having up to 12 cores, two more cores apiece than before, Apple said. A new dual 16-core Neural Engine delivers AI compute that’s up to twice as fast as the previous generation, the company said. The iMac also has a 24-inch 4.5K Retina display.

Preorders for the iMac M6 will begin Wednesday, Oct. 28, with availability to follow on Nov. 6. Pricing starts at $1,499 for an iMac with M6 featuring a 10-core CPU and 10-core GPU. It’s available in seven colors: blue, green, pink, yellow, purple, orange and silver.

MacBook Pro refresh

Apple

The new 14-inch MacBook Pro, also announced Tuesday, similarly features the M6 processor with a 12-core CPU and GPU and dual 16-core Neural Engine for AI tasks. Apple says the battery life runs up to 24 hours. The laptop features a Liquid Retina XDR display, a 12-megapixel Center Stage camera and a six-speaker sound system.

The MacBook Pro with M6 can be preordered starting Wednesday, Oct. 28, and will be in stores and delivered to customers starting Nov. 6. Pricing starts at $1,999.

Finally, a touchscreen MacBook Pro

Apple

At an event in Los Angeles on Wednesday, new Apple CEO John Ternus unveiled a new MacBook Pro with what Apple calls a PROLED XDR Display. The long-anticipated touchscreen MacBook Pro comes in 14- and 16-inch models, with a Dynamic Island that features Spotlight, Live Activities and Siri AI, up to 128GB of memory and 16TB of storage, and a choice of either the M5 Pro or M5 Max chips.

The laptops are also thinner and lighter than previous MacBook Pros, weighing 3 and 4 pounds for the 14- and 16-inch variants, respectively, and have a six-speaker sound system, Thunderbolt 5, a 12-megapixel camera and run MacOS 27 Golden Gate.

You can preorder them today, with availability on Nov. 6. For the M5 Pro chip, the 14-inch MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR starts at $2,899, and the 16-inch model starts at $3,399; for the M5 Max chip, the 14-inch laptop starts at $4,499, and the 16-inch version starts at $4,799.

Apple Creator Studio updates

This week also brought updates to the Apple Creator Studio software suite. For instance, Final Cut Pro for Mac now includes built-in MotionVFX, a collection of visual effects, plug-ins, transitions, templates and motion graphics tools; the curated Content Hub now includes video assets and is available in Final Cut Pro; Pixelmator Pro introduces Generate Fill, which lets creators transform selected areas of an image using natural language; and Keynote, Pages and Numbers introduce new AI features in beta, including assistants that understand document contexts.

The Apple Creator Studio updates will be available in November to subscribers for free.

And as for the iPhone Duo launch last week, check out CNET’s ongoing folding test — you can watch the livestream here as we continue testing how many times the iPhone Duo can fold without cracking in the CNET lab.

Tech.title: Google’s Next Mixed Reality Headset, Xreal Aura, Coming Mid-November at $1,099 to Start
Tech.content:
Ahead of the Meta VR Glasses arriving next spring, Google and Xreal are debuting a new device that also has VR-like experiences on a pair of display glasses connected with a processor puck: Xreal Aura is arriving mid-November, with preorders opening today.

The device, previously announced as costing $1,279, is going to cost less for the time being. It’s now dropped to $1,099 for early orders for the version with 256GB storage and 12GB RAM, or $1,299 for the one with 512GB/16GB (previous price: $1,500) through the end of this year.

I was impressed by the Xreal Aura during early demos over the last year. It runs a version of Android called AndroidXR, handles any Android app in either 2D or 3D VR-like modes, and can even use all the apps from the more expensive Samsung Galaxy XR released last year. It has hand tracking and can pair with keyboards and game controllers, too.

More from CNET

Also, like the Meta VR Glasses, the Xreal Aura can plug into your phone, laptop or any USB-C video-out device to display it on the glasses, either piped in as a floating display in Xreal Aura’s desktop or with just the glasses detached from the processor puck.

Chi Xu, Xreal’s founder and CEO, has been working on the idea of AR glasses for years now. I saw the company’s nReal Light glasses all the way back in 2019. But the Aura finally looks like the idea Chi’s been dreaming of.

Project Aura comes with its own travel case. The processor puck it uses is about the size of a phone. Scott Stein/CNET

“We ultimately think think this can be a tablet or laptop replacement,” Chi says to me about devices like the Xreal Aura, which tether to processing pucks and work like ultra-portable VR headsets, as opposed to wireless smart glasses like those that Meta, Google and others are also making. He also thinks that the portable nature of the Aura running camera- and display-connected Gemini will allow some ideas no one’s seen yet.

“We’re hoping Aura can be a pivoting step for this whole industry, going lightweight and very easily integrated with AI as well,” he said.

A game controller accessory comes with its own Gemini button. Xreal

The Aura also intrigues me because, although it can feel like VR while I’m wearing the glasses with their 70-degree field of view microOLED displays, they actually float their displays on top of transparent lenses that have varying degrees of electrochromic dimming. They could be worn outside more easily, to places VR headsets aren’t meant to go. And while they’re not true standalone AR glasses, they could potentially be used to try outdoor experiences using AR and AI via Gemini in ways that the Snap Specs coming later this year also aim to do.

Chi’s confidence in portable glasses computers like Xreal Aura being tablet or even laptop alternatives intrigues me. The Aura has a folding keyboard accessory, and its processor puck doubles as a trackpad. That type of on-the-go work use is exactly what I’m interested in putting to the test, along with a lot more, when I get to review the Aura.

Tech.title: How to Identify Flock Cameras (and the Lookalikes That Fool People)
Tech.content:
A Flock camera does more than photograph license plates. Depending on what a city or business pays for, the system can log a vehicle’s make, color and distinguishing features such as roof racks or bumper stickers, and some installations add audio sensors that listen for sounds such as gunshots or screaming.

That range of capabilities helps explain why some communities have canceled their Flock contracts while others keep adding cameras. If a new device has gone up near your home, a few physical details can help you identify whether it’s a Flock unit, and public maps may help confirm it.

The problem is that while there’s so much concern over Flock cameras and various abuses by law enforcement, people aren’t always great at spotting Flock cams in the real world. It leads to lots of mistaken fears about radar, traffic cameras, trail cams and other various, nontracking devices. That’s one reason I’m not a huge fan of crowdsource-dependent apps such as DeFlock, which can give conflicting information based on what people think is Flock.

More from CNET

That’s why I’m breaking down exactly what a Flock installation looks like — and how to tell whether you’re looking at one, a similar automated license plate reader camera or something else entirely.

Look for the telltale Flock camera shape and logo

You can still most Flock cameras by their distinctive design. Allen J. Schaben/Contributor/Getty Images

Flock Safety’s brand has a very clear camera shape, so with a closer look, it’s typically easy to tell if it’s a Flock automatic license plate reader camera or something else.

Watch for the classic oval, hooded shape of the camera with a circular lens, a near-universal mark of Flock camera.

Notice this competitor brand Obvio has a distinctly different design than Flock, and may not offer the same surveillance services.

Not all license plate cameras are Flock, and that can matter for your privacy. Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images

Keep in mind, Flock offers a variety of surveillance technology, including cameras that can recognize human attributes like clothes and beards, as well as devices that can detect sounds like gunshots, so not every device will look the same. But this is still one of the first and simplest ways to detect a Flock brand camera. If you get very close, you can also small, shiny, stem-like Flock logo on the front of the cameras.

Some Flock cameras don’t have the slim hood, but the color, general design and logo still give them away. Bloomberg/Getty Images

I have seen reports of other ALPR cameras hidden inside objects like fake plants, but this doesn’t appear to be Flock’s typical approach and is very rare so far.

Best DIY Home Security Systems of 2026: Install Them Yourself Dodge installation fees and take security into your own hands with these super smart security kits.

Look for Flock’s visible solar panel arrays

Flock’s solar panels often have a distinctive look. Bloomberg/Getty Images

Next, look for Flock’s large, dark-colored solar panels, which are typically angled above the camera or close by on the same mount. Many ALPR cameras use solar panels so they can be installed nearly anywhere, but Flock’s have a unique design that’s more noticeable the longer you look at the cameras.

If you see what you think is a surveillance device without a solar panel, it probably isn’t one, or at least not one associated with Flock and its camera competitors like Axon or Obvio.

For example, red-light or speed cameras may be wired into traffic-light mounts, but they are used for traffic enforcement and don’t carry the same surveillance baggage as general ALPR cameras. While they automate certain aspects of traffic enforcement and take pictures of license plates, they don’t typically have the AI recognition, broad police search capabilities, or ways to recognize individual vehicles and people like Flock can (although they can still make communities uncomfortable).

Red light and traffic cameras aren’t Flock, and don’t have the same surveillance capabilities as Flock. Robert Daemmrich Photography Inc./Getty Images

Remember, Flock and ALPR solar panels are always larger and more public than the panels people use for their home security cameras. Fortunately, there are other ways to make sure.

Check what surveillance equipment local law enforcement has bought

Searching the Atlas of Surveillance by city or county can surface Flock Safety camera locations, contract details and any reported data-sharing agreements with federal agencies. EFF

I recommend confirming your community is using Flock cameras even if you think you’ve spotted one. One of the best ways is with the Atlas of Surveillance website, which uses dedicated research to collect the different surveillance technologies that cities, police and sheriff departments have bought and are using.

The Atlas of Surveillance tries to stay as current as possible, and you can search by town or county in just a few seconds. It links to reports or public records to confirm use if possible. I’ve used it frequently to trace Flock activity in certain areas, not only with cameras but with growing numbers of surveillance drones, too. It works with multiple types of devices and platforms that law enforcement uses, making it one of the most dependable ways to corroborate that your local government recently started using Flock cameras.

When I talked to senior research Beryl Lipton from the Electronic Frontier Foundation about using the website, she said, “People should start by searching for their town and county to see what technology is in play close to home. While folks may expect some larger cities to use some of these devices, I think people will be surprised to see how common they’ve become in mid-sized and rural areas too.”

Lipton also recommended using a similar tool, the Street-Level Surveillance hub, which is more focused on the complex ways today’s agencies use surveillance technology. With both tools together, you should have a good idea what your community is facing.

Check who owns the property and what contracts they may have

Private companies like Home Depot can use Flock too, which makes it confusing when cameras are posted around parking lots. Bloomberg/Getty Images

Flock doesn’t just contract with cities or police departments. That means that while a city government may have canceled Flock Safety cameras, local businesses can use them on their private property, which can cause a lot of confusion among worried people.

If it doesn’t appear your local government is using Flock cameras, try to find out who owns the property with a camera on it, and if they contract with Flock. Home Depot and Lowe’s, for example, are very open about using ALPR cameras, including Flock’s, in their parking lots, and sometimes share that data with police.

Local businesses and neighborhood entities like HOAs can also contract with Flock, but you can often ask them directly if they have AI surveillance cameras and why.

Ask your city council

Asking your city government and showing up to meetings is a great way to find out what’s going on with Flock. The Washington Post/Getty Images

Going to your city council, especially in person, can also be helpful (even Darth Vader thinks so). You can find out about present or future connections with Flock and make your opinion heard. You may also discover that, as I’ve seen before, cities have canceled their Flock contracts and no longer use the cameras, but they still stay up because no one is sure how to legally remove them.

I’ve also seen city councils unsure what Flock cameras are or how police use them, essentially signing off on police and sheriff budgets without knowing what they’re paying for, which is a sign that auditing and accountability practices are lacking. Or, I’ve noticed some cities announce new camera or surveillance programs but carefully avoid using the word “Flock” even though they are contracting with Flock Safety.

Asking direct questions to public servants can help handle issues like these. Look for council meetings where the public is welcome, and try writing or calling your city council to ask about their plans for Flock, if any.

File a public records request

Check if your city or state supports public records requests. You may be able to use a government website to formally request access to information about ALPR cameras, installations and contract documents.

Depending on the public records portal, you may have to be very specific about the kind of information you want, and which government body has it — the police department vs. the city, for example. My other steps are a good start to the research you need if you want to access public records like this.

While not every camera is from Flock, knowing which are — and which have ALPR or person detection capabilities — is a key step in avoiding confusion and protecting your privacy.

Tech.title: Update to iOS 27.2 Now to Patch Hundreds of Bugs
Tech.content:
Apple released iOS 27.2 on Monday, Oct. 26, just a few days after the launch of the iPhone Duo. While iOS 27.2 brings Siri AI to more languages and updates a few other features, it also patches 141 bug and security issues, including some that could allow a third-party to access data or run commands on your iPhone.

You can download iOS 27.2 now by going to Settings > General > Software Update > Update Now and following the prompts on your screen.

According to Apple’s release notes, iOS 27.2 patches dozens of issues across your iPhone. Some of these issues can cause some serious problems for you and your device.

More from CNET

Nine of these bugs address issues that could lead to kernel corruption on your device. The kernel is the core of your device’s operating system, and kernel corruption can cause your device to freeze or crash. The blue screen of death, for example, could be caused by kernel corruption.

Apple also wrote that seven of these bugs could lead to arbitrary code execution. That means the bug could allow a third party to steal your data or use your device for other nefarious purposes.

The update addresses a lot of other bugs, including one that you might run into if you plug a malicious USB into your device. Apple didn’t write that any of these bugs were being actively exploited, but you should still update to iOS 27.2 now to give yourself the most protection.

For as many bugs as 27.2 fixes, it’s actually a slight decrease from earlier updates. Last month’s iOS 27 update patched even more bugs at 157. The number of bug fixes in both iOS updates are unusual based on data over the past few years. In iOS 26, the most bug fixes included in an update was 88 with iOS 26.6. The update with the next highest number of patches was iOS 18.4 with 75.

Apple didn’t say why there’s been an uptick in the number of bug fixes in iOS updates. Artificial intelligence has been used recently to find and address huge numbers of software bugs; however, that doesn’t appear to be the cause behind the surge in iOS 27.2 or iOS 27. Apple usually notes when a bug is found with the help of AI, yet OpenAI is mentioned four times in iOS 27.2’s release notes, and Claude’s Anthropic is only mentioned thrice.

Apple didn’t immediately respond to my request to comment.

For more iOS news, here’s what you should know about iOS 27.2 and iOS 27.1. You can also check out our iOS 27 cheat sheet.

Tech.title: Daylight Saving Time Ends Sunday, Nov. 1. Here’s When to Change Your Clocks
Tech.content:
Daylight saving time ends at 2 a.m. local time on Sunday, Nov. 1, when clocks across most of the US move back to 1 a.m. The timing lines up neatly with Halloween: Trick-or-treaters on Saturday still get the later sunset, and the extra hour of sleep arrives overnight. Phones and computers update on their own, but oven, microwave and car clocks usually don’t. Here’s what else to know about the switch, including which states skip it — and when the clocks spring forward again.

The time shift is notorious for disrupting sleep patterns and schedules. Some politicians are advocating for the abolition of time changes and the permanent adoption of daylight saving time, or DST. The House passed the Sunshine Protection Act in July, but it still needs Senate approval and the president’s signature to become law — meaning that, for now, we still have dark winter hours coming.

If you, too, dislike how early it gets dark each day through winter, just remember that brighter evenings will return in mid-March.

More from CNET

When does daylight saving time end?

Daylight saving time in the US ends at 2 a.m. local time Sunday, Nov. 1. It will return at 2 a.m. local time on Sunday, March 14, 2027. The end of DST is when we “fall back,” whereas in March, we “spring forward.”

The US isn’t alone in observing daylight saving time. Check out this list of other countries that use DST, along with their start and end dates.

Daylight saving time vs. standard time

The official US time website shows where time zone boundaries are located. Time.gov/Screenshot by CNET

The exact start dates for daylight saving time and standard time float a little. DST kicks off on the second Sunday of March and ends on the first Sunday of November with the return of standard time.

We spend about eight months of the year in DST. We can thank the Uniform Time Act of 1966 for bringing some order to what had been a complicated history of time changes in the US.

“Motivated by transportation improvements, this act mandated standard time within the existing time zones and established a permanent system of uniform DST, including the dates and times for twice-yearly transitions,” the Bureau of Transportation Statistics states in a history of time zones.

The country’s time zones date to the railroad boom of the late 1800s. DST formally entered the chat in 1918, but its application was inconsistent until 1966. The country tried year-round daylight saving time in January 1974 under President Richard Nixon to address the energy crisis. It didn’t go over well. Congress and President Gerald Ford restored standard time in October 1974.

If you truly hate time changes, then consider moving to Arizona (except for the Navajo Nation) or Hawaii. Those states are on standard time all year long, and their residents don’t have to deal with the physical and mental health impacts of the change. Puerto Rico, Guam, the Virgin Islands, American Samoa and the Northern Mariana Islands also skip DST.



Sleep experts seek year-round standard time

Organizations such as the National Sleep Foundation, the American Academy of Sleep Medicine and the Society for Research on Biological Rhythms are united in calling for permanent standard time, saying it’s better for human biology.

“There’s a mismatch between the outside world and our internal clocks during daylight saving time that can result in some negative health consequences,” says Joseph Dzierzewski, senior vice president of research and scientific affairs at the National Sleep Foundation.

Dzierzewski cites mental health concerns and upticks in cardiovascular events and drowsy driving. He also calls out safety issues with young children walking to school or sitting at bus stops in the dark. Those safety issues were a big reason why permanent DST didn’t last in 1974.

Will we ditch these time changes for good?

Time changes aren’t popular. An October 2024 YouGov poll (PDF) of more than 1,100 US adults found that 63% would like to see the changing of the clocks eliminated. Only 17% wanted to keep time changes, and 20% weren’t sure.

Efforts to end the time changes have so far failed to pass into law. The bipartisan Sunshine Protection Act, which would have made daylight saving time permanent, passed the Senate in 2022 — the new version of the bill passed the House earlier this year and was sent on to the Senate to review in July.

While many people agree on eliminating time changes, the schism between daylight saving time and standard time remains. Standard time may have a bit of an image issue compared to DST.

“Part of the issue is that people associate daylight saving time with summer. People love summer, right?” Dzierzewski said. “But the simple fact of the matter is, it would still be summer if we were on permanent standard time.”

President Donald Trump criticized time changes in a 2024 Truth Social post: “The Republican Party will use its best efforts to eliminate Daylight Saving Time, which has a small but strong constituency, but shouldn’t! Daylight Saving Time is inconvenient and very costly to our Nation.”

Bills and resolutions at the state level haven’t had real-world impacts yet. Politicians are still split on whether they want permanent daylight saving or standard time. Dzierzewski is hopeful that permanent standard time will win out.

“This is the first time in several years where I’ve seen more legislation introduced at a state level in support of permanent standard time as the solution,” he said.

If you’d like to see time changes end and want to advocate for either daylight saving or standard time, contact your state and national representatives and express your opinion.

"You're in a better situation to cope with the effects of the clock change if you have good sleep health generally." Joseph Dzierzewski, senior vice president of research and scientific affairs at the National Sleep Foundation

Adjust your body clock to daylight saving time

Daylight saving time is happening, so now it’s a matter of figuring out how to deal with it. It’s not just about the day of the time change.

“You’re in a better situation to cope with the effects of the clock change if you have good sleep health generally,” Dzierzewski said. He recommends exposure to bright light in the morning, physical activity during the day, eating meals at regular times and practicing a relaxing wind-down routine at night.

The majority of Americans struggle to get the National Sleep Foundation’s recommended 7 to 9 hours of sleep for most adults. A CNET survey found that more than half of US adults use some method to cope with sleep-related challenges. Check out some expert-backed tips for improving your sleep quality.

“If you’re doing these healthy sleep behaviors, you’re probably more resilient to some of these changes,” Dzierzewski said. “If you have poor sleep to begin with, you’re probably going to feel it a little bit more.”

Establishing a better sleep routine can take time. There are two things you can do in direct response to the time change. Dzierzewski suggests adjusting your bedtime and wake-up time gradually ahead of the change. For example, you could shift your schedule by 15 minutes per day and ease yourself into DST. He also recommends getting a good dose of bright morning light on the day of the time change to help set your internal body clock.

Think of DST as another kind of wake-up call, one that can motivate you to evaluate your sleep routine and quality and make positive changes. Start with these six simple habits. And don’t forget to change your clocks. Do it the night before, and you won’t have to worry about it later.

Tech.title: Fox One Will Track 2026 Midterm Election Results With New App Experience
Tech.content:
The 2026 midterm elections are less than a week away, and Fox has unveiled a new interactive experience for Fox One app subscribers on Election Day, Tuesday, Nov. 3, to keep up with the news and results as they come in across the country.

With hundreds of House, Senate, gubernatorial and local races happening all at once, it can be tough to follow along with every update. According to a statement, Fox One has launched an interface to keep track of everything, “where a race in one state reframes the math in another and where what matters most to viewers may be a ballot measure in their own county.”

The Fox One election experience will add context to Fox’s broadcast coverage. Fox One

The features that’ll appear as part of this rollout include a command center on the Fox One home screen, with widgets that update in real time on things like voter polls, contest results and Fox News “Election Insights” on key races; a curated election hub that’ll include all of Fox’s election coverage; and a new Elections Mode version of Ask Fox, the app’s AI-powered chatbot, where viewers can ask election-based questions and receive answers in real time.

More from CNET

“The results don’t arrive in order, and no two viewers are following the same set of races,” said Amit Dudakia, senior vice president and head of product at Fox Direct to Consumer. “With Fox One, we’re keeping coverage from Fox News and Fox Stations at the center and building the context around it, so viewers aren’t toggling between a stream and a second screen to understand what just happened.”

Fox One’s complete channel portfolio includes Fox News Channel, Fox Nation, Fox Sports, B1G, FS1, FS2, the Fox Network and local Fox stations. It is available at no additional cost for cable and satellite TV customers and is priced at $20 a month for a stand-alone subscription to the app. The new in-app election experience will launch on Election Day.
